courses.title: The Mool Mantar: Sikh Theology in One Breath
courses.summary: A phrase-by-phrase study of the Mool Mantar — the opening of Sri Guru Granth Sahib that names every attribute of Waheguru: one, true, creator, fearless, without enmity, timeless, unborn, self-existent, and known by grace.
outcomes: Recite and translate the full Mool Mantar from ੴ to ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ with confidence
Explain why ੴ (Ik Onkar) is the foundation of Sikh monotheism and how it differs from numeric oneness
Unpack each attribute — ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ, ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ, ਨਿਰਭਉ, ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ — and what each rules out about God
Describe the Sikh picture of God as ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ (beyond time), ਅਜੂਨੀ (unborn), and ਸੈਭੰ (self-existent)
Articulate why ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ (by the Guru's grace) makes knowledge of God a gift, not an achievement
Contrast the Mool Mantar's non-anthropomorphic, loving God with wrathful and incarnational conceptions of the divine

terms.m: The 'root formula' — the opening creedal statement of Sri Guru Granth Sahib that names the qualities of God.
Ik Onkar — the numeral One (Ik) joined to Onkar, the all-pervading Creator; the seal of Sikh theology.
Sat Naam — '(whose) Name is Truth'; the eternal, real, ever-existing nature of the Divine.
Karta Purakh — the Creator-Being; the one who makes and pervades all that is made.
Nirbhau — without fear; the Divine fears nothing and answers to no one.
Nirvair — without enmity; the Divine holds hostility toward none.
Akaal Moorat — the Form beyond Time; not subject to death or the cycle of ages.
Ajooni — unborn; not subject to birth, incarnation, or the cycle of transmigration.
Saibhang — self-existent, self-illumined; brought into being by none other than itself.
Gur Prasaad — by the Guru's grace; the Divine is realized only as a gift through the Guru.
Jap — the act of meditative repetition; the title that follows the Mool Mantar in the morning prayer.
Nirgun / Sargun — God beyond all attributes and God expressed through creation; the Mool Mantar holds both.

references: Singh, Sahib (Prof.). Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Raj Publishers, 1962-1964.
Singh, Gopal (Dr.). Sri Guru-Granth Sahib (English Version). World Sikh Centre, 1978.
Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. Oxford University Press, 2001.
Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus. HarperCollins, 1995.
Cole, W. Owen, and Piara Singh Sambhi. The Sikhs: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices. Sussex Academic Press, 1995.
McLeod, W. H. Sikhism. Penguin Books, 1997.

lessons.title: Why One Formula Holds the Whole Faith
lessons.summary: What the Mool Mantar is, where it sits in Sri Guru Granth Sahib, and why Guru Nanak opens with a definition of God.
lessons.html:
Open Sri Guru Granth Sahib at its very first page and the words that meet you are not a story, a hymn, or a prayer of petition. They are a definition. Before a single request is made of the Divine, before the day's first ਜਪੁ (Jap) begins, the Guru tells us who we are speaking to. This opening is called the ਮੂਲ ਮੰਤਰ (Mool Mantar) — literally the 'root formula' or 'root utterance.' Everything that follows in over 1,400 pages of scripture grows from this root.

Full course contents
  1. Why One Formula Holds the Whole Faith
  2. ੴ Ik Onkar and ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ — The One Whose Name Is Truth
  3. ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ — The Creator Who Pervades Creation
  4. ਨਿਰਭਉ ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ — Without Fear, Without Enmity
  5. ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ ਅਜੂਨੀ ਸੈਭੰ — Beyond Time, Unborn, Self-Existent
  6. ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ and Synthesis — The God of One Breath

The words themselves

The Mool Mantar reads:

ੴ ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ ਨਿਰਭਉ ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ ਅਜੂਨੀ ਸੈਭੰ ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ ॥

A working English rendering: One Universal Creator. Truth is the Name. The Creative Being. Without fear. Without enmity. The Form beyond Time. Unborn. Self-existent. Realized by the Guru's grace. No rendering is final — each phrase carries more than a single English word can hold, and the rest of this course exists to unpack that surplus.

Where it sits and how often it returns

The Mool Mantar is the threshold of the entire Guru Granth Sahib, and it returns — in full or in shortened forms — at the head of countless compositions throughout scripture. Scholars often distinguish the complete Mool Mantar (ੴ through ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ) from abbreviated openings such as ੴ ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ and the shortest ੴ ਸਤਿਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ, which mark sections within the text. Gurinder Singh Mann's study of the formation of Sikh scripture traces how these openings function as structural seals across the volume.

A creed of negations and affirmations

Notice the shape of the formula. Some phrases say what God is — Truth, Creator, the Form beyond Time. Others say what God is not — without fear, without enmity, unborn. This is deliberate. The Mool Mantar guards against false pictures of the Divine as much as it builds a true one. Where a tradition might imagine a jealous or vengeful deity, the Guru says ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ — no enmity. Where another might imagine God taking birth, the Guru says ਅਜੂਨੀ — unborn. The formula is simultaneously a confession of faith and a fence against idolatry of the imagination.

Not a magic spell

The word ਮੰਤਰ (mantar) can mislead readers familiar with traditions where a mantra is a sound formula recited for occult effect. The Mool Mantar is not a charm. It is the root teaching — the seed-statement from which the worldview of Sikhi unfolds. Its power is the power of truth understood and lived, not of syllables mechanically repeated. As we will see in the final lesson, even understanding it is, in the Guru's own words, a matter of ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ — grace.

How to use this course

  • Each lesson takes one cluster of attributes and asks two questions: what does this phrase affirm, and what does it deny?
  • We treat the Gurmukhi text with reverence; we explain rather than casually paraphrase.
  • By the synthesis lesson you should be able to recite the whole formula and explain, in one breath, the Sikh picture of God.
References
  • Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. Oxford University Press, 2001.
  • Singh, Sahib (Prof.). Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Raj Publishers, 1962-1964.
  • Cole, W. Owen, and Piara Singh Sambhi. The Sikhs: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices. Sussex Academic Press, 1995.

lessons.title: ੴ Ik Onkar and ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ — The One Whose Name Is Truth
lessons.summary: The first symbol of Sikhi and the nature of the Name: oneness that is unity, not mere arithmetic, and truth that is eternal reality.
lessons.html:
If a single mark could stand for an entire faith, it would be ੴ. It is the first character of Sri Guru Granth Sahib and the most recognizable symbol of Sikhi. In this lesson we unpack the opening cluster: ੴ ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ — the One whose Name is Truth.

Reading ੴ — Ik Onkar

The symbol joins two elements. The numeral ੧ (the figure 'one', Ik) is fused to ਓ (Onkar), extended by a flourishing stroke. We pronounce it Ik Onkar. Guru Nanak chose to begin not with a word but with a number, and this choice is theological. By writing the digit one, the Guru insists on oneness that cannot be split, argued away, or shared. There is no second.

Oneness as unity, not just arithmetic

It is tempting to read 'One God' as merely counting — one rather than two or many. But the Sikh One is richer. Onkar points to the One that pervades and sustains all that exists; the One from which the many emerge and into which they return. Gurbani teaches that this One is both ਨਿਰਗੁਣ (beyond all attributes) and ਸਰਗੁਣ (expressed through every form of creation). So ੴ is not a God standing apart from a separate world; it is the single reality underlying and indwelling everything. To say Ik is therefore to deny not only rival gods but also any ultimate division between Creator and creation.

A common misreadingThe Sikh meaning
One god rather than several godsOne indivisible reality, source and substance of all
A distant ruler over the worldThe One pervading and present within the world
A figure to be picturedFormless, beyond image, knowable through Name

ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ — the Name is Truth

Next comes ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ (Sat Naam). The most careful reading takes ਸਤਿ (Sat) as the predicate and ਨਾਮੁ (Naam) as the subject: (whose) Name is Truth, or 'eternal is the Name.' ਸਤਿ means truth in the deepest sense — not merely accurate statement but that which truly exists, the real that does not pass away. In Indic thought, the world of birth and death is changeable and so, in a sense, unreal; the One alone is unchangingly real. To call the Name Sat is to say the Divine is the only thing that always was, is, and shall be.

Why 'Name'?

Why locate truth in the Name rather than simply in God? Because in Sikhi the ਨਾਮੁ (Naam) is how the formless One becomes available to us. We cannot see or grasp the infinite, but we can hold the Name — remember it, sing it, live by it. The Name is the bridge between the human heart and the boundless reality. Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, in rendering the verses of the Gurus, stresses how Naam functions as the felt presence of the transcendent within ordinary life.

  • Ik rules out polytheism and ultimate division.
  • Onkar affirms a God who pervades, not merely presides.
  • Sat affirms eternal reality against the impermanent.
  • Naam gives us the way to hold the One we cannot grasp.

Already, in just three words, the Mool Mantar has set Sikhi apart: a single, formless, ever-real, all-pervading Divine, met through the Name.

References
  • Singh, Sahib (Prof.). Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Raj Publishers, 1962-1964.
  • Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus. HarperCollins, 1995.
  • McLeod, W. H. Sikhism. Penguin Books, 1997.

lessons.title: ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ — The Creator Who Pervades Creation
lessons.summary: God as Karta Purakh: the doer and the all-pervading being, holding together transcendence and immanence in two words.
lessons.html:
Having named the One whose Name is Truth, the Mool Mantar tells us what this One does and is: ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ (Karta Purakh). These two words pack the entire Sikh doctrine of creation into a single phrase.

ਕਰਤਾ — the Doer

The word ਕਰਤਾ (Karta) comes from the root meaning 'to do' or 'to make.' It names God as the active Creator — not a passive first cause set long ago, but the ongoing Doer of all that happens. In Sikh thought creation is not a single event in the distant past; the One continually creates, sustains, and dissolves. Gurbani repeatedly returns to the wonder that the same One who fashions the cosmos also watches over it with care.

ਪੁਰਖੁ — the Being who pervades

The word ਪੁਰਖੁ (Purakh) is subtle. In classical usage purusha can mean 'person' or 'cosmic being.' Here it carries the sense of the all-pervading Being — the One present throughout creation. Crucially, ਪੁਰਖੁ in the Mool Mantar is not gendered into a male deity; the Divine in Sikhi is beyond gender, addressed in Gurbani as mother and father, friend and beloved alike. So ਪੁਰਖੁ should be read as 'the pervading Being,' not 'the man.'

Two words, two truths held together

Put together, ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ does remarkable theological work. ਕਰਤਾ points to God above and beyond creation — the maker is not the made. ਪੁਰਖੁ points to God within creation — the maker pervades the made. Many theologies struggle to hold transcendence and immanence at once. The Mool Mantar simply states both in two breaths.

ਕਰਤਾ (Karta)ਪੁਰਖੁ (Purakh)
The Doer / MakerThe all-pervading Being
Emphasizes transcendenceEmphasizes immanence
Creation depends on GodGod is present in creation
Beyond the worldWithin the world

What this rules out

  • Deism — a God who builds the universe and walks away. ਪੁਰਖੁ denies the absent watchmaker.
  • Pantheism flattened — the idea that God is only the world and nothing more. ਕਰਤਾ denies that the maker is reducible to the made.
  • An idol — a created object worshipped as the Creator. The Doer cannot be one of the things done.

Living implications

If God is ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ, then creation is not an accident to escape but a sacred work shot through with the Creator's presence. This grounds the Sikh affirmation of life in the world: honest work (ਕਿਰਤ), service, and family are not distractions from God but arenas where the all-pervading Being is met. The Creator who pervades is a God you can serve at the loom, the field, and the langar — not only in retreat from the world.

References
  • Singh, Sahib (Prof.). Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Raj Publishers, 1962-1964.
  • Singh, Gopal (Dr.). Sri Guru-Granth Sahib (English Version). World Sikh Centre, 1978.
  • Cole, W. Owen, and Piara Singh Sambhi. The Sikhs: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices. Sussex Academic Press, 1995.

lessons.title: ਨਿਰਭਉ ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ — Without Fear, Without Enmity
lessons.summary: Two negations that reshape the moral character of God — and become the template for the Sikh life of fearlessness and universal goodwill.
lessons.html:
The Mool Mantar now turns from God's being to God's character, and it does so through two negations: ਨਿਰਭਉ ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ (Nirbhau Nirvair) — without fear, without enmity. These are perhaps the most morally radiant words in the formula, because they are also the ones we are called to imitate.

ਨਿਰਭਉ — without fear

The prefix ਨਿਰ (nir) means 'without,' and ਭਉ (bhau) means 'fear.' To say God is ਨਿਰਭਉ is to say the Divine fears nothing and is answerable to no higher power, for there is none. This follows directly from ੴ: if there is only One, there is nothing outside it to threaten it. Fear arises from the threat of another; the One that contains all others is beyond all threat.

ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ — without enmity

Likewise ਵੈਰੁ (vair) means 'enmity' or 'hostility,' so ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ means the Divine holds no hatred toward anyone or anything. This single word dismantles the picture of a wrathful, vengeful God who must be appeased. The God of the Mool Mantar is not angry, not jealous in the petty sense, not waiting to punish. The Divine that creates and pervades all cannot be at war with any part of itself.

PhraseWhat it affirmsWhat it denies
ਨਿਰਭਉ (Nirbhau)Absolute sovereignty and securityA God who can be coerced or threatened
ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ (Nirvair)Boundless goodwill toward allA wrathful, vengeful, hating deity

A loving, not wrathful, picture of God

Together these two words paint the moral face of the Divine. Where some imagine God as a stern judge whose default posture is anger, Sikhi imagines a Creator without fear and without hate — and therefore free to be wholly gracious. Gurbani describes the Divine as the help of the helpless, the destroyer of suffering, ever-merciful. A God without enmity is a God whose grace is not rationed by our deserving but flows from its own nature.

From theology to ethics

Here is what makes this cluster unique: it is also a command. The qualities of God become the goal of the Sikh. The one who remembers a fearless God learns to live ਨਿਰਭਉ — refusing to bow to tyranny, refusing to be ruled by anxiety. The one who remembers a God without enmity learns to live ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ — holding no hatred even toward an opponent. This pairing animates Sikh history: the courage to stand against injustice, joined to the refusal to let that struggle curdle into personal hatred.

  • Fearlessness without hatred — the Sikh fights oppression but bears no ਵੈਰੁ toward the oppressor as a person.
  • Goodwill without cowardice — universal love does not mean passivity before injustice.
  • The model is divine — these are not human ideals invented by us, but reflections of God's own character.

In two words the Mool Mantar gives both a doctrine of God and a charter for human character: be fearless, hate no one.

References
  • Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus. HarperCollins, 1995.
  • Singh, Sahib (Prof.). Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Raj Publishers, 1962-1964.
  • McLeod, W. H. Sikhism. Penguin Books, 1997.

lessons.title: ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ ਅਜੂਨੀ ਸੈਭੰ — Beyond Time, Unborn, Self-Existent
lessons.summary: Three terms that place God outside time, birth, and dependence — and quietly distinguish Sikh theology from incarnational belief.
lessons.html:
This lesson takes the metaphysical heart of the Mool Mantar: ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ ਅਜੂਨੀ ਸੈਭੰ. These three terms answer three deep questions — Is God subject to time? Is God born? Does God depend on anything?

ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ — the Form beyond Time

ਕਾਲ (kaal) means time, and also, by extension, death — for time is what brings all things to their end. The prefix ਅ (a) negates it: ਅਕਾਲ (Akaal) means 'beyond time, deathless, eternal.' ਮੂਰਤਿ (moorat) means 'form' or 'image.' So ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ is 'the Form beyond Time' — a striking phrase, because it speaks of a 'form' that is nonetheless deathless and not physical. The word ਅਕਾਲ is so central that it becomes a name of God itself — ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, the Timeless Being — and gives its name to the Akaal Takht, the seat of temporal authority for the Panth.

ਅਜੂਨੀ — unborn

ਜੂਨਿ (joon) means birth, or a 'womb' / species into which one is born. ਅਜੂਨੀ (Ajooni) means 'not subject to birth' — the Divine does not enter the cycle of birth and death, does not take physical incarnation. This is a pointed claim. In traditions that teach avatars — God descending into a human or animal form — the Divine is born. The Mool Mantar says the opposite: the One does not come into being through any womb. Sikhi therefore does not regard its Gurus as incarnations of God; they are the voice and light of the One, not God taking birth.

ਸੈਭੰ — self-existent

ਸੈਭੰ (Saibhang, from svayambhu) means 'self-existent' or 'self-illumined' — brought into being by nothing other than itself. Everything else depends on a cause; the One depends on nothing. It is its own source and its own light. This is the metaphysical floor beneath all the other attributes: only a self-existent being could be truly eternal, unborn, fearless, and one.

TermMeaningWhat it denies
ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ (Akaal Moorat)Form beyond time, deathlessThat God ages, ends, or is bound by time
ਅਜੂਨੀ (Ajooni)Unborn, never incarnatedThat God takes birth as an avatar
ਸੈਭੰ (Saibhang)Self-existent, self-illuminedThat God was created or depends on another

Why this trio matters

  • It firmly distinguishes Sikh theology from incarnational belief: the One is ਅਜੂਨੀ and is never to be pictured as having been born.
  • It rules out idolatry: a self-existent, timeless reality cannot be captured in a manufactured image, however beautiful.
  • It grounds hope: a Divine beyond time and decay is a refuge that the changes of fortune cannot touch.

A note on 'form'

Readers sometimes stumble on ਮੂਰਤਿ (form), thinking it contradicts a formless God. It does not. The phrase means the Divine is a 'form' only in the sense of being real, present, and beheld by the awakened heart — a deathless reality, not a sculpted shape. Sikhi worships no physical image; the only 'form' it bows to is the living Word, the Shabad-Guru.

References
  • Singh, Gopal (Dr.). Sri Guru-Granth Sahib (English Version). World Sikh Centre, 1978.
  • Singh, Sahib (Prof.). Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Raj Publishers, 1962-1964.
  • Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. Oxford University Press, 2001.

lessons.title: ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ and Synthesis — The God of One Breath
lessons.summary: The final phrase makes knowledge of God a gift of grace, and the whole formula is gathered into one coherent picture of the Divine.
lessons.html:
Every attribute we have studied — One, True, Creator, fearless, without enmity, beyond time, unborn, self-existent — describes a reality utterly beyond the reach of our small minds. So the Mool Mantar ends with the only honest conclusion: we cannot seize this God by effort. The final words are ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ (Gur Prasaad) — 'by the Guru's grace.'

ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ — realized by grace

ਗੁਰ (Gur) is the Guru — the light that dispels darkness — and ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ (Prasaad) is grace or gift. The phrase declares that the One described in the formula is known not through cleverness, ritual purchase, or austerity, but as a gift received through the Guru. This is the Sikh answer to a hard question: if God is beyond time, birth, and image, how could a finite human ever know such a being? Answer: only because the Guru reveals it and grace grants it.

Grace, not achievement

This single phrase reorders the spiritual life. It removes pride — no one earns God by being more learned or more austere than others. It removes despair — no one is shut out for lacking learning or status, since the gift is given by grace, not won by merit. Gurbani teaches that it is by the Guru's grace that the Name is obtained and the mind is stilled. The Mool Mantar thus closes the way it opened: humbly, pointing beyond the human to the Divine and its chosen channel, the Guru.

Gathering the whole formula

Step back and read the Mool Mantar as one breath. It moves through a deliberate sequence:

PhraseQuestion it answersThe Sikh picture of God
ੴHow many?One, indivisible, all-pervading
ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁWhat is its nature?Eternally real; known through the Name
ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁWhat does it do / where is it?Creator who pervades creation
ਨਿਰਭਉWhat rules it?Nothing — without fear
ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁHow does it relate to us?Without enmity — wholly gracious
ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿIs it bound by time?No — deathless, beyond time
ਅਜੂਨੀIs it born?No — never incarnated
ਸੈਭੰDoes it depend on anything?No — self-existent, self-illumined
ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿHow can we know it?Only as a gift, by the Guru's grace

The picture that emerges

Read together, these phrases give a God who is:

  • Not anthropomorphic — formless, beyond image, not a magnified human ruler.
  • Not wrathful — ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ, without hatred, default posture grace.
  • Not absent — ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ, present and pervading every atom.
  • Not incarnated — ਅਜੂਨੀ, never born, never to be sculpted into an idol.
  • Present and loving — eternally real, fearless, gracious, and near, met through the Name and the Guru.

One breath, one faith

This is why the Mool Mantar can be called Sikh theology in one breath. It is short enough to recite before dawn and deep enough to occupy a lifetime. Every later hymn of Sri Guru Granth Sahib elaborates some facet of this root. To understand the Mool Mantar is to hold the entire architecture of Sikh belief in your two hands — and, the Guru reminds us, even that understanding is ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ, a gift of grace.

References
  • Singh, Sahib (Prof.). Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Raj Publishers, 1962-1964.
  • Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus. HarperCollins, 1995.
  • Cole, W. Owen, and Piara Singh Sambhi. The Sikhs: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices. Sussex Academic Press, 1995.
  • McLeod, W. H. Sikhism. Penguin Books, 1997.

quiz.q: What does the term ਮੂਲ ਮੰਤਰ (Mool Mantar) literally mean, and where does it appear?
options: A magic chant recited for occult power, found at the end of scripture
The 'root formula' that opens Sri Guru Granth Sahib and defines the nature of God
A hymn of petition asking God for worldly blessings
A historical account of Guru Nanak's travels

quiz.q: Why does Guru Nanak open the Mool Mantar with the numeral ੧ in ੴ (Ik Onkar)?
options: To indicate the first of many gods in a hierarchy
To show God is distant and separate from the world
To insist on an indivisible oneness that pervades and underlies all creation
Because the number was chosen at random for decoration

quiz.q: In the phrase ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ, what pair of truths is held together?
options: God's wrath and God's mercy
God's transcendence as Doer (ਕਰਤਾ) and God's immanence as the pervading Being (ਪੁਰਖੁ)
God's maleness and femaleness as two separate deities
The created world and an entirely separate spiritual realm

quiz.q: What do the two negations ਨਿਰਭਉ and ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ tell us about God's character?
options: That God is fearful and must be appeased with offerings
That God is without fear and without enmity — sovereign and wholly gracious
That God created the world then abandoned it
That God is born repeatedly in different forms

quiz.q: How does the attribute ਅਜੂਨੀ distinguish Sikh theology from incarnational belief?
options: It teaches that God is born as an avatar in every age
It declares that God is unborn and never takes physical incarnation, so the Gurus are not God taking birth
It states that only the Gurus are God incarnate
It means God exists only in carved images

quiz.q: What does the closing phrase ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ establish about knowing God?
options: That God is known by earning merit through austerity and learning
That God can be purchased through ritual
That knowledge of God is a gift received by the Guru's grace, not a human achievement
That God cannot be known by anyone at all

courses.title: Japji Sahib: A Deep Reading of the Opening Prayer
courses.summary: A section-by-section study of Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak's foundational prayer that opens Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji: the Mool Mantar, all 38 pauris, and core concepts like Hukam, Nadar, Sach, and the Khands.
outcomes: Explain why Japji Sahib opens Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and functions as the theological foundation of Sikhi
Interpret the Mool Mantar word by word, including ੴ and the qualities of the Divine it names
Trace the argument of the early pauris on ego, ritual, and ਹੁਕਮੁ (Divine Order)
Describe the stages of spiritual development presented across the middle pauris
Distinguish the five ਖੰਡ (realms) culminating in ਸਚ ਖੰਡੁ (the Realm of Truth)
Move from rote recitation toward reflective understanding (ਵੀਚਾਰ) of Japji in daily life

terms.m: Ik Onkar — the opening symbol affirming One Universal Creator whose creative reality pervades all existence.
Mool Mantar — the 'root formula' opening Japji, a concise statement of Sikh theology describing the nature of the Divine.
Hukam — the Divine Order, Command, or Will by which all creation operates; central to Japji's worldview.
Nadar — the Grace or merciful Glance of the Divine, by which liberation is ultimately granted.
Sach — Truth; the True One. The Divine that is true beyond time, repeated throughout Japji as ਸਤਿ / ਸਚੁ.
Khand — a realm or stage of spiritual development. Japji describes five such realms.
Sach Khand — the Realm of Truth, the highest of the five Khands where the soul abides in the Divine.
Pauri — literally 'step/stanza'; the 38 numbered verses forming the body of Japji between the opening and closing Slok.
Vichar — reflective contemplation; the deep understanding of Gurbani that goes beyond mere recitation.
Haumai — egoism or 'I-am-ness', the self-centeredness Japji identifies as the root barrier to truth.
Naam — the Divine Name/Identity; loving remembrance of which is the practice Japji repeatedly commends.
Gurmukh — one who is oriented toward the Guru; the Guru-facing seeker, contrasted with the self-willed manmukh.

references: Singh, Sahib (Prof.). Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Raj Publishers, 1962-64.
Macauliffe, Max Arthur. The Sikh Religion: Its Gurus, Sacred Writings and Authors. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1909.
Singh, Gopal (trans.). Sri Guru Granth Sahib: English Version. World Sikh University Press, 1978.
Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.
Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus. San Francisco: HarperCollins, 1995.
McLeod, W. H. Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1968.
Shackle, Christopher, and Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair. Teachings of the Sikh Gurus: Selections from the Sikh Scriptures. London: Routledge, 2005.

lessons.title: Introduction — Why Japji Comes First
lessons.summary: What Japji Sahib is, its place at the opening of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, its structure, and why it is the foundation of Sikh understanding.
lessons.html:
Japji Sahib is the first composition (ਬਾਣੀ) in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, authored by Guru Nanak Dev Ji. It is recited every morning by Sikhs as the first of the Nitnem (daily prayers) and is widely held to be a distilled summary of the entire Sikh worldview. Before we read it line by line, this lesson orients us: what is Japji, how is it structured, and why does it stand at the very threshold of the Guru Granth Sahib?

Full course contents
  1. Introduction — Why Japji Comes First
  2. The Mool Mantar — Sikh Theology in One Breath
  3. Pauris 1-10 — Ego and Hukam
  4. Pauris 11-20 — Stages of Spiritual Life
  5. Pauris 21-38 — The Khands and Sachkhand
  6. Living Japji — From Recitation to Understanding

What does "Japji" mean?

The root ਜਪੁ (Jap) means to recite, repeat, or contemplate. The honorific ਜੀ (Ji) is added out of reverence, giving "Japji." The title itself signals the bani's purpose: it is something to be contemplated and lived, not merely read once and set aside.

Its place in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji

Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji opens with Japji Sahib before the rest of the scripture is arranged by musical measure (raag). Most of the Granth is organized into raags, but Japji stands apart and first, without a raag heading. Tradition understands this placement as deliberate: Japji is the doorway through which the reader enters all that follows. Its themes — the nature of the Divine, Hukam, Naam, grace, and the journey of the soul — recur throughout the entire Granth.

The structure of Japji

Japji has a clear architecture:

  • An opening ਮੂਲ ਮੰਤ੍ਰ (Mool Mantar) — the root statement of the Divine's nature.
  • An opening Slok beginning ਆਦਿ ਸਚੁ ("True in the primal beginning...").
  • Thirty-eight numbered ਪਉੜੀਆਂ (pauris, "steps"), which form the body of the composition.
  • A closing Slok beginning ਪਵਣੁ ਗੁਰੂ ("Air is the Guru...").

The word pauri means a "step" of a ladder or staircase. The image is intentional: Japji is a graded ascent. The seeker climbs from questions about ritual and ego, through stages of effort and surrender, toward the realms (Khands) of spiritual realization.

Why study it deeply?

Because Japji is recited daily, it is easy to know the sounds without knowing the meaning. This course treats Japji as theology to be understood (ਵੀਚਾਰ, vichar), not only sound to be repeated. Guru Nanak Ji himself, within Japji, contrasts mere outward practice with inner understanding. Our task across these six lessons is to honor the bani by reading it carefully, section by section.

A note on method: we will discuss the meaning and themes of the bani with reverence. We will not casually paraphrase the sacred verse as if it were ordinary prose, and where a precise location in scripture is not certain we will say "Gurbani teaches" rather than cite a specific Ang.

References
  • Singh, Sahib (Prof.). Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Raj Publishers, 1962-64.
  • McLeod, W. H. Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1968.
  • Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.

lessons.title: The Mool Mantar — Sikh Theology in One Breath
lessons.summary: A word-by-word reading of the Mool Mantar, the root statement that names the nature of the Divine and grounds all of Sikh theology.
lessons.html:
The Mool Mantar (ਮੂਲ ਮੰਤ੍ਰ, "root formula") is the opening of Japji and of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji itself. In a single sustained statement it names the essential qualities of the Divine. Sikh tradition regards it as the seed from which the rest of Gurbani unfolds. In this lesson we move through it phrase by phrase.

The phrases of the Mool Mantar

The Mool Mantar reads: ੴ ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ ਨਿਰਭਉ ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ ਅਜੂਨੀ ਸੈਭੰ ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ ॥

Phrase (Gurmukhi)TransliterationMeaning
ੴIk OnkarOne Universal Creator; the One whose creative being pervades all. The numeral "1" (੧) emphasizes absolute oneness.
ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁSat(i) NaamWhose Name/Identity is Truth; the Real, true beyond all time.
ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁKarta PurakhThe Creator-Being; the Doer who is also present within creation.
ਨਿਰਭਉNirbhauWithout fear (since nothing stands above the One).
ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁNirvairWithout enmity or hatred toward any.
ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿAkaal MooratTimeless in form; beyond death and decay (ਕਾਲ, time/death).
ਅਜੂਨੀAjooniNot subject to birth; beyond the cycle of incarnation.
ਸੈਭੰSaibhangSelf-existent; self-illumined, not created by another.
ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿGur PrasadRealized by the Guru's grace. This One is known not by intellect alone but through grace.

Why ੴ matters

The symbol ੴ joins the numeral ੧ (one) with ਓ (Onkar, the sustaining creative reality). Placing a numeral first is theologically pointed: the Divine is not merely "one among options" but absolutely, indivisibly One. Guru Nanak Ji thereby roots Sikhi in uncompromising monotheism while affirming that this One is immanent throughout creation, not distant from it.

A positive theology by negation and affirmation

Notice how the Mool Mantar works. Some terms affirm what the Divine is (Truth, Creator, self-existent); others state what the Divine is free of (fear, enmity, time, birth). This combination — saying both what God is and what God is beyond — lets the seeker hold a balanced understanding: the One is intimately creative yet utterly beyond human limitation.

Grace as the doorway

The Mool Mantar closes with ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ — by the Guru's grace. This is crucial. After naming the lofty qualities of the Divine, Guru Nanak Ji insists that this Reality is not reached by cleverness or effort alone, but is unveiled by grace through the Guru. This theme of grace (ਨਦਰਿ, Nadar) will return powerfully at the close of Japji.

References
  • Singh, Sahib (Prof.). Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Raj Publishers, 1962-64.
  • Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus. San Francisco: HarperCollins, 1995.
  • Shackle, Christopher, and Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair. Teachings of the Sikh Gurus. London: Routledge, 2005.

lessons.title: Pauris 1-10 — Ego and Hukam
lessons.summary: The opening pauris confront ritual purity and ego, introduce the central concept of Hukam (Divine Order), and present the practice of Naam and listening.
lessons.html:
Having named the Divine in the Mool Mantar, Guru Nanak Ji opens the body of Japji by asking a practical and urgent question: how does a human being become true, and break the wall of falsehood between the self and the Divine? The first ten pauris answer by dismantling reliance on ritual and ego and replacing it with surrender to Hukam and the practice of Naam.

Pauri 1 — the futility of external means

The very first pauri asks how one can become ਸਚਿਆਰਾ (sachiara, truthful/aligned with Truth) and how the wall of falsehood may fall. Guru Nanak Ji surveys the usual answers — ritual bathing, silence, accumulation — and finds them insufficient on their own. The pauri concludes that the way is to walk in accordance with the Divine Order: ਹੁਕਮਿ ਰਜਾਈ ਚਲਣਾ — to move in harmony with the Will that is already written.

Pauris 2-3 — what is Hukam?

Pauri 2 develops the concept of ਹੁਕਮੁ (Hukam), the Divine Order. By Hukam all forms come into being; by Hukam beings are made high or low; by Hukam pleasure and pain are assigned. Crucially, Guru Nanak Ji states that Hukam itself cannot be fully described. The lesson is one of humility: the order of reality is real and pervasive, even though the finite mind cannot map it completely. The seeker is invited not to decode Hukam exhaustively but to live within it without ego.

The grammar of ego

Underlying these pauris is a contrast between two postures of the heart:

PostureDescription
ਹਉਮੈ (Haumai)Ego, "I-am-ness" — the self that imagines it acts independently and seeks control. Japji presents this as the wall that obscures Truth.
ਹੁਕਮੁ (Hukam)Living in conscious harmony with the Divine Will, releasing the illusion of self-sufficiency.

To accept Hukam is precisely to dissolve haumai — and Gurbani teaches that when one understands Hukam, one no longer speaks in ego.

The Suniai and Manne pauris — listening and accepting

Among these early pauris are the celebrated sequences on ਸੁਣਿਐ (Suniai, "by listening") and ਮੰਨੈ (Manne, "by accepting/believing"). The Suniai pauris describe the transforming power of truly hearing the Divine Name — bringing wisdom, contentment, and the dissolving of sorrow. The Manne pauris go further: inward acceptance and faith cannot even be fully expressed in words, yet they reshape the whole being. Together they map a movement from outward hearing to inward conviction.

Naam, not negotiation

These pauris also reject the idea that the Divine can be bargained with or bought through ritual transactions. What is asked instead is loving remembrance of ਨਾਮੁ (Naam) and alignment with Hukam. This is the foundational ethical and spiritual turn of Japji: from the anxious, ego-driven self toward a self that listens, accepts, and lives in the Divine Order.

References
  • Singh, Sahib (Prof.). Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Raj Publishers, 1962-64.
  • McLeod, W. H. Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1968.
  • Macauliffe, Max Arthur. The Sikh Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1909.

lessons.title: Pauris 11-20 — Stages of Spiritual Life
lessons.summary: The middle pauris extend the themes of listening, acceptance, virtue, and the limits of human knowing, while affirming the cleansing power of Naam.
lessons.html:
The middle pauris of Japji deepen and broaden the themes already introduced. Guru Nanak Ji continues to weigh the value of inner practice against outer show, reflects on the vastness of creation and the limits of human reckoning, and returns repeatedly to the purifying power of the Divine Name. These pauris can be read as describing the maturing inner life of a seeker who has begun to live in Hukam.

Continuing the Suniai and Manne arcs

The reflections on ਸੁਣਿਐ (listening) and ਮੰਨੈ (acceptance) continue into this stretch of pauris. Listening, when it is true, lifts the seeker toward the company and qualities of the enlightened. Acceptance brings honor and steadiness that the world cannot grant or remove. The repetition is itself instructive: spiritual growth is not a single event but a sustained orientation, returned to again and again.

The community of the devoted

This section honors the ਪੰਚ (panch) — the accepted, realized ones who are recognized and honored in the Divine Court. Their distinction is not social rank but inner alignment. Guru Nanak Ji thereby redefines greatness: the truly elevated are those who have accepted the Divine Will and remembered the Name, regardless of worldly status.

The vastness that humbles reckoning

Guru Nanak Ji turns to the immensity of creation and of the Divine's working. He evokes countless beings, worlds, and forms beyond any counting. The repeated point is epistemic humility: human attempts to measure the Creator collapse before the scale of creation. The proper response to vastness is not calculation but wonder (ਵਿਸਮਾਦੁ) and remembrance.

The cleansing of the Name

A famous teaching in this section concerns purification. Gurbani teaches that just as hands or feet soiled with dirt are washed clean with water, and a garment stained is cleansed by soap, so a mind stained by wrongdoing is cleansed by the color of the Name (ਨਾਮੁ). The metaphor is precise and democratic: cleansing is available to anyone who turns to Naam, regardless of birth or ritual status.

Beyond merit and demerit

Guru Nanak Ji notes that good and bad deeds are recorded, and that one ultimately reaps what one sows; yet liberation is not a mechanical payout. The seeker is reminded that even our virtues are gifts, and that grace remains central. The middle pauris thus hold two truths together:

  • Action matters — what we sow, we reap, and ethical living is real.
  • Yet final reach toward the Divine rests on remembrance and grace, not on a ledger we can balance by ourselves.

By the close of this section, the seeker has been shaped: humbled before vastness, cleansed by the Name, and prepared to ascend through the realms described next.

References
  • Singh, Sahib (Prof.). Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Raj Publishers, 1962-64.
  • Singh, Gopal (trans.). Sri Guru Granth Sahib: English Version. World Sikh University Press, 1978.
  • Shackle, Christopher, and Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair. Teachings of the Sikh Gurus. London: Routledge, 2005.

lessons.title: Pauris 21-38 — The Khands and Sachkhand
lessons.summary: The closing pauris present the five Khands (realms) of spiritual ascent culminating in Sach Khand, and end with the triumph of grace in the closing Slok.
lessons.html:
The final movement of Japji brings the seeker to its most majestic teaching: the five ਖੰਡ (Khands), or realms, that map the soul's ascent toward the Divine. After continuing themes of wonder and the limits of knowing, Guru Nanak Ji describes a graded spiritual geography — not literal places, but states of consciousness through which the awakened seeker passes.

The five Khands

In the closing pauris, Guru Nanak Ji names five realms in order. They are best read as deepening stages of spiritual development:

Realm (Gurmukhi)NameCharacter of the stage
ਧਰਮ ਖੰਡDharam KhandThe Realm of Duty/Righteousness. The seeker awakens to moral responsibility within the ordered cosmos; this earth is the place where dharma is practiced.
ਗਿਆਨ ਖੰਡGian KhandThe Realm of Knowledge. The mind expands to grasp the immense diversity of creation, kindling awe and wisdom.
ਸਰਮ ਖੰਡSaram KhandThe Realm of Effort/Refinement. Consciousness, wisdom, and understanding are beautifully shaped and refined as if by a craftsman.
ਕਰਮ ਖੰਡKaram KhandThe Realm of Grace. Here grace (karam) predominates; the realm of the spiritually powerful and the devoted who are filled with the Divine.
ਸਚ ਖੰਡੁSach KhandThe Realm of Truth. The formless One abides; the seeker beholds and merges in the Divine Will. The highest realization.

How to read the Khands

The progression is meaningful. It begins with ethical duty (Dharam), proceeds through knowledge (Gian) and the refinement of the inner faculties (Saram), opens into grace (Karam), and culminates in Truth (Sach). Notice that knowledge alone does not reach the summit; refinement and, decisively, grace are required. The ascent is not a purely intellectual climb but a transformation of the whole being.

Sach Khand — the Realm of Truth

In ਸਚ ਖੰਡੁ, Guru Nanak Ji describes the Formless One dwelling and overseeing all of creation with the gaze of grace. Here the distinction between seeker and sought softens; the soul abides in harmony with the Divine Will. Guru Nanak Ji notes that to describe this state fully is as hard as steel — that is, beyond the reach of words. The Khands therefore end not in a tidy diagram but in wonder before what cannot be told.

The final pauri and the closing Slok

The thirty-eighth pauri offers a memorable image of the seeker as a disciplined craftsman, forging the self in the workshop of devotion — self-control as the furnace, patience as the goldsmith, understanding as the anvil — so that the Name may be coined in true mintage. It teaches that those upon whom grace falls are themselves made joyful and made a means of others' joy.

Japji then closes with the Slok beginning ਪਵਣੁ ਗੁਰੂ ਪਾਣੀ ਪਿਤਾ — "Air is the Guru, water the father, and the great earth the mother" — affirming that all of creation plays its role under the Divine, and that those who remember and labor truly depart with their faces radiant, carrying many others to freedom with them. Grace (ਨਦਰਿ) has the final word.

References
  • Singh, Sahib (Prof.). Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Raj Publishers, 1962-64.
  • Macauliffe, Max Arthur. The Sikh Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1909.
  • Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Name of My Beloved. San Francisco: HarperCollins, 1995.

lessons.title: Living Japji — From Recitation to Understanding
lessons.summary: How to move from daily recitation toward reflective understanding (vichar), integrating Japji's teaching on Hukam, Naam, and grace into daily life.
lessons.html:
We have read Japji from the Mool Mantar through the closing Slok. This final lesson asks the practical question Guru Nanak Ji himself cared about most: how does this bani live in us? Japji is recited every morning by millions, yet its deepest fruit is understanding (ਵੀਚਾਰ, vichar) that reshapes how one lives.

From sound to meaning

Recitation (ਪਾਠ, paath) has real value: it disciplines the day, steadies the mind, and keeps the bani on the tongue. But Guru Nanak Ji repeatedly contrasts empty outward practice with inner truth. The goal is not to abandon recitation but to let recitation become a doorway to vichar — to ask, with each pauri, "What is this teaching, and how does it change me?"

Three threads to carry forward

Across Japji, three intertwined teachings hold the whole together:

  • ਹੁਕਮੁ (Hukam): To live in conscious acceptance of the Divine Order, releasing the ego's demand for control. In daily life this looks like equanimity in gain and loss, and humility before what we cannot command.
  • ਨਾਮੁ (Naam): Loving remembrance of the Divine, which cleanses the mind and reorders desire. Japji presents Naam as available to all, independent of birth or ritual privilege.
  • ਨਦਰਿ (Nadar/Grace): The recognition that even our best efforts are completed by grace. This guards against spiritual pride and keeps the seeker grateful.

The arc, reviewed

SectionCore movement
Mool MantarNames the One: Truth, Creator, fearless, beyond time and birth, known by grace.
Pauris 1-10Dismantles ego and ritualism; introduces Hukam, listening (Suniai), and acceptance (Manne).
Pauris 11-20Deepens listening and acceptance; humbles us before vastness; affirms cleansing by Naam.
Pauris 21-38Maps the five Khands to Sach Khand; ends in the craftsman of devotion and the triumph of grace.

Why Japji is the foundation

Japji is the foundation of Sikh understanding because every major theme of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is present here in seed form: the One Divine, the centrality of Naam, the dissolution of ego, ethical living within Hukam, the irrelevance of caste and empty ritual, and the supremacy of grace. To understand Japji well is to hold a key that unlocks the rest of Gurbani.

A practice for the reader

A simple discipline of vichar: take one pauri each day. Recite it, then sit with one question — what does this ask of me today? Over thirty-eight days the whole composition passes through the heart not as sound only, but as understanding. This is the movement Guru Nanak Ji invites: from jap as repetition to Jap as living contemplation.

We close as Japji closes — with humility. The bani itself confesses that the Divine cannot be fully described. Our study is therefore an act of reverence and a beginning, not a mastery. ਨਾਨਕ ਨਾਮੁ ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ.

References
  • Singh, Sahib (Prof.). Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Raj Publishers, 1962-64.
  • McLeod, W. H. Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1968.
  • Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Name of My Beloved. San Francisco: HarperCollins, 1995.

courses.title: Khalsa Raj: Sikh Political Leadership and the Principles of Halemi Raaj
courses.summary: An advanced study of Sikh political leadership through the lens of Halemi Raaj, the realm where the weak are protected, from Banda Singh Bahadur to Maharani Jind Kaur, and its application to modern governance.
outcomes: Explain the Gurbani concept of ਹਲੇਮੀ ਰਾਜੁ (Halemi Raaj) and how it reframes the purpose of political power as service to the vulnerable
Trace the institutional development of Sikh sovereignty from the Dal Khalsa and misls to the Sarbat Khalsa and the Sarkar-e-Khalsa
Analyse the agrarian and social reforms of Banda Singh Bahadur, including the abolition of zamindari landlordism in conquered territory
Evaluate the statecraft of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, including appointment by ਮੈਰਿਟ (merit) and the pluralist character of his administration
Assess the political and military leadership of Sikh women, especially Sada Kaur and Maharani Jind Kaur, within a patriarchal age
Apply the principles of Halemi Raaj to questions of justice, pluralism, and accountability in contemporary governance

terms.m: Halemi Raaj; the realm of the gentle or humble, a just order in which the weak are protected and none oppress another
Dal Khalsa; the combined army of the Khalsa, organised under Nawab Kapur Singh into a unified fighting and governing body
Misl; one of the confederate Sikh chieftaincies that governed the Punjab in the eighteenth century
Sarbat Khalsa; the general assembly of the whole Khalsa that deliberated and passed binding resolutions (gurmatas)
Gurmata; a collective resolution passed by the Sarbat Khalsa in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib
Raj Karega Khalsa; the couplet declaring that the Khalsa shall rule, recited in the ardas
Zamindari; the landlord system of revenue and control that Banda Singh Bahadur abolished in conquered territory, granting land to the tiller
Nanakshahi; the coinage and calendar struck in the name of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh rather than a worldly king
Sarkar-e-Khalsa; the Khalsa government, the official name of the sovereign state of Maharaja Ranjit Singh
Niaau; justice; the impartial administration of right that Gurbani holds central to legitimate rule
