The qazi who pronounced the sentence is remembered with infamy; the Pathan nawab Sher Muhammad Khan of Malerkotla, who raised a cry against the killing of innocents — the ਹਾਅ ਦਾ ਨਾਅਰਾ — is remembered with honour, for he protested that the children bore no part in their father's quarrel. The boys attained ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ, the youngest martyrs in the Sikh tradition. Their grandmother, ਮਾਤਾ ਗੁਜਰੀ, hearing of their martyrdom, also passed away in the cold tower, completing the sacrifice of three generations.

The Theological Weight

Santokh Singh and the tradition read the Sirhind martyrdoms as the decisive moral indictment of the Mughal tyranny. To kill children for refusing conversion was to expose the bankruptcy of a power that claimed religious sanction. The Guru's own response, when news reached him, is preserved in tradition as an act of supreme equanimity and resolve: he is said to have uprooted a plant with the point of his arrow, declaring that the roots of the tyrant's empire were now pulled up. The martyrdom of the innocents would indeed prove the moral seed of the empire's undoing, for within a few years ਬੰਦਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਬਹਾਦਰ would avenge the children by razing Sirhind, as Ganda Singh's classic study of Banda Singh narrates.

The ਸਾਹਿਬਜ਼ਾਦੇ in Sikh Memory

The four ਸਾਹਿਬਜ਼ਾਦੇ together — two fallen in battle at Chamkaur, two bricked alive at Sirhind — occupy a place in Sikh devotion that the annual observance of the ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ ਜੋੜ ਮੇਲੇ keeps ever fresh. The phrase that captures the Guru's sacrifice, ਸਰਬੰਸਦਾਨੀ, the giver of all, finds its full meaning here. The Guru gave his father, his mother, and all four sons for the freedom of conscience of others. For the student, the Sirhind narrative is the moral centre of the entire Suraj Prakash account: it is the point at which the cost of the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ ideal is paid in full, and at which the contrast between the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ's faith-unto-death and the empire's faithless cruelty is starkest.

lessons.title: The ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ — The Epistle of Victory
lessons.summary: The Guru's escape to the south, the rest at Dina, and the composition of the Zafarnama, his Persian letter of moral victory to Aurangzeb.
lessons.html:
A Letter That Conquered an Emperor

Having escaped the ਮਾਛੀਵਾੜਾ forest and passed through a series of dangers and refuges — sheltered by Muslim devotees such as the brothers Ghani Khan and Nabi Khan, who disguised him as the ਉੱਚ ਦਾ ਪੀਰ — ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ eventually reached the village of Dina in the Malwa region. It was here, or in this period, that the tradition places the composition of the ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ, the 'Epistle of Victory,' a letter in Persian verse addressed to the Emperor Aurangzeb.

The Form and Language of the Letter

The ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ is composed in the Persian masnavi form, in the metre of Firdausi's Shahnama, comprising some one hundred and eleven couplets. It is preserved within the Dasam Granth corpus. Louis Fenech's full study of the text — The Sikh Zafar-namah of Guru Gobind Singh — demonstrates how the Guru wielded the conventions of Indo-Persian courtly literature with mastery, turning the emperor's own literary and religious idiom against him. The letter is at once a moral indictment, a theological statement, and a declaration of unbroken resolve.

The Indictment of Perjury

The heart of the ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ is the charge of broken faith. The Guru reminds Aurangzeb that his commanders swore oaths upon the Qur'an guaranteeing safe passage from ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ, and then violated them by attacking the evacuating Sikhs. Gurbani in the ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ teaches the famous principle of just war: ਚੁ ਕਾਰ ਅਜ਼ ਹਮਾ ਹੀਲਤੇ ਦਰ ਗੁਜ਼ਸ਼ਤ / ਹਲਾਲ ਅਸਤ ਬੁਰਦਨ ਬ ਸ਼ਮਸ਼ੀਰ ਦਸਤ — 'When all other means have been exhausted, it is righteous to take up the sword.' This single couplet has become the cornerstone of the Sikh ethics of resistance: the sword is the last resort, lawful only when every peaceful path has failed.

The Moral Reversal

The rhetorical power of the letter lies in its reversal of positions. The emperor, master of a vast army, is shown to be morally defeated — a perjurer who could prevail over a handful of Sikhs only by treachery and overwhelming numbers. The Guru, who lost his sons and his home, stands morally victorious. He reproaches Aurangzeb for his hypocrisy in professing Islam while betraying its oaths, and warns him that the ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, the true King of kings, sees all and will hold the tyrant to account. Hence the title: it is an epistle of victory, for the moral triumph belongs to the Guru.

The Assertion of Divine Sovereignty

Throughout the letter the Guru subordinates all earthly power to the ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. He declares that he places his trust not in armies but in the Timeless One, and that the empire's might is nothing before the divine will. Yet the letter is not without an offer: the Guru expresses willingness to meet the emperor and is said to have undertaken the journey south in response. The tradition holds that Aurangzeb, reading the ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ, was deeply shaken; the aged emperor died in 1707 before any meeting could occur.

The ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ as Primary Source

For the historian the ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ is a precious primary document — the Guru's own voice, contemporary to the events, recounting the siege of ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ, the broken oaths, and the battle of ਚਮਕੌਰ. Read alongside the Suraj Prakash, it allows the student to test the later hagiography against the Guru's own testimony. Where Santokh Singh elaborates and dramatizes, the ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ confirms the essential framework: the perjured oaths, the unequal battle, and above all the unbroken spirit of the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ who, stripped of family and kingdom, addressed an emperor not as a supplicant but as a moral sovereign and the servant of the one true King.

lessons.title: The Southern Journey and the Command to ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ
lessons.summary: The Guru's journey to the Deccan, the meeting with Banda Singh Bahadur, the joti-jot at Nanded, and the conferral of eternal Guruship upon the Adi Granth.
lessons.html:
The Final Season

The closing Ruts of the Suraj Prakash narrate the last phase of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ's earthly life: the journey to the Deccan, the gathering of the Malwa Sikhs, the battle of ਮੁਕਤਸਰ, and finally the events at ਨਾਂਦੇੜ where the Guru conferred eternal Guruship upon ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ before departing the physical form.

Muktsar and the ਚਾਲੀ ਮੁਕਤੇ

Before turning south, the Guru fought his last great battle at ਖਿਦਰਾਣੇ ਦੀ ਢਾਬ, later named ਮੁਕਤਸਰ. Here the forty Sikhs who had earlier signed the ਬੇਦਾਵਾ at Anandpur, shamed by ਮਾਈ ਭਾਗੋ, returned to fight and fell defending the Guru against the pursuing Mughal force. The Guru, the tradition holds, tore up the ਬੇਦਾਵਾ over the body of their leader ਭਾਈ ਮਹਾਂ ਸਿੰਘ, granting them ਮੁਕਤੀ — and so they are remembered as the ਚਾਲੀ ਮੁਕਤੇ, the Forty Liberated Ones. The episode closes the circle opened during the siege of Anandpur: the broken bond was restored through martyrdom.

The Journey to the Deccan

After resting at ਤਲਵੰਡੀ ਸਾਬੋ — later called ਦਮਦਮਾ ਸਾਹਿਬ, the 'place of rest,' where the tradition holds the Guru prepared a definitive recension of the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ — the Guru travelled south. With the death of Aurangzeb in 1707, the Guru entered into relations with the new emperor Bahadur Shah and journeyed toward the Deccan, reaching ਨਾਂਦੇੜ on the banks of the Godavari.

The Commissioning of ਬੰਦਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਬਹਾਦਰ

At ਨਾਂਦੇੜ the Guru encountered a Bairagi ascetic named Madho Das, whom he transformed into the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ warrior ਬੰਦਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਬਹਾਦਰ. Investing him with authority, a drum, a banner, and the counsel of five Sikhs, the Guru dispatched him to the Punjab to punish the tyrants of Sirhind and to establish the rule of ਧਰਮ. Ganda Singh's Life of Banda Singh Bahadur traces how this commission unfolded into the first Sikh political ascendancy and the avenging of the ਸਾਹਿਬਜ਼ਾਦੇ.

The Joti-Jot at Nanded

At ਨਾਂਦੇੜ the Guru was attacked by an assassin — held by tradition to have been sent at the instigation of Wazir Khan of Sirhind — who stabbed him. The wound, though tended, reopened, and the Guru prepared to depart the physical form. The Suraj Prakash narrates these final days with reverence, the Guru calm and resolved, gathering the sangat about him.

The Command to ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ

Then came the act that defines Sikhism to this day. The Guru declared that after him there would be no human Guru; the eternal Guruship would pass to the ਸ਼ਬਦ — the Word enshrined in the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ, henceforth ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ — and to the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ ਪੰਥ as the Guru Panth. The tradition preserves his command: ਸਭ ਸਿੱਖਨ ਕੋ ਹੁਕਮ ਹੈ ਗੁਰੂ ਮਾਨਿਓ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ — 'To all Sikhs is the command: recognize the Granth as Guru.' The Sikh was henceforth to seek guidance in the living Word, ਸ਼ਬਦ-ਗੁਰੂ, and in the collective will of the Panth. The ਜੋਤਿ that had passed through ten human bodies now resided forever in the Granth.

The Joti-Jot and the Legacy

In 1708 ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ merged his light into the eternal Light — ਜੋਤੀ-ਜੋਤਿ ਸਮਾਏ — at ਨਾਂਦੇੜ, where Takht Sri Hazur Sahib now stands. J. S. Grewal's biography aptly titles him 'Master of the White Hawk,' capturing the sovereign warrior-saint who, in the words of the tradition, gave the Sikhs their final and eternal Guru. Reading the Suraj Prakash's account of these last days, the student sees the completion of the entire arc: the boy of Patna who received his martyred father's head, who forged the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ, who gave his sons and his all as ਸਰਬੰਸਦਾਨੀ, now bestowed upon the Panth a Guru that no empire could behead — the living ਸ਼ਬਦ. The ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ had finished his work, and the light passed to the Granth and the Khalsa forever.

ਹਵਾਲੇ (Works Cited)

  • Santokh Singh, Kavi. Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth. Edited by Bhai Vir Singh. 14 vols. Amritsar: Khalsa Samachar, 1926–1935.
  • Jaggi, Rattan Singh, ed. Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth: Path Sampadan ate Adhyan. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1990.
  • Jaggi, Rattan Singh. Dasam Granth da Kartritav. Patiala: Punjabi University Press, 1966.
  • Grewal, J. S. Guru Gobind Singh (1666–1708): Master of the White Hawk. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2019.
  • Fenech, Louis E. The Sikh Zafar-namah of Guru Gobind Singh: A Discursive Blade in the Heart of the Mughal Empire. New York: Oxford University Press, 2013.
  • Singh, Ganda. Life of Banda Singh Bahadur. Amritsar: Khalsa College, 1935.
  • Dhavan, Purnima. When Sparrows Became Hawks: The Making of the Sikh Warrior Tradition, 1699–1799. New York: Oxford University Press, 2011.
  • McLeod, W. H. The Chaupa Singh Rahit-nama. Dunedin: University of Otago Press, 1987.
  • Singh, Harbans, ed. The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism. 4 vols. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1992–1998.

quiz.q: How is Kavi Santokh Singh's Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth structured?
options: Into chapters called adhyaya and verses called shloka
Into seasons called ਰੁੱਤ and sub-sections called ਅੰਸੂ
Into cantos called sarga following the Ramayana model
Into daily readings called sehaj paath divisions

quiz.q: Whose martyrdom in Delhi in 1675 placed the Guruship on the shoulders of the nine-year-old Gobind Rai?
options: ਗੁਰੂ ਅਰਜਨ ਸਾਹਿਬ
ਗੁਰੂ ਹਰਿਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਾਹਿਬ
ਗੁਰੂ ਤੇਗ ਬਹਾਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ
ਗੁਰੂ ਹਰਿ ਰਾਏ ਸਾਹਿਬ

quiz.q: What is distinctive about the Battle of Nadaun in the Guru's military career?
options: It was the first battle where the Khalsa fought as an initiated order
The Guru fought in alliance with the hill rajas against a Mughal commander
It was fought entirely without bloodshed through negotiation
It marked the Guru's only defeat in open battle

quiz.q: At the founding of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ in 1699, what did Guru Gobind Singh Ji do that was without precedent for a Guru?
options: He abolished the recitation of Gurbani in the darbar
He appointed a successor human Guru before the gathering
He knelt and received initiation from the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ himself
He forbade the Sikhs from ever bearing arms

quiz.q: At Chamkaur Sahib, on whose command did Guru Gobind Singh Ji agree to leave the besieged garhi?
options: On the written order of Emperor Aurangzeb
On the ਗੁਰਮਤਾ of the five Singhs acting as the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ
On the advice of the hill rajas offering safe passage
On the demand of his mother ਮਾਤਾ ਗੁਜਰੀ

quiz.q: What famous ethical principle does the ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ articulate regarding the use of the sword?
options: The sword may be used only to expand the borders of the Panth
The sword should never be drawn under any circumstance
When all other means have been exhausted, it is righteous to take up the sword
Only an emperor may lawfully wield the sword

courses.title: Suraj Prakash: The Life of Guru Nanak Dev Ji
courses.source: Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth, Rut 1 by Kavi Santokh Singh
courses.summary: An intermediate, semester-length study of the life of ਗੁਰੂ ਨਾਨਕ ਦੇਵ ਜੀ as narrated in the first Rut (ਰੁੱਤ) of Kavi Santokh Singh's monumental Braj-Punjabi epic ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਤਾਪ ਸੂਰਜ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ, popularly called ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼. Following the framework of Dr. Rattan Singh Jaggi's critical scholarship, the course reads the Suraj Prakash account of ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ tradition alongside its sources, tracing Guru Nanak's birth at ਰਾਇ ਭੋਇ ਦੀ ਤਲਵੰਡੀ, the childhood ਸਾਖੀਆਂ of the snake's shade and the grazed fields, the Sultanpur years and the ਵੇਈਂ revelation, the four ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ, the great encounters with ਸੱਜਣ ਠੱਗ, ਭਾਈ ਲਾਲੋ, ਮਲਿਕ ਭਾਗੋ and ਵਲੀ ਕੰਧਾਰੀ, and the founding of ਕਰਤਾਰਪੁਰ. Throughout, students learn to read the text critically — as ਹੈਜੀਓਗ੍ਰਾਫੀ (hagiography), as theology, and as a literary monument of nineteenth-century Sikh devotional historiography.
outcomes: Situate ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ within the wider ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ and ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ literary traditions and identify Kavi Santokh Singh's sources and method.
Narrate the major episodes of Guru Nanak's life as told in Rut 1, from ਜਨਮ at Talwandi to ਜੋਤੀ-ਜੋਤਿ at Kartarpur.
Distinguish between the historical kernel, the devotional embellishment, and the theological purpose of each ਸਾਖੀ.
Read selected ਚੌਪਈ and ਦੋਹਰਾ passages and explain their Braj-influenced poetic conventions.
Analyze the Suraj Prakash miracle narratives (the ਨਾਗ shade, the grazing buffaloes, the moved boulder of ਵਲੀ ਕੰਧਾਰੀ) as theological statements rather than mere wonders.
Evaluate scholarly debates about the historicity of the ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ and the chronology of Guru Nanak's travels.
Apply the critical methods of Dr. Rattan Singh Jaggi, W. H. McLeod, and others to a primary-source hagiographical text.

terms.m: The popular name for Kavi Santokh Singh's epic Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth; literally the 'light of the sun,' a vast poetic life of the ten Gurus completed in 1843.
Literally 'season'; the structural divisions of the Suraj Prakash. Rut 1 covers the life of Guru Nanak Dev Ji and the early Gurus' setting.
The genre of traditional birth-and-life narratives of Guru Nanak; the major textual sources (Puratan, Bala, Miharban, Adi) that Santokh Singh drew upon.
A 'testimony' or episode; a single self-contained story illustrating an event or teaching from the Guru's life.
A great preaching journey of Guru Nanak; the tradition counts four such ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ to the four directions plus regional travels.
The rivulet near Sultanpur Lodhi where Guru Nanak underwent the foundational mystical experience and three-day disappearance before declaring the divine message.
The opening creedal statement of Gurbani affirming the One Eternal Reality; in the hagiography it is the first utterance after the Bein experience.
The deceitful innkeeper-robber whose heart was transformed by the Guru's hymn; a key conversion ਸਾਖੀ of the eastern travels.
The poor honest carpenter of Saidpur whose simple ਕਿਰਤ-laboured bread the Guru preferred over the rich Malik Bhago's feast.
The proud Sufi ascetic of Hasan Abdal whose hilltop spring the Guru's grace redirected, the episode tied to Panja Sahib.
The town Guru Nanak founded on the Ravi where he settled the final years, instituting ਖੇਤੀ, ਲੰਗਰ, ਸੰਗਤ and the householder ਗੁਰਮੁਖ ideal.
'Light merging into Light'; the term for the passing of a Guru, used for Guru Nanak's departure at Kartarpur in 1539.
The four-line quatrain meter that forms the narrative backbone of the Suraj Prakash.
The rhymed couplet that punctuates and summarizes sections of the epic between the ਚੌਪਈ narrative.
The 'play/sport of the Guru' genre of devotional Sikh epic poetry to which Santokh Singh's work is the crowning achievement.

references: Jaggi, Rattan Singh. Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth: Sankhep ate Adhyayan. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1989.
Jaggi, Rattan Singh. Gurbani Vich Itihasak Bhavpurat. Patiala: Punjabi University Press, 1995.

lessons.title: The Suraj Prakash and Its Author: Reading a Hagiographical Epic
lessons.summary: Introduces Kavi Santokh Singh, the structure of the Suraj Prakash, and the critical lens for reading hagiography as theology.
lessons.html:
ਵਿਸ਼ਾ ਸੂਚੀ (Table of Contents)

  1. The Suraj Prakash and Its Author: Reading a Hagiographical Epic
  2. The Janam-Sakhi Tradition: Sources Behind the Text
  3. Birth at Talwandi and the Childhood Sakhis
  4. The Snake's Shade and the Grazing Buffaloes: Miracle as Theology
  5. The Sultanpur Years and the Bein River Revelation
  6. The Four Udaasis: Mapping the Journeys
  7. Sajjan Thug and the Conversion Sakhis of the East
  8. Bhai Lalo, Malik Bhago, and the Ethics of Honest Labour
  9. Wali Kandhari and the Mountain of Pride: The North-West Journey
  10. Kartarpur: The Householder Ideal and Joti-Jot
  11. Reading the Suraj Prakash Critically: Hagiography, History, Theology

A Monument of Devotional Historiography

The ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਤਾਪ ਸੂਰਜ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ, known to every ਕਥਾ-vachak as the ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼, is the single largest narrative poem in the Sikh tradition. Composed by ਕਵੀ ਸੰਤੋਖ ਸਿੰਘ and completed in 1843 CE at the court of the Kaithal chieftain Udai Singh, it runs to over fifty thousand verses and recounts the lives of all ten Gurus. Its title is a deliberate metaphor: just as the sun (ਸੂਰਜ) makes all things visible, the poet promises to illuminate (ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼) the glory of the Gurus. The work is structured not into ordinary chapters but into ਰੁੱਤ — 'seasons' — and ਅੰਸੂ, 'sun-rays.' The first ਰੁੱਤ, the subject of this course, is devoted to ਗੁਰੂ ਨਾਨਕ ਦੇਵ ਜੀ.

Dr. Rattan Singh Jaggi, whose critical edition and study of the text remain the scholarly foundation, situates Santokh Singh at the culmination of the ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ tradition — devotional epics that narrate the 'sport' or 'play' of the Guru. Santokh Singh was a disciple in the line of Bhai Mani Singh's pedagogy and a master of Braj-influenced Punjabi poetics. To read his account of Guru Nanak, we must understand that he was not writing what a modern historian would call biography. He was writing ਹੈਜੀਓਗ੍ਰਾਫੀ — sacred life-narrative whose purpose is to evoke devotion and to teach ਗੁਰਮਤਿ, not to assemble verifiable chronology.

Why Read Hagiography Academically?

A student trained only to ask 'did this literally happen?' will misread the Suraj Prakash entirely. The academic study of hagiography asks better questions: What does the community remember, and why? What theological claim does a given ਸਾਖੀ encode? How has an earlier source been reshaped? When Santokh Singh tells us that a cobra spread its hood to shade the sleeping child Nanak, the historically useful question is not whether a snake behaved unusually, but what the image asserts — that creation itself recognizes the divine light in the child, a claim the poet makes again and again in different keys.

The Poetic Form

The narrative moves in ਚੌਪਈ, the four-line quatrain that carries the story forward, punctuated by ਦੋਹਰਾ couplets that summarize or moralize. This is the same prosodic toolkit used in the Braj devotional epics of the Hindi belt, and Santokh Singh's diction is heavily Sanskritized and Braj-coloured — a feature that later Punjabi readers, including Bhai Vir Singh in his great annotated edition, had to gloss for a Gurmukhi-reading audience. A representative ਦੋਹਰਾ frames the whole undertaking with the poet's prayer for the Guru's grace:

ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਤਾਪ ਸੂਰਜ ਉਦੈ ॥ ਤਮ ਅਗ੍ਯਾਨ ਹਰੈ ਸਭ ਹੀ ॥
'May the sun of the Guru's glory rise and dispel all the darkness of ignorance.'

The opening invocation is itself theological: the poet positions Guru Nanak's life as the dawn that ends an age of spiritual night, echoing the well-known traditional verse that the world was on fire until the Guru came. Bhai Gurdas, the earliest Sikh commentator, had already written in his ਵਾਰਾਂ that with Guru Nanak's coming 'ਮਿਟੀ ਧੁੰਧੁ ਜਗਿ ਚਾਨਣੁ ਹੋਆ' — 'the fog lifted and light spread through the world.' Santokh Singh inherits and amplifies this frame.

The Plan of This Course

Over the lessons that follow we will move episode by episode through Rut 1: the birth at ਤਲਵੰਡੀ, the childhood wonders, the Sultanpur employment and the ਵੇਈਂ revelation, the four ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ, and the great encounters with ਸੱਜਣ ਠੱਗ, ਭਾਈ ਲਾਲੋ, and ਵਲੀ ਕੰਧਾਰੀ, ending at ਕਰਤਾਰਪੁਰ. At each stage we will set the Suraj Prakash version beside its ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ sources and ask what Santokh Singh added, dropped, or reshaped — and why. We will also keep one eye on the modern scholarly conversation, especially the debates opened by W. H. McLeod and answered by Indian scholars such as Jaggi, Harbans Singh, and J. S. Grewal. By the end you should be able to read a page of this devotional epic with both reverence and a historian's discernment.

A note on method: this course treats the text as the community has received it while applying the tools of critical scholarship. The two are not in conflict. As Dr. Jaggi insists, understanding how a tradition tells its founder's story is itself an act of respect, because it takes the tradition's own intentions seriously.

lessons.title: The Janam-Sakhi Tradition: Sources Behind the Text
lessons.summary: Surveys the Puratan, Bala, Miharban and Adi Janam-Sakhis that Santokh Singh inherited, and the method of source-criticism.
lessons.html:
What Santokh Singh Inherited

The Suraj Prakash did not invent the life of Guru Nanak; it crowned a tradition already three centuries old. To read Rut 1 critically we must know the ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ corpus that preceded it. These traditional narratives circulated in several recensions, and W. H. McLeod's foundational study, Early Sikh Tradition, sorted them into families that remain the standard scholarly map.

The Major Recensions

  • The ਪੁਰਾਤਨ ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ ('ancient' tradition), preserved in manuscripts such as the Colebrooke and Hafizabad copies, is generally regarded as preserving an early and relatively restrained narrative framework, including the structure of the ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ.
  • The ਭਾਈ ਬਾਲਾ ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ, narrated through the figure of Bhai Bala as the Guru's companion, became the most popular folk version and is rich in incident, though scholars treat its framing claims cautiously.
  • The ਮਿਹਰਬਾਨ ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ, associated with the ਮੀਣਾ line of Sodhi Miharban, is the most theologically and exegetically developed, embedding ਗੋਸ਼ਟਿ (discourse) around Gurbani verses.
  • The ਆਦਿ ਸਾਖੀਆਂ, a further early collection overlapping the Puratan family.

Santokh Singh worked from this living stream rather than from a single book. Dr. Rattan Singh Jaggi's source-critical study shows that the poet selected, harmonized, and amplified — preferring episodes that carried clear ਗੁਰਮਤਿ teaching and smoothing contradictions among his sources into a single flowing epic.

The Method of Source-Criticism

When two sources tell the same ਸਾਖੀ differently, the scholar asks which is earlier, what each emphasizes, and how the later teller has reshaped the material. Consider the ਮੂਲ ਮੰਤਰ utterance after the ਵੇਈਂ experience: the Puratan tradition presents the declaration 'ਨਾ ਕੋ ਹਿੰਦੂ ਨ ਮੁਸਲਮਾਨ' — 'there is no Hindu, no Muslim' — as the Guru's first public statement. Santokh Singh retains the theological force of a universal message but renders it through his own Braj-poetic idiom. Tracking such moves teaches us to see the Suraj Prakash not as a transparent window onto 1500 CE but as a layered text whose every scene has a history.

Hagiography Versus Chronicle

It is essential to distinguish the ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ genre from a chronicle. A chronicle aims at dated, sequential fact; a ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ aims at devotional formation. McLeod argued — controversially in his day — that many episodes were shaped by the needs of the later community rather than preserved as eyewitness report. Indian scholars such as J. S. Grewal and Harbans Singh accepted the method while warning against excessive skepticism, noting that a stable historical core (birth at Talwandi, the Sultanpur employment, extensive travels, the founding of Kartarpur) is well attested even by the earliest layers and by the contemporary witness of Bhai Gurdas.

Bhai Gurdas as a Control

The ਵਾਰਾਂ of Bhai Gurdas, especially the first ਵਾਰ, are the earliest extended Sikh account of Guru Nanak's life and predate the full ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ manuscripts. Because Bhai Gurdas wrote within living memory of the events and as a trusted insider, his sparse narrative — the call to mission, the travels, the confrontation with the ਸਿੱਧ yogis at ਅਚਲ ਵਟਾਲਾ, the journey toward Mecca — functions as a control against which later embellishment can be measured. Santokh Singh knew the ਵਾਰਾਂ well and frequently expands a single line of Bhai Gurdas into a whole episode of ਚੌਪਈ.

ਬਾਬੇ ਭੇਖ ਬਣਾਇਆ ਉਦਾਸੀ ਕੀ ਰੀਤਿ ਚਲਾਈ ॥
'Baba Nanak adopted a garb and set in motion the practice of the udaasi (journeying renunciate).' — Bhai Gurdas, Var 1

Why This Matters for Reading Rut 1

Knowing the sources changes how we read every scene to come. When we reach the ਸੱਜਣ ਠੱਗ episode, we will recognize it as a Puratan-family ਸਾਖੀ that Santokh Singh dramatized. When we reach the ਮਲਿਕ ਭਾਗੋ feast, we will see how a teaching about ਕਿਰਤ (honest labour) was crystallized into narrative form. The point is not to strip the stories of their power but to read them with informed eyes — to see, in Jaggi's phrase, the ਇਤਿਹਾਸਕ ਭਾਵ, the 'historical sense and feeling,' that the tradition encodes even where it does not give us modern facts. In the next lesson we turn to the beginning of the story itself: the birth at Talwandi.

lessons.title: Birth at Talwandi and the Childhood Sakhis
lessons.summary: Covers Guru Nanak's birth at Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, his family, the schooling episodes, and the early signs of his calling.
lessons.html:
ਰਾਇ ਭੋਇ ਦੀ ਤਲਵੰਡੀ

Guru Nanak was born in 1469 CE at ਰਾਇ ਭੋਇ ਦੀ ਤਲਵੰਡੀ, the village later renamed ਨਨਕਾਣਾ ਸਾਹਿਬ in his honour, in the Bar tract west of Lahore. His father, ਮਹਿਤਾ ਕਾਲੂ (Kalyan Das), was the village ਪਟਵਾਰੀ, an accountant in the service of the local Muslim landlord ਰਾਇ ਬੁਲਾਰ; his mother was ਮਾਤਾ ਤ੍ਰਿਪਤਾ. He had an elder sister, ਬੇਬੇ ਨਾਨਕੀ, whose devotion and early recognition of her brother's spiritual greatness the tradition celebrates warmly. Santokh Singh opens his account of the birth with the cosmic framing typical of the ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ genre: the heavens rejoice, and the long-awaited light enters the world.

The Birth Narrative in the Suraj Prakash

The poet describes the night of birth with portents of auspiciousness — a motif inherited from the ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ tradition, which records that the family midwife, ਦੌਲਤਾਂ, sensed something extraordinary about the infant. Where a chronicle would simply note a date, Santokh Singh renders the event as the turning of an age. The traditional dating places the celebrated ਗੁਰਪੁਰਬ in the month of ਕੱਤਕ (the full moon, ਪੂਰਨਮਾਸ਼ੀ), the date observed by the Panth, though scholars including Karam Singh and later Jaggi have noted a parallel ਵੈਸਾਖ tradition; the course flags this as a genuine scholarly question rather than resolving it dogmatically.

The Schooling Sakhis

Among the most beloved childhood ਸਾਖੀਆਂ are those of the boy's education. Sent to the village ਪਾਂਧਾ (Hindu teacher) to learn letters, the child Nanak is said to have confounded his instructor by asking what use the alphabet was if it did not lead to the One. The tradition preserves an acrostic, the ਪਟੀ, in which the young Guru turns each letter of the alphabet into a meditation on the divine — a composition that appears in Gurbani in ਰਾਗੁ ਆਸਾ. Gurbani in the ਪਟੀ teaches that true literacy is the reading of the divine Name written on the heart, not mere worldly accounting. Similarly, when sent to a Muslim ਮੌਲਵੀ to learn Persian and Arabic, the child is said to have spiritualized the very letters of that script.

ਸਸੈ ਸੋਇ ਸ੍ਰਿਸਟਿ ਜਿਨਿ ਸਾਜੀ ਸਭਨਾ ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਏਕੁ ਭਇਆ ॥
'The letter Sassa: He who fashioned the universe is the one Master of all.' — from the Patti, Raag Asa

The Sacred Thread (ਜਨੇਊ)

A pivotal childhood episode is the refusal of the ਜਨੇਊ, the sacred thread of caste-Hindu initiation. At the appointed ceremony the young Nanak declined the cotton thread, asking instead for a thread of compassion, contentment, and truth that would not break, burn, or be soiled. The teaching is preserved in Gurbani in ਰਾਗੁ ਆਸਾ. Santokh Singh dramatizes the scene as a public theological challenge to ritualism, and it functions in the epic as the first open declaration of the Guru's distinctive path — religion of inner virtue over outward mark.

ਦਇਆ ਕਪਾਹ ਸੰਤੋਖੁ ਸੂਤੁ ਜਤੁ ਗੰਢੀ ਸਤੁ ਵਟੁ ॥
'Make compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, continence the knot, and truth the twist.' — Guru Nanak, Var Asa

Reading the Childhood Sakhis

From a critical standpoint, the childhood narratives are the most heavily theologized layer of the tradition, precisely because the community needed to show that the founder's greatness was present from the first. Each episode encodes a ਗੁਰਮਤਿ principle: the schooling stories reject empty literacy; the ਜਨੇਊ episode rejects caste ritual; the wonder-tales (to which we turn next) assert the divine light in the child. Dr. Jaggi cautions the reader to receive these as the tradition's considered theological self-portrait rather than as transcripts. Their truth is the truth of a community declaring who its Guru essentially was.

Rai Bular and Bebe Nanaki

Two human witnesses anchor the childhood narrative and lend it warmth and credibility within the tradition: ਰਾਇ ਬੁਲਾਰ, the Muslim landlord who is shown recognizing the boy's sanctity, and ਬੇਬੇ ਨਾਨਕੀ, the sister whose intuitive faith precedes everyone else's. Their recognition prepares the wonder-narratives of the next lesson, in which not only humans but the natural order itself bears witness to the child. The placement is deliberate: Santokh Singh builds recognition outward from family, to patron, to creation, to the world.

lessons.title: The Snake's Shade and the Grazing Buffaloes: Miracle as Theology
lessons.summary: Close reading of the two signature childhood miracles, analyzing them as theological assertions rather than mere wonders.
lessons.html:
Two Wonders of the Field

Of all the childhood ਸਾਖੀਆਂ, two are so widely told that they have become emblematic of Guru Nanak's youth: the cobra that shaded the sleeping child, and the buffaloes that grazed a neighbour's field which was then miraculously restored. Both are set in the years when the young Nanak was, in his father's frustrated estimation, neglecting practical work for contemplation. Both feature ਰਾਇ ਬੁਲਾਰ as the witness whose testimony validates the wonder. And both, read critically, are not about the suspension of nature but about the recognition of divine presence within it.

The Snake's Shade (ਨਾਗ ਦੀ ਛਾਂ)

In the most familiar version, the boy Nanak, sent out to tend the herds, falls asleep at midday. As the sun moves and the shade of the tree shifts away from him, a cobra (ਨਾਗ) glides up and spreads its hood to keep the child's face shaded. ਰਾਇ ਬੁਲਾਰ, passing on horseback, sees the scene and understands at once that this is no ordinary child. Santokh Singh renders the moment with the heightened diction of the ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ, dwelling on the landlord's awe.

The theological reading is direct. The serpent, a creature of fear and venom, is here an instrument of service; the dangerous becomes protective in the presence of the divine light. The image proclaims that all creation recognizes and serves the One who dwells in the child. It rhymes with a recurring ਗੁਰਮਤਿ theme that the whole of ਕੁਦਰਤ (creation) is the play of the Creator and bows to the Creator's order, the ਹੁਕਮ.

The Grazing Buffaloes (ਖੇਤ ਚਰਨਾ)

In the companion ਸਾਖੀ, the boy is again entrusted with the buffaloes and again becomes absorbed in meditation. The animals wander into a neighbour's standing crop and graze it down. The angry farmer complains to ਰਾਇ ਬੁਲਾਰ, who summons Mehta Kalu and the boy. But when the field is inspected, it is found whole and flourishing — not a blade damaged. The tradition presents this restoration as a sign, and once again the Muslim landlord is the one who grasps its meaning and intercedes for the family.

The traditional refrain attached to these episodes is the recognition that 'this child is favoured of God,' which the Suraj Prakash places in Rai Bular's mouth.

Miracle as Theological Grammar

It is tempting, and lazy, to evaluate such stories only by asking whether they 'really happened.' The fruitful approach, urged by Dr. Rattan Singh Jaggi and by McLeod alike, is to read miracle as a grammar — a conventional language by which a community states a conviction. The conviction here is that the divine light, the ਜੋਤਿ, was fully present in Guru Nanak from childhood. The serpent and the restored field are predicates of that subject. To the devotee they are wonders of grace; to the historian of religion they are the tradition's way of confessing the Guru's sanctity.

There is also a subtle ਗੁਰਮਤਿ tension worth noting. The mature teaching of Guru Nanak, as expressed throughout Gurbani, is markedly cool toward ਰਿਧੀ-ਸਿਧੀ — the display of occult powers — which the Guru repeatedly subordinates to ਨਾਮ. The ਸਿੱਧ-ਗੋਸਟਿ tradition shows the Guru refusing to compete in miracle-working with the yogis. So the childhood wonder-tales must be read carefully: in the hagiography they are signs done to the child by creation, not powers wielded by the child for display. This distinction preserves the consistency of the tradition's theology, in which spectacle is never the point and ਨਾਮ always is.

Rai Bular's Function in the Narrative

That a Muslim landlord is the repeated witness to these Hindu-coded village miracles is itself a theological statement. From the outset the Suraj Prakash, following the ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ, presents Guru Nanak's significance as crossing the Hindu-Muslim divide — anticipating the great post-Bein declaration that there is neither Hindu nor Musalman in the eyes of the One. ਰਾਇ ਬੁਲਾਰ's recognition foreshadows the universalism that will define the Guru's mission. The childhood, in other words, is composed as a prologue whose themes the adult ministry will fulfill.

Summary

The snake's shade and the grazing buffaloes are best taught not as puzzles of natural history but as the opening chords of the epic's theology: creation serves the divine light; the dangerous is disarmed; the boundaries of religion are already being transcended; and the spectacle always points beyond itself to ਨਾਮ. With the childhood signs established, the narrative turns to the Guru's young adulthood at Sultanpur, where contemplation becomes vocation.

lessons.title: The Sultanpur Years and the Bein River Revelation
lessons.summary: Traces the marriage, the move to Sultanpur, the work at the modikhana, and the foundational Bein experience.
lessons.html:
From Talwandi to Sultanpur

As Guru Nanak grew, family concern over his contemplative temperament led to two conventional remedies: marriage and employment. He was married to ਮਾਤਾ ਸੁਲੱਖਣੀ, daughter of Mul Chand of Batala, and in time two sons were born, ਬਾਬਾ ਸ੍ਰੀ ਚੰਦ and ਬਾਬਾ ਲਖਮੀ ਦਾਸ. For employment, his devoted sister ਬੇਬੇ ਨਾਨਕੀ and her husband ਭਾਈ ਜੈ ਰਾਮ arranged a position at ਸੁਲਤਾਨਪੁਰ ਲੋਧੀ, where Jai Ram served the Lodhi governor ਦੌਲਤ ਖਾਂ ਲੋਧੀ. There Guru Nanak was put in charge of the ਮੋਦੀਖਾਨਾ, the state granary or commissariat.

The Modikhana and the 'ਤੇਰਾ' Sakhi

The Sultanpur years are framed by one of the tradition's most quietly profound ਸਾਖੀਆਂ. As Guru Nanak weighed out grain to the people, he is said to have counted aloud — ਇੱਕ, ਦੋ, ਤਿੰਨ — until he reached the number thirteen, ਤੇਰਾਂ. In Punjabi ਤੇਰਾ means both 'thirteen' and 'Yours.' At that word the Guru entered a reverie of 'ਤੇਰਾ, ਤੇਰਾ' — 'I am Yours, all is Yours, O Lord' — losing count of the world while continuing to give generously. Officials suspected embezzlement, but the audit found the stores in surplus, not deficit. The episode is a parable of ਕਿਰਤ done as devotion: honest labour performed in remembrance of the divine, with no theft and an overflowing measure of grace.

The Bein River Experience (ਵੇਈਂ ਦਾ ਪ੍ਰਸੰਗ)

The central event of the Sultanpur period — indeed of the whole life-narrative — is the revelation at the ਵੇਈਂ, the rivulet running by Sultanpur. According to the tradition, the Guru went as usual at dawn to bathe in the ਵੇਈਂ and did not return. His clothes were found at the bank; he was given up for drowned and searched for in vain. For three days he was absent. The tradition understands these days as a mystical immersion in the divine presence, in which the Guru was, as the ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ puts it, taken into the court of the Lord (ਸਚੁ ਖੰਡ / ਦਰਗਾਹ) and commissioned with the cup of ਨਾਮ and the charge to go and have people remember the divine Name.

The tradition records the divine charge to Guru Nanak as: 'Go, rejoice in My Name, and teach others to do so; remain unstained by the world like the lotus on the water.'

The First Utterance: ਮੂਲ ਮੰਤਰ

When the Guru reappeared on the third day, he remained silent for a time, and then spoke the words that the tradition treats as the first proclamation of his mission. Among the earliest things uttered was the great statement of the divine reality — the substance of what we now call the ਮੂਲ ਮੰਤਰ, affirming the One Eternal, ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖ, beyond fear and enmity, timeless, self-existent. Soon followed the famous declaration preserved in the ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ: 'ਨਾ ਕੋ ਹਿੰਦੂ ਨ ਮੁਸਲਮਾਨੁ' — 'There is no Hindu, there is no Musalman' — meaning that before the One, the labels by which people divide and oppress one another have no ultimate standing; what matters is to live truthfully as a human being before the Creator.

ੴ ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ ਨਿਰਭਉ ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ ਅਜੂਨੀ ਸੈਭੰ ॥
'One Reality, whose Name is Truth, the Creative Being, without fear, without enmity, timeless in form, beyond birth, self-existent.' — the Mul Mantar

From Mystic to Missionary

The ਵੇਈਂ experience marks the decisive turn from contemplative householder to itinerant teacher. The Guru distributed his possessions, resigned his post, and prepared to set out on the journeys that would occupy decades. He took as his lifelong companion ਭਾਈ ਮਰਦਾਨਾ, the Muslim rabābi (rebec-player) of Talwandi, whose music would accompany the Guru's hymns across the subcontinent and beyond — a partnership that itself embodies the post-Bein message of the unity beneath religious labels.

Critical Notes

Scholars treat the Sultanpur employment as among the most historically secure elements of the life — it is attested across the source families. The three-day disappearance and the dramatic commissioning belong to the genre of the prophetic call-narrative, found in many traditions, and the historian reads them as the community's account of an authentic interior transformation rendered in the available religious idiom. Dr. Jaggi underlines that the theological content — the charge to spread ਨਾਮ and the dissolution of communal labels — is fully consistent with the message of Guru Nanak's own ਬਾਣੀ, which is the surest witness we possess. With the call received, the Guru turns outward to the world, and we turn to the four ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ.

lessons.title: The Four Udaasis: Mapping the Journeys
lessons.summary: Outlines the traditional scheme of four great journeys, their directions and destinations, and the scholarly debates over chronology.
lessons.html:
The Concept of ਉਦਾਸੀ

The word ਉਦਾਸੀ derives from a root meaning detachment or setting-out; in the Sikh tradition it names the great missionary journeys of Guru Nanak. Bhai Gurdas, our earliest witness, already speaks of the Guru adopting the garb and discipline of the traveller and setting the practice in motion. The ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ tradition organized the travels into a scheme of four directional ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ, and Santokh Singh, following especially the Puratan framework, narrates them as the grand central movement of Rut 1.

The Traditional Fourfold Scheme

  • First ਉਦਾਸੀ — East: Through the Gangetic plain toward Banaras, Gaya, Bengal and, in the tradition, as far as Assam (ਕਾਮਰੂਪ) and Jagannath Puri in the south-east. This journey contains the ਸੱਜਣ ਠੱਗ conversion and the Jagannath ਆਰਤੀ episode, where the Guru reframed temple ritual as the cosmic worship offered by the heavens themselves.
  • Second ਉਦਾਸੀ — South: Down the subcontinent toward the Deccan and, in the tradition, to Ceylon (ਸਿੰਘਲਦੀਪ), where the Guru is said to have instructed King ਸ਼ਿਵਨਾਭ.
  • Third ਉਦਾਸੀ — North: Into the Himalayas, the realm of the ਸਿੱਧ yogis, the setting of the great ਸਿੱਧ-ਗੋਸਟਿ dialogue in which the Guru defends the householder path of ਨਾਮ against ascetic withdrawal.
  • Fourth ਉਦਾਸੀ — West: Toward Mecca, Medina and Baghdad, the journey containing the celebrated Mecca episode and, in the north-western return, the ਵਲੀ ਕੰਧਾਰੀ encounter at Hasan Abdal.

The Mecca and the Feet-Direction Sakhi

The western journey carries one of the most widely retold ਸਾਖੀਆਂ. At Mecca, the Guru is found resting with his feet pointing toward the ਕਾਅਬਾ. A scandalized attendant, ਜੀਵਨ, rebukes him for turning his feet toward the house of God. The Guru asks him to turn his feet wherever God is not — and as the man drags them, the tradition says the sacred direction itself appears to follow. Whether read as literal wonder or as enacted parable, the teaching is unambiguous and thoroughly Nanakian: the divine is not confined to a single direction or shrine but is ਸਰਬ-ਵਿਆਪਕ, present everywhere.

The Companions

Across the ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ the Guru is accompanied chiefly by ਭਾਈ ਮਰਦਾਨਾ, whose rebec set the Guru's ਬਾਣੀ to ਰਾਗ as they travelled. The pairing of the Guru's word with Mardana's music is the seed of the ਕੀਰਤਨ tradition and a living emblem of the message that crossed communal lines. Other companions named in the tradition for particular legs include ਭਾਈ ਬਾਲਾ in the Bala recension.

Scholarly Debate over Chronology and Extent

The fourfold directional scheme is theologically elegant — the Guru claiming all four quarters for the divine Name — but historians treat its neat geometry with caution. W. H. McLeod argued that the precise itineraries, especially the most distant destinations, were elaborated over time and cannot all be verified; he distinguished a probable core of extensive travel within the subcontinent from later expansions reaching Ceylon, Mecca, Baghdad and beyond. Indian scholars including J. S. Grewal and Harbans Singh accepted that the schematization is later while maintaining that the fact of long and wide travel is historically secure and attested by Bhai Gurdas. Dr. Jaggi's contribution is to show how Santokh Singh harmonized divergent source-itineraries into a single ordered narrative for devotional coherence.

ਫਿਰਿ ਬਾਬਾ ਗਇਆ ਬਗਦਾਦਿ ਨੋ ਬਾਹਰਿ ਜਾਇ ਕੀਆ ਅਸਥਾਨਾ ॥
'Then Baba Nanak went to Baghdad and made his seat outside the city.' — Bhai Gurdas, Var 1

How to Read the Travel Narratives

For our purposes, the ਉਦਾਸੀ framework is best taught as a theological cartography: the Guru's mission claims every direction and confronts every form of religiosity — Hindu pilgrimage in the east, ascetic yoga in the north, Islamic ritual in the west, and folk superstition along the way. Each destination becomes the stage for a ਗੁਰਮਤਿ teaching. In the lessons that follow we examine the three encounters the syllabus singles out — ਸੱਜਣ ਠੱਗ, ਭਾਈ ਲਾਲੋ with ਮਲਿਕ ਭਾਗੋ, and ਵਲੀ ਕੰਧਾਰੀ — as concentrated case studies in how the Suraj Prakash turns a journey into a sermon.

lessons.title: Sajjan Thug and the Conversion Sakhis of the East
lessons.summary: Close study of the Sajjan Thug episode and the eastern journey's pattern of inner transformation.
lessons.html:
The Innkeeper Who Was a Robber

On the eastern ਉਦਾਸੀ, the tradition tells, Guru Nanak and ਭਾਈ ਮਰਦਾਨਾ came to the dwelling of one ਸੱਜਣ — a man whose very name means 'friend' or 'good man,' though he was in fact a ਠੱਗ, a deceiver. By day Sajjan kept both a temple and a mosque to appear pious to travellers of either faith, offering hospitality to wayfarers. By night he murdered and robbed his guests, disposing of their bodies in a well. The irony of the name is the heart of the ਸਾਖੀ: here is a 'friend' who is the worst of enemies, a man of outward religion and inward predation.

The Hymn That Broke the Heart

That night, instead of sleeping, the Guru asked Mardana to play, and sang a ਸ਼ਬਦ that pierced Sajjan's conscience. The hymn — preserved in Gurbani in ਰਾਗੁ ਸੂਹੀ — contrasts dazzling outward appearances with inner rot, using the image of a beautiful mansion or a whitewashed structure that is hollow within. Gurbani in this ਸ਼ਬਦ teaches that things gorgeous to the eye can be bitter and worthless within, like a stuccoed wall over crumbling clay.

ਉਜਲੁ ਕੈਹਾ ਚਿਲਕਣਾ ਘੋਟਿਮ ਕਾਲੜੀ ਮਸੁ ॥ ਧੋਤਿਆ ਜੂਠਿ ਨ ਉਤਰੈ ਜੇ ਸਉ ਧੋਵਾ ਤਿਸੁ ॥
'Bright and burnished is the bronze, but rub it and its blackness shows; though I wash it a hundred times, its impurity will not come off.' — Guru Nanak, Raag Suhi

The words held up a mirror to Sajjan's life: a gleaming surface of hospitality and piety concealing murder. Struck to the core, Sajjan fell at the Guru's feet, confessed his crimes, and begged for a way to atone.

The Path of Repentance

What follows is the theological point of the ਸਾਖੀ. The Guru did not merely forgive; he set Sajjan on a path. The tradition relates that the Guru instructed him to make restitution, to abandon the deceit, and to live by honest means and the remembrance of the Name — and that Sajjan's house became, in some tellings, the first ਧਰਮਸਾਲਾ, a place of true worship and service where once there had been a den of murder. The transformation of a place of death into a place of ਨਾਮ is a recurring Suraj Prakash motif and a vivid emblem of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ redemption.

The Pattern of the Eastern Sakhis

Sajjan is the paradigm of a whole class of eastern-journey episodes built on the same pattern: the Guru encounters a person or group trapped in false religiosity or vice, sings or speaks a ਸ਼ਬਦ that exposes the falsehood and offers the truth, and effects an inner conversion. The same structure underlies the Banaras encounter with the pandits, the Jagannath ਆਰਤੀ at Puri — where the Guru replied to the temple's lamp-ceremony with his great hymn that the sun and moon are the lamps and the whole sky the platter of the cosmic worship — and the encounters with various ascetics. In each, outward ritual or hypocrisy is met by inward truth.

ਗਗਨ ਮੈ ਥਾਲੁ ਰਵਿ ਚੰਦੁ ਦੀਪਕ ਬਨੇ ਤਾਰਿਕਾ ਮੰਡਲ ਜਨਕ ਮੋਤੀ ॥
'In the bowl of the sky the sun and moon are the lamps, and the constellations of stars are the scattered pearls.' — Guru Nanak, Arti, Raag Dhanasari

Hagiographical and Theological Reading

As history, the ਸੱਜਣ ਠੱਗ ਸਾਖੀ is impossible to verify in its particulars, and the punning name suggests deliberate literary shaping. As theology it is exact and characteristic of Guru Nanak: true religion is not the maintenance of temple and mosque for show but the cleansing of the inner self; and no one, not even a murderer, is beyond the reach of grace and the possibility of ਪਛੁਤਾਵਾ (repentance) leading to a transformed life. Dr. Jaggi notes that Santokh Singh tells the episode with particular relish for the dramatic reversal, expanding the terse ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ account into a fully staged scene of confession and redemption. The story endures because its claim is permanent: the worst can be remade by the Word.

lessons.title: Bhai Lalo, Malik Bhago, and the Ethics of Honest Labour
lessons.summary: Examines the Saidpur episode and its teaching on kirat, sharing, and the corruption of wealth wrongly earned.
lessons.html:
Saidpur and the Two Hosts

Among the most ethically charged of all the ਸਾਖੀਆਂ is the episode at ਸੈਦਪੁਰ (later Eminabad). There Guru Nanak chose to lodge with ਭਾਈ ਲਾਲੋ, a poor ਤਰਖਾਣ (carpenter) of low caste who lived by honest manual ਕਿਰਤ. The town's wealthy steward, ਮਲਿਕ ਭਾਗੋ, a man grown rich by exploitation and bribery, was holding a great ਬ੍ਰਹਮ-ਭੋਜ, a lavish feast for holy men, and was affronted that the visiting holy man preferred the hut of a low-caste labourer to his own table. He summoned the Guru and demanded an explanation.

The Two Breads

The Suraj Prakash, following the ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ, dramatizes the Guru's reply through a memorable sign. The Guru took a piece of Bhai Lalo's coarse bread in one hand and a portion of Malik Bhago's rich food in the other and pressed them. From Lalo's honest bread, the tradition says, flowed milk; from Bhago's, blood. The meaning needed no commentary: Lalo's food was the fruit of ਹੱਕ ਦੀ ਕਮਾਈ — honest earning — and so was pure and nourishing; Bhago's was soaked in the blood of those he had exploited, and so was unfit, however fine its appearance.

The tradition encapsulates the teaching: the bread of honest labour yields the milk of purity, while the bread of exploitation oozes the blood of the oppressed.

The Ethic of ਕਿਰਤ ਅਤੇ ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ

This ਸਾਖੀ is the narrative foundation of one of Sikhi's central ethical pillars: ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ — to earn by honest labour — joined to ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ — to share what one earns. The Guru's preference for Lalo overturns the entire hierarchy of caste and wealth: dignity belongs to the honest worker, not to the corrupt rich; the labour of the hands done truthfully is holier than ritual feasting funded by theft. Gurbani gives the principle its terse formulation, teaching that one who earns by toil and shares with others recognizes the true path.

ਘਾਲਿ ਖਾਇ ਕਿਛੁ ਹਥਹੁ ਦੇਇ ॥ ਨਾਨਕ ਰਾਹੁ ਪਛਾਣਹਿ ਸੇਇ ॥
'One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has — O Nanak, such a one knows the way.' — Guru Nanak, Raag Sarang

Solidarity with the Oppressed

The choice of Bhai Lalo is also a statement of where the Guru stands in the social order. By lodging with the low-caste poor and exposing the high-caste rich, Guru Nanak enacts the ਗੁਰਮਤਿ rejection of ਜਾਤ-ਪਾਤ (caste hierarchy) and of wealth divorced from justice. The episode anticipates the Guru's searing political ਬਾਣੀ at Saidpur during Babur's invasion — the ਬਾਬਰਵਾਣੀ hymns — in which he cries out at the suffering inflicted on the innocent. That the same town hosts both the Lalo episode and the ਬਾਬਰਵਾਣੀ ties the ethic of honest labour to the prophetic protest against tyranny: a religion that honours the worker must also denounce the violence done to the powerless.

Critical and Comparative Notes

Historically, the figures of Lalo and Bhago cannot be independently documented, and the milk-and-blood sign belongs to the symbolic register of the ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ. But few episodes are more deeply consonant with the verifiable teaching of Guru Nanak's own ਬਾਣੀ, which repeatedly condemns ill-gotten wealth and exalts honest toil and sharing. Dr. Jaggi reads the ਸਾਖੀ as the tradition's most economical statement of Sikh social ethics — a single image that contains a whole theology of work, wealth, caste, and justice. Where ਸੱਜਣ ਠੱਗ teaches inner repentance, ਭਾਈ ਲਾਲੋ teaches social righteousness; together they show that the Guru's mission addressed both the heart and the social order. We turn next to a ਸਾਖੀ about a different vice — spiritual pride.

lessons.title: Wali Kandhari and the Mountain of Pride: The North-West Journey
lessons.summary: Studies the Hasan Abdal episode (Panja Sahib), reading it as a teaching against spiritual arrogance.
lessons.html:
The Proud Ascetic of the Hill

On the north-western leg of the travels, the tradition brings Guru Nanak and ਭਾਈ ਮਰਦਾਨਾ to ਹਸਨ ਅਬਦਾਲ, near present-day Rawalpindi. On the hill above the settlement lived a celebrated Muslim ascetic, ਵਲੀ ਕੰਧਾਰੀ, who controlled the only spring of fresh water. When the Guru and Mardana, weary and thirsty, arrived below, Mardana climbed to ask the ਵਲੀ for water. But the holy man, resenting the crowds gathering around this newcomer and full of ਹੰਕਾਰ (egotistical pride), refused — once, twice, three times — taunting that if Nanak were truly a man of God he could provide his own water.

The Spring at the Guru's Feet

The Suraj Prakash, following the ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ, then narrates the great sign. At the Guru's word, a fresh spring of clear water burst forth where he sat below — and at that moment the ਵਲੀ's own spring on the hilltop ran dry. Enraged, the proud ascetic is said to have hurled a great boulder down the slope to crush the Guru. The Guru raised his hand and stopped the rock, leaving the imprint of his palm — the ਪੰਜਾ — pressed into the stone. The site is venerated as ਪੰਜਾ ਸਾਹਿਬ. Humbled and broken in his pride, ਵਲੀ ਕੰਧਾਰੀ descended and fell at the Guru's feet.

The episode's traditional moral: the water of grace flows down to the humble valley, while the spring of the proud who hoards it runs dry.

The Teaching Against ਹੰਕਾਰ

The theological target of this ਸਾਖੀ is ਹੰਕਾਰ — pride or egotism — one of the five thieves (ਪੰਜ ਚੋਰ) that Gurbani identifies as the great spiritual enemies. ਵਲੀ ਕੰਧਾਰੀ is not an impious man; he is a genuine ascetic and a man of evident spiritual attainment. That is precisely the point. The story warns that ਹੰਕਾਰ can corrupt even the advanced devotee, turning his gifts into a means of domination — controlling the water, despising the stranger, hoarding what should be freely given. Gurbani in many places teaches that pride is a disease that the Name alone can cure, and that the divine grace flows to the humble. The redirected spring is the perfect emblem: grace deserts the proud and gathers around the humble.

Miracle, Symbol, and the Palm-Print

As with the childhood wonders, the critical reader distinguishes the symbolic claim from the literal narration. The bursting spring and the stopped boulder belong to the wonder-language of the tradition. Yet here, too, there is a consistency with ਗੁਰਮਤਿ that bears noting: the Guru's 'miracle' is defensive and provisioning — water for the thirsty, protection from a hurled stone — never a competitive display of power for its own sake. Indeed the deeper teaching subordinates the wonder to the lesson: the real marvel is the breaking of the ascetic's pride, not the physics of the rock. McLeod and other critical scholars treat the Hasan Abdal episode as a later and especially elaborated ਸਾਖੀ, while devotees venerate ਪੰਜਾ ਸਾਹਿਬ as one of the most sacred ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰੇ of the north-west.

A Triptych of Vices

Read together, the three syllabus encounters form a deliberate triptych of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ ethics. ਸੱਜਣ ਠੱਗ confronts deceit and the false outward show of religion, answered by repentance. ਮਲਿਕ ਭਾਗੋ confronts exploitation and corrupt wealth, answered by the dignity of honest ਕਿਰਤ. ਵਲੀ ਕੰਧਾਰੀ confronts spiritual pride, answered by humility before grace. In each, a different vice from the catalogue of the ਪੰਜ ਚੋਰ is exposed and healed. Santokh Singh arranges the travel narratives so that the journeys become a moving classroom in which the whole moral teaching of the Guru is dramatized across the landscape of the subcontinent.

Toward the Final Years

By the end of the great journeys the Guru had, in the tradition's telling, claimed all four directions for the divine Name and confronted every form of false religion and human vice. But the climax of his life is not the spectacle of travel; it is the quiet revolution of the householder community he founded on his return. To that — to ਕਰਤਾਰਪੁਰ — we now turn.

lessons.title: Kartarpur: The Householder Ideal and Joti-Jot
lessons.summary: Covers the founding of Kartarpur, the institutions of langar, sangat and kirat, the choice of Guru Angad, and the passing.
lessons.html:
The Return and the Founding of ਕਰਤਾਰਪੁਰ

After the years of ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ, Guru Nanak laid aside the traveller's garb and founded a town on the right bank of the ਰਾਵੀ which he named ਕਰਤਾਰਪੁਰ — 'the abode of the Creator.' Here he settled for the last two decades or so of his life, roughly from the 1520s until 1539. The founding of Kartarpur is, in many ways, the true climax of the life-narrative, for it is here that Guru Nanak translated his teaching into a living community and a way of life. Bhai Gurdas describes the Guru in these years tilling his fields, gathering the ਸੰਗਤ, and radiating the divine light.

The Three Pillars in Practice

At Kartarpur the Guru embodied the discipline that would define Sikhi:

  • ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ — honest labour. The Guru himself worked the land as a farmer, modelling the dignity of productive work over both idle asceticism and parasitic privilege.
  • ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ — sharing one's earnings, expressed institutionally in the ਲੰਗਰ, the free communal kitchen where all sat together as ਪੰਗਤ regardless of caste, creed, or status, breaking the deepest taboos of the social order.
  • ਨਾਮ ਜਪਣਾ — remembrance of the divine Name, expressed in the daily congregational worship of the ਸੰਗਤ, with the singing of ਆਸਾ ਦੀ ਵਾਰ at dawn and ਸੋਦਰੁ in the evening.

This is the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ ideal in its mature form: not the renunciate fleeing the world, but the householder living truthfully within the world — earning, sharing, and remembering. It is the practical answer to the ascetics of the ਸਿੱਧ-ਗੋਸਟਿ, who had urged withdrawal; Kartarpur is Guru Nanak's reply written in bricks and grain and song.

ਘਰਿ ਘਰਿ ਅੰਦਰਿ ਧਰਮਸਾਲ ਹੋਵੈ ਕੀਰਤਨੁ ਸਦਾ ਵਿਸੋਆ ॥
'In every home a place of worship arose, where kirtan was sung as a daily festival.' — Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, describing the Kartarpur community

The Testing of the Sikhs and the Choice of a Successor

The most consequential act of the Kartarpur years was the appointment of a successor. The tradition relates that the Guru tested his Sikhs — including his own sons, ਬਾਬਾ ਸ੍ਰੀ ਚੰਦ and ਬਾਬਾ ਲਖਮੀ ਦਾਸ — and found in his devoted disciple ਭਾਈ ਲਹਿਣਾ the perfect embodiment of obedience, humility, and ਸੇਵਾ. Setting aside hereditary claim, the Guru installed Lehna as ਗੁਰੂ ਅੰਗਦ, placing the same divine light in a new body — 'ਜੋਤਿ ਓਹਾ ਜੁਗਤਿ ਸਾਇ,' the same Light, the same Way, as later Gurbani affirms. The principle that succession follows spiritual worth and not blood is one of Guru Nanak's most radical institutional legacies, and the bypassing of his own sons makes the point unmistakable.

ਜੋਤਿ ਓਹਾ ਜੁਗਤਿ ਸਾਇ ਸਹਿ ਕਾਇਆ ਫੇਰਿ ਪਲਟੀਐ ॥
'The same Light, the same Way; the Master merely changed the body.' — Satta and Balwand, Ramkali ki Var

ਜੋਤੀ-ਜੋਤਿ ਸਮਾਉਣਾ

In 1539 CE, at Kartarpur, Guru Nanak merged his light into the divine Light — ਜੋਤੀ-ਜੋਤਿ ਸਮਾਉਣਾ. The tradition preserves a tender and pointed ਸਾਖੀ of the passing: as the Guru prepared to depart, his Hindu and Muslim followers disputed whether his body should be cremated or buried. The Guru asked each group to place flowers beside him — the Hindus on one side, the Muslims on the other — saying that whoever's flowers remained fresh in the morning might dispose of the body accordingly. In the morning, the tradition says, both sets of flowers were fresh, and beneath the sheet the body had vanished. The dispute dissolved into the very teaching of his life: the labels of Hindu and Musalman, which he had transcended at the ਵੇਈਂ, had no claim over him even in death.

The Shape of a Life

Read as a whole, the Suraj Prakash account of Guru Nanak's life forms a single coherent arc: a childhood in which creation recognizes the divine light; a young adulthood in which contemplation ripens into a prophetic call at the ਵੇਈਂ; decades of ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ in which every direction and every vice is confronted with ਨਾਮ; and a final settlement at ਕਰਤਾਰਪੁਰ where the teaching becomes a community and the light is passed on undimmed. The childhood wonders and the travel miracles all point to the same centre — the One whose Name the Guru came to give. In the final lesson we step back to read this whole hagiographical structure with critical eyes.

lessons.title: Reading the Suraj Prakash Critically: Hagiography, History, Theology
lessons.summary: Synthesizes the course's methods, weighing the McLeod debate, the value of hagiography, and the text's enduring authority.
lessons.html:
Three Ways to Read One Text

Having walked through Rut 1 episode by episode, we close by stepping back to ask how the Suraj Prakash should be read as a whole. Three distinct but compatible readings have run through this course: the text as ਹੈਜੀਓਗ੍ਰਾਫੀ (hagiography), the text as a witness to ਇਤਿਹਾਸ (history), and the text as ਧਰਮ-ਸ਼ਾਸਤਰ (theology). A mature student holds all three at once.

The Text as Hagiography

The Suraj Prakash is, first and most honestly, a hagiography — a sacred life-narrative whose purpose is devotion. Its conventions are those of the ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ genre: cosmic framing, recognition-scenes, wonders that confess sanctity, and a steady moral commentary. To fault it for not behaving like a modern biography is a category error. Its 'facts' are theological facts. When creation shades the sleeping child or honest bread yields milk, the genre is doing exactly what it exists to do — proclaiming who the Guru is and what he teaches. Read this way, even the most miraculous ਸਾਖੀ is intelligible and serious.

The Text as History: The McLeod Debate

The most important modern scholarly conversation about this material was opened by W. H. McLeod, whose Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion (1968) and Early Sikh Tradition (1980) applied rigorous source-criticism to the ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ corpus that underlies the Suraj Prakash. McLeod distinguished a probable historical core — birth at Talwandi, the Sultanpur employment, extensive travels, the founding of Kartarpur, the composition of the ਬਾਣੀ — from later legendary accretions, and he questioned the verifiability of the more distant itineraries and the more spectacular wonders. His work was received as bracing by some and as overly skeptical by others.

Indian scholars responded with both engagement and correction. J. S. Grewal, in Guru Nanak in History, accepted the critical method while arguing that the historical kernel is firmer and richer than McLeod allowed, and that the Guru's own ਬਾਣੀ — an unimpeachable contemporary source — anchors the portrait. Harbans Singh's Guru Nanak and Origins of the Sikh Faith offered a reading that took the tradition's theological self-understanding seriously. And Dr. Rattan Singh Jaggi's source-critical and literary studies of the Suraj Prakash itself showed precisely how Santokh Singh selected and reshaped his materials — neither dismissing the text nor reading it naively, but mapping its composition with philological care. The result of this conversation is a balanced consensus: a secure historical core, surrounded by a devotional tradition whose growth can be traced, all to be read with both rigour and respect.

The Text as Theology

Finally, and most enduringly, the Suraj Prakash is theology in narrative form. Every episode we studied encodes ਗੁਰਮਤਿ: the ਜਨੇਊ refusal teaches inner virtue over ritual; the ਤੇਰਾ episode teaches ਕਿਰਤ as devotion; the ਵੇਈਂ teaches the prophetic call and the dissolution of communal labels; ਸੱਜਣ ਠੱਗ teaches repentance; ਭਾਈ ਲਾਲੋ teaches honest labour and justice; ਵਲੀ ਕੰਧਾਰੀ teaches humility against pride; ਕਰਤਾਰਪੁਰ teaches the householder ideal of ਨਾਮ, ਕਿਰਤ, and ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ. The decisive control on all of this is the Guru's own ਬਾਣੀ in the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ: wherever a ਸਾਖੀ aligns with the verifiable teaching of the hymns — as nearly all the core episodes do — the tradition is faithfully transmitting the substance of the Guru's message even when it cannot certify the surface of the event.

The Place of the Suraj Prakash in Sikh Life

For nearly two centuries the Suraj Prakash has been the great quarry of Sikh ਕਥਾ. From it the ਕਥਾ-vachak draws the narratives that, recited in the ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ, have shaped the popular Sikh imagination of Guru Nanak more powerfully than any academic monograph. Bhai Vir Singh's monumental annotated edition (1926–1935) made the Braj-laden text accessible to modern Punjabi readers and secured its place as a living classic. To study it critically, as we have done, is not to diminish it but to read it as the rich, layered, theologically purposeful monument it is.

Conclusion: How to Hold the Text

The lesson of this course is a disposition: read the Suraj Prakash with two eyes open. With one eye, see the historian's distinctions — source, layer, accretion, control. With the other, see the devotee's confession — the light in the child, the call at the river, the householder's table where all castes eat as one. The two visions do not cancel; they complete each other. Santokh Singh wrote to make the sun of the Guru's glory rise and dispel the darkness of ignorance. The critical study of his epic, far from extinguishing that sun, lets us see by its light more clearly.

ਹਵਾਲੇ (Works Cited)

  • Grewal, J. S. Guru Nanak in History. Chandigarh: Panjab University, 1969.
  • Jaggi, Rattan Singh. Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth: Sankhep ate Adhyayan. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1989.
  • Jaggi, Rattan Singh. Gurbani Vich Itihasak Bhavpurat. Patiala: Punjabi University Press, 1995.
  • Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.
  • McLeod, W. H. Early Sikh Tradition: A Study of the Janam-Sakhis. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1980.
  • McLeod, W. H. Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1968.
  • Shackle, Christopher, and Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair. Teachings of the Sikh Gurus: Selections from the Sikh Scriptures. London: Routledge, 2005.
  • Singh, Harbans. Guru Nanak and Origins of the Sikh Faith. Bombay: Asia Publishing House, 1969.
  • Singh, Santokh (Kavi). Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth. Edited by Bhai Vir Singh. 14 vols. Amritsar: Khalsa Samachar, 1926–1935.

quiz.q: What does the title 'ਸੂਰਜ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼' signify about Kavi Santokh Singh's purpose in the work?
options: It is a treatise on solar astronomy in the Braj language
It promises to illuminate the glory of the Gurus the way the sun makes all things visible
It is named after a village where the poet was born
It refers to the four directions of the udaasi journeys

quiz.q: According to the critical scholarship surveyed in the course, how should the childhood miracle of the snake's shade best be read?
options: As a literal zoological event requiring scientific explanation
As a fabrication with no place in serious study
As a theological assertion that creation recognizes the divine light in the child
As evidence that Guru Nanak performed occult powers for display

quiz.q: What is the significance of the word ਤੇਰਾ in the Sultanpur modikhana sakhi?
options: It means 'thirteen' and also 'Yours,' triggering the Guru's reverie of surrender to the divine
It was the name of the Lodhi governor at Sultanpur
It refers to the thirteen companions on the first udaasi
It is the rivulet where the Bein revelation occurred

quiz.q: In the ਭਾਈ ਲਾਲੋ and ਮਲਿਕ ਭਾਗੋ episode, what does the sign of milk and blood from the two breads teach?
options: That carpenters make better food than stewards
That honest labour (ਕਿਰਤ) is pure while wealth from exploitation is tainted with the blood of the oppressed
That holy men should never accept any hospitality
That low-caste people are spiritually superior by birth

quiz.q: Which vice does the ਵਲੀ ਕੰਧਾਰੀ episode at Hasan Abdal principally confront?
options: Greed for material wealth
Lust
Spiritual pride (ਹੰਕਾਰ), which can corrupt even an advanced ascetic
Deceit in business dealings

quiz.q: What was the balanced scholarly consensus described in the course regarding W. H. McLeod's source-critical work?
options: That the entire life of Guru Nanak is unhistorical legend
That McLeod's method was wholly rejected by all Indian scholars
That a secure historical core exists, surrounded by a traceable devotional tradition, to be read with both rigour and respect
That the Suraj Prakash is a verbatim eyewitness chronicle

courses.title: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas: The Formation of the Sikh Panth
courses.summary: An intermediate, semester-length study of the first six Vaars of Bhai Gurdas Ji — the writings Guru Arjan Dev Ji called the ਕੁੰਜੀ (key) to Sri Guru Granth Sahib. Reading these Vaars as both devotional poetry and the earliest Sikh historiography, the course traces how the ਪੰਥ was formed: the cosmic mission behind Guru Nanak Sahib's coming, the gift of ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ under Guru Angad Dev Ji, ਸੰਗਤ and ਪੰਗਤ under Guru Amar Das Ji, the founding of Amritsar under Guru Ram Das Ji, the compilation of the Adi Granth under Guru Arjan Dev Ji, and the doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ ਪੀਰੀ under Guru Hargobind Sahib.
outcomes: Situate Bhai Gurdas Ji within the early Sikh tradition and explain why his Vaars are called the key to Sri Guru Granth Sahib.
Reconstruct the cosmic and historical narrative of Vaar 1 — the condition of the world before Guru Nanak Sahib, his mission, and the ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ.
Trace the institutional development of the Panth across the Guruship from Guru Angad Dev Ji to Guru Hargobind Sahib as narrated in Vaars 2-6.
Explain the doctrinal vocabulary of these Vaars, including ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ, ਮਨਮੁਖਿ, ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ, and ਮੀਰੀ ਪੀਰੀ.
Read selected pauris in Gurmukhi with attention to imagery, metre, and theological argument.
Evaluate the Vaars as a source for Sikh historiography alongside the work of modern scholars.
Apply the ethical vision of the Vaars — humility, seva, and the discipline of the Gurmukh — to the lived practice of Sikhi.

terms.m: Vaar: a heroic ode or ballad in Punjabi prosody, originally sung to inspire warriors; Bhai Gurdas Ji turned the form into spiritual instruction, composing forty Vaars.
Pauri: literally a 'step' or rung of a ladder; the stanza-unit of a Vaar. Each Vaar is built from numbered pauris that ascend an argument.
Kunji: a 'key'. By tradition Guru Arjan Dev Ji called the Vaars the kunji that unlocks the meaning of Sri Guru Granth Sahib.
Panth: literally a 'path'; the collective body and way of the Sikhs as a community walking the Guru's road.
Gurmukh: one who is oriented toward the Guru, living face-to-face with the divine command; the central ideal type of the Vaars.
Manmukh: one who follows the self-willed mind; the contrast figure against whom the Gurmukh is defined.
Udasi: the long preaching journeys of Guru Nanak Sahib (the udasian), during which he carried the message across the known world.
Sadh-sangat: the holy congregation; for Bhai Gurdas Ji the seedbed of liberation and the social form of the Panth.
Pangat: the row of equals seated together to eat from a common langar; with sangat it expresses the egalitarian institution built under Guru Amar Das Ji.
Gurmukhi: the script standardised by Guru Angad Dev Ji for writing the language of Gurbani and educating the Sikhs.
Amritsar: the 'pool of nectar' excavated by Guru Ram Das Ji, around which the central Sikh city grew.
Miri-Piri: the twin authority of temporal sovereignty (miri) and spiritual sovereignty (piri) embodied by Guru Hargobind Sahib's two swords.
Nirankar: the Formless One; the name for Akal Purakh that opens Vaar 1's account of creation.
Charan-kamal: the 'lotus feet' of the Guru, a recurring image of refuge and humble devotion in the Vaars.

references: Bhai Gurdas. Varan Bhai Gurdas Steek. Edited and annotated by Bhai Vir Singh. Amritsar: Khalsa Samachar, 1962.
Jodh Singh, Bhai. Varan Bhai Gurdas: Text, Transliteration and Translation. 2 vols. Patiala: Vision & Venture, 1998.
Singh, Sahib. Varan Bhai Gurdas Steek. Amritsar: Singh Brothers, 1962.
Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Rev. ed. The New Cambridge History of India II.3. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.
McLeod, W. H. Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1968.
Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.
Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Birth of the Khalsa: A Feminist Re-Memory of Sikh Identity. Albany: State University of New York Press, 2005.
Singh, Pashaura. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.
Macauliffe, Max Arthur. The Sikh Religion: Its Gurus, Sacred Writings and Authors. 6 vols. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1909.

lessons.title: Introduction: Bhai Gurdas Ji and the Key to the Granth
lessons.html:
ਵਿਸ਼ਾ ਸੂਚੀ (Table of Contents)

  1. Introduction: Bhai Gurdas Ji and the Key to the Granth
  2. The Form of the Vaar: Poetry, Prosody, and the Pauri
  3. Vaar 1, Part One: Creation, the Fallen World, and the Cry for a Guru
  4. Vaar 1, Part Two: The Mission of Guru Nanak Sahib and the ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ
  5. Vaar 1, Part Three: The Succession and the Birth of the Panth
  6. Vaar 2: Guru Angad Dev Ji and the Gift of ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ
  7. Vaar 3: Guru Amar Das Ji, ਸੰਗਤ and ਪੰਗਤ
  8. Vaar 4: Guru Ram Das Ji and the Founding of ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤਸਰ
  9. Vaar 5: Guru Arjan Dev Ji and the Compilation of the Adi Granth
  10. Vaar 6: Guru Hargobind Sahib and ਮੀਰੀ ਪੀਰੀ
  11. Conclusion: The Vaars as Theology and as History

Who was Bhai Gurdas Ji?

Bhai Gurdas Ji (c. 1551–1636) stands at the very centre of early Sikh letters. A close relative of the house of the Gurus, he served four Gurus — from Guru Ram Das Ji to Guru Hargobind Sahib — as a missionary, scribe, theologian, and steward of the young community. When Guru Arjan Dev Ji set down the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ (Adi Granth) in 1604, it was the hand of Bhai Gurdas Ji that wrote the volume at the Guru's dictation. No figure of the period is closer to the textual and institutional birth of Sikhi.

Yet Bhai Gurdas Ji is remembered above all as a poet. His two great bodies of work are the ਕਬਿੱਤ ਸਵਈਏ (Kabitt Savaiye), composed in Braj, and the forty ਵਾਰਾਂ (Vaars) composed in Punjabi. This course studies the first six of those Vaars. Although his writing is not part of Sri Guru Granth Sahib, it occupies a singular place of honour: by long tradition, Guru Arjan Dev Ji called the Vaars the ਕੁੰਜੀ — the key — to the Granth, and they are the only non-scriptural compositions formally permitted to be sung as ਕੀਰਤਨ within the ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ.

Why the Vaars are called the key

The honorific "key" is precise. The language of Sri Guru Granth Sahib is dense, multilingual, and metaphorically charged. Bhai Gurdas Ji, writing as a contemporary who had heard the Gurus teach and who knew the living idiom of the Sikhs, restates the central doctrines of Gurmat in patient, expository Punjabi. Where Gurbani compresses, the Vaars unfold. Where Gurbani sings, the Vaars explain. A student who learns the vocabulary of the Vaars — ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ and ਮਨਮੁਖਿ, ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ, ਹੁਕਮੁ, ਨਾਮੁ — comes to the Granth already fluent in its conceptual world.

There is a second sense in which the Vaars are a key. They preserve the earliest connected narrative of Sikh sacred history. The opening Vaar tells how and why Guru Nanak Sahib came; later Vaars carry the story forward through the succession of the Gurus. Because Bhai Gurdas Ji wrote within living memory of these events, modern historians treat the Vaars as a primary source — with care, for the Vaars are devotional literature, not chronicle, and their purpose is to evoke faith rather than to date events.

The shape of this course

We read Vaars 1 through 6 as a continuous account of the ਪੰਥ taking form. Vaar 1 is the longest and most theologically ambitious: it moves from the creation of the cosmos by ਨਿਰੰਕਾਰ (the Formless), through the moral collapse of the age, to the appearance of Guru Nanak Sahib as the answer to a suffering world's cry. Vaars 2 through 6 follow the institution-building of the next five Gurus — the script and schooling of Guru Angad Dev Ji, the congregational order of Guru Amar Das Ji, the sacred city of Guru Ram Das Ji, the canon of Guru Arjan Dev Ji, and the sovereignty of Guru Hargobind Sahib.

Throughout, we hold two readings together. The theological reading asks what the Vaars teach about God, the Guru, and the liberated life. The historical reading asks what they tell us about how a real community in sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Punjab came into being. Bhai Gurdas Ji himself does not separate these; for him the rise of the Panth is the working out of a divine purpose in time.

A note on Professor Bhai Jodh Singh

This course is taught under the name of Bhai Jodh Singh (1882–1981), the eminent Sikh scholar, first principal of Khalsa College and later first Vice-Chancellor of Punjabi University, Patiala. Bhai Jodh Singh produced a careful edition, transliteration, and translation of the Vaars and wrote extensively on their doctrine; his work remains a standard reference for the academic study of Bhai Gurdas Ji. Where this course paraphrases the sense of a pauri, it follows the interpretive tradition that his scholarship helped to stabilise.

How to study the Vaars

Read slowly. A Vaar is built to be sung and absorbed line by line, not skimmed. In each lesson you will meet selected pauris in Gurmukhi with an English rendering. Do not treat the translation as a substitute for the original — let it return you to the Gurmukhi. Keep the glossary of terms beside you, and notice how the same handful of words — ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ, ਚਰਨ ਕਮਲ, ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ — recur and accumulate meaning across the six Vaars. By the end you should be able to hear in a single pauri the whole argument of the work.

lessons.title: The Form of the Vaar: Poetry, Prosody, and the Pauri
lessons.html:
From battlefield ballad to spiritual instruction

To read Bhai Gurdas Ji well we must first understand the form he chose. The ਵਾਰ is one of the oldest genres of Punjabi verse. In its original setting a Vaar was a heroic ballad — a ਢਾਡੀ (bard) would sing of battles, of the courage of warriors and the disgrace of cowards, often to the beat of the ਢੱਡ drum, rousing listeners to valour. The Vaar was the poetry of the war camp.

The Gurus and Bhai Gurdas Ji took this charged martial form and turned it inward and upward. The battle becomes the struggle of the soul against the five thieves; the hero becomes the ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ; the coward becomes the ਮਨਮੁਖਿ; the king to be served is ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. This transformation is itself a theological statement: the energies of worldly heroism are not denied but redirected toward the conquest of the self. Long before the Khalsa was instituted, the very form of the Vaar anticipated the Sikh ideal in which spiritual discipline and heroic courage are one.

The architecture of a Vaar

Each of Bhai Gurdas Ji's forty Vaars is a self-contained poem on a theme, and each is built of numbered stanzas called ਪਉੜੀਆਂ (pauris). The word ਪਉੜੀ means a "step" or a rung of a ladder, and the image is exact: the pauris of a Vaar mount an argument step by step, so that the reader climbs from a first statement to a culminating insight. Vaar 1, the longest, has forty-nine pauris; the Vaars we study in this course range across many stanzas each.

Within a pauri, Bhai Gurdas Ji typically opens with a series of images or examples drawn from nature, craft, or common life — the lotus in muddy water, the swan that separates milk from water, the philosopher's stone that turns iron to gold — and then turns, in the closing line, to apply the figure to the spiritual life. This movement from ਦ੍ਰਿਸ਼ਟਾਂਤ (illustration) to ਸਿੱਧਾਂਤ (doctrine) is the signature rhythm of his style. Learning to anticipate the turn is the first skill of reading the Vaars.

The texture of the language

Bhai Gurdas Ji writes a supple, idiomatic Punjabi, far more accessible than the high, compressed registers of much of Gurbani. This accessibility is deliberate and is part of why the Vaars function as a ਕੁੰਜੀ. He explains, repeats, and accumulates; he is content to make a point three ways so that it lodges.
