Guru Nanak Dev Ji and his successors had already adapted the form within Gurbani, repurposing its martial energy to celebrate the victory of the soul over ਹਉਮੈ and the triumph of ਨਾਮ. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ ਜੀ inherited this transformed Vaar and made it the vehicle for an extended, systematic exposition of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ across forty separate poems.

Forty Vaaran, Many Pauris

The corpus consists of forty ਵਾਰਾਂ. Each Vaar is built of ਪਉੜੀਆਂ — stanzas — and the number of pauris varies from Vaar to Vaar, with the whole running to several hundred stanzas. The word ਪਉੜੀ means a step or the rung of a ladder, and the image is deliberate: each stanza is a step by which the seeker climbs toward the Divine. A Vaar is thus not a flat sequence but an ascent, the pauris accumulating toward a spiritual summit.

The Internal Shape of a ਪਉੜੀ

A typical pauri of Bhai Gurdas Ji follows a recognisable rhythm. It opens with an image or premise drawn from the natural or social world — a tree, a river, a craftsman, a merchant, the relation of servant to master. It develops the image across several lines, often piling up parallel instances. Then it executes a turn, applying the image to the spiritual life and frequently closing with a refrain-like phrase such as ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ ਸੁਖ ਫਲੁ ("the Gurmukh's fruit of bliss") or a benedictory line. Learning to anticipate this shape lets the reader follow the argument of even an unfamiliar pauri.

Thematic Arrangement

The forty Vaaran are not random. The very first Vaar is foundational: it surveys creation, the futility of the world's many paths, the advent of Guru Nanak Dev Ji as the one who dispelled the darkness, and the lineage of the Gurus. Later Vaaran take up specific themes — the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ and ਮਨਮੁਖ, the glory of the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ, the disease of ਹਉਮੈ, the marks of the true disciple, the relationship of disciple and Guru, and ethical conduct. There is a broadly catechetical logic to the whole: the corpus equips the ਗੁਰਸਿੱਖ with a complete conceptual and moral education.

The First ਵਾਰ as Foundational History

The opening Vaar deserves special note because of its sweeping account of religious history and its celebrated stanzas on the coming of Guru Nanak Dev Ji. In lines treasured by the tradition, Bhai Gurdas Ji depicts the world groaning in darkness until the Guru arose — ਸਤਿਗੁਰ ਨਾਨਕ ਪ੍ਰਗਟਿਆ — "the True Guru Nanak became manifest, and the mist lifted and light spread in the world." Here biography, theology, and poetry fuse, and we glimpse why the Vaaran are read as a primary witness to how the early Panth understood the mission of Guru Nanak Dev Ji.

Language of the Vaaran

The forty Vaaran are composed in a literary Punjabi accessible to the ordinary disciple, rich in the proverbs and imagery of Punjab's rural and mercantile life. This is a deliberate choice. Gurbani draws on many registers and languages; the Vaaran, as a key, speak the people's own tongue. Their vocabulary of fields, looms, wells, merchants, and seasons grounds the highest theology in the textures of everyday experience — the same strategy by which Gurbani itself often teaches.

For the Student

As you begin to read individual Vaaran, identify three things in each pauri: the opening image, the development, and the turn. Track how the same handful of theological concepts recur across many Vaaran, each time illuminated from a fresh angle. The architecture rewards both close reading of a single step and a panoramic view of the whole ascent.

lessons.title: The ਕਬਿੱਤ-ਸਵਈਏ and the Two Languages
lessons.summary: The 556 Braj poems distinct from the Vaaran, and the bilingual genius of Bhai Gurdas Ji.
lessons.html:
Beyond the Forty Vaaran

The forty Punjabi ਵਾਰਾਂ are not the whole of ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ ਜੀ's poetic output. He also composed 556 ਕਬਿੱਤ-ਸਵਈਏ — poems in the Braj Bhasha literary idiom, using the ਕਬਿੱਤ and ਸਵਈਆ metres favoured in the devotional poetry of north India. These form a distinct corpus, separate in language, metre, and tone from the Vaaran, and are studied as a body in their own right.

Why Braj?

Braj Bhasha was the prestige literary language of devotional (ਭਗਤੀ) poetry across northern India in the period. By composing in Braj, Bhai Gurdas Ji placed ਗੁਰਮਤਿ in conversation with the wider devotional culture of his age and reached audiences beyond Punjab. The choice reflects his scholarly range and the universalising impulse of Sikhi, which from Guru Nanak Dev Ji onward addressed all of humanity rather than a single region or tongue. The ਕਬਿੱਤ-ਸਵਈਏ thus extend the reach of the same theology the Vaaran teach, now clothed in the elevated diction of Braj.

Differences of Texture

The two corpora differ in texture. The Punjabi Vaaran are expansive, narrative, proverbial, and catechetical, building arguments image by image. The Braj ਕਬਿੱਤ-ਸਵਈਏ tend toward concentrated devotional intensity, lyrical celebration of the Guru, the ਸ਼ਬਦ, and the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ, and ecstatic meditation on the experience of love for the Divine. Where the Vaaran often teach, the ਕਬਿੱਤ often sing. A student who reads both gains a fuller portrait of the poet: the patient teacher of the Vaaran and the rapt devotee of the ਕਬਿੱਤ.

The Bilingual Achievement

That one author commanded both a vernacular Punjabi suited to the village ਸੰਗਤ and a sophisticated Braj suited to the pan-Indian literary world is a remarkable achievement. It mirrors the linguistic generosity of the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ itself, which Bhai Gurdas Ji had written by hand and which gathers ਬਾਣੀ in many languages and registers. His bilingual output is an extension into his own voice of the multilingual inclusiveness he had transcribed in scripture.

A Shared Theology

Despite their differences of language and tone, both corpora teach the same ਗੁਰਮਤਿ. The supremacy of the ਸ਼ਬਦ, the necessity of the Guru, the centrality of ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ, the saving power of the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ, the contrast of ਗੁਰਮੁਖ and ਮਨਮੁਖ, and the dissolution of ਹਉਮੈ run through both. The ਕਬਿੱਤ-ਸਵਈਏ are, in this sense, the Vaaran's lyrical companion — the same wine in a different cup.

Place in the Tradition

In practice, the forty Vaaran have enjoyed wider currency in the Panth than the Braj poems, partly because their Punjabi is more immediately accessible to the ਸੰਗਤ and partly because of the celebrated saying naming the Vaaran the key. The ਕਬਿੱਤ-ਸਵਈਏ, while less often quoted in ordinary discourse, are prized by students of Gurmat poetry for their devotional depth and their evidence of Bhai Gurdas Ji's literary mastery. Both are sung in ਕੀਰਤਨ within the tradition, always with the understanding that they are the inspired words of a great ਗੁਰਸਿੱਖ and not Gurbani.

For the Student

For most of this course we focus on the forty Vaaran, since these are the texts named the key to Gurbani. But the serious student should be aware of the ਕਬਿੱਤ-ਸਵਈਏ as a parallel achievement, and should sample them to appreciate the full bilingual genius of the man who wrote the first Sikh scripture and then sang its meaning in two tongues.

lessons.title: The Theology of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ
lessons.summary: The central ideal of the Guru-oriented being, and its opposite the manmukh.
lessons.html:
The Organising Polarity

If one had to name the single concept that organises the Vaaran, it would be the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ. The word combines ਗੁਰ (Guru) and ਮੁਖ (face): the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ is the one whose face is turned toward the Guru, who orients the whole of life around the Guru's word. Its opposite is the ਮਨਮੁਖ — the one whose face is turned toward the ਮਨ, the self-willed mind, governed by appetite and ego. Across the forty Vaaran, Bhai Gurdas Ji returns again and again to this polarity, defining the spiritual life as the journey from ਮਨਮੁਖ to ਗੁਰਮੁਖ.

The Marks of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ

Bhai Gurdas Ji does not define the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ abstractly; he paints a portrait through accumulated traits. The ਗੁਰਮੁਖ rises in the ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ (the ambrosial hours before dawn), bathes, and meditates on ਨਾਮ; joins the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ; speaks sweetly and lives humbly; earns an honest living and shares it; sees the Divine in all and harms none; bears slander without resentment and returns good for evil. The ਗੁਰਮੁਖ is, in short, ਗੁਰਮਤਿ made flesh — the abstract teaching realised in a living person.

The Path, Not Just the Goal

Crucially, ਗੁਰਮੁਖ names both a goal and a path — ਗੁਰਮੁਖ ਪੰਥ, the Guru-oriented way. To become a ਗੁਰਮੁਖ is not a sudden acquisition but a discipline practised over a lifetime under the Guru's guidance. Bhai Gurdas Ji often compares it to slow, patient processes: the ripening of fruit, the polishing of metal, the disciple's gradual transformation in the company of the holy. This emphasis on process makes the Vaaran practical rather than merely inspirational; they are a manual of formation.

The ਮਨਮੁਖ as Mirror

The ਮਨਮੁਖ is not introduced to condemn but to instruct. By drawing the self-willed person — restless, proud, enslaved to the five thieves (ਕਾਮ, ਕ੍ਰੋਧ, ਲੋਭ, ਮੋਹ, ਅਹੰਕਾਰ), forever seeking outside what can only be found within — Bhai Gurdas Ji holds up a mirror in which the reader recognises their own unredeemed condition. The contrast sharpens the appeal of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ ideal. Often a single pauri sets the two side by side, so that the choice before every soul stands starkly revealed.

A Representative Teaching

Gurbani in the Vaaran teaches that the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ finds the fruit of bliss — the recurring phrase ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ ਸੁਖ ਫਲੁ — by surrendering the ego and living in remembrance. Bhai Gurdas Ji writes, in lines the tradition cherishes, of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ who, like the lotus, grows in the water of the world yet remains untouched by it, and who, like the swan, discerns the real from the false. These natural images make the ideal concrete: the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ is in the world but not of it.

Theological Roots in Gurbani

The ਗੁਰਮੁਖ–ਮਨਮੁਖ polarity is not Bhai Gurdas Ji's invention; it is pervasive in Gurbani itself, from the ਜਪੁ ਜੀ onward. His contribution is to expand and dramatise it — to take a polarity that Gurbani states with luminous concision and render it as an extended gallery of portraits the ordinary disciple can study and emulate. This is the work of the key: making the doctrine of Gurbani walkable.

For the Student

As you read, collect the traits Bhai Gurdas Ji assigns to the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ across different Vaaran; you will find they compose a complete ethic and spirituality. Notice, too, that the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ is never solitary — the ideal is realised in community, in the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ, which is the subject of our next lesson.

lessons.title: ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ and the Cure of ਹਉਮੈ
lessons.summary: The holy congregation as the crucible of transformation and the dissolution of ego.
lessons.html:
The Disease and Its Diagnosis

At the heart of Bhai Gurdas Ji's theology, as of Gurbani, lies the diagnosis of the human condition: the soul is separated from the Divine by ਹਉਮੈ — egoity, the deep conviction of being a separate, self-sufficient "I." From ਹਉਮੈ flow the five thieves and all suffering. Gurbani famously states that ਹਉਮੈ is a chronic disease — and that within the disease lies its own remedy. Bhai Gurdas Ji takes up this diagnosis and devotes much of his poetry to its cure.

The Remedy: ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ

The remedy he sets above all others is the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ, the company of the holy. The self cannot heal itself, for the surgeon and the disease are the same ਹਉਮੈ; what is needed is an environment in which ਨਾਮ is sung, the ਸ਼ਬਦ is heard, and the ego is steadily worn away through humble service and association. The ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ is, for Bhai Gurdas Ji, the crucible in which base metal is transmuted into gold, the school in which the ਮਨਮੁਖ becomes ਗੁਰਮੁਖ.

Images of the Congregation

Bhai Gurdas Ji's praise of the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ is among the most beautiful poetry in the corpus. He likens the company of the holy to a fragrance that perfumes whatever it touches, to a touchstone that turns iron to gold, to the sandalwood whose nearness makes neighbouring trees fragrant. In a celebrated image he describes how the worthless ਰੀਠਾ and the ਮਜੀਠ and the iron are all transformed by association — the lesson being that no soul is so fallen that the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ cannot raise it. The teaching is radically hopeful.

Why Community, Not Solitude

It is significant that Sikhi locates liberation not in isolated asceticism but in community. The Nath yogis of Bhai Gurdas Ji's milieu sought salvation in the cave and the forest; Gurmat sends the seeker into the ਸੰਗਤ. The ਗੁਰਮੁਖ does not flee the world but joins the holy congregation within it, earning an honest living, raising a family, and sharing with others, all while keeping ਨਾਮ in the heart. The ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ is the social form of the spiritual life, and its centrality marks Sikhi off from the renunciant traditions around it.

The Mechanism of the Cure

How does the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ cure ਹਉਮੈ? Through ਸੇਵਾ (selfless service) the ego's grip on the self loosens; through ਕੀਰਤਨ and ਸਿਮਰਨ the mind is filled with the Divine rather than the self; through the humbling experience of placing others first, the "I" shrinks until, in the language of Gurbani, it is annihilated and only the Divine remains. Bhai Gurdas Ji presents this not as theory but as observed reality — the transformation he had witnessed in countless disciples at Goindwal, Amritsar, and Agra.

A Representative Teaching

Gurbani in the Vaaran teaches that in the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ the unutterable ਨਾਮ is realised, ਹਉਮੈ departs, and the soul merges in the Divine as water merges in water. The ਸੰਗਤ is therefore not optional ornament but the very means of grace. To join it sincerely is already to be on the road from ਮਨਮੁਖ to ਗੁਰਮੁਖ.

For the Student

The pairing of disease (ਹਉਮੈ) and cure (ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ) gives the Vaaran their therapeutic structure. As you read, watch how nearly every spiritual problem Bhai Gurdas Ji raises is finally resolved in the company of the holy and the remembrance of ਨਾਮ. This is the practical heart of his teaching, and the reason the Vaaran have remained a living guide for the ਸੰਗਤ for four centuries.

lessons.title: Parable, Metaphor, and Reading a ਪਉੜੀ Closely
lessons.summary: A close-reading workshop on Bhai Gurdas Ji's poetic method.
lessons.html:
The Method of the Image

ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ ਜੀ teaches almost entirely through images. Rather than argue abstractly, he reaches for the lotus, the swan, the deer, the rain-bird (ਚਾਤ੍ਰਿਕ), the philosopher's stone, the merchant, the river, and the changing seasons. His genius is to draw a precise spiritual lesson from each, so that the natural and social world becomes a vast book of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ. This lesson is a workshop in reading his method.

The Lotus and the Swan

Two of his most frequent images deserve attention. The ਕਮਲ (lotus) grows rooted in muddy water yet floats above it, unstained — the figure of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ who lives amid the world's attachments yet remains detached, devoted to the Divine. The ਹੰਸ (swan), in Indian poetic convention, can separate milk from water and feeds only on pearls — the figure of the discerning soul who, guided by the Guru, distinguishes the real from the illusory and consumes only what is true. When you meet these images, you can predict the teaching: detachment in the world, discernment of the true.

The Deer and the Musk

A poignant image is the ਮ੍ਰਿਗ (deer) that carries musk in its own navel yet runs through the forest searching for the source of the scent. This is the human soul, which contains the Divine within yet searches for fulfilment in the outer world of objects and rituals. The lesson — that what we seek is already within, accessible through the Guru and ਨਾਮ — is delivered not as a proposition but as an unforgettable picture of misdirected longing. This is why parable is so powerful a key: it lodges the teaching in memory.

The ਚਾਤ੍ਰਿਕ and Single-minded Devotion

The ਚਾਤ੍ਰਿਕ, the rain-bird of Indian poetry, is said to drink only the ਸ੍ਵਾਂਤੀ raindrop and to cry for it even amid rivers and lakes. Bhai Gurdas Ji uses it for the devotee whose longing fixes on the Divine alone and refuses all substitutes. The image teaches single-mindedness (ਇਕ-ਮਨ) in devotion — a quality central to ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ. Again the doctrine is conveyed entirely through the creature's behaviour.

A Close Reading in Practice

Let us model the close reading the course asks of you. Take a pauri built on the touchstone. The opening lines present the ਪਾਰਸ (philosopher's stone) that turns iron to gold. The middle develops the marvel — even base, rusted iron is transmuted at a touch. The turn applies it: such is the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ, or such is the Guru, whose touch transforms the fallen soul. The pauri closes, often, on the fruit of bliss for the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ. Notice the three movements — image, development, turn — and notice how the spiritual claim gains force from the concreteness of the metaphor. Iron really does seem to become gold; so really, says the poet, does the soul change in holy company.

Why This Matters for Interpreting Gurbani

This method is exactly why the Vaaran serve as the key. Gurbani uses many of the same images — the lotus, the swan, the deer, the rain-bird — but often in a single compressed line. Bhai Gurdas Ji unfolds the image at length, teaching the reader the conventional meaning and spiritual application. Having studied his expanded treatment, the reader returns to Gurbani and now understands the compressed allusion. The Vaaran train the eye to read Gurbani's imagery.

For the Student

Practise this week by selecting any pauri, identifying its central image, and writing out the three movements and the doctrine taught. Then find, if you can, the same image in Gurbani and observe how concisely it is used there. You will discover in your own reading why Guru Arjan Dev Ji called these poems a key.

lessons.title: The Vaaran as Witness to History
lessons.summary: How the Vaaran record the early Panth, the Gurus, and the events of their age.
lessons.html:
Poetry as Historical Source

Beyond their theology, the Vaaran are a precious historical source for the early Sikh tradition, valued by historians such as J. S. Grewal for the window they open onto how the community understood itself in the early seventeenth century. Because ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ ਜੀ lived through the events and served at the centre of the community, his poetry preserves the self-understanding of the Panth at a formative moment — not as a later reconstruction but as contemporary testimony.

The Lineage of the Gurus

The first Vaar contains the tradition's celebrated account of the advent of Guru Nanak Dev Ji and the succession of the Gurus. Bhai Gurdas Ji narrates how the Guru travelled to the corners of the earth on his ਉਦਾਸੀਆਂ (journeys), confronting the religious establishments of his day and calling all to the worship of the One. He depicts the world before Guru Nanak Dev Ji as sunk in darkness and falsehood, and the Guru's coming as the rising of the sun that scatters the night. This is theology in the form of history: the mission of Guru Nanak Dev Ji is framed as a cosmic intervention.

The ਸੰਗਤ Across the Land

The Vaaran also testify to the geographic spread of the early ਸੰਗਤ. Bhai Gurdas Ji, who himself served as a ਪਰਚਾਰਕ in Agra, describes a community established across northern India, bound together by devotion to the Guru and the practice of ਨਾਮ. This evidence of an organised, far-flung network of Sikhs in his lifetime is important for historians reconstructing the institutional growth of the tradition under Guru Arjan Dev Ji.

The Transition to ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ

As discussed earlier, Bhai Gurdas Ji witnessed the martyrdom of Guru Arjan Dev Ji and the assumption of temporal authority by Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji. The Vaaran are read as engaging the questions this transformation raised among the ਸੰਗਤ — the puzzlement of disciples who saw their Guru now bearing arms, keeping horses, and holding court. The tradition treasures a passage understood to reassure such doubters that the Guru's outward change served an inner and eternal purpose, and that the same divine light shone in the warrior-Guru as in his peaceful predecessors. This makes the Vaaran a witness to the very moment Sikhi articulated its doctrine of dual sovereignty.

The Polemical Edge

Bhai Gurdas Ji also engages the rival paths of his age — the Vaishnav devotionalism, the Nath yogis, the ritualism of brahmanical religion, and the practices he regarded as empty. He does so not from ignorance but from learning; his refutations show intimate knowledge of the traditions he critiques. For the historian, this polemic maps the religious landscape within which early Sikhi defined itself, and shows the Panth asserting a distinct identity over against the surrounding options.

Limits of the Historical Reading

A caution: the Vaaran are theology first and chronicle second. Bhai Gurdas Ji writes to teach ਗੁਰਮਤਿ, not to compile annals, and his historical references are selective and interpretive, framed always by his devotional purpose. The careful historian, as Grewal and Pashaura Singh both note, reads the Vaaran for the community's self-understanding rather than as a neutral record of dates and deeds. Used with this discipline, they are an irreplaceable source.

For the Student

When you read the historical passages of the Vaaran, ask two questions: what does this tell us about the events, and what does it tell us about how the early Panth understood those events? The second question is often where the richest insight lies, for in the Vaaran we hear the first Sikh community speaking, through its greatest poet, about who it believed itself to be.

lessons.title: Authority, Reception, and Reading the Vaaran Today
lessons.summary: The place of the Vaaran in the Panth, their reception history, and their use now.
lessons.html:
A Unique Status

The Vaaran occupy a status unlike any other text in the Sikh tradition. They are not Gurbani and are never accorded the reverence reserved for the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ. Yet, alone among the writings of the ਗੁਰਸਿੱਖ, they are sanctioned to be sung in ਕੀਰਤਨ within the ਦਰਬਾਰ alongside Gurbani, and they are quoted with special authority in ਕਥਾ and exegesis. This intermediate status — below scripture, above all other commentary — flows directly from the saying that named them the ਕੁੰਜੀ, the key.

Reception in the Tradition

From Guru Arjan Dev Ji's time onward, the Vaaran were studied by those who taught and interpreted Gurbani. Taran Singh places Bhai Gurdas Ji at the fountainhead of the indigenous exegetical schools (ਵਿਆਖਿਆ ਪ੍ਰਣਾਲੀਆਂ). The great commentators of later centuries drew on his expansions; the ਨਿਰਮਲੇ and ਉਦਾਸੀ scholars who developed the ਟੀਕਾ tradition assumed familiarity with his teaching. In the modern era, Bhai Vir Singh produced an influential annotated edition, and Professor Sahib Singh, the celebrated grammarian of Gurbani, wrote a ਸਟੀਕ (commentary) on the Vaaran, embedding them in the academic study of the tradition.

Modern Scholarly Editions

The student today is well served. Bhai Jodh Singh's two-volume Varan Bhai Gurdas, with text, transliteration, and translation, makes the corpus accessible to readers without classical training. The editions of Bhai Vir Singh and Sahib Singh provide annotation and commentary in Punjabi. Western scholarship — Gurinder Singh Mann on the making of scripture, Pashaura Singh on canon and authority, J. S. Grewal on the history — situates the Vaaran within critical study. A serious course can therefore move between the primary text and a rich secondary literature.

Distinguishing the Key from the Treasure

The most important interpretive discipline, repeated throughout this course, is to honour the Vaaran without confusing them with Gurbani. When a question of doctrine arises, Gurbani rules; the Vaaran illuminate but do not legislate. This is not a demotion of Bhai Gurdas Ji but the very humility he himself insisted upon. He never claimed his words were Guru's word; he claimed only to serve at the Guru's door. To read him rightly is to receive his help in understanding Gurbani while keeping our final gaze fixed on the ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ.

Why the Vaaran Still Matter

Four centuries on, the Vaaran remain a living guide. Their portraits of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ still describe an attainable ideal; their praise of the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ still calls the disciple into community; their diagnosis of ਹਉਮੈ still names the modern malady with uncomfortable precision. Their plain Punjabi and vivid images make them more immediately graspable than the densest Gurbani, which is exactly why they continue to serve beginners as a doorway and to reward the learned with fresh depths.

A Program of Continued Study

This intermediate course is an introduction; a full mastery would involve reading all forty Vaaran in the original, studying the ਕਬਿੱਤ-ਸਵਈਏ, comparing the imagery of the Vaaran with its sources in Gurbani, and engaging the commentarial tradition from Sahib Singh onward. The student who completes this course should be equipped to undertake that program, opening any Vaar with confidence, identifying its image and argument, and using it — as Guru Arjan Dev Ji intended — as a key to the inexhaustible treasure of the ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ.

For the Student

End this course by returning to where we began: the metaphor of the key. You have now seen the man who cut the key, the lock it fits, the metal it is made of, and the door it opens. Carry that image into your own reading of Gurbani, and let the Vaaran of ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ ਜੀ accompany you as the faithful servant they were always meant to be.

ਹਵਾਲੇ (Works Cited)

  • Bhai Gurdas. Vaaran Bhai Gurdas Ji. Annotated edition by Bhai Vir Singh. Amritsar: Khalsa Samachar.
  • Jodh Singh, Bhai. Varan Bhai Gurdas: Text, Transliteration and Translation. 2 vols. Patiala: Vision & Venture, 1998.
  • Singh, Sahib. Vaaran Bhai Gurdas Steek. Amritsar: Singh Brothers.
  • Ashok, Shamsher Singh. Bhai Gurdas: Jivan te Rachna. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1977.
  • Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.
  • Singh, Pashaura. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.
  • Singh, Taran. Gurbani dian Viakhia Pranalian. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1980.
  • Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1990.
  • McLeod, W. H. The Chaupa Singh Rahit-nama. Dunedin: University of Otago Press, 1987.

options: Because they were included as part of the Adi Granth canon

Ghazals in Persian
