When ਹਉਮੈ no longer demands to be first, one is free to let others be first.

The Social and the Spiritual Are One

The deepest teaching of Vaars 13-14 is the inseparability of the spiritual and the social. Bhai Gurdas refuses any division between an inner piety and an outer ethics. The same transformation that turns the face toward the Guru turns the hands toward service and the heart toward compassion. To grow in remembrance is to grow in kindness; to deepen in humility is to deepen in justice. There is one movement, not two. Gurbani in Salok Mahalla 9 teaches that the one in whose heart compassion and the Name dwell together is rare and blessed; Bhai Gurdas builds his entire social vision on this unity. As we approach the final Vaar of our study, we find Bhai Gurdas gathering all these social virtues into their single root — ਨਿਮਰਤਾ, the humility that is the crown of the whole inner life.

lessons.title: Vaar 15: ਨਿਮਰਤਾ — Humility as the Crown of the Inner Life
lessons.summary: Studies Bhai Gurdas's culminating teaching that humility is both the root and the crown of spiritual attainment, gathering all the disciplines into one.
lessons.html:
The Virtue Beneath All Virtues

If a single thread runs through the nine Vaars we have studied, it is ਨਿਮਰਤਾ — humility. Vaar 15 gathers this thread and makes it explicit, presenting humility as both the soil in which every other virtue grows and the crown that completes the spiritual life. ਨਿਮਰਤਾ is the precise opposite of ਹਉਮੈ; where egoity is the root disease, humility is the root cure. To understand Bhai Gurdas's vision of the inner life is finally to understand his vision of humility.

The Paradox of Greatness

Bhai Gurdas teaches a paradox the Gurus made central to Gurmat: that the way up is down. The one who would be exalted must become small; the one who would be first must take the last place. This is not strategic self-deprecation but a profound reordering of the self. Greatness, in Bhai Gurdas's reckoning, belongs to ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ alone; the human being who grasps at greatness usurps what is not his and falls into ਹਉਮੈ. The humble person, claiming nothing, becomes the vessel through which the Divine greatness can flow. Emptiness is the condition of being filled.

The Figures of Humility

Bhai Gurdas's similes for humility are among his most beautiful:

  • Water — it flows ever to the lowest place, and so it gathers, nourishes, and sustains all life. The humble person seeks the low place and so becomes a source of life to others.
  • The fruit-laden tree — it bends low under the weight of its fruit; the more it bears, the lower it bows. The truly accomplished person grows more humble, not more proud, with attainment.
  • The dust of the feet — Bhai Gurdas's most frequent image; the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ counts himself the dust beneath everyone's feet, the lowest of the low, and in that lowliness finds peace.

ਹੋਇ ਨਿਮਾਣਾ ਭਗਤਿ ਕਰਿ ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ ਧਿਆਏ ॥

"Becoming utterly humble, the Guru-oriented performs devotion and meditates."

The phrase ਹੋਇ ਨਿਮਾਣਾ — "becoming humble," literally "becoming without honour/status" — names the precondition of true devotion. One cannot truly worship while still clinging to one's own honour. The ਗੁਰਮੁਖ first lays down all claim to status, and only then does devotion become real. Humility is not a stage one passes through but the permanent ground on which the whole life of the spirit stands.

ਪੈਰੀ ਪੈਣਾ — Humility Embodied

Bhai Gurdas gives humility a characteristic Sikh embodiment in ਪੈਰੀ ਪੈਣਾ — the practice of falling at the feet, of bowing, of greeting others as one's superiors. This is not empty etiquette but a discipline of the body that trains the heart. By repeatedly enacting lowliness, the seeker wears down the reflexes of pride. The body teaches the soul. In the ਸੰਗਤ, where all bow to all and all serve all, humility becomes a shared atmosphere, each person's lowering supporting the others'.

The Completion of the Disciplines

We can now see how Vaar 15 completes the arc of the nine Vaars. ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ (Vaar 7) softens ਹਉਮੈ; the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ (Vaar 8) is defined by surrender of the self; ਸੇਵਾ (Vaar 9) is humility made physical; ਸੰਗਤ (Vaar 10) is the community of mutual lowliness; the inner ਤੀਰਥ (Vaar 11) is reached by bowing at the feet of the holy; ਧਰਮ (Vaar 12) wills the good of others rather than the self; the social ethics (Vaars 13-14) lower the self and raise the other. Every discipline, traced to its root, is a discipline of humility. ਨਿਮਰਤਾ is thus not the last virtue in a list but the single virtue that all the others express.

Humility and Grace

Finally, humility is the meeting-point of effort and grace, the theme with which our study began. The humble heart makes no claim upon the Divine; it does not earn or demand, but receives. And precisely because it claims nothing, grace (ਗੁਰਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ) flows to it freely. The proud heart, full of itself, has no room for grace; the humble heart, emptied of ਹਉਮੈ, is all room. This is the final wisdom of Bhai Gurdas's inner life: that the whole labour of the disciplines is to make us small enough to receive what was always being given. In the concluding lesson we will gather these threads into a single architecture and reflect on what Bhai Gurdas offers the seeker today.

lessons.title: Synthesis: The Architecture of Spiritual Discipline in the Vaaran
lessons.summary: Draws together Vaars 7-15 into a coherent practical theology and reflects on Bhai Gurdas's enduring contribution to Sikh spiritual life.
lessons.html:
One Integrated Path

Having read Vaars 7 through 15 in turn, we are now positioned to see them whole. Bhai Gurdas did not compose a random anthology of pious counsels; he built an integrated architecture of the inner life, in which each discipline supports and completes the others. In this final lesson we draw the threads together and reflect on what this seventeenth-century theology offers the seeker of any age.

The Logic of the Nine Vaars

Recall the movement we have traced. Vaar 7 lays the foundation in ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ, the remembrance that softens the ego and orients the whole self. Vaar 8 defines the goal and its opposite — the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ turned toward the Guru, the ਮਨਮੁਖ turned toward the self. Vaars 9 and 10 give the two outward disciplines, ਸੇਵਾ and ਸੰਗਤ, through which the turning is accomplished. Vaar 11 interiorises ਤੀਰਥ, locating purification within rather than at distant shrines. Vaar 12 defines ਧਰਮ as righteous householder living grounded in remembrance. Vaars 13-15 carry the disciplines into society as ਦਇਆ, just dealing, and supremely ਨਿਮਰਤਾ. The structure is not linear but concentric: every Vaar circles the same centre, which is the dissolution of ਹਉਮੈ and the reception of ਗੁਰਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ.

The Diagnosis and the Cure

At the root of Bhai Gurdas's entire system lies a single diagnosis: the human predicament is ਹਉਮੈ, the self mistaking itself for the centre. Every discipline he teaches is, at bottom, a medicine for this one disease. Remembrance turns the self toward another centre; service deflates the self's pretensions; congregation reshapes the self in good company; the inner pilgrimage washes the self's defilement; righteous living turns the self's energies toward others' good; humility lays the self down entirely. The unity of the Vaaran is the unity of a single cure applied through many means. This is why Bhai Gurdas can move so fluidly between themes — they are all facets of one work.

Effort and Grace, Held Together

Throughout, Bhai Gurdas maintains the delicate balance with which our course began: the disciplines are real, necessary, and demanding, yet they do not earn liberation. They prepare the heart; the gift is given. Gurbani in Japji Sahib teaches that all happens within the ਹੁਕਮ, the Divine Order, and that grace cannot be commanded. Bhai Gurdas honours this fully. The seeker labours not to compel the Divine but to become receptive to it — to grow small enough, humble enough, empty enough that grace may flow. The whole architecture of discipline serves this single end: receptivity.

Bhai Gurdas as Theologian

We may now appreciate why Guru Arjan Sahib called the Vaaran the ਕੁੰਜੀ to Sri Guru Granth Sahib. Bhai Gurdas takes the soaring, mystical utterance of Gurbani and renders it teachable — orders it into doctrine, illustrates it with images drawn from common life, and shows the disciple the actual path of practice. He is the first systematic theologian of Sikhi, and Vaars 7-15 are his most sustained treatment of the practical question every faith must answer: how does a person actually grow? His answer is comprehensive, psychologically acute, socially radical, and devotionally warm. He never reduces the inner life to technique, nor inflates it into vague mysticism; he keeps it grounded, livable, and within reach of the ordinary householder.

The Enduring Gift

What does Bhai Gurdas offer the seeker today? First, an integrated path — not a scattered set of practices but a coherent way in which remembrance, service, community, ethics, and humility reinforce one another. Second, a profound psychological realism — his diagnosis of ਹਉਮੈ and its symptoms remains startlingly accurate to the human condition. Third, a radical egalitarianism — by relocating holiness from shrines and castes to the heart and the ਸੰਗਤ, he makes the highest attainment available to everyone equally. Fourth, the dignity of ordinary life — his insistence that the householder, not the ascetic, embodies the ideal. And finally, the primacy of humility — his teaching that the whole journey is, in the end, a descent into smallness that becomes a doorway to grace.

A Closing Word

To study Vaars 7-15 is to receive a complete spiritual education in miniature. Bhai Gurdas asks of us not admiration but practice — that we rise in the ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ to remember, that we serve without seeking reward, that we sit in the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ, that we deal justly and compassionately with all, and that we become, in his recurring image, the dust of the feet of the holy. The Vaaran are not a text to be mastered but a path to be walked. May this study be, for each who undertakes it, a true ਤੀਰਥ — an inner crossing place from the worldly toward the eternal.

quiz.q: Why did Guru Arjan Sahib reportedly call the Vaaran Bhai Gurdas the ਕੁੰਜੀ (key) to Sri Guru Granth Sahib?
options: Because the Vaaran are considered scripture equal in authority to Gurbani
Because the Vaaran function as an interpretive key that opens and explains the meaning of Gurbani without adding to it
Because Bhai Gurdas physically held the key to the room where the Adi Granth was stored
Because the Vaaran were composed before any of the Guru Sahibs' compositions

quiz.q: In Vaar 7, what is the relationship Bhai Gurdas maintains between disciplined practice and spiritual attainment?
options: Attainment is purely the result of human effort and can be earned through practice alone
Practice is irrelevant; only grace matters and effort is discouraged
Practice prepares and readies the heart, but the fruit arrives as ਗੁਰਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ (grace), not as a purchase
Practice and grace are unrelated and operate in completely separate domains

quiz.q: According to Bhai Gurdas in Vaar 8, what fundamentally distinguishes the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ from the ਮਨਮੁਖ?
options: The ਗੁਰਮੁਖ is wealthy and high-caste while the ਮਨਮੁਖ is poor
The ਗੁਰਮੁਖ has renounced family life while the ਮਨਮੁਖ remains a householder
The ਗੁਰਮੁਖ is turned toward the Guru in surrendered humility while the ਮਨਮੁਖ is turned toward the self and ruled by ਹਉਮੈ
The ਗੁਰਮੁਖ performs more elaborate rituals than the ਮਨਮੁਖ

quiz.q: In Vaar 11, how does Bhai Gurdas reinterpret the sixty-eight (ਅਠਸਠਿ) ਤੀਰਥ of classical tradition?
options: He declares that all sixty-eight pilgrimage sites are gathered in the feet of the holy and the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ
He provides a detailed travel itinerary for visiting all sixty-eight in the correct order
He argues that only the Ganga among them is truly purifying
He claims the sixty-eight ਤੀਰਥ must be visited before one can join the ਸੰਗਤ

quiz.q: What is distinctive about Bhai Gurdas's ਪਾਰਸ (philosopher's stone) simile for the ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ in Vaar 10?
options: The ਸੰਗਤ is weaker than the philosopher's stone and only sometimes transforms people
The ਸੰਗਤ surpasses the philosopher's stone because it makes the transformed person into another transformer, reproducing holiness
The philosopher's stone is condemned as a worldly distraction from true devotion
The simile teaches that transformation is impossible without literal gold

quiz.q: In Vaar 15, why does Bhai Gurdas present ਨਿਮਰਤਾ (humility) as both the root and the crown of the spiritual life?
options: Because humility is a social custom required only when greeting elders
Because humility is the precise opposite of ਹਉਮੈ, so every discipline traced to its root is a discipline of humility, and the humble heart alone is empty enough to receive grace
Because humility is the easiest virtue to achieve and requires no effort
Because Bhai Gurdas considered all other virtues unnecessary once humility was attained

courses.title: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas: Social Ethics and Community Life
courses.summary: This intermediate course examines Vaars 26-40 of ਵਾਰਾਂ ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ as a social charter for the early Sikh community. Reading ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ as the first authoritative interpreter of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, students explore how the Vaars articulate a revolutionary social ethic: the rejection of ਜਾਤ-ਪਾਤ, the dignity of women, the economy of ਲੰਗਰ and ਸੇਵਾ, the ethics of the Sikh merchant and householder, and the institutions—the ਧਰਮਸਾਲ, the ਸੰਗਤ, and the ਗ੍ਰੰਥੀ—that bound the ਪੰਥ together. The course treats the Vaars not as abstract poetry but as a lived constitution for the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ within the ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤ.
outcomes: Explain why ਵਾਰਾਂ ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ are called the ਕੁੰਜੀ (key) to ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ and how they function as the earliest exegesis of the ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ.
Analyze the rejection of ਜਾਤ-ਪਾਤ and ਵਰਨ-ਆਸ਼ਰਮ in Vaars 26-40 and contrast it with prevailing Brahmanical social order.
Describe the social economy of ਲੰਗਰ, ਸੇਵਾ, and ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ as a model of redistributive community life.
Evaluate the status and dignity of women in the early Sikh community as reflected in the Vaars and contemporary Gurmat.
Assess the business ethics of the Sikh merchant and householder (ਗ੍ਰਿਹਸਤੀ) including ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ and honest trade.
Articulate the role of the ਧਰਮਸਾਲ, ਸੰਗਤ, and ਗ੍ਰੰਥੀ in institutionalizing the early ਪੰਥ as a social charter.

terms.m: A Punjabi ballad or epic-heroic poetic form; the principal genre of Bhai Gurdas's compositions, here repurposed for theological and social instruction.
The caste system and its hierarchy of birth-based status, decisively rejected in the social vision of the Vaars.
The Brahmanical fourfold caste order (varna) and four life-stages, which the Sikh ਪੰਥ replaces with a single egalitarian community.
The free community kitchen where all sit and eat together regardless of caste, status, or gender; a central institution of Sikh social equality.
Selfless service rendered to the ਸੰਗਤ and humanity without expectation of reward; the ethical core of community life.
The holy congregation of seekers; the social and spiritual matrix in which the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ is formed.
One oriented toward the ਗੁਰੂ; the ideal Sikh whose conduct embodies the social and spiritual ethic of the Vaars.
The self-willed person turned away from the ਗੁਰੂ; the ethical counter-type whose egoism fractures community.
The early Sikh place of assembly and worship, precursor to the ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ, where ਸੰਗਤ gathered for ਕੀਰਤਨ and ਲੰਗਰ.
To earn one's living by honest labor; the first of the three foundational Sikh ethical practices.
To share one's earnings with others before consuming; the ethic of redistribution underpinning Sikh economy.
Remembrance and meditation upon the Divine Name; the spiritual discipline that grounds ethical action.
The custodian and reader of scripture who serves the ਸੰਗਤ; a key functionary of Sikh institutional life.
The householder; the Sikh ideal of spiritual life lived within family and society rather than renunciation.
The collective body and path of the Sikh community as an organized social and spiritual order.

references: Bhai Gurdas. Vaaran Bhai Gurdas Ji. Edited by Bhai Vir Singh. Amritsar: Khalsa Samachar, 1962.
Singh, Jodh. Varan Bhai Gurdas: Text, Transliteration and Translation. 2 vols. Patiala: Vision & Venture, 1998.
Hawley, John Stratton, and Gurinder Singh Mann, eds. Studying the Sikhs: Issues for North America. Albany: State University of New York Press, 1993.
Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.
McLeod, W. H. The Evolution of the Sikh Community: Five Essays. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1976.
Singh, Pashaura. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.
Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Rev. ed. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.
Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Feminine Principle in the Sikh Vision of the Transcendent. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1993.

lessons.title: Bhai Gurdas and the Vaars as Social Charter
lessons.summary: Introduces Bhai Gurdas, the nature of the Vaars, and the framing of Vaars 26-40 as a social constitution for the early Panth.
lessons.html:
ਵਿਸ਼ਾ ਸੂਚੀ (Table of Contents)

  1. Bhai Gurdas and the Vaars as Social Charter
  2. The Rejection of ਜਾਤ-ਪਾਤ in the Vaars
  3. ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤ: The Congregation as Social Body
  4. ਲੰਗਰ and the Economy of Sharing
  5. ਸੇਵਾ: The Ethic of Selfless Service
  6. Women in the Early Sikh Community
  7. ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ and the Ethics of the Sikh Merchant
  8. The ਗ੍ਰਿਹਸਤੀ Ideal: Spirituality in the World
  9. The ਧਰਮਸਾਲ and the Institutions of the Panth
  10. The ਗੁਰਮੁਖ and the ਮਨਮੁਖ as Social Types
  11. Sikhs and Non-Sikhs: Boundaries and Neighbourliness
  12. The Vaars as a Living Constitution: Synthesis

The First Interpreter of Gurbani

ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ (c. 1551-1636) stands at the foundation of Sikh intellectual life. A contemporary and confidant of four Gurus—from ਗੁਰੂ ਰਾਮਦਾਸ to ਗੁਰੂ ਹਰਿਗੋਬਿੰਦ—he served as the scribe of the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ as it was compiled under ਗੁਰੂ ਅਰਜਨ in 1604. His own poetic corpus, the forty ਵਾਰਾਂ and the several hundred ਕਬਿੱਤ-ਸਵੱਯੇ, earned the unique blessing attributed to ਗੁਰੂ ਅਰਜਨ that they are the ਕੁੰਜੀ, the key, to ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ. To read the Vaars is to read the earliest authoritative exegesis of the Sikh scripture, written by one who breathed the air of the Guru's court.

The ਵਾਰ as a poetic form was inherited from the Punjabi bardic tradition: a ballad of heroic struggle, sung to rouse warriors. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ took this martial vessel and filled it with a different heroism—the inner conquest of ਹਉਮੈ (egoism) and the outward building of a just community. Each ਵਾਰ comprises a series of ਪਉੜੀਆਂ (stanzas), and within them the poet weaves illustration, analogy, and exhortation drawn from everyday Punjabi life: the merchant's ledger, the farmer's field, the spinning wheel, the marketplace.

Why Vaars 26-40 Form a Social Charter

While the earlier Vaars (especially 1 and 11) narrate the lives of the Gurus and the formation of the early ਸੰਗਤ, the later Vaars turn insistently toward the texture of communal life. Here ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ describes how a Sikh should earn, share, serve, marry, trade, worship, and relate to neighbours. Read together, Vaars 26-40 constitute something like a constitution for the ਪੰਥ—not a legal code, but a moral charter that defines the obligations of membership in the ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤ.

The poet repeatedly contrasts two figures: the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ, whose life is oriented toward the ਗੁਰੂ and the welfare of others, and the ਮਨਮੁਖ, whose self-will dissolves community. Gurbani in the Vaars teaches that the measure of a person is not birth, ritual purity, or wealth, but the quality of their conduct within the ਸੰਗਤ. As ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ writes in a celebrated line, ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ ਸੁਖ ਫਲੁ ਪਿਰਮ ਰਸੁ—the fruit of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ's life is the joy of loving devotion, a joy that overflows into service of others.

Method of This Course

Over the following lessons we will read the social vision of Vaars 26-40 thematically. We treat each theme—caste, congregation, kitchen, service, women, work, household, institution, and inter-community relations—as a chapter in a single argument: that the Guru founded not merely a religion of belief but a reordered society. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ is our guide because he wrote from within that society as it was being born.

A word of method on citation. The numbering of ਪਉੜੀਆਂ varies slightly across printed editions, and out of fidelity to the tradition we will quote ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ by theme and image rather than asserting precise stanza numbers where we are not certain. What matters for our purpose is the social ethic the Vaars articulate, which is consistent and unmistakable across the corpus.

The Stakes of the Reading

It is easy to read the Vaars as devotional poetry and miss their social radicalism. In sixteenth-century Punjab, to seat a Brahmin and an outcaste at the same row in ਲੰਗਰ, to honour a labouring woman as the equal of a man before the ਗੁਰੂ, to declare honest trade a form of worship—these were not pieties but provocations. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ records and defends this new order. To study his Vaars is to study the social imagination of early Sikhism at its source. In the lessons that follow we will see how thoroughly the everyday—food, work, marriage, neighbourliness—became, in the Guru's ਪੰਥ, a theatre of the sacred.

lessons.title: The Rejection of ਜਾਤ-ਪਾਤ in the Vaars
lessons.summary: Examines how Vaars 26-40 dismantle caste hierarchy and replace ਵਰਨ-ਆਸ਼ਰਮ with a single egalitarian Panth.
lessons.html:
The Inherited Order

The social world into which the Gurus spoke was governed by ਵਰਨ-ਆਸ਼ਰਮ ਧਰਮ—the fourfold division of society into ਬ੍ਰਾਹਮਣ, ਖੱਤਰੀ, ਵੈਸ਼, and ਸ਼ੂਦਰ, with the so-called untouchables outside the scheme altogether. Birth determined occupation, marriage, the food one could share, and one's spiritual standing. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ confronts this order directly and declares it dissolved within the ਸੰਗਤ of the ਗੁਰੂ.

One Status Before the Guru

A recurring theme across Vaars 26-40 is that within the ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤ ਜਾਤ-ਪਾਤ has no purchase. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ uses the famous image of rivers losing their separate names upon joining the Ganges: just as many streams become one water, so persons of every caste, upon entering the ਸੰਗਤ, become simply Sikhs of the ਗੁਰੂ. In one of his most quoted lines he writes, ਚਾਰਿ ਵਰਨ ਇਕ ਵਰਨ ਕਰਾਇਆ—the four castes were made into one. The Guru's achievement, in ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ's reading, was precisely to collapse the fourfold ਵਰਨ into a single human community.

Crucially, this is not a private spiritual equality that leaves the social order intact. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ insists on practical, visible equality: shared food, shared seating, shared worship, intermarriage of formerly separated groups within the ਸੰਗਤ. The Brahmanical world located purity and pollution in the body and its contacts; the Vaars relocate value to conduct and devotion. Gurbani in the Vaars teaches that the lowest by birth, if a ਗੁਰਮੁਖ, stands higher than the highest-born ਮਨਮੁਖ.

The Critique of Ritual Status

ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ does not merely ignore caste; he satirizes the pretensions that sustain it. He mocks the Brahmin who guards his cooking-square against the touch of the low while harbouring greed and deceit within. He ridicules the notion that an external thread or mark confers worth. The poet's logic is consistent: that which is held sacred by ਵਰਨ-ਆਸ਼ਰਮ—pedigree, ritual purity, the privileges of the twice-born—is morally empty if the heart is full of ਹਉਮੈ.

The Positive Vision: ਗੁਰੂ ਕਾ ਸਿੱਖ

In place of caste identity, ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ offers a new identity: ਗੁਰੂ ਕਾ ਸਿੱਖ, the Sikh of the Guru. This identity is achieved, not inherited. It is constituted by initiation into the ਸੰਗਤ, by the practice of ਨਾਮ ਜਪਣਾ, ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ, and ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ, and by service. He describes early Sikhs of every former caste—merchants, farmers, weavers, and those once despised as outcaste—seated together and honoured equally. The transformation he celebrates is sociological as well as spiritual: a new people brought into being across the old lines of division.

Historical Significance

Scholars such as J. S. Grewal and W. H. McLeod have noted that this dismantling of caste was among the most consequential features of early Sikhism, attracting in particular those marginalized by the Brahmanical order. The institution of ਲੰਗਰ, which we examine in Lesson 4, was the practical engine of this equality. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ is our earliest internal witness to the deliberate, theologically grounded rejection of ਜਾਤ-ਪਾਤ.

A Caution and a Realism

The Vaars present the ideal, and we should not naively assume the early community fully realized it; caste consciousness proved stubborn in Punjabi society and resurfaced repeatedly. Yet the normative force of ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ's teaching is unambiguous: within the ਪੰਥ, ਜਾਤ-ਪਾਤ is to be abolished, and any Sikh who reintroduces it betrays the ਗੁਰੂ. This normative clarity is what makes the Vaars a charter rather than a mere description. The reader who internalizes Vaar after Vaar comes away with one conviction hammered home from every angle: birth confers nothing, conduct confers everything, and the ਸੰਗਤ is the place where this truth is enacted in shared bread and shared worship.

lessons.title: ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤ: The Congregation as Social Body
lessons.summary: Explores the centrality of the holy congregation as the social and spiritual matrix of the early Panth.
lessons.html:
The Heart of the Social Order

If ਜਾਤ-ਪਾਤ is what the Vaars dissolve, the ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤ is what they build in its place. Across Vaars 26-40, the congregation is not a backdrop to spiritual life but its very condition. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ returns again and again to the transformative power of the company of the holy. In a line beloved by ਪਾਠੀ and ਪ੍ਰਚਾਰਕ alike he declares, ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤਿ ਸਚਿ ਖੰਡੁ ਹੈ—the holy congregation is the realm of Truth, the very ਸਚ ਖੰਡ described in ਜਪੁਜੀ.

The Alchemy of Company

ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ is the great poet of ਸੰਗਤ. His favourite images are transformations effected by proximity: iron carried across the ocean in the boat of wood; base metal touched by the philosopher's stone (ਪਾਰਸ) and turned to gold; the wild ਰੀਠਾ tree near sandalwood acquiring fragrance. By each image he makes a single point—that human beings are formed by their company, and that the ਸੰਗਤ is the company that elevates. The ਮਨਮੁਖ alone is lost; the same person within the ਸੰਗਤ becomes a ਗੁਰਮੁਖ.

This is a profoundly social anthropology. Salvation, in the Vaars, is not achieved by the solitary ascetic in the forest but by the ordinary person embedded in a community of seekers. The forest renunciant, so honoured in the Indic traditions, is gently displaced by the householder who sits in ਸੰਗਤ. Gurbani in the Vaars teaches that ਨਾਮ is realized in company, through ਕੀਰਤਨ and the shared remembrance of the congregation, not in isolation.

The Discipline of Belonging

Membership in the ਸੰਗਤ carries obligations. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ describes the conduct of the good Sikh within the congregation: humility, the willingness to take the lowest seat, readiness to serve, restraint of the tongue, and the suppression of ਹਉਮੈ. He famously likens the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ to one who walks the path as if treading the edge of a sword—the demanding discipline of selflessness. The ਸੰਗਤ is thus not a comfortable club but a school of character, in which the ego is filed away through encounter with others.

Equality Enacted

The ਸੰਗਤ is where the abolition of caste, discussed in Lesson 2, becomes visible and habitual. In the congregation all sit upon the same floor; none is seated above another; the ਲੰਗਰ that follows feeds all from one kitchen. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ presents this not as a symbolic gesture but as the routine practice of the community. The ਸੰਗਤ is the social body in which the doctrine of equality is rehearsed daily until it becomes second nature.

The Authority of the Sangat

The Vaars also intimate the collective authority of the ਸੰਗਤ. The Guru is present in the congregation; the will of the Guru is discerned in and through the gathered Sikhs. This seed—the sacral status of the ਸੰਗਤ—would later flower into the doctrine of ਗੁਰੂ ਪੰਥ. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ stands at the origin of the Sikh conviction that the community itself, when gathered in the Guru's name, is a vehicle of the Guru's authority.

Why It Matters

For our study of social ethics, the ਸੰਗਤ is the foundational institution: it is the context in which every other ethic—sharing, service, work, marriage—acquires meaning. To understand ਲੰਗਰ, ਸੇਵਾ, and the rest, we must first see them as activities of the ਸੰਗਤ. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ teaches that the individual Sikh is unintelligible apart from the congregation; the Sikh is constituted as a social being. In the next lesson we turn to the most concrete expression of ਸੰਗਤ life: the free kitchen, where doctrine becomes food, and where the boundaries that ਜਾਤ-ਪਾਤ erected are dismantled meal by meal.

lessons.title: ਲੰਗਰ and the Economy of Sharing
lessons.summary: Analyzes the free community kitchen as the practical engine of equality and a model of redistributive economy.
lessons.html:
Doctrine Made Edible

No institution expresses the social ethic of the Vaars more vividly than the ਲੰਗਰ, the free kitchen where all sit in a single row (ਪੰਗਤ) and eat together. Established by ਗੁਰੂ ਨਾਨਕ and developed by his successors—most famously by ਗੁਰੂ ਅਮਰਦਾਸ, who required that even the Mughal emperor eat in ਪੰਗਤ before audience—the ਲੰਗਰ converts the abstract teaching of equality into the concrete act of shared eating. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ, writing from within the Guru's establishment at ਗੋਇੰਦਵਾਲ and ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤਸਰ, knew this institution intimately.

Why Food Was the Frontier

In the world of ਵਰਨ-ਆਸ਼ਰਮ, food was the chief site of caste regulation. Who could cook for whom, who could eat with whom, whose touch polluted the meal—these rules policed the boundaries of hierarchy more rigorously than almost any other. By instituting a kitchen where Brahmin and outcaste, rich and poor, man and woman ate the same food in the same row, the Gurus struck at the very nerve of the caste system. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ celebrates this: in the ਲੰਗਰ, the distinctions that the world holds sacred are simply set aside, and humanity eats as one family.

The Three Pillars and Sharing

The ਲੰਗਰ embodies one of the three foundational practices of Sikh life: ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ, to share before one eats. Alongside ਨਾਮ ਜਪਣਾ (remembrance) and ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ (honest labour), ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ completes the triad that structures the Sikh's relation to God, to work, and to others. The Vaars present the Sikh economy as fundamentally redistributive: one earns honestly and gives freely, and the surplus flows through the ਲੰਗਰ and the ਸੰਗਤ to those in need. Gurbani in the Vaars teaches that what is shared is multiplied, while what is hoarded is lost.

The Economy of ਦਸਵੰਧ

Connected to this ethic is the practice of ਦਸਵੰਧ, the dedication of a tenth of one's earnings to the ਗੁਰੂ and the community. While the formal system of ਦਸਵੰਧ and the ਮਸੰਦ network developed over the period in which ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ lived, the underlying principle—that the individual's wealth carries a communal obligation—pervades the Vaars. The ਲੰਗਰ is sustained by this flow: the offerings of the ਸੰਗਤ become the bread of the ਸੰਗਤ. The economy is circular and communal rather than acquisitive and private.

Service in the Kitchen

The ਲੰਗਰ is also a school of ਸੇਵਾ, the subject of our next lesson. The cooking, serving, and cleaning are performed by volunteers of every rank, and the highest-born may be found washing the dishes of the lowest. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ holds up this voluntary, menial service as the very form of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ's humility. There is no separate servant class; the ਸੰਗਤ serves itself, and in serving learns to dissolve ਹਉਮੈ.

A Living Witness

The historical importance of ਲੰਗਰ can hardly be overstated. It made the Sikh community visibly distinct, materially attractive to the poor and marginalized, and structurally egalitarian. Travellers and chroniclers across centuries remarked on the open kitchen that fed all comers without question of creed or caste. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ is the contemporary voice that explains its meaning from within: the ਲੰਗਰ is not charity dispensed from above but the table of a single family seated as equals.

The Charter Implication

For the social charter we are reconstructing, ਲੰਗਰ is the keystone. It joins together equality (Lesson 2), congregation (Lesson 3), sharing economy (this lesson), and service (Lesson 5) in a single daily practice. To eat in ਪੰਗਤ is to enact, with the body, the entire social theology of the Vaars. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ teaches that the kitchen is a sanctuary, and the shared meal a sacrament of equality, in which the Guru's vision of one humanity is tasted by all who come.

lessons.title: ਸੇਵਾ: The Ethic of Selfless Service
lessons.summary: Examines ਸੇਵਾ as the ethical core of community life and the chief discipline of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ.
lessons.html:
Service as Spiritual Path

At the moral centre of the Vaars stands ਸੇਵਾ, selfless service. For ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ, ਸੇਵਾ is not an optional virtue but the defining activity of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ. The one who has truly remembered ਨਾਮ expresses that remembrance in service of the ਸੰਗਤ and of all creation. Gurbani in the Vaars teaches that ਸੇਵਾ performed without desire for reward—ਨਿਸ਼ਕਾਮ ਸੇਵਾ—purifies the heart and dissolves ਹਉਮੈ as no ritual can.

The Forms of Service

ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ describes ਸੇਵਾ in concrete, often humble forms: drawing water and grinding grain for the ਲੰਗਰ, fanning the ਸੰਗਤ, sweeping the ਧਰਮਸਾਲ, washing the feet and dishes of fellow Sikhs, carrying loads for the weary. He deliberately exalts the lowliest tasks, for it is precisely in menial service that the ego is most thoroughly humbled. The poet praises the Sikh who considers no service beneath them and who serves the lowest with the reverence due to the Guru.

Service as the Inversion of Status

This exaltation of menial service is a direct assault on the logic of ਵਰਨ-ਆਸ਼ਰਮ, in which manual and menial labour was assigned to the low-born and avoided by the high. By making voluntary menial service the highest spiritual act, ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ inverts the social pyramid. The proud Brahmin who would never touch a broom is, in the Guru's order, spiritually beneath the Sikh who sweeps the ਸੰਗਤ's floor with love. ਸੇਵਾ thus carries forward the caste-dissolving work of ਲੰਗਰ.

The Threefold Service

Sikh tradition, drawing on the spirit of the Vaars, distinguishes ਤਨ, ਮਨ, ਧਨ—service by body, by mind, and by wealth. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ touches each: the labour of the body in the ਲੰਗਰ and ਧਰਮਸਾਲ; the service of the mind in counsel, teaching, and ਕੀਰਤਨ; and the service of wealth through ਦਸਵੰਧ and giving. The complete Sikh serves with all three, holding nothing back. The poet warns that wealth given without humility, or labour given for praise, is service corrupted by ਹਉਮੈ.

The Test of Sincerity

ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ is acute about the dangers of false service. Service performed for reputation, for reward, or with an eye to recognition is not ਸੇਵਾ but a subtler form of self-seeking. True ਸੇਵਾ is silent, unselfconscious, and indifferent to thanks. He illustrates with the image of the tree that gives fruit to the one who throws stones at it, and the sandalwood that perfumes even the axe that fells it—service returned for injury, given without calculation. The ਗੁਰਮੁਖ serves in this manner, expecting nothing.

Service and the Common Good

Importantly, ਸੇਵਾ in the Vaars is not confined to the religious community. While the ਸੰਗਤ is its first sphere, the ethic extends outward to all in need. The principle of ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ, the welfare of all, is implicit throughout: the Sikh serves humanity, not merely co-religionists. This universalism distinguishes Sikh ਸੇਵਾ from mere in-group solidarity and gives it its enduring social power.

The Charter Implication

For the social charter, ਸੇਵਾ supplies the motive force. Equality, congregation, and the sharing economy would be inert without the active, self-giving disposition that ਸੇਵਾ instils. It is the engine that drives the ਲੰਗਰ, sustains the ਸੰਗਤ, and binds the community into a body that cares for its members and for the stranger. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ teaches that to serve is to worship, and that the hands made rough by service are dearer to the Guru than the folded hands of the idle devotee. In the early ਪੰਥ, to be a Sikh was to be a servant.

lessons.title: Women in the Early Sikh Community
lessons.summary: Explores the dignity and status of women in the social vision reflected in the Vaars and contemporary Gurmat.
lessons.html:
A Revolution in Dignity

The social charter of early Sikhism included a reordering of the status of women. The Gurus rejected the contemporary teachings that treated woman as spiritually inferior, ritually polluting, or fit only for subordination. While ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ writes within a patriarchal age and his imagery sometimes reflects its assumptions, the deeper logic of the Vaars—and of the ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ they interpret—affirms the spiritual equality and dignity of women within the ਸੰਗਤ.

The Foundational Teaching

The bedrock here is ਗੁਰੂ ਨਾਨਕ's celebrated declaration in ਆਸਾ ਦੀ ਵਾਰ that woman is the one through whom kings and all humanity are born, and that she who gives birth to the great should not be called inferior—ਸੋ ਕਿਉ ਮੰਦਾ ਆਖੀਐ ਜਿਤੁ ਜੰਮਹਿ ਰਾਜਾਨ. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ, as the first interpreter of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, carries this affirmation into his vision of community life. The woman is a full member of the ਸੰਗਤ, partakes of ਲੰਗਰ in the same ਪੰਗਤ, performs ਸੇਵਾ, and walks the path of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ.

Women in the ਸੰਗਤ

The Vaars assume the presence and participation of women in the congregation. Unlike traditions that secluded women or barred them from sacred space, the ਸੰਗਤ described by ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ included women who heard ਕੀਰਤਨ, served in the kitchen, and pursued ਨਾਮ. The ਧਰਮਸਾਲ was open to them. The household ideal that the Vaars champion (Lesson 8) necessarily honours the wife as a spiritual partner, not a mere instrument.

The Spiritual Use of the Feminine

ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ employs the imagery of the devoted wife (ਸੁਹਾਗਣ) longing for her Beloved Lord as the model of the ideal soul. As scholars such as Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh have shown, this feminine voice of devotion is not incidental: the soul before God is figured as the bride, and every Sikh, male or female, is called to adopt this loving, surrendered posture. The elevation of the feminine as the very form of the ideal devotee carries an implicit affirmation of woman's spiritual capacity and worth.

The Rejection of Harmful Customs

The social charter implied a rejection of the customs that degraded women. ਸਤੀ (the burning of widows), female infanticide, the veil (ਪਰਦਾ), and the contempt for widows were practices that the Gurus' teaching undermined, and the later ਰਹਿਤ tradition would explicitly forbid. The logic is already present in the Vaars: if woman is not ਮੰਦਾ (low), if she is a full member of the ਸੰਗਤ and a ਗੁਰਮੁਖ in her own right, then the customs that treat her as disposable are incompatible with the Guru's way.

Honesty About Limits

A scholarly reading must be candid. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ wrote in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and his texts at times reflect the gendered assumptions of his milieu; some passages use the figure of woman in conventional ways. We do the tradition no service by anachronistically projecting modern egalitarianism onto every line. Yet the trajectory is unmistakable and was radical for its time: a movement toward the recognition of women as full spiritual and social persons within the ਪੰਥ.

The Charter Implication

For our charter, the inclusion of women completes the universality of the ਸੰਗਤ. Just as ਜਾਤ-ਪਾਤ is dissolved, so the spiritual subordination of women is rejected in principle. The ਸੰਗਤ that ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ describes is, in its ideal form, a community in which neither caste nor gender determines worth, and in which the path of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ is open to all. Gurbani in the Vaars teaches that the Beloved looks upon the heart, and the heart has no gender. This affirmation, planted in the early ਪੰਥ, remains a resource and a challenge for the community across the centuries.

lessons.title: ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ and the Ethics of the Sikh Merchant
lessons.summary: Analyzes honest labour, the dignity of work, and the business ethics of the Sikh trader in the Vaars.
lessons.html:
Work as Worship

The Sikh social charter is built upon ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ, the obligation to earn one's living by honest labour. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ, drawing on the example of ਗੁਰੂ ਨਾਨਕ—who farmed at ਕਰਤਾਰਪੁਰ—and on the merchant and artisan members of the early ਸੰਗਤ, treats honest work not as a worldly necessity to be transcended but as a spiritual discipline. The Sikh does not beg, does not renounce work for the begging bowl of the ascetic, and does not live off others. To labour honestly and to share the fruit is itself a form of worship.

The Rejection of Renunciation

This ethic is pointedly opposed to the renunciant ideal. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ has sharp words for the ਜੋਗੀ and ਸੰਨਿਆਸੀ who abandon the world and live on alms. He sees in such renunciation a hidden parasitism: the renunciant who eats without working is sustained by the labour of the householder he claims to have transcended. By contrast, the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ remains in the world, earns honestly, and supports both family and ਸੰਗਤ. The dignity of productive labour is a cornerstone of the charter.

The Mercantile World of the Vaars

ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ's imagery is saturated with the world of the merchant. He speaks constantly of the ਵਣਜਾਰਾ (the travelling trader), the ਸਉਦਾ (merchandise), the ਪੂੰਜੀ (capital), the ਖਰਾ ਅਤੇ ਖੋਟਾ (the genuine and the counterfeit coin), the ledger, profit and loss. He uses these to figure the spiritual life—the true merchant trades in ਨਾਮ, his capital is the breath, his profit is the love of God. But the very fluency of this imagery reflects the centrality of trade to the early ਸੰਗਤ, much of which was drawn from the ਖੱਤਰੀ mercantile communities.

The Ethics of Honest Trade

From this mercantile imagery ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ draws an explicit business ethic. The Sikh merchant must deal in the ਖਰਾ—the genuine, the true—and shun the ਖੋਟਾ, the counterfeit and the dishonest. False weights, adulteration, deceit, and the exploitation of the buyer are condemned. Gurbani in the Vaars teaches that the wealth earned by deceit is poison, while even modest earnings won honestly and shared are blessed. He invokes the principle, central to ਗੁਰਮਤਿ, that one must not consume what rightly belongs to another—ਹਕੁ ਪਰਾਇਆ is forbidden as surely as carrion.

Wealth Without Attachment

The Sikh merchant is to earn and even to prosper, but without ਲੋਭ (greed) and without attachment. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ holds up the ideal of one who handles wealth as a steward rather than an owner—earning much, perhaps, but holding it lightly, giving freely through ਦਸਵੰਧ and ਲੰਗਰ. The lotus that floats on water yet is not wetted by it is his image for the Sikh in the marketplace: engaged in commerce, yet inwardly detached.

Labour, Sharing, and Remembrance

ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ is meaningless in isolation; it is one of the three pillars and must be joined to ਨਾਮ ਜਪਣਾ and ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ. The honest earning is to be sanctified by remembrance and completed by sharing. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ presents the integrated life: hands at work, tongue in ਨਾਮ, and a portion of every earning given to the ਸੰਗਤ. This is the householder's path of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ.

The Charter Implication

For our charter, ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ establishes the economic ethic of the community: a society of honest workers and ethical traders who reject both idleness and exploitation. It dignifies labour, disciplines commerce, and feeds the redistributive economy of ਲੰਗਰ and ਦਸਵੰਧ. The Sikh merchant of the Vaars is a moral figure—prosperous perhaps, but honest, generous, and detached. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ thus offers one of the earliest articulations of a distinctly Sikh business ethics, grounded in truthfulness, fairness, and the obligation of the wealthy to the community.

lessons.title: The ਗ੍ਰਿਹਸਤੀ Ideal: Spirituality in the World
lessons.summary: Examines the householder ideal as the Sikh path of spiritual life lived within family and society.
lessons.html:
The Path of the Householder

Central to the social vision of the Vaars is the ideal of the ਗ੍ਰਿਹਸਤੀ, the householder. Against the long Indic tradition that located the highest spiritual life in renunciation and the forest, the Gurus taught that liberation is to be sought within the home, the family, and society. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ is the great expositor of this ideal: the perfected being is not the world-fleeing ascetic but the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ householder who lives amid wife, children, work, and ਸੰਗਤ while keeping the heart fixed on ਨਾਮ.

The Lotus and the Water-Fowl

ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ's favourite images for the householder ideal are the lotus (ਕਮਲ) that grows in the mud and floats on the water yet remains unstained, and the water-fowl (ਮੁਰਗਾਈ) that swims in the pond yet keeps its feathers dry. By these he teaches the art of being in the world but not of it—fully engaged in family and trade, yet inwardly detached and devoted. This is harder, he insists, than fleeing to the forest. To remain pure amid temptation requires more than to avoid temptation altogether.

Marriage as Spiritual Partnership

Within the householder ideal, marriage is dignified as a spiritual relationship. The Sikh ideal, later crystallized in the doctrine of ਅਨੰਦ ਕਾਰਜ and the teaching that husband and wife are ਏਕ ਜੋਤਿ ਦੁਇ ਮੂਰਤੀ—one light in two bodies—has its roots in this elevation of the married state. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ honours the faithful householder and the chaste, devoted partnership. Sexual fidelity (the rejection of ਪਰ ਇਸਤ੍ਰੀ and ਪਰ ਪੁਰਖ, the other's spouse) is a recurring ethical demand of the Vaars, binding alike on man and woman.

Family and Community

The household is not a private retreat but the basic cell of the ਸੰਗਤ. The ਗ੍ਰਿਹਸਤੀ raises children in ਗੁਰਮਤਿ, extends hospitality to the traveller and the needy, and contributes to the ਲੰਗਰ and ਦਸਵੰਧ. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ presents an interlocking social order in which honest households, joined in ਸੰਗਤ, constitute the ਪੰਥ. The family is where the virtues of service, sharing, and remembrance are first learned and practised.

Against Asceticism and Excess Alike

The householder path steers between two errors. On one side stands the ascetic who flees the world; on the other, the worldling who is enslaved by it. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ rejects both. The ਗੁਰਮੁਖ neither renounces the world nor is consumed by it, but lives within it as a trustee, enjoying its gifts with gratitude and detachment. The Five Thieves—ਕਾਮ, ਕ੍ਰੋਧ, ਲੋਭ, ਮੋਹ, ਅਹੰਕਾਰ—are to be conquered not by withdrawal but by inner discipline amid the very situations that provoke them. Gurbani in the Vaars teaches that the true renunciation is renunciation of ਹਉਮੈ, not of home and labour.

The Social Significance

The householder ideal has profound social consequences. By rejecting renunciation, the Vaars keep the spiritually serious within society as productive, responsible members—as workers, parents, neighbours, and citizens. The community is not drained of its best into monasteries; rather, its saints are its householders, fully embedded in the social fabric. This is one reason early Sikhism could grow into a robust social and, later, political community: its ideal of holiness was an ideal of engaged, worldly life.

The Charter Implication

For our charter, the ਗ੍ਰਿਹਸਤੀ ideal supplies the basic social unit and the model of integrated life. The Sikh is a worker (Lesson 7), a member of the ਸੰਗਤ (Lesson 3), a server (Lesson 5), and a householder—all at once, without contradiction. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ weaves these into a single life of ਰਾਜ ਜੋਗ, the union of worldly engagement and spiritual realization. The home, sanctified by ਨਾਮ and service, becomes a ਧਰਮਸਾਲ in miniature, and the householder a ਗੁਰਮੁਖ in the midst of the world.

lessons.title: The ਧਰਮਸਾਲ and the Institutions of the Panth
lessons.summary: Examines the institutions—the place of worship, the role of the ਗ੍ਰੰਥੀ, and emerging organizational structures—that bound the early Panth.
lessons.html:
From Movement to Institution

A social charter requires institutions, and the Vaars witness the institutional consolidation of the early ਪੰਥ. The central institution is the ਧਰਮਸਾਲ, the place of assembly and worship that ਗੁਰੂ ਨਾਨਕ established at ਕਰਤਾਰਪੁਰ and that multiplied across Punjab and beyond as the ਸੰਗਤ grew. The term ਧਰਮਸਾਲ—the hall of ਧਰਮ—names a space where Sikhs gathered for ਕੀਰਤਨ, the recitation of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, the taking of ਲੰਗਰ, and the conduct of community life. It is the ancestor of the later ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ.

The ਧਰਮਸਾਲ as Social Centre

The ਧਰਮਸਾਲ was far more than a building for prayer. It was the social and economic hub of the local ਸੰਗਤ: the site of ਲੰਗਰ, the place where the needy were fed and travellers housed, where disputes might be settled and the community's affairs ordered. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ describes the ਧਰਮਸਾਲ as the place where the ਸੰਗਤ assembles in the ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ (the ambrosial early hours) for remembrance. The institution gave the dispersed ਸੰਗਤ a fixed centre and a regular rhythm of communal life.

The Reading of Scripture

The compilation of the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ in 1604—an event in which ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ himself served as scribe—gave the community an authoritative scripture and, with it, the centrality of scriptural reading to congregational life. The installation of the ਗ੍ਰੰਥ at ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ established the pattern of the scripture as the focus of the ਧਰਮਸਾਲ. From this flows the role of the ਗ੍ਰੰਥੀ.

The Role of the ਗ੍ਰੰਥੀ

The ਗ੍ਰੰਥੀ is the custodian and reader of the scripture, the one who recites and expounds ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ for the ਸੰਗਤ and tends the ਧਰਮਸਾਲ. Importantly, in the Sikh order the ਗ੍ਰੰਥੀ is not a priest in the sacerdotal sense—not a mediator who alone may approach the sacred, nor a member of a separate priestly caste. The rejection of ਜਾਤ-ਪਾਤ and of Brahmanical priesthood means that any committed Sikh, regardless of birth, may serve in this role. The ਗ੍ਰੰਥੀ serves the ਸੰਗਤ; he does not rule it. This is consonant with ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ's vision of a community without a priestly hierarchy, in which the scripture is open to all and the congregation collectively bears authority.

Networks and Functionaries

The period of ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ saw the development of organizational structures to link the growing and geographically scattered ਸੰਗਤ to the centre. The ਮਸੰਦ system—local representatives appointed to gather offerings (ਦਸਵੰਧ) and lead the regional ਸੰਗਤ—knit the ਪੰਥ into a coordinated body, though it would later require reform. ਮੰਜੀਆਂ and ਪੀੜ੍ਹੀਆਂ, the seats of authority established by earlier Gurus, similarly extended the community's reach. These structures show the ਪੰਥ acquiring the institutional sinews of an organized society.

The Authority of the Word and the Sangat

ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ locates ultimate authority in the ਸ਼ਬਦ (the divine Word) and in the ਸੰਗਤ gathered around it. The ਧਰਮਸਾਲ is sacred because the ਸ਼ਬਦ is recited there and the ਸੰਗਤ assembles there. The functionaries—ਗ੍ਰੰਥੀ, ਮਸੰਦ—are servants of this Word and this congregation, not lords over them. This anti-hierarchical institutionalism is distinctive: the Vaars build a structured community while resisting the priestly domination characteristic of the surrounding religious order.

The Charter Implication

For our charter, the institutions described here give the social ethic durable form. Equality, congregation, sharing, service, and honest work are not left to individual goodwill but are housed in the ਧਰਮਸਾਲ, sustained by the ਲੰਗਰ, focused on the ਗ੍ਰੰਥ, served by the ਗ੍ਰੰਥੀ, and linked through the ਮਸੰਦ network into a ਪੰਥ. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ shows us a movement becoming an institution without becoming a hierarchy—a community organized around the Word and the congregation rather than around birth and priesthood. This institutional vision is among the most enduring legacies of the Vaars.

lessons.title: The ਗੁਰਮੁਖ and the ਮਨਮੁਖ as Social Types
lessons.summary: Analyzes the contrast between the Guru-oriented and self-willed person as the ethical centre of the Vaars' social vision.
lessons.html:
The Two Ways of Being

The deepest organizing contrast in the entire corpus of ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ is between the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ and the ਮਨਮੁਖ. These are not merely spiritual categories but social types: two opposite orientations that produce two opposite kinds of community life. The ਗੁਰਮੁਖ—literally, one whose face is turned toward the ਗੁਰੂ—lives for others and builds community; the ਮਨਮੁਖ—one who follows the ਮਨ, the self-willed mind—lives for the self and fractures it. The entire social ethic of the Vaars can be read as a portrait of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ.

The Portrait of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ

ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ lavishes his finest poetry on the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ. The ਗੁਰਮੁਖ is humble, taking the lowest place; truthful in word and trade; tireless in ਸੇਵਾ; generous in sharing; faithful in the household; steadfast in ਨਾਮ. He bears insult without retaliation, returns good for evil, and treats every person as an equal regardless of caste or station. He is the lotus in the mud, the sandalwood that scents the axe, the tree that gives fruit to those who stone it. In the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ, all the virtues we have studied—equality, service, sharing, honesty, detachment—are gathered into a single character.

The Portrait of the ਮਨਮੁਖ

Against this stands the ਮਨਮੁਖ, driven by the Five Thieves—ਕਾਮ (lust), ਕ੍ਰੋਧ (anger), ਲੋਭ (greed), ਮੋਹ (attachment), ਅਹੰਕਾਰ (pride). The ਮਨਮੁਖ is proud of birth and wealth, clings to caste distinctions, deals dishonestly, serves only himself, and is ungrateful. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ catalogues the ਮਨਮੁਖ's failings with vivid satire: the false guru who fleeces disciples, the hypocrite whose outer piety masks inner corruption, the ingrate who bites the hand that feeds. The ਮਨਮੁਖ is the dissolver of community, the one in whom ਹਉਮੈ has triumphed.

Ingratitude as the Cardinal Vice

ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ reserves special condemnation for the ungrateful—the ਬੇਮੁਖ and the ਅਕਿਰਤਘਣ (the one who forgets benefits received). In a memorable series of comparisons he declares that even the worst of creatures has some redeeming trait, but the ingrate has none. This emphasis is socially significant: gratitude is the glue of community, the recognition that one is sustained by the ਸੰਗਤ, by the ਗੁਰੂ, by others' labour. The ਮਨਮੁਖ's ingratitude is the denial of this interdependence, and thus the deepest threat to the social body.

The Social Stakes of Character

The genius of ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ is to show that the spiritual and the social are one. The inner conquest of ਹਉਮੈ and the outer building of community are not two tasks but one. The ਗੁਰਮੁਖ, by dissolving the ego, becomes capable of equality, service, and sharing; the ਮਨਮੁਖ, ruled by ego, is incapable of them. Gurbani in the Vaars teaches that the reform of society begins with the reform of the self, and that the just community is simply a community of ਗੁਰਮੁਖ. There is no social ethic without character, and no character without the ਗੁਰੂ.

A Calling, Not a Caste

Crucially, ਗੁਰਮੁਖ and ਮਨਮੁਖ are not fixed categories of birth but chosen orientations. Anyone may become a ਗੁਰਮੁਖ by turning toward the ਗੁਰੂ; anyone may fall into the ways of the ਮਨਮੁਖ by following self-will. This is the engine of the caste-dissolving ethic: worth is determined by the orientation of the heart, which is open to all, and not by the accident of birth, which is given to none by choice.

The Charter Implication

For our charter, the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ is the citizen and the ਮਨਮੁਖ the anti-citizen of the ਪੰਥ. The whole social order described in this course—the egalitarian ਸੰਗਤ, the open ਲੰਗਰ, the economy of sharing, the ethic of service, the honest marketplace, the faithful household, the non-hierarchical institutions—is sustainable only if peopled by ਗੁਰਮੁਖ. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ thus grounds his social charter in personal transformation: the just society is the visible form of transformed selves gathered in ਸੰਗਤ.

lessons.title: Sikhs and Non-Sikhs: Boundaries and Neighbourliness
lessons.summary: Explores how the Vaars define Sikh identity while teaching respect and good relations with non-Sikhs.
lessons.html:
Identity and Openness

A social charter must answer two questions at once: who belongs, and how do members relate to those outside? The Vaars of ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ are notable for holding together a clear sense of distinct Sikh identity with a generous ethic toward non-Sikhs. The early ਪੰਥ was neither a closed sect indifferent to outsiders nor a vague universalism without boundaries; it was a defined community with porous, hospitable edges.

The Distinctiveness of the Sikh Way

ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ is emphatic that the Guru's way is a distinct path, the ਨਿਰਾਲਾ ਪੰਥ, the unique path, different from both the dominant Hindu traditions and from Islam. He describes the Sikh way as a third way that supersedes the existing systems—not a reform of ਵਰਨ-ਆਸ਼ਰਮ nor a branch of the prevailing faiths, but a new dispensation. He is critical of the corruptions he perceives in the religious establishments around him: the empty ritualism of the Brahmin, the hypocrisy of the ਪਾਖੰਡੀ, the formalism that mistakes outer observance for inner truth. The Sikh ਗੁਰਮੁਖ is defined against these.

Critique Aimed at Hypocrisy, Not Peoples

It is essential to read ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ's criticism rightly. His polemic targets ਪਾਖੰਡ (hypocrisy), empty ritual, and the abuses of religious authority—wherever they are found, including within the nominal Sikh fold. It is not an indictment of Hindus or Muslims as peoples, nor a license for contempt toward them. The Guru's teaching, which ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ interprets, recognizes the divine in all and holds that there is neither Hindu nor Muslim before God, only human beings to be judged by their deeds.

The Ethic of Neighbourliness

Toward non-Sikhs the Vaars teach respect, honesty, and the same ethical conduct demanded within the community. The Sikh merchant must deal honestly with all customers, not only with co-religionists. The ਲੰਗਰ feeds all comers without question of creed; the open kitchen is the practical emblem of an open community. The principle of ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ, the welfare of all, governs the Sikh's relation to the wider world. ਸੇਵਾ is owed to humanity, not merely to the ਸੰਗਤ.

Hospitality and the Stranger

Hospitality to the stranger and the traveller is a marked feature of the social ethic. The ਧਰਮਸਾਲ housed travellers of any background; the ਲੰਗਰ fed them. This institutionalized hospitality expresses a theology in which the guest is honoured and the needy served regardless of identity. Gurbani in the Vaars teaches that the Lord dwells in all hearts, and so service to any person is service to the Divine.

Boundaries That Include

The Sikh community thus drew its boundary not by birth, ethnicity, or exclusion of outsiders, but by commitment to the Guru's way—a boundary anyone could cross by becoming a ਗੁਰਮੁਖ. This is a fundamentally different kind of boundary from that of caste, which is closed by birth. The ਪੰਥ is bounded yet open: bounded by its distinctive ethic and devotion, open to all who would embrace them. Many of the early ਸੰਗਤ came from both Hindu and Muslim backgrounds, drawn by precisely this openness.

The Charter Implication

For our charter, this lesson defines the community's external relations. The ਪੰਥ is a distinct community with a clear identity and a critique of surrounding corruptions, yet it practises honesty, service, and hospitality toward all, feeds the stranger, and holds its doors open to any who would join. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ models a posture that later Sikh history would test severely: firm in identity, generous in conduct, principled in critique, and humane toward the neighbour. The distinctiveness of the ਨਿਰਾਲਾ ਪੰਥ does not contradict its openness; the two together define the social charter's relation to the world.

lessons.title: The Vaars as a Living Constitution: Synthesis
lessons.summary: Synthesizes the course into an integrated account of the Vaars as a social charter and considers their enduring significance.
lessons.html:
Drawing the Threads Together

Across this course we have read Vaars 26-40 of ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ as a social charter for the early ਪੰਥ. We may now gather the threads into a single vision. The charter begins by dissolving the old order: ਜਾਤ-ਪਾਤ and ਵਰਨ-ਆਸ਼ਰਮ are abolished within the ਸੰਗਤ (Lesson 2). In their place rises a new social body, the ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤ (Lesson 3), where equality is enacted daily in the ਲੰਗਰ (Lesson 4) and sustained by the ethic of ਸੇਵਾ (Lesson 5). Women are affirmed as full members of this body (Lesson 6). The community's economy rests on ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ and honest trade (Lesson 7), and its basic social unit is the ਗ੍ਰਿਹਸਤੀ, the engaged householder (Lesson 8). Durable institutions—the ਧਰਮਸਾਲ, the ਗ੍ਰੰਥ, the ਗ੍ਰੰਥੀ, the ਮਸੰਦ network—give the ethic lasting form without erecting a priestly hierarchy (Lesson 9). All of this is peopled and powered by the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ, the transformed self oriented to the ਗੁਰੂ (Lesson 10), and the community relates to the wider world with distinct identity yet open hospitality (Lesson 11).

The Unity of the Vision

The genius of ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ is the seamlessness of this vision. Spiritual and social, inner and outer, individual and communal are not separate domains but aspects of one life. ਨਾਮ ਜਪਣਾ, ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ, and ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ—remembrance, labour, sharing—form a single integrated discipline. The conquest of ਹਉਮੈ and the building of the just ਸੰਗਤ are one work. The Vaars refuse the divorce of religion from ethics, of worship from work, of devotion from justice. To be a Sikh is to live this integrated life.

A Charter, Not a Code

We have called the Vaars a charter rather than a legal code, and the distinction matters. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ does not legislate detailed rules; he forms character and casts a vision. He works by image, exhortation, and the portrait of the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ, persuading the reader to internalize an ethic rather than merely obey a rule. This is why the Vaars remained the ਕੁੰਜੀ to ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ for centuries: they do not date as legislation dates, but speak to the heart in every age.

The Historical Achievement

The social order the Vaars describe was a genuine historical achievement, not merely an ideal on paper. Scholars from J. S. Grewal to Pashaura Singh have documented how early Sikhism created a distinct community across caste lines, with its own institutions, scripture, and ethic, that grew into a major social and eventually political force in Punjab. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ is our indispensable contemporary witness to the meaning of this achievement, written from inside the Guru's court. His Vaars let us hear how the early community understood itself.

The Enduring Challenge

The charter remains a challenge as well as a heritage. The abolition of ਜਾਤ-ਪਾਤ, the dignity of women, the economy of sharing, the ethic of honest work and selfless service, the openness to the neighbour—these are ideals against which the community measures itself in every generation, and often finds itself wanting. The Vaars are not a monument to a perfected past but a living constitution that continues to summon the ਪੰਥ to its own best self. Gurbani in the Vaars teaches that the work of becoming a ਗੁਰਮੁਖ, and of building the ਸੰਗਤ in which the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ flourishes, is never finished.

Conclusion

To read Vaars 26-40 is to encounter the social imagination of early Sikhism at its source: a vision of one humanity, gathered across the lines of caste and creed and gender, eating from one kitchen, serving one another, working honestly, living in the world without bondage to it, and turning together toward the ਗੁਰੂ. ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ gave this vision enduring poetic form. It stands as one of the great social charters of the religious traditions, and as a perennial summons to justice, equality, and service lived as worship.

ਹਵਾਲੇ (Works Cited)

  • Bhai Gurdas. Vaaran Bhai Gurdas Ji. Edited by Bhai Vir Singh. Amritsar: Khalsa Samachar, 1962.
  • Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Rev. ed. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.
  • Hawley, John Stratton, and Gurinder Singh Mann, eds. Studying the Sikhs: Issues for North America. Albany: State University of New York Press, 1993.
  • Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.
  • McLeod, W. H. The Evolution of the Sikh Community: Five Essays. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1976.
  • Singh, Jodh. Varan Bhai Gurdas: Text, Transliteration and Translation. 2 vols. Patiala: Vision & Venture, 1998.
  • Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Feminine Principle in the Sikh Vision of the Transcendent. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1993.
  • Singh, Pashaura. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.

quiz.q: Why are the ਵਾਰਾਂ ਭਾਈ ਗੁਰਦਾਸ traditionally described as the ਕੁੰਜੀ (key) to ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ?
options: Because they were written before the Guru Granth Sahib existed
Because they are the earliest authoritative exegesis of Sikh scripture by a contemporary of the Gurus
Because they replace the Guru Granth Sahib in worship
Because they were composed by Guru Arjan himself

quiz.q: How does Bhai Gurdas characterize the effect of the ਗੁਰੂ on the fourfold caste order?
options: The four castes were preserved but ranked differently
The four castes were made into one (ਚਾਰਿ ਵਰਨ ਇਕ ਵਰਨ)
Only the lower castes were admitted to the Sangat
Caste was retained for marriage but abolished for worship

quiz.q: Which practice in the Vaars most directly attacked the caste system's regulation of purity and pollution?
options: The recitation of Japuji
The shared ਲੰਗਰ where all eat together in one ਪੰਗਤ
The appointment of ਮਸੰਦ representatives
The composition of ਕਬਿੱਤ-ਸਵੱਯੇ

quiz.q: What does Bhai Gurdas identify as the cardinal vice that most threatens the social body?
options: Poverty
Ingratitude (the ਅਕਿਰਤਘਣ who forgets benefits received)
Manual labour
Marriage

quiz.q: How does the householder (ਗ੍ਰਿਹਸਤੀ) ideal of the Vaars relate to renunciation?
options: It requires renunciation of family before liberation
It rejects renunciation, teaching liberation within home, work, and society like the lotus unstained by water
It treats the ascetic as the highest spiritual type
It forbids all engagement in trade and commerce

quiz.q: What distinguishes the boundary of the ਪੰਥ from the boundary of caste in the Vaars?
options: The Panth's boundary is fixed by birth and cannot be crossed
The Panth's boundary is defined by commitment to the Guru's way and is open to anyone who becomes a ਗੁਰਮੁਖ
The Panth excludes all non-Sikhs from the ਲੰਗਰ
The Panth requires a priestly caste to mediate entry

courses.title: Bhai Nand Lal Goya: Life, Times, and Literary Legacy
courses.source: Collected Works of Bhai Nand Lal Goya
courses.summary: A comprehensive intermediate study of ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਜੀ "ਗੋਯਾ" (c. 1633-1713), the Persian-trained scholar of Ghazni who became one of the most beloved Sikhs of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ and one of the ਪੰਜ ਵਿਦਵਾਨ of the Anandpur court. The course traces his youth on the Mughal frontier, his service at the imperial court of Bahadur Shah, his transformative arrival at Anandpur Sahib, and his Persian and Punjabi compositions — ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ, ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ, ਗੰਜਨਾਮਾ, ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ and others — situating him as the bridge between the classical Persian literary tradition and Sikh theology.
outcomes: Reconstruct the biography of ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਜੀ from Ghazni to Anandpur Sahib, distinguishing documented fact from later hagiographic tradition.
Explain the literary-historical context of Indo-Persian ਫ਼ਾਰਸੀ poetry and the ਤਸੱਵੁਫ਼ (Sufi) tradition that shaped his idiom.
Analyze the major works — ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ, ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ, ਗੰਜਨਾਮਾ, ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ, ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ — for their theology, form, and audience.
Evaluate how ਗੋਯਾ translated Sikh concepts of ਨਾਮ, ਗੁਰੂ and ਪ੍ਰੇਮ into the vocabulary of Persian mysticism.
Assess his historical significance as a cultural bridge and as a primary witness to the court of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ.
Apply critical methods to the textual transmission and authenticity debates surrounding works attributed to him.

terms.m: The takhallus (pen-name) of Bhai Nand Lal, a Persian word meaning 'one who speaks' or 'the eloquent speaker' — a fitting signature woven into the final couplets of his ghazals.
His principal Persian collection: a divan of around sixty-three ghazals expressing love and longing for the Guru and the Divine in classical Persian poetic form.
The 'Book of Life,' a Persian masnavi of spiritual counsel originally titled Bandginama ('Book of Devotion'), teaching the path of ਨਾਮ and remembrance.
The 'Book of Treasure,' a Persian work in prose and verse offering devotional homage to the ten Gurus, ang by ang of praise.
A Punjabi rahit-text in verse attributed to him, listing transgressions (tankhah) and the conduct expected of a Gursikh; debated in authorship.
'The Radiance of the Light' — a short Persian piece celebrating the spiritual illumination received through the Guru.
Persian, the language of Mughal administration, scholarship and high poetry, in which Goya composed the bulk of his work.
The Islamic mystical tradition (Sufism) whose vocabulary of divine love, annihilation of the self, and the beloved Goya adapted to Sikh devotion.
The classical Persian and Urdu lyric form of rhymed couplets sharing a refrain, the dominant form of the ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ.
The 'five scholars' said to grace the court of Guru Gobind Singh Ji at Anandpur; tradition counts Bhai Nand Lal among the fifty-two poets (ਬਵੰਜਾ ਕਵੀ).
The 'fifty-two poets' traditionally associated with the literary court (darbar) of Guru Gobind Singh Ji at Anandpur and Paonta Sahib.
A secretary or scribe skilled in Persian composition; Nand Lal's profession in Mughal service before and after Anandpur.
A Persian narrative or didactic poem in rhyming couplets, the form of the ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ and ਗੰਜਨਾਮਾ.
The city in the Punjab where Nand Lal was born and spent his early life before frontier service and his journey to Anandpur (sources vary between Ghazni and Multan).

references: Ganda Singh, ed. Bhai Nand Lal Granthavali. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1968.
Hans, Surjit. A Reconstruction of Sikh History from Sikh Literature. Jalandhar: ABS Publications, 1988.
Macauliffe, Max Arthur. The Sikh Religion: Its Gurus, Sacred Writings and Authors. Vol. 5. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1909.
Singh, Pritam, ed. and trans. Diwan-e-Goya of Bhai Nand Lal. Amritsar: Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, 1962.
Fenech, Louis E. The Sikh Zafar-namah of Guru Gobind Singh: A Discursive Blade in the Heart of the Mughal Empire. New York: Oxford University Press, 2013.
McLeod, W. H. Sikhs of the Khalsa: A History of the Khalsa Rahit. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2003.
Singh, Bhai Vir, ed. Bhai Nand Lal Granthavali. Reprint, Amritsar: Khalsa Samachar, 1953.
Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. The New Cambridge History of India, II.3. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1990.
Ashta, Dharam Pal. The Poetry of the Dasam Granth. New Delhi: Arun Prakashan, 1959.

lessons.title: Introduction: Why Bhai Nand Lal Matters
lessons.summary: Course overview, the figure of ਗੋਯਾ as a bridge between Persian letters and Sikh devotion, and the source-critical problems ahead.
lessons.html:
ਵਿਸ਼ਾ ਸੂਚੀ (Table of Contents)

  1. Introduction: Why Bhai Nand Lal Matters
  2. The World of Indo-Persian Letters and ਤਸੱਵੁਫ਼
  3. Birth, Youth, and the Frontier: Ghazni and ਮੁਲਤਾਨ
  4. Service at the Mughal Court and the ਮੁਨਸ਼ੀ's Craft
  5. The Turn to Anandpur: Meeting ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ
  6. The Darbar of the Tenth Guru: ਬਵੰਜਾ ਕਵੀ
  7. The ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ: Love in the Persian Ghazal
  8. The ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ and the Path of ਨਾਮ
  9. The ਗੰਜਨਾਮਾ: Treasury of Praise for the Ten Gurus
  10. Punjabi Voice: ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ, ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ and the Question of Authenticity
  11. Later Years, Death, and Transmission of the Corpus
  12. Legacy: The Bridge Between Two Worlds

A Speaker at the Threshold

Among the constellation of figures who gathered around ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ at Anandpur Sahib at the close of the seventeenth century, few are as striking as the poet who signed his verses ਗੋਯਾ — "the speaker, the eloquent one." Born into a Persian-literate household on the western edge of the Mughal world, trained in the classical sciences of his age, fluent in the idiom of ਫ਼ਾਰਸੀ that ruled the chanceries of an empire, ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਜੀ chose to lay his learning at the feet of a Guru whose Sikhs were then being forged into the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ. His life, spanning roughly 1633 to 1713, is therefore a study in crossing thresholds: between Persian and Punjabi, between the Mughal court and the Guru's darbar, between the inherited vocabulary of ਤਸੱਵੁਫ਼ and the living revelation of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ.

This course treats ਗੋਯਾ not as a footnote to the history of the tenth Guru but as a major literary figure in his own right and as a primary witness to one of the most consequential moments in Sikh history. To read him well is to read across two of the great traditions of South Asian devotion at the very point where they met.

The Shape of the Course

We will move in three broad movements. First, we reconstruct the man and his times: the world of Indo-Persian letters into which he was born, the frontier and the court that shaped his early career, and the journey that brought him to Anandpur. Second, we read his works closely — the Persian ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ, the didactic ਮਸਨਵੀ poems ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ and ਗੰਜਨਾਮਾ, and the Punjabi rahit-texts attributed to him. Third, we weigh his legacy and confront the source-critical problems that surround his corpus.

A Warning About Sources

A serious student must begin with a caution. Much of what is popularly told about ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਜੀ comes from ਸਾਖੀ (anecdote) and later hagiography, set down generations after his death. The professor of this course, ਸੁਰਜੀਤ ਹੰਸ (Surjit Hans), has argued forcefully in his A Reconstruction of Sikh History from Sikh Literature that Sikh literary sources must be read critically, with attention to when and why they were composed. We will honor that method. Where the evidence is firm, we will say so; where tradition outruns documentation — for instance over whether he was born at Ghazni or at ਮੁਲਤਾਨ, or over the exact circumstances of his first meeting with the Guru — we will mark the uncertainty rather than smooth it over.

This is not skepticism for its own sake. It is the discipline that allows ਗੋਯਾ to emerge as a real historical person rather than a pious silhouette. His poetry is intimate, urgent, and self-revealing; the more honestly we situate it, the more powerfully it speaks.

The Central Claim

The thesis that will organize our reading is this: ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਜੀ performed an act of translation in the deepest sense. He took the ready-made imagery of Persian mystical poetry — the wine, the beloved, the moth and the flame, the annihilation of the self — and re-centered it entirely upon the ਗੁਰੂ and upon ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ as revealed in Sikh teaching. The beloved of the Persian ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲ becomes, in his hands, the Guru and the Timeless One; the longing of the lover becomes the longing of the disciple for ਨਾਮ. In doing so he did not merely decorate Sikh ideas in Persian dress. He demonstrated that the deepest aspirations of the Persian devotional tradition found their fulfilment in the path opened by ਗੁਰੂ ਨਾਨਕ ਸਾਹਿਬ and carried forward by ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ. That is why, three centuries on, his ਸ਼ਬਦ are still sung in Gurdwaras and his name is spoken with love. By the end of this course you should be able to explain precisely how he accomplished this and why it mattered then and matters now.

lessons.title: The World of Indo-Persian Letters and ਤਸੱਵੁਫ਼
lessons.summary: The literary and mystical context — Persian as the language of empire and poetry, and the Sufi idiom Goya inherited and transformed.
lessons.html:
Persian: The Language of Empire and of the Soul

To understand ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਜੀ we must first understand the medium he commanded. By the seventeenth century, ਫ਼ਾਰਸੀ (Persian) had been for centuries the prestige language of administration, scholarship, and high culture across the Mughal domains. A boy of his background did not learn Persian as a foreign tongue but as the very air of educated life: the language in which revenue was recorded, letters were written, history was composed, and — crucially for us — in which poetry of extraordinary refinement was made. Persian was the Latin of Mughal India, and to be a ਮੁਨਸ਼ੀ (a master of its prose and verse) was to hold a key that opened the doors of the court.

The poetic inheritance was immense. Behind any Indo-Persian poet stood the towering presence of Hafiz of Shiraz, of Sa'di, of Jami, and above all of the mystical masnavi of Rumi. These were not distant influences but the daily companions of any literate man's imagination. Their forms — the ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲ of rhymed couplets bound by a single refrain, the ਮਸਨਵੀ of narrative or didactic couplets — and their stock of images supplied a ready vocabulary that a new poet could inhabit, vary, and turn to his own purposes.

The Imagery of ਤਸੱਵੁਫ਼

Most important of all was the tradition of ਤਸੱਵੁਫ਼, the mystical strand of Islam whose poetry sang of the soul's love for the Divine. Its imagery is famous and recognizable: the lover (ਆਸ਼ਿਕ) consumed by longing for the beloved (ਮਾਸ਼ੂਕ); the wine and the tavern that stand for spiritual intoxication; the moth that immolates itself in the candle's flame; the annihilation of the ego so that only the Divine remains. This was a poetry of intimacy and of self-abandonment, in which the boundary between human and divine love was deliberately and productively blurred.

A student should grasp that this imagery is a language — a code with shared meanings. When a Persian poet wrote of wine, no informed reader thought of literal drunkenness; they understood the intoxication of nearness to the Divine. When ਗੋਯਾ later took up these same figures, his original audience read them fluently. His genius lay in keeping the form and the resonance while redirecting the object of devotion.

Points of Contact and Difference

It would be a mistake, however, to imagine that ਗੋਯਾ simply poured Sikh content into a Sufi mould without friction. Sikh theology, as it had developed from ਗੁਰੂ ਨਾਨਕ ਸਾਹਿਬ to the tenth Guru, holds distinctive commitments. Gurbani teaches that ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ is ਨਿਰੰਕਾਰ (without form) yet wholly present; that liberation comes through ਨਾਮ and the grace of the ਸਤਿਗੁਰੂ; that the householder's life of honest labor, remembrance, and sharing is the arena of the spiritual path. The ਗੁਰੂ in Sikh thought is not merely a spiritual guide among many but the very channel of the Divine Word, the ਸ਼ਬਦ-ਗੁਰੂ. When ਗੋਯਾ writes of the beloved, then, the beloved is at once ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ and the living Guru through whom the Timeless One is known.

A Poet at the Confluence

Here lies the deep interest of his work. The Persian tradition gave him a peerless instrument for expressing yearning, surrender, and ecstatic love. Sikh teaching gave him a specific object and a specific path: ਨਾਮ, the Guru, the company of the ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤ. Where some Sufi poetry can dissolve into a generalized pantheism or an abstract union, ਗੋਯਾ's verse is anchored. It always returns to a concrete devotion — to the feet of the Guru, to the practice of remembrance, to the conduct of a Gursikh. As Gurbani in the wider Sikh tradition teaches, the Divine is found through the Guru's grace and the discipline of ਨਾਮ; ਗੋਯਾ takes the soaring vocabulary of Persian love-poetry and ties it firmly to that ground.

In the lessons that follow we will watch this confluence at work line by line. But the reader who keeps in mind this double inheritance — the splendor of the Persian poetic instrument and the specificity of the Sikh path — will already possess the master key to ਗੋਯਾ's art.
