He is neither a Persian poet who happened to admire a Guru nor a Sikh devotee who happened to know Persian. He is the rarest of things: a fully accomplished master of one tradition who became a wholehearted disciple within another, and who made the first serve the second.

lessons.title: Birth, Youth, and the Frontier: Ghazni and ਮੁਲਤਾਨ
lessons.summary: Reconstructing his early life on the Mughal frontier, his education, and the source debates over his birthplace and family.
lessons.html:
The Problem of Beginnings

The early life of ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਜੀ is precisely where the historian must be most careful. Tradition and the principal modern editors place his birth around 1633 (the year 1633 is the most commonly cited; some sources differ), and most accounts associate his family with Ghazni, the famous city of the Afghan frontier, where his father is said to have served as a ਮੁਨਸ਼ੀ in the administration of the Mughal governor. Other traditions and some scholars connect his early life with ਮੁਲਤਾਨ in the southern Punjab. We should hold both possibilities in view rather than insist on a single tidy answer; the documentary record for a private individual of this period is thin, and later biographers had reasons to round the story into shape.

What is not in doubt is the cultural milieu. He was raised in a household where Persian learning was the family trade. His father, by the common account named Diwan Chhajju Ram (the names given in tradition vary), held a respectable secretarial post, and the boy was given a thorough education in Persian and Arabic letters, in the literary classics, and in the administrative arts that such a position required.

An Education in Two Worlds

The young Nand Lal's schooling would have immersed him in the canon we surveyed in the previous lesson: the ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲ and the ਮਸਨਵੀ, the great names of Persian poetry, and the conventions of ਤਸੱਵੁਫ਼. Accounts agree that he showed unusual gifts early, composing verse while still young and earning the takhallus ਗੋਯਾ — "the eloquent speaker" — a name that would outlast every other title he held. To be honored with a pen-name was itself a mark of recognized poetic standing in that world.

At the same time, he grew up in the religiously plural society of the frontier and the Punjab, where Hindu, Muslim, and the rising Sikh community lived in close proximity and where the language of devotion crossed communal lines freely. This plural formation matters: it helps explain how a man so deeply at home in the Islamicate Persian tradition could later embrace, without any sense of contradiction, the path of the Sikh Gurus.

Early Loss and Movement

The traditional accounts tell of early hardship. The death of his father while he was still young is said to have thrown family responsibilities onto his shoulders and prompted moves in search of livelihood — from the frontier toward ਮੁਲਤਾਨ, and later toward the centers of Mughal power. Whatever the exact itinerary, the picture that emerges is of a talented young man making his way by his pen, dependent on patronage, navigating the precarious career of the professional ਮੁਨਸ਼ੀ in a competitive world.

Reading the Hagiography Critically

Here the method advocated by our professor, ਸੁਰਜੀਤ ਹੰਸ, becomes practical. Later ਸਾਖੀ literature tends to retroject his future sanctity onto his childhood, supplying portents and precocious piety. The careful reader recognizes these as the conventions of devotional biography rather than as transcripts of fact. This does not make them worthless — they tell us how the Sikh community remembered and honored him — but it means we cannot mine them for hard chronology without corroboration.

What we can say with confidence is structural rather than anecdotal. ਗੋਯਾ was a product of the Indo-Persian frontier intelligentsia: highly literate, mobile, dependent on service, and formed by a cosmopolitan culture in which Persian poetry and mystical devotion were the common currency of the educated. These facts of formation are far more revealing than any single dated event, because they explain the man he became.

Why the Frontier Matters

The frontier upbringing left two durable marks on his work. First, his Persian was not provincial but accomplished, the equal of any court poet's — a fact that would secure his place both in Mughal service and, later, in the literary darbar at Anandpur. Second, his early exposure to a society where Hindu, Muslim, and Sikh devotion mingled gave him an instinctive ease in moving between religious vocabularies. When he later wrote of ਨਾਮ and the ਗੁਰੂ in the imagery of the Persian ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲ, he was drawing on a lifetime of living at confluences. The boy of the frontier became the poet of the threshold. As we turn next to his years in Mughal service, keep in mind that everything he learned in this formative period — the craft, the imagery, the plural sensibility — was being prepared, though he could not have known it, for a single destination: the court of the tenth Guru.

lessons.title: Service at the Mughal Court and the ਮੁਨਸ਼ੀ's Craft
lessons.summary: His career in imperial service, the tradition of his employment under prince Mu'azzam (later Bahadur Shah), and what the ਮੁਨਸ਼ੀ's profession entailed.
lessons.html:
The Career of a Master Secretary

Having been formed as a Persian scholar of the first rank, ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਜੀ followed the natural path of his class: service in the Mughal administration as a ਮੁਨਸ਼ੀ. The profession deserves explanation, for it was both humble and exalted. A ਮੁਨਸ਼ੀ was a secretary, a drafter of correspondence and documents, but at the highest level he was far more — a stylist whose command of elegant Persian could make or break a patron's reputation, a confidential adviser, and often a man of real influence behind the formal hierarchy of office. The best munshis were prized possessions, recruited and retained by the most powerful patrons.

In the Household of a Prince

The strongest strand of tradition places ਗੋਯਾ in the service of prince Mu'azzam, the son of the emperor Aurangzeb who would later ascend the throne as Bahadur Shah. According to these accounts, Nand Lal's brilliance as a Persian stylist brought him to the prince's notice and into a position of trust at the imperial establishment in or around Delhi and Agra. A well-known ਸਾਖੀ tells of a moment when his learning was tested — a challenge to interpret a Qur'anic verse that had baffled the court's scholars, which he is said to have resolved with such insight that it both elevated him and provoked dangerous envy. Whether or not the episode is literally true, it dramatizes a real condition of his life: he was a Hindu (in the broad sense of the time) excelling in a Muslim court, admired and resented in equal measure.

This tension — the brilliant outsider whose very excellence made him vulnerable — is historically plausible and helps explain his eventual movement away from imperial service toward Anandpur. The court was a place of patronage but also of peril, where the favor that raised a man could be withdrawn, and where religious difference could be turned into a weapon by rivals.

What the Craft Gave Him

However we weigh the particular anecdotes, the years of Mughal service had concrete and lasting effects on ਗੋਯਾ as a writer. Three are worth naming.

  • Mastery of register. Drafting at the highest level disciplined his Persian into precision and flexibility. The same pen that could compose a formal imperial letter could turn to the intimacy of the ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲ. This range is everywhere visible in his work.
  • Knowledge of power. He saw the Mughal state from the inside — its grandeur and its cruelties, its patronage and its intrigues. This first-hand knowledge gives weight to his later choice. When such a man turns from the imperial court to the Guru's darbar, the turn is not naïve; it is made with open eyes.
  • A network and a reputation. His standing as a Persian poet of the front rank, earned in these years, is what made him a credible and welcome figure when he later joined the literary circle of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ. He arrived at Anandpur not as an unknown seeker but as an established master.

The Pull of a Different Court

The Mughal world offered ਗੋਯਾ everything a man of his training could want: status, livelihood, proximity to power. And yet the trajectory of his life is a movement away from that world toward another kind of court entirely. The historian must resist both extremes here — neither reducing his turn to Sikhism to mere flight from court danger, nor inflating it into a sudden miraculous conversion stripped of all human context. The truth, as far as we can reconstruct it, lies in between. A man who knew the imperial court intimately, who had tasted both its rewards and its insecurities, encountered in the person and teaching of the tenth Guru something the court could not give: a path of devotion, a community of equals in the ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤ, and a beloved worthy of the longing his poetry had always expressed.

The Threshold of Anandpur

We should also note that, by tradition, ਗੋਯਾ did not abandon the practical world of service even after his attachment to the Guru; some accounts have him returning to administrative work, even in the service of Bahadur Shah, in later years. His life was not a clean break but a layered double belonging — a man of the Mughal chancery whose heart had been claimed by Anandpur. That very doubleness is what makes him such a valuable witness and such a singular poet. In the next lesson we follow him across the decisive threshold: the journey to Anandpur Sahib and the meeting that reoriented his life and his art.

lessons.title: The Turn to Anandpur: Meeting ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ
lessons.summary: The journey to Anandpur Sahib, the traditions of his first meeting with the Guru, and the spiritual reorientation that followed.
lessons.html:
The Journey to the Guru

The pivot of ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਜੀ's life is his arrival at Anandpur Sahib and his acceptance as a Sikh of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ. Anandpur in the closing decades of the seventeenth century was no ordinary place. Founded by the ninth Guru, ਗੁਰੂ ਤੇਗ਼ ਬਹਾਦਰ ਜੀ, it had become under the tenth Guru a vibrant center of devotion, learning, martial preparation, and literary creativity. To it came seekers, soldiers, scholars, and poets from across northern India. For a man of ਗੋਯਾ's gifts and inclinations, Anandpur was a magnet.

The traditional accounts describe his coming as the culmination of a deepening longing. Whether he came first drawn by the fame of the Guru's court, or whether — as some ਸਾਖੀ relate — he came seeking refuge from the dangers that his very brilliance had stirred up in Mughal circles, the result was the same. In the presence of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ he found the beloved his poetry had always been seeking.

The Meeting and Its Meaning

Here again we must read the tradition with care. The hagiographies render the meeting in the language of instant and total recognition: the accomplished Persian master humbled and completed in the Guru's presence, his learning at last finding its true object. Such accounts are theological portraits as much as historical reports. Yet beneath the conventions lies something we can affirm. ਗੋਯਾ's own poetry testifies, more reliably than any ਸਾਖੀ, to a profound and transformative attachment to the Guru. The intensity of devotion in the ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ is not borrowed convention; it is lived experience set to verse.

The spiritual logic of the turn is worth drawing out. Everything in ਗੋਯਾ's formation had prepared him to recognize and to love a perfect spiritual master. The Persian tradition had taught him to long for a beloved; ਤਸੱਵੁਫ਼ had taught him that the self must be surrendered; his years at court had taught him the emptiness of worldly favor. In ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ all of these found their resolution. The Guru was the beloved who was also the channel of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ; surrender to him was surrender to the Divine; and the community of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ offered a belonging deeper than any patronage.

The Guru's Court as Spiritual Home

What ਗੋਯਾ found at Anandpur was not only a master but a milieu suited to his whole being. The tenth Guru gathered around himself a remarkable literary establishment, and a Persian poet of the first rank was not merely welcome but valued. He could continue to be entirely himself — a master of ਫ਼ਾਰਸੀ, a poet of the ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲ — while pouring that mastery into a new devotion. He did not have to renounce his art to become a Sikh; rather, his art was redeemed and reoriented. This is a crucial point for understanding his significance. Sikhism did not ask the Persian poet to fall silent; it gave his poetry its truest theme.

Devotion in His Own Words

The character of his attachment is best heard in his verse rather than described from outside. Across the ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ he returns again and again to the longing of the disciple for the Guru and for the vision of the Divine. In the spirit of his refrain, ਗੋਯਾ speaks as one who has tasted nearness and cannot bear separation: "ਬੇ ਤੂ ਯਕ ਦਮ ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀ ਕਰਦਨ ਮੁਹਾਲ" — "Without You, to live even for a single breath is impossible." The line distills the whole of his spiritual posture: a life that has found its center and can no longer conceive of itself apart from the beloved. (We will examine such verses closely in later lessons; here it is enough to register the depth of feeling.)

A Reoriented Life

The turn to Anandpur did not, as we have noted, mean a simple departure from the world. Tradition has ਗੋਯਾ continuing in practical service and moving between worlds even after his attachment to the Guru. But the center of gravity of his life and his art had shifted decisively. From this point on, the great subject of his poetry is the Guru and the Divine made known through the Guru; the great practice it commends is ਨਾਮ; and the great community it presupposes is the ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤ. The Persian master had become ਗੋਯਾ the Sikh — and it is as ਗੋਯਾ the Sikh that he speaks to us still. In the next lesson we step into the darbar itself, to see the literary culture of Anandpur within which his work took shape.

lessons.title: The Darbar of the Tenth Guru: ਬਵੰਜਾ ਕਵੀ
lessons.summary: The literary court of Guru Gobind Singh Ji, the tradition of the fifty-two poets, and Goya's place among them.
lessons.html:
A Court of Poets

To appreciate ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਜੀ fully we must see him in company. ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ was himself a poet of extraordinary power and a patron of literature on a grand scale. At Anandpur Sahib and earlier at ਪਾਉਂਟਾ ਸਾਹਿਬ, the Guru gathered a literary establishment that Sikh tradition remembers as the ਬਵੰਜਾ ਕਵੀ — the "fifty-two poets." The number is traditional and should be treated as emblematic rather than as an exact census; what it conveys is the scale and seriousness of the Guru's literary court. Among these poets, ਗੋਯਾ holds an honored place, often named together with a handful of the most distinguished as one of the leading scholars (ਵਿਦਵਾਨ) of the establishment.

The Programme of the Darbar

The literary work of the Guru's court had purpose and direction. The Guru commissioned and inspired translations and original compositions that retold the great narratives of heroism and devotion, that celebrated the Divine in martial and ecstatic registers, and that equipped the emerging ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ with a literature adequate to its spirit. This was poetry in the service of a community's self-understanding and courage. The darbar was thus not a leisured salon but a workshop of cultural formation, producing the texts that would shape Sikh imagination for generations.

Within this programme, ਗੋਯਾ occupied a distinctive niche. Most of the court's major output was in the Braj-influenced poetic idiom of the day. ਗੋਯਾ's special contribution was ਫ਼ਾਰਸੀ — the Persian language and its high mystical poetry. He brought to the Guru's court the prestige and the resources of the dominant literary culture of the Mughal world and placed them at the service of Sikh devotion. In doing so he extended the reach of the darbar's literature into the very idiom of the imperial elite.

The Significance of a Persian Voice

Why did it matter that the Guru's court should include a master of Persian? Several reasons stand out.

  • Reach. Persian was the language of the educated across northern India and beyond. A Persian poet of ਗੋਯਾ's calibre could carry the devotion of the Guru's house into circles that the vernacular could not easily reach.
  • Prestige. By producing first-rate Persian poetry on Sikh themes, the darbar demonstrated that the path of the Gurus could be expressed in the most refined idiom of the age, on equal terms with anything the imperial court could show.
  • Translation of the tradition. ਗੋਯਾ's work made the concepts of Sikh devotion — ਨਾਮ, ਗੁਰੂ, ਪ੍ਰੇਮ, surrender — available in the vocabulary of ਤਸੱਵੁਫ਼, building a bridge across which understanding could pass.

Relationship with the Guru

The tradition preserves a memory of genuine warmth between ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ and ਗੋਯਾ. The poet is remembered as a beloved Sikh, close to the Guru, honored for his learning and his devotion alike. Some accounts attach particular sayings and incidents to their relationship; as always, these should be received as the community's affectionate memory rather than as documented transcript. But the affection itself is well-founded, for it is written into ਗੋਯਾ's own verse, which speaks of the Guru with an intimacy that cannot be feigned.

A Workshop of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ Era

It is worth situating ਗੋਯਾ's years at the darbar within the larger history unfolding around him. This was the era of the founding of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ in 1699 — the transformation of the Sikh community into a disciplined order with its distinctive form and code of conduct. The literary court did not stand apart from these momentous developments; it was part of the same creative ferment. The poetry produced there, including ਗੋਯਾ's, belongs to the cultural dimension of the Khalsa's birth. When we later examine the Punjabi rahit-texts attributed to him — works concerned with the conduct of a Gursikh — we will see his writing touching directly on the disciplinary life of this new community.

The Poet Among Poets

To read ਗੋਯਾ as a solitary genius would be to misread him. He was a member of a brilliant company, contributing a particular and precious voice to a collective enterprise directed by the Guru himself. His Persian poetry is one instrument in a great orchestra. Yet it is an instrument no one else in that court could play with his mastery, and the music he made on it has outlasted much of the rest in the living devotion of the Sikh community. Having placed him in his court, we are now ready to turn to the works themselves, beginning with his crowning achievement, the ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ.

lessons.title: The ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ: Love in the Persian Ghazal
lessons.summary: Close study of his principal Persian divan — its form, its imagery, and its transformation of the Sufi ghazal into Sikh devotion.
lessons.html:
The Crown of His Work

The ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ is the masterpiece on which ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਜੀ's literary fame chiefly rests. A ਦੀਵਾਨ, in the Persian tradition, is a collected body of a poet's ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲ, and Goya's divan gathers some sixty-odd lyrics (the count is usually given as around sixty-three ghazals) in which the language of love-poetry is wholly given over to devotion. Several of its ਸ਼ਬਦ have entered the living devotional life of the Sikh community and are sung in kirtan to this day, which is the surest testimony to their spiritual power.

The Form: The ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲ

The ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲ is a lyric of rhyming couplets bound together by a shared rhyme and refrain, in which the final couplet customarily contains the poet's takhallus. ਗੋਯਾ works within this strict and beautiful form with complete mastery. The convention of naming oneself in the closing couplet allows him a characteristic gesture: again and again the poem turns at its end to ਗੋਯਾ himself — "the speaker" — as one who can only speak because he has been given something to say by the Guru. The signature thus becomes a small act of humility, the eloquent one confessing that his eloquence is a gift.

The Imagery Transformed

The deep interest of the divan lies in what we anticipated in Lesson 2: the redirection of the entire apparatus of Persian love-poetry onto the Guru and the Divine. The familiar figures are all present — the beloved whose face is light, the lover sleepless with longing, the separation that is agony and the union that is bliss, the wine of devotion, the moth and the flame. But the beloved is now ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ and the Guru through whom the Timeless One is known. The intoxication is the intoxication of ਨਾਮ. The annihilation of the self is the dissolving of ਹਉਮੈ (egoism) in remembrance.

Consider the refrain we glimpsed earlier: "ਬੇ ਤੂ ਯਕ ਦਮ ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀ ਕਰਦਨ ਮੁਹਾਲ" — "Without You, to live even for a single breath is impossible." In a purely human love-poem this would be a lover's hyperbole. In ਗੋਯਾ's hands it is a theological statement: the soul cannot live apart from the Divine beloved; remembrance is the very breath of spiritual life. The form remains that of the love-lyric; the meaning has been raised to the level of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ's teaching that life without ਨਾਮ is no life at all.

The Centrality of the Guru

What distinguishes ਗੋਯਾ from a generic mystical poet is the concrete centrality of the Guru. His longing is not for an abstract Absolute but for the beloved Guru in whom the Absolute is made present and accessible. This is thoroughly Sikh. In Sikh teaching the ਸਤਿਗੁਰੂ is the indispensable means by which ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ is realized; the disciple's love for the Guru and love for the Divine are not two loves but one. ਗੋਯਾ's divan is in a sense an extended meditation on this single truth, sung in the most exquisite Persian.

Reading a Ghazal Spiritually

A student approaching the divan should learn to read on two levels at once, as its first audience did. On the surface is the immemorial drama of love and separation, with all its sensuous imagery. Beneath and through that surface is the spiritual reality: the soul's relationship to the Guru and to ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. The pleasure of the poetry lies precisely in holding both levels together — in feeling the human intensity of the longing while knowing its divine object. This is the genius of the ਤਸੱਵੁਫ਼ tradition, here placed wholly at the service of Sikh devotion.

Why It Endures

The ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ has endured for three centuries for reasons both literary and spiritual. As literature it is Persian poetry of a high order, the work of a true master of the ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲ. As devotion it gives voice, with rare beauty and intensity, to the love of the Guru and the longing for ਨਾਮ that lie at the heart of Sikh spiritual life. That some of its compositions are sung in kirtan means that ਗੋਯਾ's love-poetry has become the community's prayer — a fate granted to very few poets. When a sangat raises one of his ਸ਼ਬਦ, the bridge he built between Persian letters and Sikh devotion is crossed anew, and the eloquent speaker speaks again. In the next lesson we turn from his lyric to his didactic poetry, where the same devotion takes the form of counsel.

lessons.title: The ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ and the Path of ਨਾਮ
lessons.summary: Study of his major didactic masnavi — its teaching on remembrance, devotion, and the conduct of the spiritual life.
lessons.html:
From Lyric to Counsel

If the ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ is the song of ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਜੀ's love, the ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ is its teaching. This Persian ਮਸਨਵੀ — a poem of rhyming couplets in the didactic tradition — is among his most substantial works. Tradition holds that it was originally titled ਬੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ, the "Book of Devotion," and that the Guru himself suggested renaming it ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ, the "Book of Life," since true devotion is true life. The story, whatever its historicity, captures the work's theme exactly: that the life worth living is the life of remembrance.

The Form of the Didactic ਮਸਨਵੀ

The ਮਸਨਵੀ form, made supreme in Persian by Rumi, is ideally suited to sustained spiritual instruction. Its rhyming couplets carry the reader forward through an unfolding argument or meditation, accumulating force through repetition and variation. ਗੋਯਾ uses the form to lay out, with eloquence and warmth, the essentials of the devotional path as he had received them from ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ.

The Centrality of ਨਾਮ

The heart of the ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ is the practice of ਨਾਮ — the remembrance of the Divine Name. This is the central discipline of Sikh spiritual life as taught throughout ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, and ਗੋਯਾ makes it the axis of his counsel. He urges the constant remembrance of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, the keeping of the Divine in the heart at all times, the turning of every breath into an act of devotion. In the spirit of his teaching, the remembrance of the Name is the treasure beside which all worldly gain is poverty.

This emphasis places ਗੋਯਾ squarely within the mainstream of Sikh teaching. Gurbani teaches that liberation and peace come through ਨਾਮ, through the grace of the ਸਤਿਗੁਰੂ, and through the company of the ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤ. The ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ is, in effect, an extended Persian elaboration of this teaching, addressed to readers who would receive it in the idiom of ਤਸੱਵੁਫ਼.

Devotion and Conduct

The work is not a treatise of abstract mysticism but a guide to a life. Alongside the call to remembrance, ਗੋਯਾ counsels humility, the renunciation of ਹਉਮੈ, love for the Divine and for fellow seekers, and the orientation of the whole self toward the beloved. The devotional life he describes is intense and total, demanding the surrender of the ego, yet it is also a life of love rather than mere austerity. The reader is drawn not driven, persuaded by the sweetness of the beloved rather than frightened by threat.

The Sufi Vocabulary in Service of Sikh Teaching

Here again we see ਗੋਯਾ's characteristic act of translation. The vocabulary of the ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ is drawn from the world of Persian mysticism: the language of the lover and beloved, of annihilation and subsistence, of the heart as the seat of the Divine. But the content is Sikh. The remembrance he commends is ਨਾਮ; the master through whom the Divine is reached is the ਗੁਰੂ; the community of seekers is the ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤ. He demonstrates that the Persian mystical tradition's deepest insights — that the self must be surrendered, that the Divine is to be sought within, that love is the highest path — find their proper completion in the discipline of remembrance taught by the Sikh Gurus.

The Pastoral Voice

One should notice the tone of the ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ. It is pastoral, addressed to a fellow traveler, warm and encouraging. ਗੋਯਾ writes not as a remote authority but as one who has walked the path and longs for others to know its joy. This pastoral warmth is part of why the work has been cherished. It does not merely instruct; it invites. The reader feels addressed as a friend and beckoned toward a treasure the poet has himself found.

A Book to Live By

The ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ thus complements the ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ perfectly. Where the divan sings the experience of love, the ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ teaches the way of life that makes such love possible and fruitful. Together they show ਗੋਯਾ whole: the lover and the teacher, the poet of ecstasy and the guide of conduct. And both rest on the same foundation — the centrality of ਨਾਮ, the indispensability of the ਗੁਰੂ, and the transformation of the self through devotion. The "Book of Life" earns its title: it teaches that to remember the Divine is to live, and to forget is to be, however busy, already dead. We turn next to a third major Persian work, the ਗੰਜਨਾਮਾ, in which ਗੋਯਾ's devotion takes the form of praise for the ten Gurus in succession.

lessons.title: The ਗੰਜਨਾਮਾ: Treasury of Praise for the Ten Gurus
lessons.summary: Study of the 'Book of Treasure' — its praise of the ten Gurus, its theology of Guruship, and its prose-and-verse form.
lessons.html:
A Treasury of Praise

The ਗੰਜਨਾਮਾ, the "Book of Treasure," is among the most theologically interesting of ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਜੀ's Persian works. Its subject is the ten Gurus, from ਗੁਰੂ ਨਾਨਕ ਸਾਹਿਬ to ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ, each praised and celebrated in turn. The work is distinctive in form, combining passages of ornate Persian prose with verse, so that praise rises and falls between the two registers. Its title declares its theme: the Gurus are the treasure, and to contemplate them is to grow rich in the one wealth that matters.

The Theology of ਗੁਰੂ

To understand the ਗੰਜਨਾਮਾ a student must grasp the Sikh doctrine of Guruship that underlies it. In Sikh theology the ten Gurus are understood to share a single spiritual light (ਜੋਤਿ), passed from one to the next, so that though the human persons differ, the Guruship is one. The Gurus are the means by which ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ is made known; to praise them is therefore to praise the Divine working through them. ਗੋਯਾ's successive celebration of each Guru is built upon this understanding. He does not praise ten separate teachers but the one light shining through ten windows.

This is why the ਗੰਜਨਾਮਾ can lavish such exalted language on the Gurus without any impropriety. The praise is ultimately directed beyond the human persons to the Divine reality they embody and reveal. Gurbani in the Sikh tradition teaches that the Guru and ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ are to be understood together, the Guru as the very form through which the formless is known. ਗੋਯਾ's treasury of praise is an extended poetic enactment of this teaching.

Praise as Devotion

In the devotional traditions of South Asia and the Persianate world alike, praise (ਸਿਫ਼ਤਿ-ਸਾਲਾਹ in the broader Sikh vocabulary) is itself a spiritual discipline. To recount the glory of the beloved is to fix the heart upon the beloved, to kindle love, and to be transformed by contemplation. The ਗੰਜਨਾਮਾ is praise of this kind. Its ornate Persian is not mere decoration; it is the offering of the poet's highest art as an act of devotion. The beauty of the language is itself a form of worship, the finest words laid at the feet of the Gurus.

A Persian Frame for Sikh History

The ਗੰਜਨਾਮਾ also performs a quiet historiographical function. By moving through the ten Gurus in succession, ਗੋਯਾ presents, in Persian, the shape of Sikh sacred history — the unbroken transmission of the light from Nanak to Gobind Singh. For a Persian-reading audience this was a way of grasping the coherence and continuity of the Sikh tradition. The ten Gurus are shown as a single unfolding reality, culminating in the Guru under whom ਗੋਯਾ himself lived. The work thus carries Sikh self-understanding into the language and literary world of the Mughal elite.

The Place of the Tenth Guru

There is a special intimacy in ਗੋਯਾ's praise of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ, his own living Guru and beloved. The reader senses that the whole succession of praise has been building toward the Guru whom the poet knew face to face, in whose darbar he served, and whose love had reoriented his life. The theological doctrine of the one light passing through ten Gurus becomes, for ਗੋਯਾ, a lived reality, for the light that shone in ਗੁਰੂ ਨਾਨਕ ਸਾਹਿਬ shone before his own eyes in the tenth Master.

The Treasure Defined

The ਗੰਜਨਾਮਾ completes a triad with the ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ and the ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ. The divan sings the love; the ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ teaches the path; the ਗੰਜਨਾਮਾ praises the Gurus through whom love and path alike are given. All three rest on the same foundation and serve the same devotion. Reading them together, we see the wholeness of ਗੋਯਾ's vision: ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ to be loved, ਨਾਮ to be remembered, the ਗੁਰੂ to be praised and followed. The treasure of the title is finally nothing other than this — the Guru, and through the Guru the Divine, possessing which the soul possesses everything. Having surveyed the great Persian works, we turn next to a different and more contested part of his legacy: the Punjabi rahit-texts attributed to his name.

lessons.title: Punjabi Voice: ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ, ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ and the Question of Authenticity
lessons.summary: The Punjabi rahit-texts attributed to Goya, their content on Sikh conduct, and the scholarly debates over their authorship.
lessons.html:
A Different Register

Alongside the Persian masterpieces stands a body of Punjabi writing attributed to ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਜੀ, of which the best known is the ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ. These texts belong to a quite different genre and serve a different purpose from the Persian poetry. Where the ਦੀਵਾਨ sings of mystical love and the ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ teaches inward devotion, the ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ and related ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ texts concern the outward conduct and discipline of the Gursikh — the rules of the Sikh way of life as it crystallized in the era of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ.

What the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ Genre Is

A ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ is a text setting out the ਰਹਿਤ — the code of conduct binding upon Sikhs, and especially upon the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ. The word ਤਨਖਾਹ in this context means a transgression of the code and the penance due for it; a ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ thus enumerates faults to be avoided and the conduct expected of a faithful Sikh. These texts are precious sources for the history of Sikh practice, recording — or prescribing — the norms of the community in its formative period. The scholar W. H. McLeod devoted careful study to this whole body of rahit-literature, and his work is essential reading for anyone approaching these texts seriously.

The Content of the ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ

The ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ attributed to ਗੋਯਾ is a Punjabi verse text, cast in the form of instruction, that lays out the conduct of a true Gursikh and warns against various transgressions. It touches on devotion, discipline, ethical behavior, and loyalty to the Guru and the Panth. The text is notable for its memorable formulations of Sikh ideals, and certain of its lines have become proverbial in the community as expressions of the Sikh spirit of devotion and service. As a witness to the ethos of the Khalsa era, it is of considerable interest whatever its precise authorship.

The Problem of Authenticity

Here we must engage directly with one of the central source-critical problems of our subject, in the spirit of our professor ਸੁਰਜੀਤ ਹੰਸ's insistence on critical reading. The Persian works — the ਦੀਵਾਨ, the ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ, the ਗੰਜਨਾਮਾ — are securely associated with ਗੋਯਾ; their language, style, and devotional voice are consistent and bear his unmistakable signature. The Punjabi rahit-texts are a different matter. The ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ literature as a whole had a complex history of transmission, with texts being copied, expanded, and reattributed over time, and with later material sometimes accruing to honored names. Scholars have therefore debated whether the ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ and similar works in their received form are genuinely the composition of ਗੋਯਾ, or whether they represent later material attached to his prestigious name, or some layered combination of the two.

A responsible student does not resolve this debate by fiat. The honest position is to recognize that these texts are attributed to ਗੋਯਾ within Sikh tradition, that they are valuable historical sources for the rahit regardless of authorship, and that the question of their precise origin remains genuinely open and contested among scholars. To claim certainty in either direction would be to abandon the critical method this course upholds.

Why the Attribution Is Plausible — and Why Caution Remains

There are reasons the attribution to ਗੋਯਾ is not unreasonable. He was a close and beloved Sikh of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ during the very period when the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ's discipline was being articulated; a man so placed might well have set down such instruction. Yet the linguistic and stylistic gulf between the polished Persian of the divan and the Punjabi of the rahit-texts, together with the known fluidity of rahit-transmission, rightly keeps scholars cautious. The two bodies of work address different audiences in different languages for different purposes, and it is possible that not all that bears his name in the Punjabi corpus flowed from his pen.

The Lesson of the Debate

This question is more than a technicality; it is a model of how Sikh literary history must be done. The student who learns to distinguish the securely attributed Persian masterpieces from the more complex Punjabi rahit-corpus, and to hold the latter's authorship as an open question, has learned the essential discipline of the field. ਗੋਯਾ's greatness rests securely on his Persian achievement; the Punjabi texts add a further, more debated dimension to his legacy. Both deserve study; each deserves to be read with the appropriate degree of confidence. In the final two lessons we turn to the close of his life and to the question of his enduring significance.

lessons.title: Later Years, Death, and Transmission of the Corpus
lessons.summary: His later life and return to service, the traditions of his death around 1713, and how his works were preserved and transmitted.
lessons.html:
The Later Years

The closing decades of ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਜੀ's life are, like its beginning, imperfectly documented. The broad picture preserved in tradition is of a man who, after his transformative years in connection with ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ, continued to move between the world of practical service and the world of devotion. Some accounts place him again in administrative employment in his later years, including service connected with Bahadur Shah after that prince became emperor in 1707. Tradition also associates his later life with ਮੁਲਤਾਨ, where he is said to have established a center of learning. As always, these details come to us through the filter of later memory and should be held with appropriate caution.

What the period reveals, if the traditions are even broadly reliable, is the same doubleness that marked his whole life: a man at home in two worlds, the Mughal and the Sikh, never wholly leaving either. His heart belonged to the Guru; his profession kept him tied to the chancery. This is not contradiction but the texture of a real life lived at a confluence of worlds.

The Turbulent Background

The student should remember the momentous and tragic events that framed these years. ਗੋਯਾ lived through the period of the great sacrifices of the Guru's house — the martyrdoms of the ਸਾਹਿਬਜ਼ਾਦੇ, the evacuation of Anandpur, and in 1708 the passing of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ himself and the vesting of eternal Guruship in the ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ. To have loved the tenth Guru as ਗੋਯਾ did and to have outlived him was to bear a profound loss. His poetry of longing and separation acquires a further poignancy when read against this background, though we must be careful not to read specific later events into verses whose dating is uncertain.

The Tradition of His Death

ਗੋਯਾ is generally said to have died around 1713 (the year 1713 is the most commonly cited, with some variation in the sources), some years after his beloved Guru. The accounts of his death, like those of his birth, are wrapped in the conventions of devotional memory. What matters for us is that he died as he had lived for his last decades — a Sikh of the tenth Guru and a poet of the Guru's praise, his great works complete and ready to be passed on.

The Transmission of the Corpus

The survival of ਗੋਯਾ's writings is itself a significant chapter. Persian manuscripts of the ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ, the ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ, and the ਗੰਜਨਾਮਾ were copied and preserved within the Sikh community and beyond, treasured for their devotional power. The Punjabi rahit-texts circulated within the more fluid manuscript tradition of the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ literature. Over the generations the corpus was gathered, copied, and eventually edited and printed.

Modern scholarship owes a particular debt to the editors who assembled and published his works. The great collected edition prepared by ਗੰਡਾ ਸਿੰਘ (Ganda Singh), the Bhai Nand Lal Granthavali, brought the corpus together for critical study, and earlier the labors of ਭਾਈ ਵੀਰ ਸਿੰਘ (Bhai Vir Singh) had served the same end. The translation and edition of the ਦੀਵਾਨ by ਪ੍ਰੀਤਮ ਸਿੰਘ (Pritam Singh) and the inclusion of ਗੋਯਾ in Max Arthur Macauliffe's monumental The Sikh Religion carried his name and work to wider scholarly and English-reading audiences. Through these efforts the words of the eloquent speaker were saved from the hazards of manuscript transmission and made available to the modern world.

The Critical Task Continues

The transmission history also explains why the source-critical problems we have noted exist. A corpus that passed through generations of copying, that crossed languages and genres, and that gathered around it the affection and the embellishments of a devoted community, inevitably presents the scholar with questions of authenticity, dating, and original form. The work of editors like ਗੰਡਾ ਸਿੰਘ and critical historians like ਸੁਰਜੀਤ ਹੰਸ is precisely the work of sorting the secure from the doubtful, the original from the accreted. That work is not finished, and a student of ਗੋਯਾ today inherits both the treasure and the responsibility of its critical care.

A Life Completed

By his death around 1713, ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਜੀ had completed one of the most remarkable literary and spiritual journeys of his age: from the Persian-literate frontier, through the Mughal court, to the darbar of the tenth Guru and a body of devotional poetry that the Sikh community would cherish for centuries. In the final lesson we step back to assess the meaning of that journey and the legacy of the bridge he built.

lessons.title: Legacy: The Bridge Between Two Worlds
lessons.summary: Synthesis of his historical and literary significance as a bridge between Persian tradition and Sikh theology, and his living legacy.
lessons.html:
Taking the Measure of ਗੋਯਾ

We come at last to the question with which we began: why does ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਜੀ matter? Having traced his life from the frontier to Anandpur and read his works from the ਦੀਵਾਨ to the ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ, we are now in a position to answer with precision. His significance is at once historical and literary and spiritual, and it can be summed up in the image with which we opened — the bridge.

The Literary Bridge

First, ਗੋਯਾ stands as a bridge between two of the great literary traditions of South Asia: the classical Persian poetry of the Mughal world and the devotional literature of the Sikhs. He was a master of the ਫ਼ਾਰਸੀ ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲ and ਮਸਨਵੀ, the equal of the court poets of his age, and he placed that complete mastery at the service of Sikh devotion. In doing so he created something genuinely new: a body of first-rate Persian mystical poetry whose beloved is the Guru and whose treasure is ਨਾਮ. He proved that the loftiest idiom of the age could carry the deepest content of the Sikh path. No one before or after has done quite what he did, with quite his mastery.

The Theological Bridge

Second, and more profoundly, ਗੋਯਾ built a theological bridge. He took the vocabulary of ਤਸੱਵੁਫ਼ — the lover and the beloved, the wine of devotion, the annihilation of the self — and showed that its deepest aspirations find their fulfilment in the path of the Sikh Gurus. The Persian mystical tradition longed for union with the Divine and for the surrender of the ego; ਗੋਯਾ demonstrated that this longing is answered in the remembrance of ਨਾਮ, in love of the ਗੁਰੂ, and in the company of the ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤ. He did not water down Sikh teaching to fit a foreign mould; he raised the foreign idiom to express Sikh truth. The result is a kind of dialogue between traditions conducted within a single poetic voice.

The Historical Witness

Third, ਗੋਯਾ is a precious historical witness. As a member of the literary darbar of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ and a beloved Sikh of the tenth Master, he stands close to one of the most consequential moments in Sikh history — the era of the founding of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ. His Persian works show us the devotional and intellectual culture of that court from the inside, and the Punjabi rahit-texts attributed to him touch directly on the disciplinary self-fashioning of the new community. Read critically, as our professor ਸੁਰਜੀਤ ਹੰਸ insists they must be, his writings illuminate the spirit of the age that made the modern Sikh community.

The Living Legacy

Fourth, and most movingly, ਗੋਯਾ's legacy is living, not merely historical. His ਸ਼ਬਦ are sung in kirtan in Gurdwaras to this day; his Persian love-poetry has become the prayer of the sangat. Few poets achieve this. That a Persian ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲ written three centuries ago should rise from the throats of a worshipping community is the surest sign that ਗੋਯਾ touched something real and enduring. The bridge he built is not a monument to be admired from a distance but a path still walked, every time his words are sung.

A Model of Confluence

There is, finally, a larger lesson in ਗੋਯਾ's life for our own time. He shows what becomes possible when deep mastery of one tradition meets wholehearted devotion within another — not syncretism that blurs all distinctions, nor sectarianism that walls them off, but a generous confluence in which the resources of one tradition are placed in service of the truth found in another. ਗੋਯਾ remained the consummate Persian poet even as he became the wholehearted Sikh, and each identity enriched the other. In an age that too often forces a choice between cosmopolitan learning and rooted devotion, his example reconciles them.

The Eloquent Speaker

He signed himself ਗੋਯਾ — the speaker, the eloquent one — yet his eloquence was always, by his own confession, a gift received at the feet of the Guru. In studying him we have watched a man of the world's finest learning lay that learning down as an offering, and receive it back transformed into prayer. That is his enduring lesson and his enduring gift. The student who has worked through this course should now be able to read his verses with understanding, to situate him in his time, to weigh the evidence for his life critically, and above all to hear in his Persian couplets the voice of a Sikh in love with the Guru and the Timeless One. The bridge stands; we are invited to cross.

  • Fenech, Louis E. The Sikh Zafar-namah of Guru Gobind Singh: A Discursive Blade in the Heart of the Mughal Empire. New York: Oxford University Press, 2013.
  • Ganda Singh, ed. Bhai Nand Lal Granthavali. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1968.
  • Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. The New Cambridge History of India, II.3. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1990.
  • Hans, Surjit. A Reconstruction of Sikh History from Sikh Literature. Jalandhar: ABS Publications, 1988.
  • Macauliffe, Max Arthur. The Sikh Religion: Its Gurus, Sacred Writings and Authors. Vol. 5. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1909.
