quiz.q: What is the meaning of the takhallus (pen-name) ਗੋਯਾ that Bhai Nand Lal wove into the final couplets of his ghazals?
options: 'The wanderer' or 'traveler'
'The speaker' or 'the eloquent one'
'The servant of the Guru'
'The poet of Multan'

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes Bhai Nand Lal's central literary-theological achievement?
options: He translated the Guru Granth Sahib into Persian prose
He invented an entirely new poetic form unknown to Persian tradition
He redirected the imagery of Persian mystical (ਤਸੱਵੁਫ਼) love-poetry onto the Guru and the Divine
He rejected Persian poetry in favor of writing only in Punjabi

quiz.q: The ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ ('Book of Life') is, by tradition, a renaming of which earlier title, and centers on which practice?
options: ਗੰਜਨਾਮਾ; the praise of the ten Gurus
ਬੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ ('Book of Devotion'); the remembrance of ਨਾਮ
ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ; the code of conduct
ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ; the love-ghazal

quiz.q: Why do scholars treat the authorship of the Punjabi ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ differently from the Persian ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ?
options: The ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ was written in a language Bhai Nand Lal never knew
The ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ literature had a fluid transmission, and later material was sometimes attached to honored names, leaving the attribution genuinely contested
The Persian works are universally rejected as forgeries
The ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ is securely dated while the divan is not

quiz.q: What is the theological foundation underlying the ਗੰਜਨਾਮਾ's successive praise of the ten Gurus?
options: That each Guru taught a different and competing doctrine
That the ten Gurus share a single spiritual light (ਜੋਤਿ), so praising them is praising the one Divine reality working through them
That only the tenth Guru was truly divine
That the Gurus should be worshipped as separate deities

quiz.q: According to the critical method emphasized in this course (associated with Surjit Hans), how should the traditional ਸਾਖੀ accounts of Bhai Nand Lal's life be read?
options: As literal, fully documented transcripts of historical fact
Critically — as devotional memory valuable for showing how the community honored him, but not minable for hard chronology without corroboration
As entirely worthless and to be discarded completely
As Persian poetry rather than biography

courses.title: Ghazaliyat of Bhai Nand Lal: Sikh Persian Poetry
courses.source: Ghazaliyat by Bhai Nand Lal Goya
courses.summary: An advanced literary and theological study of the ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲੀਆਤ (Ghazaliyat) of ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਗੋਯਾ, the foremost Persian poet of the court of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ. The course reads the Persian ghazal as a vessel for ਗੁਰਮਤਿ: students master the formal architecture of the ghazal (ਮਤਲਾ, ਰਦੀਫ਼, ਕਾਫ਼ੀਆ, ਮਕਤਾ, ਤਖ਼ੱਲੁਸ), trace how Goya transforms the Sufi vocabulary of divine love into devotion to the Guru as ਮਹਿਬੂਬ (Beloved), and situate his verse beside ਰੂਮੀ and ਹਾਫ਼ਿਜ਼. Special attention is given to how Goya names ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ within Persian imagery, the doctrine of ਫ਼ਨਾ (annihilation of the self) recast as merger in the Guru, and the place of his ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ in the broader Sikh literary canon.
outcomes: Analyze the formal structure of the Persian ghazal — ਮਤਲਾ, ਰਦੀਫ਼, ਕਾਫ਼ੀਆ, ਬੈਤ, and ਮਕਤਾ — and identify these elements within Bhai Nand Lal's ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ.
Explain how ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ adapts the Sufi conceit of the divine ਮਹਿਬੂਬ to express devotion to the Guru and to ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ.
Compare Goya's mysticism of love and ਫ਼ਨਾ with that of ਰੂਮੀ and ਹਾਫ਼ਿਜ਼, noting both inheritance and theological departure.
Interpret key Persian-Sikh images — wine, the cup-bearer, the moth and flame, the face of the Beloved — as ਗੁਰਮਤਿ symbols rather than literal indulgence.
Situate the Ghazaliyat within the wider corpus of Bhai Nand Lal (ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ, ਤਨਖ਼ਾਹਨਾਮਾ, ਜੋਤਿ ਬਿਗਾਸ) and within Persianate Sikh literature.
Evaluate the use of ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ and ਨਾਮ in a Persian poetic register and assess what is gained theologically by writing Sikh devotion in Persian.
Read selected ਅਸ਼ਆਰ (couplets) closely, attending to sound, the turn of the radif, and the signature of the ਮਕਤਾ.

terms.m: A lyric poem of rhyming couplets (often 5–15) sharing a single metre, each couplet a self-contained unit of thought; the dominant form of Bhai Nand Lal's Persian Divan.
The collected Persian ghazals of Bhai Nand Lal, arranged in classical Divan order; 'Goya' (the speaker, the eloquent one) is his poetic pen-name.
The poet's pen-name woven into the final couplet of a ghazal; Bhai Nand Lal's takhallus is 'Goya' (ਗੋਯਾ).
The opening couplet of a ghazal in which both lines rhyme, establishing the qafia and radif that govern the whole poem.
The closing couplet of a ghazal, where the poet inscribes his takhallus, often addressing himself.
The fixed refrain word or phrase repeated at the end of each rhyming line of the ghazal, after the qafia.
The rhyme syllable preceding the radif, recurring at the close of each rhyming line of the ghazal.
The Beloved; in Goya's verse the Guru and ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, inheriting the form of the Sufi-Persian beloved while transforming its meaning.
Annihilation of the ego-self, a Sufi term Goya recasts as the merging of the disciple into the Guru and the Divine.
The Sikh name of the Divine; Goya invokes it within Persian poetic imagery, anchoring the ghazal in ਗੁਰਮਤਿ.
The Timeless Being, the Sikh formless Divine, the ultimate referent of Goya's love-poetry.
The Divine Name and its remembrance; for Goya the substance of mystical life, woven through the Persian register as zikr of the Beloved.
Bhai Nand Lal's longer Persian mathnavi 'Book of Life', a didactic-devotional companion to the ghazals.
The poet; Bhai Nand Lal stands in the line of Persianate court poets while serving the ਦਰਬਾਰ of Guru Gobind Singh.
The court; Bhai Nand Lal was a luminary of the ਦਰਬਾਰ of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ at Anandpur Sahib.

references: Ganda Singh, ed. Bhai Nand Lal Granthavali. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1968.
Hans, Surjit. A Reconstruction of Sikh History from Sikh Literature. Jalandhar: ABS Publications, 1988.
Singh, Pritam. Bhai Nand Lal Goya: Jeevan te Rachna. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1983.
Schimmel, Annemarie. Mystical Dimensions of Islam. Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1975.
Lewis, Franklin D. Rumi: Past and Present, East and West. Oxford: Oneworld, 2000.
Singh, Trilochan, trans. The Turban and the Sword of the Sikhs: Bhai Nand Lal and His Works. Amritsar: International Sikh Centre, 1967.
Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1990.
Bowering, Gerhard. "The Concept of Love in Sufism." In Encyclopaedia Iranica. New York: Columbia University, 2007.
Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.

lessons.title: Bhai Nand Lal Goya and the Persianate Sikh World
lessons.summary: Introduces Bhai Nand Lal, his place in the Darbar of Guru Gobind Singh, and the historical setting of Persian-language Sikh devotion.
lessons.html:
ਵਿਸ਼ਾ ਸੂਚੀ (Table of Contents)

  1. Bhai Nand Lal Goya and the Persianate Sikh World
  2. The Architecture of the Ghazal: ਮਤਲਾ, ਰਦੀਫ਼, ਕਾਫ਼ੀਆ, ਮਕਤਾ
  3. The Divine ਮਹਿਬੂਬ: Love for the Guru as Beloved
  4. ਫ਼ਨਾ and Mystical Union in the Ghazaliyat
  5. The Wine, the Cup-Bearer, and the Symbolic Lexicon
  6. ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ in Persian Imagery: Naming the Divine
  7. Goya and ਰੂਮੀ: Inheritance and Departure
  8. Goya and ਹਾਫ਼ਿਜ਼: The Ghazal of Longing
  9. The Signature Couplet: Reading the ਮਕਤਾ of Goya
  10. The Wider Corpus: ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ, ਤਨਖ਼ਾਹਨਾਮਾ, ਜੋਤਿ ਬਿਗਾਸ
  11. The Ghazaliyat in the Sikh Literary Canon
  12. Close Reading and Synthesis

Who Was Bhai Nand Lal?

ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਗੋਯਾ (c. 1633–1713) stands among the foremost ਸ਼ਾਇਰ (poets) of the Sikh tradition and is universally counted among the fifty-two poets of the ਦਰਬਾਰ of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ at Anandpur Sahib. Born in Ghazni and raised in a Persian-literate household, he was a master of the Persian language at a time when Persian was the prestige tongue of letters, administration, and mystical poetry across the Indo-Iranian world. His mastery of that idiom is precisely what makes his work so remarkable: he turned the most refined instrument of Persianate culture toward the praise of the Guru and the love of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ.

His pen-name, ਗੋਯਾ — "the one who speaks," "the eloquent" — is more than convention. It names a vocation: to give speech to a love that the heart cannot contain. In the Persian Divan he signs nearly every ghazal with this ਤਖ਼ੱਲੁਸ, so that the very last breath of each poem returns us to the speaking self dissolved in the Beloved.

The Persianate Setting

To read Goya we must first understand the world that produced him. By the seventeenth century, Persian poetry had a thousand-year-old grammar of love. The ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲ, perfected by poets such as ਹਾਫ਼ਿਜ਼ of Shiraz and the spiritual epic of ਰੂਮੀ, had developed a dense symbolic vocabulary: the Beloved whose face is the locus of beauty, the wine that intoxicates without grapes, the moth that immolates itself in the flame, the lover who counts separation as his only wealth. Sufi poets had long read these images as a veiled theology of ਇਸ਼ਕ — love as the engine of the soul's return to God.

Bhai Nand Lal inherits this entire apparatus. Yet he is not a Sufi writing for a khanqah; he is a Sikh of the Guru's court writing ਗੁਰਮਤਿ in Persian dress. The tension and the genius of his work lie exactly here. When Goya writes of the Beloved's face, he means the radiant presence of the Guru; when he writes of wine, he means the intoxication of ਨਾਮ; when he writes of annihilation, he means ਫ਼ਨਾ understood not as absorption into an abstract Absolute but as merger into ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ through the grace of the Guru.

Why Persian, Why the Ghazal?

A natural question for the advanced student: why would a Sikh devotee write in Persian rather than the Gurmukhi of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ? Several answers converge. First, Persian was Goya's native literary language and the language of the educated elite he could reach. Second, the ghazal offered a ready-made vocabulary of total, consuming love that mapped onto the Sikh experience of devotion to the Guru. Third, by writing Sikh theology in the highest register of Persianate culture, Goya demonstrated that the message of the Gurus could command the most sophisticated literary form of the age. As Surjit Hans observes in his study of Sikh literature, the Persian works of the period are not marginal curiosities but evidence of a confident tradition speaking across linguistic frontiers.

The Shape of This Course

Over the coming lessons we will move from form to content to comparison. We begin with the mechanics of the ghazal — its ਮਤਲਾ, ਰਦੀਫ਼, ਕਾਫ਼ੀਆ, and ਮਕਤਾ — because one cannot read Goya without hearing the architecture. We then turn to his central theme, the Guru as ਮਹਿਬੂਬ, and to the doctrine of ਫ਼ਨਾ. We will decode his symbolic lexicon, attend to how he names ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ within Persian imagery, and set him beside ਰੂਮੀ and ਹਾਫ਼ਿਜ਼. Finally we will widen the frame to his complete corpus and his place in the Sikh canon. Throughout, the discipline is the same: to read closely, to honor the form, and never to mistake the metaphor for the meaning. The wine of Goya is not the tavern's wine; it is, in the words of the tradition, the ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ of the Name — "the cup of love that never empties."

lessons.title: The Architecture of the Ghazal
lessons.summary: Teaches the formal grammar of the Persian ghazal and locates each element within Bhai Nand Lal's Divan.
lessons.html:
The Couplet as Universe

The ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲ is built from the ਬੈਤ — the couplet, two hemistichs (ਮਿਸਰਾ) that together form a complete thought. Unlike a Western stanza that flows into the next, each couplet of a ghazal is, in principle, a self-standing pearl. A ghazal is therefore less a single argument than a string of pearls sharing one thread of metre and rhyme. This structural fact has enormous interpretive consequences for reading Goya: we should not always expect linear development across couplets, but rather a circling and deepening around a single emotional center — separation from, and longing for, the ਮਹਿਬੂਬ.

ਮਤਲਾ: The Opening Couplet

The first couplet, the ਮਤਲਾ, is special: in it both hemistichs rhyme. This double rhyme announces the two governing sound-elements of the entire poem — the ਕਾਫ਼ੀਆ (the rhyme proper) and the ਰਦੀਫ਼ (the refrain that follows it). Once the ਮਤਲਾ sets these, every subsequent couplet must echo them in its second line. The ear, having heard the pattern twice at the outset, then waits across each couplet for its satisfying return.

ਕਾਫ਼ੀਆ and ਰਦੀਫ਼: Rhyme and Refrain

The ਕਾਫ਼ੀਆ is the rhyming syllable; the ਰਦੀਫ਼ is a word or phrase repeated unchanged after it. Persian ghazals frequently carry a radif — for example a recurring word for "the Beloved," or "again," or "of love" — and the radif becomes a kind of refrain-bell that tolls at the end of every couplet. In Goya's hands the radif often carries the theological payload: by ending couplet after couplet on the same devotional word, he hammers the single point home, so that the form itself enacts ਸਿਮਰਨ, the repeated remembrance of the Name. The student should train the ear to catch the radif first; it is the spine of the poem.

ਮਕਤਾ and ਤਖ਼ੱਲੁਸ: The Signature

The final couplet, the ਮਕਤਾ, contains the poet's ਤਖ਼ੱਲੁਸ. Goya almost always addresses himself by name here — "O Goya..." — folding the poet into the poem as both speaker and subject. This is not vanity; in the Persian-Sufi convention the maqta is the moment the lover confesses his own helplessness, his own annihilation. When Goya names himself in the maqta, he simultaneously dissolves himself: the eloquent one falls silent before the Beloved. We will devote a full lesson later to reading these signature couplets.

Metre: The ਬਹਿਰ

Persian prosody is quantitative, organized by patterns of long and short syllables into named metres (ਬਹਿਰ). A ghazal holds a single metre throughout. For the advanced student of Goya, the practical point is that meaning and metre are inseparable: the swing of the long syllables, the caesura, the lengthening of a vowel on the Beloved's name — these are expressive choices, not mere scaffolding. Even in translation we should try to recover the rhythm of yearning that the metre carries.

How the Elements Work Together

Consider how these parts cohere. The ਮਤਲਾ throws open the door with its double rhyme. Each succeeding ਬੈਤ presents a fresh image — the face, the wine, the wound of separation — yet every one lands on the same ਕਾਫ਼ੀਆ and ਰਦੀਫ਼, so the listener is repeatedly returned to the poem's still center. Finally the ਮਕਤਾ signs and silences the speaker. The form thus mirrors the mystical path itself: many approaches, one goal; many images, one Beloved; and at last the self surrendered. As Annemarie Schimmel notes of Persian mystical verse generally, the ghazal's formal discipline is itself a spiritual discipline — the binding of multiplicity to unity.

Applying the Grammar to Goya

When we open the ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ, we should approach each ghazal with three questions. What is the ਰਦੀਫ਼, and what theological weight does its repetition carry? How does the chain of couplets circle the central longing? And what confession does the ਮਕਤਾ make in Goya's own name? With this grammar in hand, the seemingly ornate surface of the verse opens into a precise devotional instrument. In the next lesson we turn from the vessel to what it carries: the love of the Guru as ਮਹਿਬੂਬ.

lessons.title: The Divine Beloved: Love for the Guru
lessons.summary: Explores how Goya transforms the Persian-Sufi figure of the Beloved into devotion to the Guru and Akal Purakh.
lessons.html:
The Beloved at the Center

Every great ghazal tradition revolves around a single figure: the ਮਹਿਬੂਬ, the Beloved. In secular Persian verse the beloved may be a human face; in Sufi verse the beloved is God veiled in that face; in Goya the beloved is the Guru, and through the Guru, ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. This is the hinge of the entire Ghazaliyat. To miss it is to read Goya as a love poet of the tavern; to grasp it is to read him as a poet of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ.

The Guru as the Face of the Divine

In Sikh theology the Guru is the door to ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ — the one through whom the formless ਨਿਰੰਕਾਰ becomes knowable and loveable. Gurbani in the ਜਪੁਜੀ teaches that without the Guru's grace none crosses the ocean of existence. Goya takes this theology and gives it the body of the Persian beloved. When he praises the radiance of the Beloved's countenance, he is not describing a human lover; he is describing the ਦਰਸ਼ਨ of the Guru, in whose presence the disciple's darkness is undone. The Persian topos of the lover dying for one glance of the beloved becomes, in Goya, the disciple who lives only for the Guru's ਦਰਸ਼ਨ.

From ਇਸ਼ਕ to ਪ੍ਰੇਮ

The Persian-Sufi vocabulary of ਇਸ਼ਕ — overwhelming, ruinous, total love — maps with surprising precision onto the Sikh ਪ੍ਰੇਮ of the Guru. The ਭਗਤ of Gurbani also speaks of love that consumes the self, of the soul-bride longing for her Husband-Lord. Goya stands at the meeting point of these two streams. He writes in the imagery of one and the theology of the other. The lover's sleeplessness, his tears, his indifference to the world's opinion, his readiness to be ruined — all of these the Sikh tradition recognizes as the marks of true devotion. Goya's achievement is to show that the Persian love-lyric, stripped of the tavern and turned toward the Guru, becomes a faithful expression of Sikh ਭਗਤੀ.

A Representative Image

Goya repeatedly figures the disciple as the moth (ਪਰਵਾਨਾ) and the Guru as the flame (ਸ਼ਮਾ). The moth's love is proven only in its self-destruction; it cannot love the flame and survive. In Goya's verse this is the proof of true devotion to the Guru: "ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਉਹੀ ਸੱਚਾ ਹੈ ਜੋ ਆਪੇ ਨੂੰ ਮਿਟਾ ਦੇਵੇ" — love is true only when it effaces the self. The image is wholly Persian; the doctrine is wholly ਗੁਰਮਤਿ, for the dissolution of ਹਉਮੈ (egoism) is the heart of the Sikh path.

The Beloved Who Is Also the Guide

One crucial difference from secular Persian verse deserves emphasis. In the tavern-ghazal the beloved is often cruel, capricious, withholding — a tyrant of beauty. In Goya the Beloved is the Guru, and the Guru is grace itself. The withholding, where it appears, is read as the disciple's own unreadiness, not the Beloved's cruelty. Thus the emotional weather of Goya's ghazals tends toward longing-in-hope rather than longing-in-despair. The separation is real and painful, but the Beloved is known to be merciful, and union is the promised end. This theological optimism, rooted in the Sikh understanding of the Guru's ਕਿਰਪਾ, subtly reshapes the inherited form.

Love as the Whole of Religion

For Goya, as for the ਭਗਤ of Gurbani, love is not one virtue among many but the substance of religion itself. Ritual without love is empty; learning without love is dry. Gurbani in the ਆਸਾ ਕੀ ਵਾਰ teaches that the Lord is found through love and surrender, not through cleverness. Goya's entire Divan is an extended commentary on this truth. He writes, in effect, that the only knowledge worth having is the knowledge of the Beloved, and the only path to it is to be undone by love. In this he is at once a Persian ghazal-poet and a teacher of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ.

Reading Forward

Having established the Beloved as the Guru, we are prepared in the next lesson to examine the mechanism by which the lover reaches the Beloved: ਫ਼ਨਾ, the annihilation of the self. The Persian-Sufi doctrine of fana will be tested against the Sikh understanding of merging into ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ, and we will see both how much Goya borrows and where, decisively, he departs.

lessons.title: ਫ਼ਨਾ and Mystical Union
lessons.summary: Examines the doctrine of self-annihilation in Goya and how it is recast in Sikh terms as merger into the Guru and Waheguru.
lessons.html:
The Problem of the Self

At the heart of every mystical poetry lies a single obstacle: the self. The ego, the ਹਉਮੈ, is what stands between the lover and the Beloved. The Persian-Sufi tradition names the overcoming of this obstacle ਫ਼ਨਾ — annihilation. To attain the Beloved, the lover must cease to be a separate "I." Goya inherits this doctrine fully, and it is the engine of his Ghazaliyat. Yet the way he understands annihilation is shaped decisively by ਗੁਰਮਤਿ.

What ਫ਼ਨਾ Means in Sufism

In classical Sufi thought, ਫ਼ਨਾ is the passing-away of the individual self in the divine reality, often followed by ਬਕਾ — subsistence, a renewed existence now lived in and through God. The lover is extinguished as a drop and survives as the ocean. Annemarie Schimmel describes this as the central drama of Sufi spirituality: the moth must burn to become one with the flame. The vocabulary is one of dissolution, drowning, burning, melting — all images of a bounded self losing its boundary.

How Goya Recasts It

Goya takes this vocabulary but routes annihilation through the Guru. For the Sikh, one does not dissolve directly into an abstract Absolute; one merges into ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ through the grace of the Guru and the practice of ਨਾਮ. So in Goya the moment of ਫ਼ਨਾ is also the moment of total surrender to the Guru. The self is not erased into an impersonal void but joined to the ਜੋਤਿ — the Divine Light — that the Guru embodies and transmits. Gurbani in the ਸੁਖਮਨੀ teaches that he who effaces his ego and takes refuge in the Lord is liberated; Goya gives this teaching the shape of the lover consumed before the Beloved.

The Drop and the Ocean

The favorite Persian image for union is the drop returning to the ocean. Goya uses it, but with a Sikh inflection. The drop does not lose its preciousness in merging; rather, it discovers that it was always of the ocean's substance. This resonates with the Sikh teaching that the soul (ਆਤਮਾ) is of the same light as the Supreme Soul (ਪਰਮਾਤਮਾ) — "ਮਨ ਤੂੰ ਜੋਤਿ ਸਰੂਪੁ ਹੈਂ," Gurbani in Guru Amar Das's ਅਸਟਪਦੀ teaches: O mind, you are the very embodiment of light. Annihilation, then, is not destruction but homecoming. The self that is annihilated is only the false self, the ਹਉਮੈ; what remains is the true self, the light, now united with its source.

Annihilation as Joy, Not Terror

Because the Beloved in Goya is the gracious Guru rather than a fearsome Absolute, ਫ਼ਨਾ in his verse carries a note of joy. The lover does not dread his dissolution; he longs for it as the consummation of love. To be undone before the Guru is the disciple's deepest wish. This colors the whole emotional register of the Ghazaliyat. Where some Sufi poetry trembles before the abyss of self-loss, Goya leans into it with the confidence of one who knows the Beloved is merciful. The terror of annihilation is transmuted into the sweetness of surrender.

The Living Liberation

One further Sikh note distinguishes Goya. The Sikh ideal is ਜੀਵਨ ਮੁਕਤਿ — liberation while living. Annihilation of the ego is not a postponement of life but its true beginning; the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ lives in the world, serving and remembering, ego dissolved, light united. Goya's lover, then, is not a recluse who has fled existence but a disciple transformed within it. The ਫ਼ਨਾ he sings is compatible with the active, ethical life the Gurus enjoin — earning honestly, sharing, remembering. This is a quiet but profound departure from any reading of annihilation as world-denial.

Summary

ਫ਼ਨਾ in Goya is the Persian-Sufi doctrine of self-annihilation, received in full vocabulary but transformed in substance: it is the effacement of ਹਉਮੈ, accomplished through the Guru's grace, issuing not in a void but in merger with ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ, experienced as joyful homecoming and compatible with ਜੀਵਨ ਮੁਕਤਿ. With this doctrine clear, we turn next to the symbolic lexicon — wine, cup-bearer, tavern — through which Goya stages the drama of love and annihilation.

lessons.title: The Wine, the Cup-Bearer, and the Symbolic Lexicon
lessons.summary: Decodes the recurring symbols of Goya's ghazals — wine, the saqi, the tavern, the moth and flame — as Gurmat metaphors.
lessons.html:
Reading the Symbols Correctly

No aspect of Goya's Ghazaliyat is more liable to misreading than its symbolic vocabulary. The verse is full of wine, intoxication, the cup-bearer, the tavern, the wine-house. A reader unschooled in the Persian-Sufi convention might conclude that Goya celebrates literal drinking — a conclusion both false and offensive to ਗੁਰਮਤਿ, which forbids intoxicants. The advanced student must therefore learn to translate the symbolic lexicon. In the Persian mystical tradition, and emphatically in Goya, these are spiritual ciphers with fixed devotional meanings.

Wine: The Intoxication of ਨਾਮ

The wine of the ghazal is not the grape's wine but the wine of love — the intoxication of ਨਾਮ, the Divine Name. To be drunk on this wine is to be absorbed in the remembrance of the Beloved, oblivious to the world's distractions. Gurbani itself uses the metaphor of intoxication for the bliss of the Name; the ਭਗਤ speaks of being dyed in the Lord's love as in a deep color. Goya's wine belongs to this family of images. When he writes of the cup that never empties, he means the inexhaustible bliss of ਸਿਮਰਨ. The point of the metaphor is precisely the contrast: ordinary wine dulls the mind and passes; the wine of the Name awakens the soul and never fails.

The Cup-Bearer: The Guru

The ਸਾਕੀ, the cup-bearer who pours the wine, is the Guru. The disciple cannot reach the intoxication of the Name by himself; it is given, poured, by the grace of the Guru. This is a precise theological claim dressed in tavern imagery. The lover at the wine-house begs the cup-bearer for one more cup — the disciple at the Guru's door begs for the gift of ਨਾਮ. The whole scene of the Persian tavern is thus transfigured into the ਸੰਗਤ, the holy congregation, where the Guru dispenses the wine of love.

The Tavern: The ਸੰਗਤ

The wine-house or tavern (ਮੈਖ਼ਾਨਾ) is, in Goya, the gathering of lovers of the Beloved — the company of the devout. To go to the tavern is to seek the company where the Name is poured and drunk. Far from a place of dissolution, it is the place of true sobriety in the spiritual sense: the only place where one's real thirst is quenched. The reversal is deliberate and characteristic of Sufi-Persian poetics, where the tavern outranks the mosque because love outranks formal observance. Goya inherits this provocative move and gives it Sikh content: the ਸੰਗਤ surpasses empty ritual because there the living wine of the Name is shared.

The Moth and the Flame

We have met the ਪਰਵਾਨਾ (moth) and ਸ਼ਮਾ (flame) already, in the lesson on the Beloved. In the symbolic lexicon they form a complete teaching: the moth's love is proven only by its self-immolation. The flame is the Guru, the light of ਜੋਤਿ; the moth is the disciple whose love must consume his separate self. This image binds the theme of love (the Beloved) to the theme of annihilation (ਫ਼ਨਾ) in a single picture. It is perhaps the most economical emblem of Goya's whole devotional vision.

Other Recurring Figures

Several further symbols deserve note. The ਜ਼ੁਲਫ਼ (the Beloved's curling lock) figures the bewildering beauty of the Divine, the snare in which the lover is willingly caught. The ਨਰਗਿਸ (narcissus, the Beloved's eye) figures the gaze of grace that wounds and heals. The ਦਾਗ਼ (the brand or scar on the lover's heart) figures the mark of love that the disciple wears with pride. The ਖ਼ਾਕ (dust) at the Beloved's threshold figures the humility of the devotee, who counts the dust of the Guru's feet his highest station. Each of these is a fixed coin in the currency of Persian mysticism, and Goya spends them all in the service of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ.

A Method of Reading

The practical lesson is this: when reading Goya, never take the sensual surface literally. Build a glossary. Wine equals the bliss of ਨਾਮ; the cup-bearer equals the Guru; the tavern equals the ਸੰਗਤ; the moth equals the disciple; the flame equals the Guru's light; dust equals humility; the scar equals the cherished wound of love. With this key, the apparently worldly verse reveals itself as a sustained meditation on devotion. As Surjit Hans cautions, the historian and the literary reader alike must respect the conventions of the genre, or they will badly misjudge the poet's intent. In the next lesson we examine how, within this symbolic world, Goya inscribes the explicitly Sikh name of the Divine: ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ.

lessons.title: ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ in Persian Imagery
lessons.summary: Studies how Goya names the Sikh Divine within Persian poetic conventions, anchoring the ghazal in Gurmat.
lessons.html:
Naming the Unnameable in a Borrowed Tongue

A central question of this course is whether a Persian ghazal can remain authentically Sikh. The answer turns on how Goya handles the Name. Persian mystical verse has its own rich vocabulary for God — ਯਾਰ (the friend), ਦੋਸਤ (the beloved friend), ਮਹਿਬੂਬ (the beloved), ਜਾਨਾਨ (the soul's darling). Goya uses these freely. But he also, decisively, anchors his verse in the specifically Sikh Name: ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ, the Wondrous Lord, the ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ of the Gurus. By naming ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ within the Persian frame, Goya marks his ghazals unmistakably as ਗੁਰਮਤਿ.

ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ as the Cry of Wonder

The Name ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ is itself an exclamation of wonder — "Wah!" before the Guru, before the marvel of the Divine. This is theologically perfect for the ghazal, a form whose native emotion is astonishment before the Beloved's beauty. The Persian poet's gasp of wonder at the face of the beloved becomes, in Goya, the very utterance of the Name. Where a secular poet would cry out at beauty, Goya cries ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ. The form's emotional grammar and the Sikh Name fuse seamlessly. The wonder that the ghazal exists to express is, for Goya, precisely the wonder that the Name encodes.

The Friend Who Is the Guru

The Persian ਯਾਰ — the Friend — is one of the tenderest names for the Divine in Sufi verse. Goya embraces it, but for him the Friend is the Guru and ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ together. The intimacy of friendship, the closeness of the beloved companion, expresses the Sikh experience of the Guru as nearer than one's own breath. Gurbani in the ਸੁਖਮਨੀ teaches that the Lord is the help of the helpless, the companion of the forsaken; Goya's ਯਾਰ is this ever-present friend, robed in Persian tenderness.

The Formless in Imagery

Here lies a genuine tension. Sikh theology is firmly ਨਿਰਗੁਣ at its core — the Divine is ਨਿਰੰਕਾਰ, without form. Yet the ghazal trades in images: the face, the eye, the lock of hair. How does Goya, a Sikh, reconcile the formless God with the embodied imagery of the beloved? The answer is that he uses the imagery as the Bhagats of Gurbani themselves do — as ਸਰਗੁਣ language pointing beyond itself to the ਨਿਰਗੁਣ reality. The Beloved's face is not a literal face but the radiance of the Divine made loveable; the eye is the gaze of grace; the lock is the bewildering mystery. The imagery is a ladder, kicked away at the top. Goya never lets the reader rest in the image; the ਮਕਤਾ regularly recalls us to the formless Beloved and to the Name.

ਨਾਮ as the Persian zikr

The Sufi practice of zikr — the rhythmic repetition of the divine name — has an obvious counterpart in the Sikh ਸਿਮਰਨ of ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ. Goya exploits this convergence. The ਰਦੀਫ਼, the repeated refrain of the ghazal, becomes a kind of zikr-in-form: each couplet ends by returning to the Beloved or the Name, and the poem as a whole performs the remembrance it commends. To read Goya aloud is thus to practice a literary ਸਿਮਰਨ. The form does not merely describe devotion; it enacts it. This is one of the deepest ways the Ghazaliyat is Sikh: its very structure is remembrance.

The Theological Gain

What is gained by writing ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ in Persian dress? First, reach: the message of the Gurus enters the prestige literature of the age. Second, demonstration: the Sikh faith is shown able to inhabit and master the highest form of Persianate culture without dilution. Third, depth: the inherited Sufi vocabulary of love supplies an emotional intensity that enriches the expression of ਭਗਤੀ. And fourth, dialogue: Goya implicitly converses with the whole Persian mystical tradition, claiming its forms for the Guru. As Surjit Hans and later scholars have argued, this is not syncretism that blurs Sikhi into Sufism, but appropriation that bends Persian form to Sikh substance.

Conclusion

Goya names the Divine in two registers at once — the Persian ਯਾਰ and ਮਹਿਬੂਬ, and the Sikh ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ and ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ — and the genius of his verse is to make them speak as one voice without erasing the difference. The imagery serves the formless; the refrain performs the remembrance; the wonder of the ghazal becomes the wonder of the Name. With this settled, we are ready to set Goya in conversation with the two giants whose shadow falls across all Persian mystical verse: ਰੂਮੀ and ਹਾਫ਼ਿਜ਼.

lessons.title: Goya and ਰੂਮੀ: Inheritance and Departure
lessons.summary: Compares Goya's mysticism of love and annihilation with that of Jalal al-Din Rumi, marking both debt and divergence.
lessons.html:
The Towering Precedent

No poet casts a longer shadow over Persian mysticism than ਜਲਾਲ-ਉਦ-ਦੀਨ ਰੂਮੀ (1207–1273), whose ਮਸਨਵੀ and ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਸ਼ਮਸ are the summit of Sufi poetry. Any later poet of Divine love in Persian writes in the air Rumi made. Goya is no exception. To read Goya beside Rumi is to see clearly both what the Sikh poet inherits and where he turns away. Franklin Lewis's authoritative study of Rumi reminds us how thoroughly Rumi's idiom — the reed torn from its bed, the lover dissolved in the Beloved, the dance of annihilation — saturated the Persianate world for centuries.

Shared Ground: Love as Cosmic Force

Goya and Rumi agree on first principles. For both, ਇਸ਼ਕ — love — is the fundamental force of reality, the gravity that draws all things back to their Source. For both, the self is the obstacle and its annihilation the goal. For both, music and poetry are not decoration but vehicles of the soul's ascent. For both, the Beloved is at once unbearably near and agonizingly veiled. When Goya writes of the lover consumed, of separation as the soul's wound, of the wine of love, he is speaking a language Rumi perfected. The continuity is real and deep, and the advanced student should feel the family resemblance.

The Reed and the Disciple

Rumi's most famous image is the ਨੇ, the reed-flute, torn from the reed-bed and crying in its separation — the soul severed from God, longing to return. Goya's lover, severed from the Beloved-Guru and crying in the night, is kin to Rumi's reed. Both turn the pain of separation (ਫ਼ਿਰਾਕ) into the very proof and engine of love. Both insist that the wound is precious, that the longing is itself a form of nearness. This shared theology of longing is perhaps the strongest thread connecting the two poets.

The Decisive Departure: The Guru

Yet here is the divergence. Rumi's path to annihilation runs through love itself and through the figure of the spiritual master Shams — but it is framed within the Islamic theological world, with its prophetology and its understanding of the divine-human relation. Goya's path runs explicitly through the ਗੁਰੂ as the Sikhs understand the Guru: not merely a human master but the embodied ਜੋਤਿ, the channel of ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ's grace, ten in form and one in light. The mediator is different, and the difference is theological, not merely nominal. For Goya, there is no union with the Beloved except through the Guru of the Sikhs; the whole architecture of grace is ਗੁਰਮਤਿ.

Departure in Ethics and Liberation

A second departure concerns the shape of liberation. Rumi's mysticism, in its dominant key, tends toward ecstatic absorption. Goya, formed by the Khalsa ideal at the court of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ, holds annihilation together with the active, ethical, householder life — ਜੀਵਨ ਮੁਕਤਿ, liberation while living and serving. The Sikh insistence on ਕਿਰਤ (honest labor), ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ (sharing), and ਨਾਮ together as a single path subtly reorients the inherited mysticism. Goya's lover is not only a burning moth but, implicitly, a disciple of the Guru who lives righteously in the world. The ecstasy is real, but it is wedded to a discipline of life that Rumi's verse does not foreground in the same way.

Departure in the Name

Finally, the Name itself differs. Where Rumi's God is addressed within the names and idiom of Islam, Goya anchors his verse in ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ and ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. This is not a trivial substitution; it carries the whole distinctive Sikh understanding of the Timeless, ਅਕਾਲ, beyond birth and death, sovereign and self-existent. The emotional surface may echo Rumi, but the theological substance is the Gurus'.

How to Read the Two Together

The most fruitful method is neither to collapse Goya into Rumi nor to deny the kinship. Read the shared idiom as evidence of a common Persian mystical inheritance, and read the departures as the marks of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ asserting itself within that inheritance. Goya is a Sikh poet fluent in Rumi's language who speaks, in that language, a different and distinctively Sikh truth. In the next lesson we turn to the other great precedent, ਹਾਫ਼ਿਜ਼, master of the ghazal form itself, against whom Goya's craft can best be measured.

lessons.title: Goya and ਹਾਫ਼ਿਜ਼: The Ghazal of Longing
lessons.summary: Sets Goya beside Hafiz of Shiraz, the supreme ghazal craftsman, to measure form, ambiguity, and devotional aim.
lessons.html:
The Master of the Form

If Rumi is the master of the mystical epic, ਹਾਫ਼ਿਜ਼ of Shiraz (c. 1315–1390) is the supreme master of the ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲ itself. His Divan is the most beloved book of poetry in the Persian world, prized for its musicality, its layered ambiguity, and its perfect command of radif and qafia. To measure Goya's craft we set him beside Hafiz, the standard against which all ghazal-makers are judged. The comparison is humbling and illuminating in equal measure.

Shared Craft

Goya clearly studied the Hafizian ghazal. He commands the same machinery: the resonant ਮਤਲਾ, the tolling ਰਦੀਫ਼, the self-addressing ਮਕਤਾ. Like Hafiz, he can pivot in a single couplet from the wine-cup to the wound of the heart; like Hafiz, he uses the tavern against the pulpit, love against cold piety. The Hafizian celebration of the ਰਿੰਦ — the holy rogue who scorns hypocrisy and seeks only the Beloved — finds an echo in Goya's preference for sincere love over empty observance. Both poets exalt the lover who is ruined by love above the respectable believer who has never burned.

The Famous Ambiguity of ਹਾਫ਼ਿਜ਼

Hafiz is celebrated — and endlessly debated — for his ambiguity. Is a given wine literal or mystical? Is the beloved earthly or divine? Hafiz keeps the registers in suspension, and centuries of readers have quarreled over whether he is a libertine, a Sufi, or both at once. This deliberate undecidability is part of his genius and his charm. It allows the verse to be read at the tavern and at the shrine alike.

Goya's Resolved Devotion

Here Goya parts company with Hafiz in a revealing way. Where Hafiz cultivates ambiguity, Goya resolves it. There is, finally, little doubt in Goya about what the wine is or who the Beloved is: the wine is ਨਾਮ, the Beloved is the Guru and ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ. The ਮਕਤਾ regularly closes the question by naming the Name or recalling the Guru. Goya uses the Hafizian surface — the tavern, the wine, the beloved's beauty — but he does not leave the reader suspended; he tips the verse decisively toward ਗੁਰਮਤਿ. This is a difference of purpose. Hafiz writes a poetry that can be read many ways; Goya writes a poetry of devotion that wears the many-wayed surface but means one thing. The student should notice this contrast carefully, for it marks the line between the consummate aesthete of Shiraz and the devotee of Anandpur.

Longing as the Common Key

What both poets share above all is the emotion of longing — ਫ਼ਿਰਾਕ, the ache of separation that is the ghazal's native mood. Hafiz's lover and Goya's lover both live in the gap between desire and union, and both make that gap sing. But the longing points differently. Hafiz's longing often hovers, exquisite and unresolved; Goya's longing strains toward a known and gracious Beloved, the Guru whose union is promised. The same emotional string is plucked, but it is tuned to a different theological pitch.

Craft in the Service of Doctrine

A fair literary judgment, which the advanced student should be able to defend, is this: Goya may not surpass Hafiz in the sheer musical perfection and bottomless ambiguity that make the Shirazi master unique. But Goya achieves something Hafiz does not attempt — he bends the most sophisticated lyric form of the Persian world entirely to the service of a specific, articulate theology of the Guru, without sacrificing beauty. His craft is real and high; it is craft in the service of ਭਗਤੀ. In this he is closer in aim to the ਭਗਤ of Gurbani than to the courtly aesthetes of Persia, even as he speaks their language.

Conclusion

Set beside ਹਾਫ਼ਿਜ਼, Goya emerges as a poet who fully inherits the ghazal's craft and its provocative surface, yet refuses its ambiguity in favor of a resolved devotion to the Guru and ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ. The tavern is the ਸੰਗਤ; the wine is the ਨਾਮ; the Beloved is the Guru; and the longing, however Hafizian its ache, is tuned to the Sikh hope of union. Having compared Goya to both great precedents, we turn next to the most intimate moment of his own verse: the signature couplet, the ਮਕਤਾ, where Goya speaks his own name.

lessons.title: The Signature Couplet: Reading the ਮਕਤਾ of Goya
lessons.summary: A focused study of how Bhai Nand Lal inscribes his takhallus in the closing couplet and what it accomplishes.
lessons.html:
The Most Personal Verse

Every ghazal ends with the ਮਕਤਾ, and in the maqta the poet speaks his ਤਖ਼ੱਲੁਸ. For Goya this is the most intimate verse of each poem — the moment when the eloquent one (ਗੋਯਾ) turns to address himself. Where the body of the ghazal sings of the Beloved in the third person or the second, the maqta often turns inward: "O Goya..." This turn is the subject of the present lesson, for in it the whole devotional logic of the Ghazaliyat is concentrated.

The Function of the ਤਖ਼ੱਲੁਸ

The pen-name serves several functions at once. Practically, it signs the poem and secures the poet's authorship in a tradition of oral and manuscript transmission. Aesthetically, it provides the satisfying close that the form demands. But spiritually — and this is what matters for Goya — the takhallus is the site of the poet's self-confession. By naming himself, the poet makes himself a character in his own poem, and almost always a humbled one. The act of self-naming becomes an act of self-effacement. He who is called "the eloquent" confesses, in the end, that before the Beloved he has nothing to say.

Self-Naming as Self-Annihilation

Here the maqta connects directly to the doctrine of ਫ਼ਨਾ we studied earlier. The convention of addressing oneself by name might seem like the height of self-assertion; in the mystical ghazal it is the opposite. To say "O Goya, be silent before the Beloved" or "O Goya, count yourself the dust of the Guru's door" is to stage the annihilation of the self in the very verse that bears the self's name. The form thus performs the paradox at the heart of the mysticism: the self appears precisely in order to be surrendered. The signature is also the erasure.

Characteristic Moves of Goya's ਮਕਤਾ

Several recurring gestures mark Goya's signature couplets. First, the gesture of humility: Goya names himself only to lower himself — as the dust (ਖ਼ਾਕ) of the Beloved's threshold, as the least of lovers, as one unworthy of the gift he has received. Second, the gesture of total dependence: Goya confesses that his eloquence, his very speech, is itself the Beloved's gift, not his own attainment — a beautiful turn, since his pen-name means "the speaking one," and he confesses that the speech is borrowed. Third, the gesture of longing-as-wealth: Goya declares that his only possession is his love, his only riches the wound of separation, his only hope the Guru's grace. These three gestures — humility, dependence, longing — constitute the emotional signature of his Divan.

An Illustrative Pattern

A typical Goya maqta runs in spirit: "ਗੋਯਾ, ਤੇਰੀ ਜ਼ਬਾਨ ਉੱਤੇ ਜੋ ਨਾਮ ਹੈ, ਉਹ ਵੀ ਉਸੇ ਮਹਿਬੂਬ ਦੀ ਦਾਤ ਹੈ" — O Goya, even the Name upon your tongue is the gift of that same Beloved. The structure is exemplary: the poet is named, then immediately dispossessed of any credit, then returned to the Beloved as the source of all. In a single couplet the ego is raised and dissolved, and the Name is exalted. This is the maqta doing its full theological work.

The Maqta as Teaching

Because the maqta is where Goya speaks most directly, it is often where his teaching is most explicit. The ambiguity that might color the body of the ghazal is here resolved (recall our comparison with ਹਾਫ਼ਿਜ਼). The closing couplet frequently names ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ, recalls the Guru, or states the lesson plainly: that love is all, that the self must be surrendered, that the Name is the only wealth. For the student, the maqta is therefore the best place to begin reading any Goya ghazal — read it last in the poem, but read it first for the meaning, and let it illuminate the images that precede it.

Conclusion

The ਮਕਤਾ of Goya is the hinge of his art and his devotion: the place where the eloquent speaker names himself in order to surrender himself, confesses his dependence, exalts the Name, and resolves the ghazal's longing toward the gracious Beloved. To read the maqta well is to hold the key to the Ghazaliyat. With this craft mastered, we widen the lens in the next lesson to Goya's complete corpus, of which the ghazals are the lyric heart.

lessons.title: The Wider Corpus: ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ, ਤਨਖ਼ਾਹਨਾਮਾ, ਜੋਤਿ ਬਿਗਾਸ
lessons.summary: Places the Ghazaliyat within Bhai Nand Lal's complete body of work, in both Persian and Punjabi.
lessons.html:
Beyond the Ghazals

The ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲੀਆਤ are the lyric heart of Bhai Nand Lal's output, but they are part of a larger corpus that ranges across genre and even language. To read the ghazals well, the advanced student should know the company they keep. The standard scholarly gathering of his works is the ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਗ੍ਰੰਥਾਵਲੀ edited by Ganda Singh, which assembles the Persian and Punjabi compositions and remains the foundation of all serious study.

ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ: The Persian Ghazals

The ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ is the collection of Persian ghazals proper, arranged in the classical Divan order. It is the work we have been studying. Its register is intensely lyrical and devotional: the love of the Beloved, the longing of separation, the intoxication of the Name, the surrender of the self. If one wants the music of Goya's mysticism, it is here.

ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ: The Book of Life

The ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ, the "Book of Life," is a longer Persian work in the ਮਸਨਵੀ form — rhymed couplets sustained over a continuous didactic-devotional discourse rather than the discrete couplets of the ghazal. Where the ghazals sing, the Zindaginama teaches. It expounds the life of love and devotion at greater length, instructing the disciple in the way of remembrance and surrender. Reading it alongside the ghazals shows the same theology in two modes: the lyric cry and the sustained sermon. Trilochan Singh's translations made these Persian works accessible to English readers and underscored their doctrinal seriousness.

ਤਨਖ਼ਾਹਨਾਮਾ: The Rehatnama

Of a quite different character is the ਤਨਖ਼ਾਹਨਾਮਾ attributed to Bhai Nand Lal — a ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ, a code of conduct for the Sikh, composed in Punjabi. Here the mystic of the Persian ghazals appears as the teacher of ਰਹਿਤ, the discipline of Khalsa life. The famous lines on the greatness of the ਸੰਗਤ and on the Guru being present where the Khalsa gather belong to this tradition of his work. The contrast with the ghazals is instructive: the same author who sings of annihilation in love also lays down the practical ethics of the community. This is the Sikh integration of the inner and the outer — ਭਗਤੀ and ਰਹਿਤ — embodied in one writer.

ਜੋਤਿ ਬਿਗਾਸ: The Radiance of Light

The ਜੋਤਿ ਬਿਗਾਸ exists in versions associated with Bhai Nand Lal and treats the theme of the Divine Light — the ਜੋਤਿ — and its illumination of the devoted soul. The very title points to the heart of his vision: the kindling of the inner light through the Guru. Whatever the textual complexities, the thematic unity with the ghazals is plain: it is the same light, the same Beloved, the same surrender.

Persian and Punjabi Together

One of the most striking features of Goya's corpus is its bilingual reach. He writes the loftiest Persian and also composes in Punjabi for the practical instruction of the Khalsa. This range tells us something important about the Sikh literary world of the period: it was confidently plurilingual, able to speak in the prestige language of the empire and in the mother tongue of the Panth, and to address both the mystic's longing and the disciple's daily discipline. As J. S. Grewal's history of the Sikhs makes clear, the period of Guru Gobind Singh was one of remarkable cultural production, and Bhai Nand Lal stands among its finest fruits.

Reading the Ghazals in Context

Knowing the wider corpus changes how we read the ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲੀਆਤ. The intoxication of the ghazals is not escapism, because the same poet wrote the ਤਨਖ਼ਾਹਨਾਮਾ; the love is disciplined, the ecstasy is ethical. The teaching of the Zindaginama tells us how to live the love that the ghazals sing. The light of the Jot Bigas is the light the ghazals' moth seeks in the flame. The corpus is one body, and the ghazals are its singing heart. With this whole in view, we turn in the next lesson to Goya's place in the larger Sikh literary canon.

lessons.title: The Ghazaliyat in the Sikh Literary Canon
lessons.summary: Assesses Bhai Nand Lal's standing within Sikh literature and the question of Persianate Sikh writing.
lessons.html:
A Place of Honor

Where does the Ghazaliyat stand in the canon of Sikh literature? Bhai Nand Lal occupies a place of distinct honor: a poet of the Guru's own ਦਰਬਾਰ, the foremost Persian voice of the tradition, and a figure beloved by the Panth across the centuries. His verses are sung in ਕੀਰਤਨ and quoted in ਅਰਦਾਸ-adjacent tradition; the line affirming that the Guru is present wherever the Khalsa gather, drawn from his work, is among the most cherished in Sikh life. Yet his standing also raises real questions of canon and category that the advanced student should weigh.

The Question of Authority

It is essential to be precise about authority. The compositions of Bhai Nand Lal are not part of ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ; the canon of scripture was sealed by the Gurus, and only the Gurus' and the Bhagats' bani included therein carries the authority of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ. Bhai Nand Lal's writings, however revered, belong to a different and lower order of authority — the cherished literature of a great Gursikh, not the eternal Shabad. Gurinder Singh Mann's study of the making of Sikh scripture clarifies precisely this distinction between the sealed canon and the wider devotional literature that grew around it. To honor Goya is not to confuse his ghazals with Gurbani; the advanced student must hold this line clearly.

Persianate Sikh Literature

Goya is the supreme example of a Persianate Sikh literature that flourished in the period — Sikh devotion and Sikh history written in the Persian language and forms. This body of writing reflects the multilingual, cosmopolitan character of the Sikh tradition at the turn of the eighteenth century. It demonstrates that Sikhi was never linguistically parochial; it could and did speak in the high idiom of the wider Indo-Persian world. Surjit Hans's reconstruction of Sikh history from Sikh literature treats such works as serious historical and theological sources, not ornaments, and the modern student should do the same.

The Charge of Syncretism, Answered

Because Goya writes in Persian forms saturated with Sufi vocabulary, some have been tempted to read him as a syncretist who blends Sikhi and Sufism into one. This reading should be resisted as imprecise. As we have seen across this course, Goya borrows the form and the vocabulary of Persian-Sufi mysticism but bends them to ਗੁਰਮਤਿ: the Beloved is the Sikh Guru, the Name is ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ, the annihilation is merger into ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ through the Guru's grace, and the life that issues is the ethical householder discipline of the Khalsa. Form is shared; substance is Sikh. The right word is not syncretism but appropriation — the confident claiming of a great literary instrument for the Guru's message.

Goya and the ਭਗਤ Tradition

It is illuminating to set Goya beside the ਭਗਤ whose bani is in Guru Granth Sahib. Like them, he sings of the soul's love for the Divine in the imagery of his own milieu; like them, he exalts love and surrender over ritual; like them, he points always beyond the image to the formless. The difference is one of authority and language, not of fundamental spirit. Goya is, in a sense, a later voice in the long Sikh tradition of devotional poetry — writing in Persian rather than in the languages of Gurbani, and standing outside the sealed canon, but kindled by the same flame.

Goya in Sikh Devotional Life

Beyond the academy, Goya lives in Sikh practice. His verses are sung; his teaching on the ਸੰਗਤ and the Khalsa is treasured; his image of the disciple consumed in love for the Guru shapes the affective life of the Panth. This living reception is itself part of his canonical standing. A literature is canonized not only by scholars but by the community that keeps it alive in song and memory, and the Sikh community has kept Goya alive for three centuries.

Conclusion

The Ghazaliyat stands as the crown of Persianate Sikh literature: a revered, non-scriptural body of devotional verse by a poet of the Guru's court, distinct in authority from ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ yet kindred to the ਭਗਤ tradition in spirit, and best understood as the appropriation of Persian form for Sikh substance. With its place in the canon assessed, our final lesson gathers the threads through close reading and synthesis.

lessons.title: Close Reading and Synthesis
lessons.summary: Consolidates the course through method of close reading and a synthesis of Goya's achievement, ending with Works Cited.
lessons.html:
Bringing the Course Together

This final lesson consolidates what we have learned by practicing the discipline at the center of the course: the close reading of Goya's verse, integrating form, content, symbol, and comparison. A student who has worked through these lessons should now be able to take any ghazal of the ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ and read it with full equipment.

A Method for Close Reading

The method has four movements. First, hear the form: identify the ਮਤਲਾ, fix the ਕਾਫ਼ੀਆ and ਰਦੀਫ਼, and feel how the refrain tolls across the couplets. Second, read the ਮਕਤਾ for the meaning: find Goya's signature, see how he humbles himself and names the Beloved or the Name, and let the closing couplet resolve the poem's ambiguity. Third, decode the symbols: translate the wine as ਨਾਮ, the cup-bearer as the Guru, the tavern as the ਸੰਗਤ, the moth and flame as the disciple consumed in the Guru's light. Fourth, situate the poem: hear behind it the inheritance of ਰੂਮੀ and ਹਾਫ਼ਿਜ਼, and mark the departure into ਗੁਰਮਤਿ — the Guru as mediator, ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ as the Name, ਜੀਵਨ ਮੁਕਤਿ as the shape of liberation.

A Worked Synthesis

Apply this to a representative Goya movement. A ghazal opens with a ਮਤਲਾ that establishes a refrain on the Beloved; each couplet then circles the single ache of separation — the night without the Beloved's face, the cup begged from the cup-bearer, the moth drawn to the flame. We do not look for linear argument; we feel the deepening of one longing. Then the ਮਕਤਾ arrives: "ਗੋਯਾ, ਤੇਰਾ ਸਭ ਕੁਝ ਉਸੇ ਮਹਿਬੂਬ ਦਾ ਹੈ" — Goya, all that you are belongs to that Beloved. The signature humbles the speaker, names the Beloved, and resolves the wine and the flame into the love of the Guru and ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ. The Persian surface is complete; the Sikh substance is unmistakable. That double achievement, held in a single couplet, is the essence of Goya.

What Goya Accomplished

Standing back, we can state Goya's achievement in a sentence the advanced student should be able to defend: Bhai Nand Lal took the most refined lyric form of the Persianate world — the ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲ, with its inherited vocabulary of love, wine, and annihilation — and bent it, without dilution and without sacrificing beauty, to the expression of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ, making the Guru the Beloved, ਨਾਮ the wine, the ਸੰਗਤ the tavern, ਫ਼ਨਾ the merger into ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, and ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ the wonder the whole form exists to utter. He converses with ਰੂਮੀ and ਹਾਫ਼ਿਜ਼ as an equal in craft and departs from them as a Sikh in substance.

Why It Matters

Goya matters for several reasons. He proves the literary range and confidence of the Sikh tradition. He enriches Sikh devotion with the intensity of the Persian love-lyric. He provides a bridge of dialogue with the wider mystical world, claiming its forms for the Guru. And he gives the Panth, in song, an enduring image of the disciple consumed by love for the Guru. To study his Ghazaliyat is to study how a tradition can master a borrowed instrument and make it sing its own truth.

For Further Study

The student who wishes to go further should work with the Persian text and a reliable translation side by side, read the ghazals aloud to feel the metre and refrain, study the ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀਨਾਮਾ for the doctrine at length, and read Goya beside the ਭਗਤ bani of Guru Granth Sahib to feel both the kinship and the difference. The scholarship listed below is the foundation for all of this. Above all, the student should remember the discipline of this course: honor the form, decode the symbol, and never mistake the metaphor for the meaning. The wine of Goya is the ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ of the Name; the Beloved is the Guru; and the longing, however Persian its dress, is the longing of the Sikh soul for ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ.

ਹਵਾਲੇ (Works Cited)

  • Ganda Singh, ed. Bhai Nand Lal Granthavali. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1968.
  • Hans, Surjit. A Reconstruction of Sikh History from Sikh Literature. Jalandhar: ABS Publications, 1988.
  • Singh, Pritam. Bhai Nand Lal Goya: Jeevan te Rachna. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1983.
  • Schimmel, Annemarie. Mystical Dimensions of Islam. Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1975.
  • Lewis, Franklin D. Rumi: Past and Present, East and West. Oxford: Oneworld, 2000.
  • Singh, Trilochan, trans. The Turban and the Sword of the Sikhs: Bhai Nand Lal and His Works. Amritsar: International Sikh Centre, 1967.
  • Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1990.
  • Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.
  • Bowering, Gerhard. "The Concept of Love in Sufism." In Encyclopaedia Iranica. New York: Columbia University, 2007.

quiz.q: In the structure of the ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲ, what is the ਰਦੀਫ਼?
options: The opening couplet in which both lines rhyme
The fixed refrain word or phrase repeated at the end of each rhyming line after the qafia
The poet's pen-name woven into the final couplet
The quantitative metre governing the whole poem

quiz.q: How does Bhai Nand Lal primarily transform the Persian-Sufi figure of the Beloved (ਮਹਿਬੂਬ)?
options: He rejects the figure of the Beloved entirely
He makes the Beloved a literal human lover of the tavern
He makes the Beloved the Guru, and through the Guru, ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ
He replaces the Beloved with abstract philosophical argument

quiz.q: In Goya's symbolic lexicon, what does the cup-bearer (ਸਾਕੀ) represent?
options: The hypocritical preacher
The Guru, who pours the wine of the Name by grace
The disciple seeking the Beloved
The earthly king or emperor

quiz.q: How does Goya recast the Sufi doctrine of ਫ਼ਨਾ (annihilation)?
options: As the destruction of the soul into an impersonal void with no remainder
As effacement of ਹਉਮੈ through the Guru's grace, issuing in joyful merger with ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ and compatible with ਜੀਵਨ ਮੁਕਤਿ
As a purely intellectual exercise unrelated to love
As a rejection of all mystical experience

quiz.q: What is a key DIFFERENCE between Goya and ਹਾਫ਼ਿਜ਼ in their handling of imagery?
options: Goya does not use the ghazal form at all
Hafiz writes only about the Guru while Goya writes about wine
Where Hafiz cultivates deliberate ambiguity, Goya resolves it decisively toward devotion to the Guru and ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ
Goya never uses a radif or qafia

quiz.q: What is the correct statement about the authority of Bhai Nand Lal's writings within the Sikh tradition?
options: They are part of the sealed canon of ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ
They carry the same authority as ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ
They are revered devotional literature of a great Gursikh, distinct in authority from and not part of Gurbani
They were rejected by the Sikh community and are not preserved

courses.title: Zindagi Nama: Bhai Nand Lal's Autobiography in Verse
courses.source: Zindagi Nama by Bhai Nand Lal Goya
courses.summary: An advanced literary and devotional study of the Zindagi Nama (Book of Life), the great Persian masnavi of ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਗੋਯਾ, court-poet of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ. Reading the poem as a versified spiritual autobiography, the course traces Goya's journey from Persianate scholar of Ghazni and Multan to a ਗੁਰਸਿੱਖ at Anandpur Sahib, and examines how the masnavi form carries an interior account of the ਗੁਰੂ-ਸਿੱਖ relationship, ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ, and the ethics of devotion. Students learn to read the Zindagi Nama both as world literature in the masnavi tradition and as a unique first-person witness to life in the Guru's court, while attending to its theology of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, ਹੁਕਮ, and ਬੰਦਗੀ. Key concepts and terms are presented in Gurmukhi Unicode throughout.
outcomes: Situate the Zindagi Nama within the corpus of ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਗੋਯਾ and within the wider Persianate and Sikh literary worlds.
Explain the conventions of the masnavi form and analyze how its rhyming couplets shape the work as a versified spiritual autobiography.
Trace the spiritual milestones of Goya's life from Persian scholar to ਗੁਰਸਿੱਖ as the poem itself narrates them.
Interpret the Zindagi Nama's theology of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, ਨਾਮ, ਹੁਕਮ, and ਬੰਦਗੀ in relation to mainstream ਗੁਰਮਤਿ.
Analyze how the poem portrays the ਗੁਰੂ-ਸਿੱਖ relationship and the figure of the ਮੁਰਸ਼ਿਦ-Guru.
Assess the Zindagi Nama as a historical source for life in the court of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ at Anandpur Sahib.
Evaluate problems of language, translation, and reception that shape how the poem is read today.
Compose a sustained scholarly close reading of a passage from the Zindagi Nama using primary text and secondary scholarship.

terms.m: Zindagi Nama, the 'Book of Life,' Bhai Nand Lal's long Persian masnavi of devotional and autobiographical verse on the path of the Guru-oriented life.
Bhai Nand Lal 'Goya,' poet-scholar of the court of Guru Gobind Singh Ji; 'Goya' (the one who speaks) was his Persian pen-name (takhallus).
Masnavi, a Persian narrative or didactic poem in rhyming couplets, the verse form in which the Zindagi Nama is composed.
Takhallus, the pen-name a Persian or Urdu poet inserts into the verse; here 'Goya,' meaning eloquent or speaking.
Akal Purakh, the Timeless Being, the one formless God whose remembrance is the heart of the Zindagi Nama.
Nam Simran, loving remembrance and repetition of the Divine Name, the central spiritual discipline the poem urges.
Murshid, the Persian Sufi term for the spiritual guide; in the Zindagi Nama it is reoriented onto the Sikh ਗੁਰੂ.
Bandagi, devotion, worshipful servitude before Akal Purakh, a recurring keyword of the poem's ethics.
Hukam, the Divine Order or Will; surrender to Hukam structures the poem's vision of the surrendered life.
Gursikh, a disciple of the Guru; the identity into which the Zindagi Nama narrates Goya's transformation.
Diwan-e-Goya, Goya's collection of Persian ghazals, the companion lyric work to the longer Zindagi Nama.
Farsi, the Persian language of the Mughal court and of Goya's poetry, the linguistic medium of the Zindagi Nama.
Ishq, ardent love; the Zindagi Nama channels the Sufi vocabulary of ਇਸ਼ਕ toward love of Akal Purakh and the Guru.
Anandpur Sahib, the seat of Guru Gobind Singh Ji where Goya served and where much of the poem's witness is set.

references: Ganda Singh, ed. Bhai Nand Lal Granthavali. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1989.
Hans, Surjit. A Reconstruction of Sikh History from Sikh Literature. Jalandhar: ABS Publications, 1988.
Nabha, Bhai Kahn Singh. Gurushabad Ratnakar Mahankosh. Patiala: Bhasha Vibhag Punjab, 1930.
Fenech, Louis E. The Sikh Zafar-namah of Guru Gobind Singh: A Discursive Blade in the Heart of the Mughal Empire. New York: Oxford University Press, 2013.
Singh, Bhai Vir. Bhai Nand Lal: Jiwan te Rachna. Amritsar: Khalsa Samachar, n.d.
Schimmel, Annemarie. Mystical Dimensions of Islam. Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1975.
Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Rev. ed. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.
