lessons.title: Introduction: The Book of Life and Its Poet
lessons.html:
ਵਿਸ਼ਾ ਸੂਚੀ (Table of Contents)

  1. Introduction: The Book of Life and Its Poet
  2. Goya's Life: From Ghazni and Multan to the Guru's Darbar
  3. The ਮਸਨਵੀ Form: How Persian Couplets Carry a Life
  4. Reading the Zindagi Nama as Spiritual Autobiography
  5. Theology of the Poem: ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, ਨਾਮ, and ਹੁਕਮ
  6. The ਗੁਰੂ-ਸਿੱਖ Relationship and the ਮੁਰਸ਼ਿਦ Reimagined
  7. Sufi Vocabulary, Gurmat Substance: ਇਸ਼ਕ and ਬੰਦਗੀ
  8. The Zindagi Nama as Witness to the Court of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ
  9. The Goya Corpus: ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ and the Companion Works
  10. Language, Translation, and Reception
  11. Close Reading Workshop: Method and Practice
  12. Legacy: The Zindagi Nama in Sikh Devotional and Literary Life

What the Zindagi Nama Is

The ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀ ਨਾਮਾ, or 'Book of Life,' is among the most remarkable works of devotional literature produced in the orbit of the Sikh Gurus. Composed in elegant ਫ਼ਾਰਸੀ (Persian) by ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਗੋਯਾ, a learned poet who became a beloved Sikh of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ, it is a long poem in rhyming couplets that reads at once as a meditation on the purpose of human life and as the interior record of one soul's transformation. To open the Zindagi Nama is to encounter a man speaking directly about why he was born, what he sought, and where he finally found rest.

This course treats the poem as a versified spiritual autobiography. That phrase needs care. The Zindagi Nama does not tell its story the way a modern memoir does, with dates, places, and a chain of external events. Instead, it narrates an inner journey: the movement from restlessness to ਬੰਦਗੀ (devotion), from learning to love, from the seeking self to the surrendered ਗੁਰਸਿੱਖ. The 'life' of the title is less a biography than a teaching about what a life is for.

Why Study It at an Advanced Level

For the advanced student, the Zindagi Nama sits at a fascinating crossroads. It belongs to the great Persianate literary world that stretched from Anatolia to Bengal, drawing on the conventions of the ਮਸਨਵੀ and the vocabulary of Sufi poetry. Yet its substance is thoroughly ਗੁਰਮਤਿ: its God is ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, its discipline is ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ, and its spiritual master is the Sikh Guru. Studying the poem therefore means holding two literacies at once: a literacy in Persian poetic form and a literacy in Sikh theology. The reward is a deeper understanding of how Sikh thought expressed itself across languages, and of how a single gifted poet could pour Mughal courtly eloquence into the service of the Khalsa's spiritual vision.

The Poet Behind the Name

The author signs himself ਗੋਯਾ, a Persian ਤਖ਼ੱਲੁਸ or pen-name meaning 'the one who speaks' or 'the eloquent.' The choice is telling. Goya is a poet acutely aware that speech, when purified, becomes praise, and that the highest eloquence is the remembrance of the Name. Across his works the takhallus recurs as a kind of signature humility: the speaker reminds himself, again and again, that his words are worth nothing unless they turn toward ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ.

Goya served in the ਦਰਬਾਰ (court) of Guru Gobind Singh Ji at ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ, where, by long Sikh tradition, he was honored among the cultured circle of poets the tenth Guru gathered. This gives the Zindagi Nama a unique value: it is one of the very few first-person testimonies we possess from within that court, written not by a chronicler looking back but by a participant looking up at his Guru.

How This Course Proceeds

We begin with the poet's life and the masnavi form, then turn to the poem's autobiographical architecture and its theology. We examine how Goya reimagines the Sufi ਮੁਰਸ਼ਿਦ as the Sikh Guru, how he borrows Persian devotional vocabulary while filling it with Gurmat meaning, and how the poem testifies to court life. Later lessons address the wider Goya corpus, problems of language and translation, the practice of close reading, and the poem's enduring place in Sikh devotional life. Throughout, Gurbani in the Guru Granth Sahib and the teachings of the Gurus will serve as our touchstone for measuring the poem's theology, and we will be careful never to attribute citations we cannot verify.

A note on method: the Zindagi Nama survives in Persian manuscripts and in many later editions and translations into Punjabi, Hindi, and English. Where we quote, we present the substance of the poem's teaching, and where a precise wording is uncertain we describe what the poem says rather than inventing a citation. This discipline matters, because the poem's reception has sometimes blurred the line between Goya's verse and later devotional elaboration. The advanced reader learns to keep that line clear.

By the end of this introduction the student should grasp three things: that the Zindagi Nama is a Persian masnavi, that it functions as a spiritual autobiography rather than a factual one, and that its religious heart is unambiguously Sikh. These three claims will be tested and refined in every lesson that follows.

lessons.title: Goya's Life: From Ghazni and Multan to the Guru's Darbar
lessons.html:
The Shape of a Life

Before we can read the Zindagi Nama as autobiography, we must assemble what is known of ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਗੋਯਾ from tradition and scholarship. The picture is part documented history and part hagiographic memory, and the advanced student must learn to weigh the two. The editor Ganda Singh, in his standard Bhai Nand Lal Granthavali, gathered the available testimonies, and Surjit Hans, whose critical eye informs this course, taught us to read such testimonies for what they reveal about Sikh self-understanding as much as for bare fact.

Origins and Early Learning

By widely repeated tradition, Goya was born in ਗ਼ਜ਼ਨੀ (Ghazni), in the Persianate cultural world of Afghanistan, into a family connected with administrative and scholarly service. He was raised in an environment saturated with ਫ਼ਾਰਸੀ learning, where mastery of Persian poetry, prose, and the chancery arts was the mark of an educated man. The family's path led to ਮੁਲਤਾਨ (Multan), a great Punjabi entrepôt of Persian culture and Sufi devotion, and it is here that the young Nand Lal's gifts as a poet and stylist matured.

This early formation is essential to understanding the Zindagi Nama. Goya did not stumble into Persian verse; he was a trained master of it before he ever reached the Guru. The poem's polished couplets, its command of Sufi imagery, its rhetorical control, all flow from this education. When such a man turns his art toward ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ and the Guru, the result is not naive devotion but the deliberate offering of a connoisseur's craft.

Service and Reputation

Tradition records that Goya's abilities won him employment in Mughal administrative circles, and he is associated in several accounts with service connected to the prince who would become the emperor Bahadur Shah. Whatever the precise arrangements, the point for our reading is that Goya moved easily in the highest Persianate scholarly society of his age. He was a man of the world of courts, letters, and patronage, not a recluse.

The Turn to the Guru

The decisive event of Goya's life, in the tradition, is his arrival at the ਦਰਬਾਰ of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ at ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ. Here the accomplished Persian scholar became a ਗੁਰਸਿੱਖ. Sikh memory cherishes him as one of the ਕਵੀ (poets) of the tenth Guru's circle, and the Guru is said to have held his verse in affection. Whether or not every detail of the traditional accounts can be documented, the structural fact is secure and is confirmed by the poetry itself: a Persianate intellectual gave his heart and his art to the Sikh Guru.

It is this turn that the Zindagi Nama makes into its spiritual subject. The poem is the inner record of why such a turn happens and what it means. When Goya writes of the soul finding its true master, he writes from the lived experience of a learned man who had everything the Persianate world prized and found it incomplete until he reached the Guru's feet.

Reading Life Against Poem

A central methodological lesson of this course is that we read the life and the poem together but not naively. The Zindagi Nama is not a diary; it gives us the meaning of Goya's life as he came to understand it, not its calendar. Surjit Hans's approach to Sikh literature, his insistence on reading texts as historical artifacts that disclose the mind of a community, guides us here. We treat the traditional biography as the frame the community built around a poet it loved, and we treat the poem as the poet's own distilled testimony to his transformation.

Hagiography also surrounds Goya: stories of his devotion, of the Guru's recognition of his verse, of his place in the company of the court poets. These stories are valuable not because every detail is verifiable but because they show how later Sikhs understood the meaning of a learned man's surrender to the Guru. The advanced reader holds the documented, the traditional, and the poetic in productive tension.

Why the Biography Matters for the Poem

Knowing that Goya came from ਗ਼ਜ਼ਨੀ and ਮੁਲਤਾਨ, that he was a master of ਫ਼ਾਰਸੀ before he was a Sikh, changes how we read every couplet. The Sufi vocabulary in the Zindagi Nama is not borrowed clumsily from outside; it is the native idiom of a man reborn. The Persian forms are not a costume; they are his mother tongue of art, now devoted to a new Master. In the next lesson we examine the form itself, the ਮਸਨਵੀ, to see how its structure became the vessel for this devoted life.

lessons.title: The Masnavi Form: How Persian Couplets Carry a Life
lessons.html:
The Vessel and Its Shape

The Zindagi Nama is a ਮਸਨਵੀ, and to read it well one must understand what that means. The masnavi is one of the great forms of Persian and Persianate literature: a poem built of rhyming couplets in which each couplet rhymes within itself (AA, BB, CC) rather than across the whole poem. This simple structural choice has enormous consequences. Because the rhyme resets with every couplet, the masnavi is free to run on at length, making it the natural form for narrative, for didactic teaching, and for sustained spiritual meditation.

The Great Models

Every educated Persian reader of Goya's age carried the masnavi tradition in memory. The towering model was the Masnavi-i Ma'navi of Jalal al-Din Rumi, the 'spiritual couplets' that became a second scripture for many. Before and alongside Rumi stood the romances and didactic masnavis of Nizami, the ethical poems of Sa'di, the mystical allegories of Attar and Jami. Annemarie Schimmel's study of these traditions reminds us how the masnavi became the chosen vehicle for the inner life, a form long enough to follow the soul through all its stages.

Goya wrote in full consciousness of this lineage. When he chose the masnavi for his Book of Life, he placed his work within a recognizable genre of spiritual teaching in couplets. His readers would have expected a poem that instructs, that moves through stages, that returns repeatedly to the love of the Divine. The Zindagi Nama fulfills these expectations while redirecting them toward ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ and the Sikh Guru.

How the Couplet Works

The independence of each masnavi couplet makes the form both flexible and demanding. Each ਬੈਤ (couplet) is a complete unit of sense, a small jewel that can stand alone, yet the couplets accumulate into a sustained argument. This is why so many masnavi lines circulate as proverbs and as single quotations: each couplet is built to be both whole in itself and part of a larger flow.

For the Zindagi Nama, this structure is perfectly suited to spiritual autobiography. A life of devotion is not a single plot but a series of realizations, and the masnavi's couplet-by-couplet movement mirrors the way insight comes: one truth at a time, each complete, each leading on. Goya can pause on a single teaching, polish it into a memorable couplet, and then move forward, much as a soul moves from one station of ਬੰਦਗੀ to the next.

Meter and Music

The masnavi is composed in quantitative Persian meter, where the pattern of long and short syllables creates the poem's music. This musicality matters for our subject. The Zindagi Nama is not merely argument; it is meant to be recited, to be heard, to enter the ear and the heart. The discipline the poem teaches is ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ, the rhythmic remembrance of the Name, and the rhythmic couplet itself enacts something of that remembrance. Form and content rhyme: a poem about repetition is built from repeated metrical units.

Didactic and Devotional Registers

Masnavis typically move between two registers. In the didactic register the poet instructs, advises, and exhorts; in the devotional or ecstatic register the poet praises, longs, and surrenders. The Zindagi Nama uses both. It teaches the reader how to live, what to renounce, how to remember ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, and it breaks repeatedly into pure praise and longing. The student should learn to notice these shifts of register, because they map the poem's emotional architecture.

Form as Argument

It is tempting to treat poetic form as mere packaging, but in the Zindagi Nama the form is part of the meaning. The choice of the masnavi declares an allegiance: Goya announces, simply by his form, that he writes within the great tradition of spiritual instruction in Persian couplets, a tradition associated with the inner life and the love of God. He then claims that tradition for the Sikh path. The masnavi form is, in this sense, Goya's first theological statement, made before a single word of doctrine: the form says that the deepest things are best carried in the patient, accumulating music of the couplet.

Reading Couplets as a Sikh Text

One caution for the advanced reader: because masnavi couplets travel so easily as detached quotations, individual lines of the Zindagi Nama have sometimes been lifted, paraphrased, and embellished in later devotional usage. The disciplined reader returns each couplet to its place in the poem's argument and reads it within Goya's own flow rather than within later accretions. In the next lesson we turn from the form to the autobiographical content it carries, asking what kind of 'life' the Book of Life actually narrates.

lessons.title: Reading the Zindagi Nama as Spiritual Autobiography
lessons.html:
What Kind of Autobiography?

To call the ਜ਼ਿੰਦਗੀ ਨਾਮਾ an autobiography is both true and in need of qualification. It is not the autobiography of events but of meaning. Where a modern memoirist asks 'what happened to me?', Goya asks 'what is a life, and what was mine for?' The poem is the answer a soul gives when it has found its center. This lesson develops the tools for reading such a text.

The Two Selves of the Poem

Spiritual autobiography classically stages a drama between two selves: the old self lost in the world and the new self awakened to the Divine. Augustine's Confessions, the spiritual narratives of the Sufis, and the self-accounts of many devotional traditions all turn on this hinge. The Zindagi Nama enacts the same drama in the idiom of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ. The old self is the ਮਨਮੁਖ, the one turned toward the ego and the world; the new self is the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ, the one turned toward the Guru. The poem's 'I' moves from restlessness and incompleteness toward the peace of ਨਾਮ.

Crucially, this movement is universalized. Goya tells his own story in a way that becomes the reader's story. When he describes the soul's hunger and its finding, he speaks for any seeker. This is a deliberate feature of spiritual autobiography: the particular life becomes a map others can follow. The Book of Life is meant to be the reader's life too.

The Architecture of the Journey

The poem can be read as a series of spiritual milestones, though it does not march through them mechanically. We can discern a movement from a meditation on the purpose of human birth, to the recognition of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ as the one reality, to the necessity of the Guru as guide, to the discipline of ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ, to the surrender of the ego in ਬੰਦਗੀ, and finally to the settled state of one who lives in the Divine Will, in ਹੁਕਮ. The Zindagi Nama is the story of how a learned man passed through these stations.

We can summarize the poem's narrated arc in the words of its own teaching: that the human being is born to remember the Creator, that without such remembrance life is wasted, and that the Guru alone awakens the soul to its purpose. Where the precise Persian wording of any one couplet is uncertain in transmission, we hold to the substance: the Zindagi Nama teaches that a life is measured by its remembrance of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ.

The Confessional Voice

What makes the poem autobiography rather than mere doctrine is its voice. Goya does not stand outside his teaching; he confesses his own need of it. He speaks as one who has felt the emptiness of worldly attainment and the fullness of devotion. The ਤਖ਼ੱਲੁਸ 'Goya' appears as a recurring self-address, the poet calling himself by name to remember, to humble himself, to return to the Name. This habit of self-address is one of the surest marks of the autobiographical mode: the speaker is also the one spoken to.

Memory and Witness

Spiritual autobiography is an act of memory in two senses: it remembers the speaker's own past, and it performs ਸਿਮਰਨ, the remembrance of God. In the Zindagi Nama these two memories fuse. To recall his journey is, for Goya, already to praise the One who drew him on. The poem's backward glance at the self and its upward glance toward ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ are a single motion. This is why the Book of Life can be at once a memoir and a manual of devotion.

Comparison and Caution

It is illuminating to compare the Zindagi Nama with the Sufi tradition of spiritual self-narrative and with the autobiographical impulses in Punjabi devotional literature. But the advanced reader must avoid flattening Goya into a generic mystic. His autobiography is anchored in a specific allegiance: to ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ and the Sikh path. The shape may be shared with other traditions of spiritual autobiography; the substance is particular and Sikh.

The Reader's Task

Reading the Zindagi Nama as autobiography therefore means three things at once: tracking the inner journey of its 'I,' hearing the confessional and self-addressing voice, and recognizing that the poem invites the reader to make that journey their own. In the next lesson we descend into the poem's theology, the doctrinal substance that the autobiography exists to convey, and we test it against the teaching of Gurbani.

lessons.title: Theology of the Poem: Akal Purakh, Nam, and Hukam
lessons.html:
The God of the Zindagi Nama

The Zindagi Nama is, at its core, a poem about God and the soul's relation to God. Its theology is the heart that the autobiographical and literary features serve. This lesson sets out that theology and measures it against mainstream ਗੁਰਮਤਿ as taught in Gurbani.

One Formless Reality

The God of the Zindagi Nama is ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, the Timeless Being: one, formless, beyond birth and death, the sole reality from which all else proceeds. Goya, writing in Persian, draws on the rich Persian and Sufi vocabulary for the Divine, words for the Beloved, the Truth, the Eternal, but the conception he serves is the ਇੱਕ ਓਅੰਕਾਰ of Sikh teaching. The Zindagi Nama is uncompromisingly monotheistic. There is no created intermediary worthy of worship; there is only the One and the soul's longing for the One.

This aligns the poem with the opening declaration of the Guru Granth Sahib, the ਮੂਲ ਮੰਤਰ, which proclaims the one Creator who is timeless, unborn, self-existent. Gurbani in the Japji Sahib teaches that this One is beyond reckoning and is known through the Guru's grace. Goya's poem breathes the same conviction: the Divine is one, formless, and approached through love and remembrance, not through ritual machinery.

Nam: The Name as the Way

If ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ is the poem's God, then ਨਾਮ is its way to God. The discipline the Zindagi Nama urges above all is ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ, the loving remembrance of the Divine Name. In Goya's vision, the Name is not a mere word but the living presence of the Divine made available to the heart. To remember the Name is to be remade by it.

This too is central Gurmat. Gurbani throughout the Guru Granth Sahib exalts ਨਾਮ as the supreme treasure, the medicine for all ills, the means by which the soul is united with the Divine. The Zindagi Nama, though written in Persian and clothed in Sufi imagery, places ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ at the center exactly as Gurbani does. The poem's many exhortations to remember, to repeat, to never let the heart be empty of the Name, are Goya's Persian rendering of the Sikh way.

Hukam: Surrender to the Divine Order

The third pillar of the poem's theology is ਹੁਕਮ, the Divine Order or Will. The mature soul in the Zindagi Nama is one who has surrendered its own will into the ਹੁਕਮ of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. This is the resolution of the poem's autobiographical drama: the restless self finds peace not by getting what it wants but by wanting what the Divine wills.

Gurbani in the Japji Sahib teaches that all exists within ਹੁਕਮ and that to understand and accept the Hukam is to be freed from ਹਉਮੈ, the ego. The Zindagi Nama makes the same move. The surrender of ਹਉਮੈ is the poem's quiet climax, the point at which the seeking 'I' dissolves into devotion.

Grace and Love

For all its emphasis on discipline, the Zindagi Nama is no manual of earning. The soul reaches ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ by grace and by love, ਇਸ਼ਕ, not by transaction. The Guru's grace awakens the soul; the soul responds with love; love deepens into remembrance; remembrance flowers into surrender. This circle of grace and love is wholly congruent with Gurbani's teaching that union comes by the Guru's ਕਿਰਪਾ, grace, and not by human striving alone.

What the Poem Is Not

It is worth stating the negatives. The Zindagi Nama does not teach incarnation, idol worship, or ritual salvation. It does not locate the Divine in image or place. It does not make any human being the object of worship; even the Guru, supremely honored, is the window to the Divine and not the Divine's replacement. These negations matter because the poem's Sufi vocabulary could be misread as pantheism or as the worship of the master. Read against Gurbani, the poem's theology is disciplined Sikh monotheism.

A Theology in Verse

The achievement of the Zindagi Nama is to present this theology not as a creed but as a lived movement of the heart. ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, ਨਾਮ, and ਹੁਕਮ are not abstract doctrines in the poem but the very stations of Goya's journey. To learn the theology is to follow the autobiography, and to follow the autobiography is to absorb the theology. In the next lesson we examine the relationship at the poem's emotional center: the bond between the ਸਿੱਖ and the Guru.

lessons.title: The Guru-Sikh Relationship and the Murshid Reimagined
lessons.html:
The Heart of the Matter

If theology is the poem's mind, the ਗੁਰੂ-ਸਿੱਖ relationship is its heart. The Zindagi Nama exists because a learned man met his Guru, and everything the poem says about God flows through that meeting. This lesson examines how Goya portrays the bond between disciple and Guru, and how he takes the Sufi figure of the ਮੁਰਸ਼ਿਦ and reimagines it as the Sikh Guru.

The Sufi Murshid

In the Persian Sufi world Goya inherited, the ਮੁਰਸ਼ਿਦ was the spiritual guide, the ਪੀਰ who initiated the seeker, the ਮੁਰੀਦ, into the path and led the soul stage by stage toward the Divine. Schimmel's account of Sufi devotion shows how central this relationship was: the guide was the soul's physician, mirror, and gateway, and devotion to the guide was understood as devotion to God flowing through a human channel. The vocabulary of love between ਮੁਰਸ਼ਿਦ and ਮੁਰੀਦ filled Persian poetry.

Goya knew this vocabulary intimately. When he reached ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ, he did not abandon it; he transformed it. The Sufi grammar of guide and disciple became, in his hands, the language of the ਗੁਰੂ-ਸਿੱਖ bond.

The Sikh Guru Is Different

Yet the transformation is real and not merely a relabeling. The Sikh Guru in the Zindagi Nama is not a Sufi ਪੀਰ with a new name. The Guru is the embodiment of the Word, the ਸ਼ਬਦ, the one through whom ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ reveals the way of ਨਾਮ. Where the Sufi master often stood at the head of a lineage tariqa with its rituals of initiation, the Sikh Guru stands within the ਗੁਰੂ lineage that culminates in the eternal Guruship of the Word. Goya's devotion to ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ is devotion to a Guru who points wholly beyond himself to the One.

This is the crucial theological safeguard in the poem. The intensity of Goya's love for his Guru never tips into worship of a man. The Guru is supremely honored as the means of grace, the awakener, the one whose glance turns the soul toward God, but the object of worship remains ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. The Sikh Guru is the perfect ਮੁਰਸ਼ਿਦ precisely because he hides himself in the Word and reveals only the Divine.

The Drama of Surrender

The poem stages the disciple's surrender as the turning point of the spiritual life. The proud, accomplished scholar lays his learning at the Guru's feet and finds that all his Persian mastery is worth nothing beside the Guru's gift of ਨਾਮ. This is a recurring movement in spiritual autobiography, the surrender of worldly attainment, but Goya gives it a specific Sikh shape: the surrender is to the Guru who teaches remembrance and the discarding of ਹਉਮੈ.

The Zindagi Nama teaches that without the Guru the soul cannot find the way, that the Guru's grace is the door, and that the disciple's whole duty is loving obedience and remembrance. This is fully congruent with Gurbani, which teaches throughout the Guru Granth Sahib that ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ is realized through the ਗੁਰੂ and the ਸ਼ਬਦ, and that the ਗੁਰਮੁਖ is the one who lives by the Guru's word.

Love as the Bond

The relationship is bound by ਪ੍ਰੇਮ and ਇਸ਼ਕ, love. Goya's portrayal of the disciple's longing for the Guru, the joy of the Guru's presence, the ache of separation, draws on the full emotional palette of Persian love poetry. But the love is purified: it is love of the Guru as the gate to the Beloved, ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. The reader feels the warmth of a real human devotion and is led through it to the love of God.

A Unique Testimony

What makes Goya's portrait of the ਗੁਰੂ-ਸਿੱਖ relationship precious is that it is written from inside. This is not a theologian's account of what the relationship should be; it is a disciple's account of what it felt like to live in the presence of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ. The Zindagi Nama lets us hear the voice of one who actually sat in that ਦਰਬਾਰ, and that intimacy is its enduring gift.

Method Note

The advanced reader should resist two errors: collapsing the Sikh Guru into the Sufi ਮੁਰਸ਼ਿਦ as if they were identical, and denying any relationship between the two as if Goya's vocabulary were accidental. The truth is a creative transformation: Goya took a living devotional language and reoriented it toward the Sikh Guru and ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. In the next lesson we examine this transformation at the level of vocabulary, asking how Sufi words come to carry Gurmat substance.

lessons.title: Sufi Vocabulary, Gurmat Substance: Ishq and Bandagi
lessons.html:
Borrowed Words, Native Faith

One of the most intellectually rich features of the Zindagi Nama is the way it uses the vocabulary of Persian Sufi poetry to express a Sikh devotional vision. This lesson studies that interplay closely, because mastering it is essential to reading the poem without distortion. The danger is twofold: to assume the Sufi words mean exactly what they mean in Sufi poetry, or to ignore them as empty ornament. The truth lies between: Goya pours ਗੁਰਮਤਿ into Persian devotional forms.

The Word Ishq

Consider ਇਸ਼ਕ, ardent passionate love. In Persian Sufi verse, ਇਸ਼ਕ is the burning love of the soul for the Divine Beloved, often expressed through the imagery of human passion, the cup of wine, the moth and the flame, the lover destroyed in love. Goya uses this whole vocabulary. But the Beloved is ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, and the intoxication is the intoxication of ਨਾਮ. The wine is not wine; it is the Name. The annihilation of the lover is not a metaphysical absorption that erases the soul but the dissolving of ਹਉਮੈ, the ego, so that the soul lives in ਹੁਕਮ.

This matters theologically. Some strands of Sufi thought speak of ਫ਼ਨਾ, the annihilation of the self in God, in ways that can suggest the soul's identity is simply erased or that the soul becomes God. Gurmat teaches union and merger, the drop returning to the ocean, while preserving the Creator-creature distinction and the reality of loving relationship. The advanced reader watches how Goya uses the intense language of ਇਸ਼ਕ and self-loss while keeping the Sikh frame: the soul is fulfilled in loving remembrance and surrender, not abolished.

The Word Bandagi

Consider ਬੰਦਗੀ, devotion or worshipful servitude. The word literally evokes the posture of the ਬੰਦਾ, the servant or slave, before the Master. In the Zindagi Nama, ਬੰਦਗੀ is the soul's whole vocation: to stand as a servant before ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, to remember, to obey, to love. This is fully Sikh; Gurbani repeatedly exalts the posture of the ਦਾਸ, the servant, and the ਸੇਵਕ who finds greatness in service. The Persian ਬੰਦਗੀ and the Gurmat ideal of ਸੇਵਾ and loving submission converge.

Imagery and Its Reorientation

Persian devotional poetry comes with a stock of images: the tavern and the wine, the Beloved's face and tresses, the candle and the moth, the rose and the nightingale, the dust of the Beloved's path. Goya inherits these and reorients them. The tavern becomes the company of the devout, the ਸਾਧ ਸੰਗਤ; the wine becomes ਨਾਮ; the dust of the path becomes the humble dust of the Guru's feet. The reader trained only in Sufi convention will catch the imagery but miss the redirection; the reader trained only in Gurmat will catch the doctrine but miss the artistry. The Zindagi Nama demands both literacies.

Why Goya Did This

Why use Sufi vocabulary at all? Three reasons. First, it was Goya's native poetic idiom; a master of ਫ਼ਾਰਸੀ naturally composed in its devotional language. Second, it made the Sikh message legible to the Persianate world, a kind of bridge by which the wider culture could glimpse the depth of the Guru's path. Third, the Sufi vocabulary of love and longing genuinely suited the emotional truth Goya wished to express; the language of ਇਸ਼ਕ can carry the heat of real devotion. Goya's genius was to use a shared devotional idiom without surrendering the distinctness of his faith.

The Comparative Question

Scholars have long discussed the relationship between Sikh devotion and the Sufi and ਭਗਤੀ currents around it. The Guru Granth Sahib itself includes the compositions of Bhagats and of Baba Farid, a Sufi voice, showing that Gurmat could embrace what was true in surrounding traditions while subordinating all to its own vision of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. Goya's Zindagi Nama operates in this same spirit at the level of a single poet's art: it gratefully uses the surrounding devotional language and bends it toward the Guru.

Reading Discipline

The practical lesson is a habit of double reading. For each charged Persian word in the Zindagi Nama, the student asks two questions: what does this word mean in the Sufi tradition, and what does Goya make it mean here? The gap between the two answers is where the poem's meaning lives. ਇਸ਼ਕ and ਬੰਦਗੀ are our model cases; the method extends to the whole vocabulary. In the next lesson we turn from inner devotion to outer witness, reading the Zindagi Nama as a record of life in the Guru's court.

lessons.title: The Zindagi Nama as Witness to the Court of Guru Gobind Singh Ji
lessons.html:
A Voice from Inside the Darbar

Among the many values of the Zindagi Nama, one is uniquely historical: it is a first-person witness from within the ਦਰਬਾਰ of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ at ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ. This lesson examines what kind of historical source the poem is and how to read it responsibly, drawing on Surjit Hans's method of reconstructing Sikh history from Sikh literature.

The Court of the Tenth Guru

The court of Guru Gobind Singh Ji at Anandpur was, by tradition and by the surviving literature, a center of remarkable cultural activity. The Guru gathered poets and scholars, sponsored the translation and composition of works, and presided over a flowering of devotional and martial literature. The age was also one of gathering conflict, as the Guru founded the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ in 1699 and faced mounting pressure from hill rajas and the Mughal state. Into this charged and creative environment came ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਗੋਯਾ, a master of Persian letters, who took his place among the Guru's ਕਵੀ.

What the Poem Witnesses

The Zindagi Nama does not give us a chronicle of events; it gives us something rarer, the texture of devotion as experienced by a participant. From it we learn how the relationship between the cultured disciple and the Guru was felt, how ਨਾਮ and ਬੰਦਗੀ stood at the center of the community's spiritual life, and how a Persianate intellectual understood his transformation into a ਗੁਰਸਿੱਖ. This is the history of an inner world, and it is precious precisely because such testimonies are so rare.

To set the witness in context, the advanced student reads the Zindagi Nama alongside the other Persian work associated with this court, the ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ, the Epistle of Victory addressed by Guru Gobind Singh Ji to the emperor Aurangzeb. Louis Fenech's detailed study of the Zafar-namah illuminates how Persian, the language of empire, became in Sikh hands a vehicle of moral and spiritual challenge. The Zindagi Nama belongs to this same phenomenon: Persian, the courtly tongue, turned to the praise of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ and the witness of the Guru's path.

The Hans Method

Surjit Hans's A Reconstruction of Sikh History from Sikh Literature models how to use a text like the Zindagi Nama. Hans argued that Sikh literature must be read as a historical source for the mentality and self-understanding of the community, not merely mined for datable facts. A devotional poem tells us less about what happened on a given day than about how the community thought, valued, and believed. Applied to the Zindagi Nama, this method yields a portrait of the spiritual ideals alive in the Guru's circle: the centrality of ਨਾਮ, the ethic of ਬੰਦਗੀ, the bond of ਗੁਰੂ and ਸਿੱਖ.

Cautions for the Historian

The poem must be handled with critical care. First, it is a devotional and didactic work, not a report; its 'I' is the spiritual self, and its scenes are interior. Second, the text comes to us through manuscripts and editions of varying authority, and later devotional tradition has sometimes added stories about Goya that the poem itself does not contain. The disciplined reader distinguishes what the Zindagi Nama actually says from what tradition has wrapped around it. Third, we must resist the temptation to extract precise biographical events from a poem whose purpose is spiritual rather than documentary.

These cautions do not diminish the poem's value; they refine it. The Zindagi Nama is a superb source for the inner life of the Guru's court and a poor source for its calendar, and the wise historian asks of it only what it can give.

The Significance of a Persian Witness

That this witness comes in ਫ਼ਾਰਸੀ is itself historically significant. It shows that the Sikh path drew to itself the most cultivated minds of the Persianate world and that those minds expressed their new faith in their inherited language of high culture. The Zindagi Nama is evidence that the Guru's court was not parochial but cosmopolitan, capable of speaking to and through the dominant literary culture of the age while remaining wholly devoted to ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ.

Summary

Read as history, the Zindagi Nama is best understood as a witness to a mentality, a first-person record of devotion from within the court of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ. Following Hans, we read it for what it discloses about the Sikh spiritual imagination at a formative moment. In the next lesson we widen our view to the rest of Goya's corpus, especially the ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ, to see the Zindagi Nama in the company of its author's other works.

lessons.title: The Goya Corpus: Diwan-e-Goya and the Companion Works
lessons.html:
The Poet's Whole Output

The Zindagi Nama does not stand alone. ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਗੋਯਾ left a body of Persian works, and reading the Book of Life within that body sharpens our understanding of it. This lesson surveys the corpus as gathered in standard editions such as Ganda Singh's Bhai Nand Lal Granthavali, and asks how the works illuminate one another.

The Diwan-e-Goya

The companion masterpiece to the Zindagi Nama is the ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ, Goya's collected ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲs. Where the Zindagi Nama is a long masnavi of teaching and autobiography, the Diwan is a collection of ghazals, the lyric form par excellence of Persian poetry, each a short, intense, self-contained poem of love and longing. If the masnavi is the river of the spiritual journey, the ghazals are pools of concentrated feeling.

In the ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ Goya pours out the ardor of ਇਸ਼ਕ for the Divine Beloved and for the Guru. The ghazals are prized in Sikh devotional life, and verses from them are sung in ਕੀਰਤਨ. They reveal the same theology as the Zindagi Nama, the love of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, the centrality of ਨਾਮ, the devotion to the Guru, but in a more compressed and ecstatic register. Reading the Diwan alongside the Zindagi Nama, we see a single devotional vision expressed in two complementary forms.

The Other Works

The Goya corpus, as traditionally gathered, includes several further Persian works of devotion and praise, among them shorter masnavis and prose-and-verse compositions in honor of the Guru and on the nature of the spiritual life. Two short works in Punjabi are also traditionally associated with Goya and describe aspects of the Guru's court and the daily devotional discipline of the Sikh, though questions of authorship and transmission attach to parts of the corpus and the advanced student should treat attributions with scholarly caution.

The general point is that Goya was a prolific devotional poet whose works circle the same center from different angles. Some praise the Guru directly; some meditate on the Name; some, like the Zindagi Nama, narrate the spiritual journey. Together they form one of the richest bodies of Persian devotional literature produced within the Sikh tradition.

Genre and Function

Comparing the genres clarifies the Zindagi Nama's distinctive work. The ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲ excels at the lyric moment, the flash of longing or union; the ਮਸਨਵੀ excels at the sustained journey and the patient teaching. Goya needed both. His ecstasy found its form in the ghazals of the Diwan; his teaching and his life-story found their form in the masnavi of the Zindagi Nama. The student who reads only one form misunderstands the poet; the two forms are the two lungs of his devotion.

The Takhallus Across the Corpus

The pen-name ਗੋਯਾ threads through the whole corpus, appearing characteristically in the closing verses where the poet addresses himself. Tracking this signature across the works reveals a consistent self-understanding: Goya the eloquent speaker who knows that all his eloquence is dust unless it praises the One. This recurring self-address binds the Zindagi Nama to the Diwan and to the rest, marking them all as the utterance of a single devoted voice.

Editions and Access

For the advanced student, the gateway to the corpus is the critical editorial work, above all Ganda Singh's collection, which assembles the Persian texts with scholarly apparatus. Bhai Vir Singh's studies of Goya's life and work in Punjabi opened the poet to a wide modern Sikh readership and remain influential. The student should be aware that popular editions and translations vary in fidelity, and that for serious study one returns to the best-attested texts.

Why the Corpus Matters for the Zindagi Nama

Placing the Zindagi Nama within Goya's corpus does three things. It confirms the consistency of its theology across the poet's output, so that the Book of Life is not an isolated statement but the narrative crown of a unified devotional vision. It clarifies the masnavi's distinctive function as the form of journey and teaching. And it reminds us that Goya was, above all, a poet, a maker, whose every work was an offering of craft to ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ and the Guru. In the next lesson we turn to the practical problems of meeting this poet across the barriers of language, translation, and reception.

lessons.title: Language, Translation, and Reception
lessons.html:
Meeting the Poem Across Distances

Most readers today meet the Zindagi Nama not in Goya's Persian but in translation, and almost always at the end of a long chain of transmission, editing, and devotional use. This lesson addresses the problems and responsibilities that come with reading the poem across the distances of language, manuscript, and reception. For the advanced student, these are not dry technicalities; they shape what we can responsibly claim about the poem.

The Persian Barrier

The Zindagi Nama is a work of high ਫ਼ਾਰਸੀ art. Its meaning lives in its meter, its rhyme, its allusions to the Persian poetic tradition, and the precise resonances of its vocabulary. A translation, however skilled, cannot carry all of this. The music of the ਮਸਨਵੀ couplet, the way a single word can summon the whole Sufi imaginary, the interplay of sound and sense, these are largely untranslatable. The reader who works only from translation must hold their conclusions about the poem's art with humility, while the reader who can approach the Persian gains access to a dimension the translation can only gesture toward.

The Problem of the Text

Before translation comes the question of the text itself. The Zindagi Nama survives in manuscripts that differ, and the various printed editions reflect editorial choices about which readings to follow. Critical editions, such as the work gathered by Ganda Singh, attempt to establish a reliable text, but the advanced student should know that no single popular edition is simply 'the' Zindagi Nama. When we quote the poem, we must be aware of which text we are quoting and how secure the wording is. This is why, in this course, we are careful to convey the substance of the poem's teaching and to avoid presenting any specific wording or numbered citation as certain when it is not.

Layers of Translation

The Zindagi Nama has been translated and paraphrased into Punjabi, Hindi, Urdu, and English, often for devotional rather than scholarly purposes. Devotional translations sometimes smooth, expand, or interpret the text to draw out its piety, which is valuable for worship but can mislead the scholar. The student must distinguish a close scholarly rendering from a free devotional paraphrase. A useful discipline is to compare several translations of the same passage; where they diverge widely, one has found a place where interpretation is doing heavy work, and where caution is required.

Reception in Sikh Devotional Life

The Zindagi Nama and the ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ have lived, above all, as devotional texts. Verses of Goya are sung in ਕੀਰਤਨ and quoted in ਕਥਾ, and the poet is honored in Sikh memory as a model of the learned man who surrendered to the Guru. This living reception is a strength: the poem has never been a museum piece but a breathing part of Sikh devotion. Yet reception also reshapes a text. Favorite couplets are detached and recirculated, stories accrete around the poet, and the popular image of the Zindagi Nama can drift from its actual contents. The scholar honors the devotional life of the text while keeping a clear eye on what the poem itself, in its best-attested form, says.

Translation as Interpretation

Every translation is already an interpretation, and the charged vocabulary of the Zindagi Nama makes this especially acute. How one renders ਇਸ਼ਕ, whether as 'love,' 'passion,' or 'ardor,' already nudges the reader toward a reading. How one translates the language of self-loss can make Goya sound more like a particular school of Sufi metaphysics or more like mainstream ਗੁਰਮਤਿ. The advanced reader learns to see the interpretive choices embedded in any translation and to ask whether they are faithful to Goya's Sikh frame.

A Responsible Practice

From all this follows a practice. Read the best-attested text where possible; compare translations; distinguish scholarly from devotional renderings; honor the living reception while not confusing it with the text; and never present an uncertain wording or citation as fact. This discipline is not pedantry. It is the respect a great poem deserves, and it protects both the integrity of Goya's work and the integrity of our own scholarship. In the next lesson we put these principles to work in the practice of close reading.

lessons.title: Close Reading Workshop: Method and Practice
lessons.html:
From Survey to Close Reading

Having surveyed the poet, the form, the theology, and the problems of text and translation, we now turn to the central scholarly skill of this course: the close reading of the Zindagi Nama. This lesson sets out a method and then models it, so that the student can produce sustained, evidence-based interpretation of the poem's verse.

The Five Movements of a Close Reading

A disciplined close reading of a passage from the Zindagi Nama moves through five steps. First, establish the text: identify the passage, note which edition and translation you are using, and flag any uncertainty in the wording. Second, describe the form: observe the couplets, the movement of thought from line to line, the register (didactic or ecstatic), and any patterning of sound or image. Third, read the vocabulary doubly: for each charged term, ask what it means in the Persian Sufi tradition and what Goya makes it mean in his Sikh frame. Fourth, locate the theology: identify how the passage handles ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, ਨਾਮ, ਹੁਕਮ, the Guru, and measure it against Gurbani. Fifth, situate the autobiography: ask where in the soul's journey this passage falls and how it advances the poem's narrative of transformation.

Worked Example: A Passage on the Purpose of Life

Consider a representative teaching of the Zindagi Nama, that the human being is born to remember the Creator and that a life without such remembrance is wasted. We do not here pin this to a specific numbered couplet, because the wording varies across editions; instead we read the poem's clear and repeated teaching. Goya in substance declares: the breath that passes without the remembrance of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ is breath wasted; the purpose of being born a human is to remember the One who gave the breath.

Apply the method. Form: such teachings come in the masnavi's didactic register, a couplet that states a truth and a following couplet that drives it home, the patient hammer-blows of instruction. Vocabulary: the language of breath and remembrance draws on the Persian devotional vocabulary of ਦਮ, the breath, and ਯਾਦ, remembrance, terms a Sufi reader would recognize; Goya makes them carry ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ, the Sikh discipline of remembering the Name. Theology: the passage centers ਨਾਮ and the purpose of human birth, which we can measure against Gurbani in the Guru Granth Sahib, where the teaching that the human birth is a precious opportunity to remember the Divine recurs throughout. Autobiography: this teaching belongs near the poem's foundational layer, the recognition of what a life is for, which sets in motion the whole journey.

Worked Example: A Passage of Surrender

Take a second representative movement: the surrender of the ego, the dissolving of ਹਉਮੈ into ਬੰਦਗੀ. The Zindagi Nama in substance teaches that the soul finds peace only when it lays down its own will and lives in the ਹੁਕਮ of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. Applying the method, we notice the shift into the ecstatic register, the imagery of ਇਸ਼ਕ and self-loss, the double reading required to keep the Sufi language within the Sikh frame of merger-without-erasure, and the theology of ਹੁਕਮ measured against the teaching of the Japji Sahib that all is within the Divine Order. In the autobiography, this passage marks the climax, the point where the seeking self yields.

Common Errors to Avoid

Close reading of the Zindagi Nama has characteristic pitfalls. Over-Sufizing: reading every term in its Sufi sense and missing the Sikh redirection. Over-flattening: ignoring the Persian artistry and treating the poem as bare doctrine. False precision: citing a couplet number or exact wording as if it were secure when the text is uncertain. Hagiographic drift: importing later stories about Goya into the reading of the verse. The five-step method guards against each by demanding evidence, double reading, textual honesty, and attention to the poem's own argument.

The Student's Assignment

The capstone exercise of this course is a sustained close reading of a passage of the Zindagi Nama using the five movements. The student selects a passage in a stated edition and translation, describes its form, reads its vocabulary doubly, locates its theology against Gurbani, and situates it in the poem's autobiographical arc, all while observing the discipline of textual honesty. The aim is not to praise the poem but to understand it, to show in detail how Goya's Persian art carries his Sikh devotion. In the final lesson we step back to consider the poem's legacy and enduring significance.

lessons.title: Legacy: The Zindagi Nama in Sikh Devotional and Literary Life
lessons.html:
The Afterlife of the Book of Life

We end where a great poem always points, beyond itself, to its life in the community that has cherished it. The Zindagi Nama has lived for three centuries as scripTural companion, devotional resource, literary monument, and emblem of a learned man's surrender to the Guru. This final lesson assesses its legacy and gathers the threads of the course.

A Living Devotional Text

The Zindagi Nama and the ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ have never been merely studied; they have been loved, sung, and lived. Verses of ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਗੋਯਾ hold an honored place in Sikh devotional life, recited in ਕਥਾ and sung in ਕੀਰਤਨ. Goya is remembered with deep affection as the model of the cultivated intellectual who found that all his learning was empty until he reached the Guru's feet. This living reception is the surest sign of the poem's power: it continues to do spiritual work in the hearts of readers and listeners.

A Literary Monument

As literature, the Zindagi Nama is a landmark. It demonstrates that Sikh devotion could express itself at the highest level of Persian art, taking the prestige language of the Mughal world and turning it to the praise of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. Alongside the ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ, it stands as evidence of the cosmopolitan reach of the Guru's court and of the capacity of the Sikh vision to speak through the great literary forms of its age. For the historian of literature, Goya is a major Persian poet of the Indian subcontinent; for the historian of Sikhism, he is a witness to a formative moment.

A Bridge Between Worlds

Part of the poem's enduring fascination is its position on a frontier. It draws on the Sufi vocabulary of ਇਸ਼ਕ and ਮੁਰਸ਼ਿਦ and ਬੰਦਗੀ while remaining wholly committed to ਗੁਰਮਤਿ. In an age of religious division, the Zindagi Nama shows a Sikh poet confidently using a shared devotional language to express a distinct faith, neither retreating into isolation nor dissolving into the surrounding traditions. For modern readers interested in how religious traditions meet without merging, the poem is an instructive case.

What the Course Has Established

Across these lessons we have established several claims. The Zindagi Nama is a Persian ਮਸਨਵੀ, a poem of rhyming couplets in the great tradition of spiritual instruction in verse. It functions as a spiritual autobiography, narrating not events but the meaning of a life transformed, the movement from the accomplished Persian scholar to the surrendered ਗੁਰਸਿੱਖ. Its theology is disciplined Sikh monotheism: ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, ਨਾਮ, and ਹੁਕਮ at its center, measured throughout against Gurbani. It reimagines the Sufi ਮੁਰਸ਼ਿਦ as the Sikh Guru while guarding against any worship of the human master. And it offers a rare first-person witness to the inner life of the court of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ.

The Scholar's Continuing Task

We have also learned a discipline: to read the poem with double literacy, Persian form and Sikh substance; to handle text, translation, and reception with care; and never to claim a citation or wording we cannot verify. This discipline is the gift of advanced study. It allows us to love the poem as devotion while understanding it as scholarship, holding both without confusion.

A Final Word

The Zindagi Nama ends, as it begins, by turning the reader toward the One. Its 'Book of Life' is finally an invitation: to make of one's own life a remembrance of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, to find a true Guru, and to let the ego dissolve in ਬੰਦਗੀ. That a master of Persian letters wrote such a book in such a form, from within the court of the tenth Guru, is among the treasures of the Sikh literary heritage. The student who has worked through this course is now equipped to enter that treasure with both reverence and rigor.

quiz.q: What verse form is the Zindagi Nama composed in, and what is its defining structural feature?
options: The ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲ, with a single rhyme running across the whole poem
The ਮਸਨਵੀ, built of self-rhyming couplets (AA, BB, CC) suited to long narrative and teaching
The ਵਾਰ, an epic ballad in alternating stanzas and refrains
Free verse without meter or rhyme

quiz.q: In what sense is the Zindagi Nama best understood as an autobiography?
options: As a dated chronicle of external events in Goya's career
As a spiritual autobiography of inner meaning, narrating the soul's transformation rather than a calendar of facts
As a fictional romance with an invented narrator
As a courtly history of the Mughal administration

quiz.q: How does the Zindagi Nama treat the Sufi figure of the ਮੁਰਸ਼ਿਦ (spiritual guide)?
options: It rejects the concept entirely as incompatible with Sikh teaching
It identifies the ਮੁਰਸ਼ਿਦ with God and urges worship of the master
It creatively reorients the figure onto the Sikh Guru, who points wholly beyond himself to ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ
It replaces the guide with self-directed meditation needing no Guru

quiz.q: Which three concepts form the theological core of the Zindagi Nama, consistent with mainstream ਗੁਰਮਤਿ?
options: ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, ਨਾਮ, and ਹੁਕਮ
Incarnation, idol worship, and ritual sacrifice
Caste, pilgrimage, and astrology
Renunciation of the world, celibacy, and silence

quiz.q: What is the relationship between the Zindagi Nama and the ਦੀਵਾਨ-ਏ-ਗੋਯਾ?
options: They are two names for the same single poem
The Diwan is a prose chronicle while the Zindagi Nama is its verse summary
The Zindagi Nama is a long teaching-and-autobiography masnavi, while the Diwan is Goya's collection of lyric ਗ਼ਜ਼ਲs; together they express one devotional vision in two forms
The Diwan was written by a different poet and only attributed to Goya

quiz.q: According to the course, what is the most responsible way to handle quotations from the Zindagi Nama given its textual history?
options: Always cite a specific couplet number from any available edition to appear precise
Convey the substance of the poem's teaching and avoid presenting uncertain wordings or numbered citations as secure
Rely exclusively on free devotional paraphrases because they capture the piety best
Refuse to quote the poem at all since it survives only in Persian

courses.title: Jot Bigas and Rah-i-Rast: Bhai Nand Lal's Punjabi Works
courses.source: Jot Bigas and Rah-i-Rast by Bhai Nand Lal Goya
courses.summary: This intermediate course examines the two Punjabi compositions of ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਗੋਯਾ, the celebrated court poet of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ: the ਜੋਤਿ ਬਿਗਾਸ (Expansion of Divine Light) and the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ known as ਰਹਿ-ਇ-ਰਾਸਤ (The Straight Path). While ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ is best remembered as a master of Persian verse, these two works reveal him writing in Punjabi for the Sikh ਸੰਗਤ, articulating the metaphysics of ਜੋਤਿ, the centrality of ਨਾਮ, devotion to the ਗੁਰੂ, and the ethical discipline of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ. Students will analyze the theological content, the contrast between his Persian and Punjabi registers, his place in the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ tradition, and his lasting contribution to early Sikh literature. The course situates these texts in the historical context of the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries at ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ.
outcomes: Identify the historical and biographical context of ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ ਗੋਯਾ and his service at the court of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ
Distinguish the theological themes of the ਜੋਤਿ ਬਿਗਾਸ, especially the metaphysics of ਜੋਤਿ and the role of ਨਾਮ and ਸਿਮਰਨ
Analyze the ethical and ਰਹਿਤ content of the ਰਹਿ-ਇ-ਰਾਸਤ within the wider ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ tradition
Compare ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ's Punjabi register with his Persian masterpieces and assess questions of authorship and attribution
Evaluate the contribution of these Punjabi works to the formation of early Sikh literary and devotional culture
Apply scholarly source-critical methods to ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ literature and the problems of redaction
