courses.title: Guru Granth Darpan: Prof Sahib Singh's Life Work
courses.source: Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan by Prof Sahib Singh
courses.summary: A comprehensive intermediate study of Prof Sahib Singh (1892-1977) and his monumental ten-volume ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਦਰਪਣ, the standard Punjabi word-for-word commentary (ਟੀਕਾ) on the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ. The course traces his improbable journey from a Hindu Pohuwindi family to becoming the foremost grammarian of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, examines the grammatical methodology that anchors the Darpan, and evaluates why his ਟੀਕਾ became the most trusted Punjabi commentary among Sikh scholars, ਟਕਸਾਲ traditions, and ordinary ਸੰਗਤ alike.
outcomes: Reconstruct the biography of Prof Sahib Singh and explain how his life as a teacher and ਪ੍ਰਿੰਸੀਪਲ shaped the Darpan
Describe the grammatical methodology (ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ ਵਿਆਕਰਣ) that underlies every entry in the ਦਰਪਣ
Explain the word-for-word (ਪਦ-ਅਰਥ) and paraphrase (ਅਰਥ) structure of a typical Darpan entry
Evaluate why the Darpan became the standard Punjabi ਟੀਕਾ and how it differs from earlier commentaries
Analyze how Prof Sahib Singh resolves difficult or contested ਤੁਕਾਂ of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ using grammar rather than tradition alone
Assess the present status of the Darpan among academic scholars, ਟਕਸਾਲਾਂ, and critics

terms.m: Darpan, literally 'mirror' — the title Prof Sahib Singh gave his ten-volume commentary, presenting Gurbani's meaning as a clear reflection.
Teeka: a line-by-line scriptural commentary or exegesis in the Punjabi-Sikh tradition.
Pad-arath: the word-for-word meaning of each term in a verse, listed before the running translation in the Darpan.
Gurbani Viakaran: the grammar of the sacred text, the systematic linguistic framework Prof Sahib Singh derived and applied.
Lagaan-matraan: the vowel signs and diacritics of Gurmukhi, which Sahib Singh argued carry grammatical and therefore semantic meaning.
Adi Granth: the first compilation of the scripture by ਗੁਰੂ ਅਰਜਨ ਦੇਵ ਜੀ, the text the Darpan explains.
Aunkar: the short 'u' vowel sign beneath a consonant, whose presence or absence Sahib Singh showed marks grammatical case and number.
Sihari: the short 'i' vowel sign, another diacritic Sahib Singh demonstrated to be grammatically meaningful in Gurbani.
Taksal: the traditional Sikh seminary lineages of recitation and exegesis, against whose oral readings the Darpan is often compared.
Khalsa College, Amritsar, where Prof Sahib Singh taught and served, the institutional home of his scholarship.
Panth: the collective Sikh community, the readership and final arbiter of the Darpan's authority.
Arath: the running paraphrase or sense-translation of a verse that follows the word-for-word gloss.

references: Singh, Sahib. Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. 10 vols. Jalandhar: Raj Publishers, 1962-1964.
Singh, Sahib. Gurbani Viakaran. Amritsar: Singh Brothers, 1939.
Singh, Sahib. Meri Jeevan Kahani (My Life Story). Amritsar: Singh Brothers, 1968.
Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.
Singh, Pashaura. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.
Shackle, Christopher. A Guru Nanak Glossary. London: School of Oriental and African Studies, 1981.
Singh, Taran. Gurbani dian Viakhia Pranalian. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1980.
Mann, Gurinder Singh, and Kamalroop Singh. The Granth of Guru Gobind Singh: Essays, Lectures and Translations. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2015.

lessons.title: Introduction: A Mirror Held to Gurbani
lessons.summary: Overview of the Darpan, its place in Sikh scholarship, and the course roadmap.
lessons.html:
ਵਿਸ਼ਾ ਸੂਚੀ (Table of Contents)

  1. Introduction: A Mirror Held to Gurbani
  2. From Pohuwindi to the Panth: The Life of Prof Sahib Singh
  3. Khalsa College and the Making of a Scholar
  4. Gurbani Viakaran: The Grammar Beneath the Darpan
  5. The Power of the Lagaan-Matraan
  6. Anatomy of a Darpan Entry: Pad-Arath and Arath
  7. Earlier Teekas and Why the Darpan Surpassed Them
  8. How the Darpan Handles Difficult Gurbani
  9. Reception, Critics, and the Taksal Debate
  10. The Darpan Today: Digital Life and Enduring Authority
  11. Conclusion and Works Cited

A Mirror Held to Gurbani

When a student of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ in the twentieth or twenty-first century reaches for a single Punjabi reference to settle the meaning of a difficult ਤੁਕ (line), the volume most likely to be pulled from the shelf is one of the ten that make up Prof Sahib Singh's ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਦਰਪਣ. The very title is a claim about method: a ਦਰਪਣ is a mirror, and Sahib Singh offered his commentary not as a screen of his own opinions but as a polished surface in which the meaning already present in the scripture could be seen clearly. This course examines both the man and the monument he left behind.

The ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ, compiled by ਗੁਰੂ ਅਰਜਨ ਦੇਵ ਜੀ in 1604 and given its final form as ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ by ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ, is a text of extraordinary linguistic range. Its verses draw on Sant Bhasha, Old Punjabi, Braj, Persian, Sanskritic vocabulary, and regional dialects, set into thirty-one ਰਾਗ (musical measures). For centuries its meaning was transmitted chiefly through oral ਟਕਸਾਲ traditions and a handful of written ਟੀਕੇ. What Sahib Singh attempted was different in kind: a complete, internally consistent, grammatically argued explanation of every line, from the ਮੂਲ ਮੰਤਰ to the closing ਸਲੋਕ.

Why a Whole Course on One Commentary?

It may seem unusual to devote a full intermediate-level course to a single work of exegesis. But the Darpan is not merely a book; it is a method, a turning point, and a continuing presence in Sikh intellectual life. To understand the Darpan is to understand a particular answer to a deep question: how should the ਪੰਥ read its own scripture? Should meaning be fixed by inherited oral tradition, by mystical intuition, by sectarian preference, or by something more publicly checkable? Sahib Singh's answer was that the scripture itself encodes its meaning through a consistent internal grammar, and that this grammar — what he called ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ ਵਿਆਕਰਣ — can be recovered, taught, and applied by anyone willing to learn it.

This was a democratizing and at times controversial claim. By insisting that the ਲਗਾਂ ਮਾਤਰਾਂ (the vowel signs of Gurmukhi) are not decorative but grammatically load-bearing, Sahib Singh made it possible to argue about meaning with evidence rather than authority. As one of his own dictums in the Darpan repeatedly implies, the text is its own best interpreter.

What This Course Covers

Over the following lessons we will: reconstruct Sahib Singh's biography, including the remarkable fact that the foremost expositor of Sikh scripture was born into a Hindu Pohuwindi family and embraced ਸਿੱਖੀ as a young man; trace his years at ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ ਕਾਲਜ and his rise to ਪ੍ਰਿੰਸੀਪਲ; study the grammatical apparatus of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ ਵਿਆਕਰਣ; dissect the structure of a Darpan entry into its ਪਦ-ਅਰਥ and ਅਰਥ components; compare the Darpan to earlier ਟੀਕੇ such as those of the Faridkot tradition; analyze specific cases where the Darpan resolves notoriously difficult verses; and weigh both its scholarly reception and the criticisms raised by some ਟਕਸਾਲ traditions.

The course assumes that students can read Gurmukhi script and have basic familiarity with ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, but it does not assume prior training in linguistics. Where technical grammatical terms appear, they are explained. Throughout, key concepts are given in their Gurmukhi forms, because the Darpan's argument is itself inseparable from the script in which Gurbani is written.

A Note on Method and Humility

Studying a commentary is not the same as treating it as infallible. Sahib Singh himself, in the introductions to his volumes, framed his work as an offering to the ਪੰਥ open to correction. Part of the intellectual maturity this course hopes to cultivate is the ability to use the Darpan as a powerful tool while remaining aware of its assumptions and its debates. We approach it, in other words, the way Sahib Singh approached the scripture: with reverence, but also with careful, evidence-seeking attention. In the lessons that follow, the Darpan will serve both as our subject and, repeatedly, as our example of how rigorous reading is done.

lessons.title: From Pohuwindi to the Panth: The Life of Prof Sahib Singh
lessons.summary: The biography of Sahib Singh from his 1892 birth through his embrace of Sikhi and scholarly vocation.
lessons.html:
The Life of Prof Sahib Singh (1892-1977)

The life of the man who would write the most authoritative Punjabi ਟੀਕਾ of the ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ began far from any seminary. He was born in 1892 in the village of Phattewali, in the Sialkot district of present-day Pakistan, into a Hindu family of the Pohuwindi (Khatri) community. The boy who became Sahib Singh was originally given a name within that household; his journey to ਸਿੱਖੀ was a deliberate, considered embrace rather than an inheritance. This detail matters profoundly for understanding the Darpan: its author came to ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ as one who had to learn it, argue his way into it, and master its language from the outside in. The convert's rigor — the refusal to take any reading for granted — became the scholar's signature.

Education and the Turn to Sikhi

Sahib Singh received a sound classical education, gaining command of Sanskrit and Persian alongside Punjabi. This linguistic breadth was not incidental; the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ draws on exactly these traditions, and a commentator equipped with Sanskrit morphology and Persian vocabulary could see structures invisible to a reader of Punjabi alone. As a young man he took ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ and formally entered the Khalsa, an act that for him was bound up with intellectual conviction as much as devotion. He recounts aspects of this journey in his autobiography ਮੇਰੀ ਜੀਵਨ ਕਹਾਣੀ, a candid account that scholars still mine for insight into how his method took shape.

A Teacher by Vocation

Sahib Singh's working life was that of an educator. He taught for years, eventually associated with ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ ਕਾਲਜ and rising to the position of ਪ੍ਰਿੰਸੀਪਲ. The classroom shaped the Darpan in a way that is easy to overlook: its explanations are pedagogical. They do not merely assert a meaning; they walk a reader through the reasoning, isolating each word, naming the grammatical form, and only then offering the running sense. The Darpan reads, at its best, like the notes of a master teacher who has anticipated every place a student might stumble.

This pedagogical instinct was sharpened by the religious reform climate of his era. Sahib Singh worked in the period shaped by the ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ movement and its successors, when Sikh scholars were urgently concerned to recover and clarify the distinct meaning of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ. The reformers' insistence that Sikhs should understand their scripture directly, rather than through inherited ਨਿਰਮਲਾ or ਉਦਾਸੀ filters, created exactly the audience the Darpan would serve.

The Decades of Labor

The Darpan was not a young man's project completed in a season. It was the fruit of decades of grammatical study that first crystallized in his 1939 ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ ਵਿਆਕਰਣ, and only later flowered into the full ten-volume commentary published in the early 1960s. Between the grammar and the Darpan lay years of testing: applying his rules to verse after verse, refining them where they failed, and building the confidence that a single consistent system could account for the whole text. By the time the volumes appeared, Sahib Singh was an elderly scholar offering the distilled work of a lifetime.

ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ ਵਿਚ ਹਰੇਕ ਲਫ਼ਜ਼ ਦੀ ਆਪਣੀ ਬਣਤਰ ਹੈ।
"In Gurbani every word has its own structure."

This conviction — paraphrasing the spirit of his prefatory remarks — is the thread running from his earliest grammatical notes to the final volume of the Darpan.

Death and Legacy

Prof Sahib Singh died in 1977, having lived to see his ਟੀਕਾ accepted across a remarkably wide swath of the ਪੰਥ. He left behind not only the Darpan and the ਵਿਆਕਰਣ but numerous other writings, including expositions of individual ਬਾਣੀਆਂ and historical works. Yet it is the Darpan that secured his place. The boy from a Pohuwindi village had become, by the end of his life, the figure to whom Sikhs of every background turned when they wanted to know, with confidence, what a line of their scripture means. The following lessons turn from the life to the work, beginning with the institution that housed his scholarship.

lessons.title: Khalsa College and the Making of a Scholar
lessons.summary: How Sahib Singh's institutional home and the Singh Sabha milieu shaped his exegetical project.
lessons.html:
Khalsa College and the Making of a Scholar

No major work of scholarship arises from a vacuum. The ਦਰਪਣ was produced by a particular man, but it was also produced within a particular institutional and intellectual ecosystem. To understand why the Darpan looks the way it does — systematic, grammar-first, pedagogically structured, addressed to an educated Sikh public — we must understand ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ ਕਾਲਜ and the reform movement that gave it purpose.

The Singh Sabha Inheritance

The late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries saw the ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ movement reshape Sikh self-understanding. Confronted by Christian missionary activity, by the ਆਰੀਆ ਸਮਾਜ, and by what reformers saw as the blurring of Sikh distinctiveness, ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ scholars set out to define ਸਿੱਖੀ on its own terms. Central to this project was the scripture. If Sikhs were a distinct ਪੰਥ, then ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ had to be read as carrying a distinct theology — ਇੱਕ ਓਅੰਕਾਰ, the formless ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, the rejection of ritualism and caste — and not assimilated into a generic devotional Hinduism.

This created an urgent scholarly need: reliable, accessible explanation of what Gurbani actually says. The older ਟੀਕੇ produced within ਨਿਰਮਲਾ and ਉਦਾਸੀ traditions, learned as they were, often read Gurbani through Vedantic categories that the reformers found alien to the Gurus' message. Sahib Singh's grammatical method offered a way to argue for distinctively Sikh readings not by assertion but by linguistic evidence drawn from the text itself.

Khalsa College as a Workshop

ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ ਕਾਲਜ, Amritsar, founded in 1892 — the very year of Sahib Singh's birth — was the flagship institution of modern Sikh education. It gathered teachers and students committed to combining traditional learning with modern methods. As a teacher and eventually ਪ੍ਰਿੰਸੀਪਲ in this environment, Sahib Singh was surrounded by the questions, debates, and pedagogical pressures that shaped the Darpan. A college demands explanations that can be taught and tested; it rewards systems over intuitions. The Darpan's relentless consistency is, in part, a classroom virtue.

Contemporaries and Conversations

Sahib Singh did not work alone. He was part of a generation of Sikh scholars — figures associated with the ਚੀਫ਼ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ ਦੀਵਾਨ, with the burgeoning Punjabi print culture, and with institutions that would later include Punjabi University — who together built modern Sikh studies. Earlier reference works, most notably Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's monumental encyclopedia the ਮਹਾਨ ਕੋਸ਼, provided lexical resources Sahib Singh could lean on and refine. His own contribution was to move from lexicon to grammar: not just what a word means, but what its form tells us about its function in a sentence.

ਜਿਥੇ ਅਰਥ ਔਖਾ ਹੋਵੇ, ਉਥੇ ਵਿਆਕਰਣ ਰਾਹ ਵਿਖਾਂਦਾ ਹੈ।
"Where the meaning is difficult, grammar shows the way."

The Print Revolution

The Darpan also belongs to the age of the Punjabi printing press. Earlier ਟੀਕੇ circulated in manuscript or limited editions, accessible mainly to specialists. By the time the Darpan appeared, Punjabi publishing could put a ten-volume reference set into the hands of ordinary literate ਸੰਗਤ, ਗ੍ਰੰਥੀ, ਰਾਗੀ, and ਕਥਾਵਾਚਕ across Punjab and the diaspora. The medium suited the message: a public, checkable method deserved a public, widely available text. The reach of the Darpan is inseparable from the technology that distributed it.

An Institutionally Grounded Authority

The result of all this is that the Darpan carried a particular kind of authority. It was not the authority of a ਟਕਸਾਲ lineage transmitted from teacher to disciple, nor the charisma of a ਸੰਤ. It was the authority of an educator at the leading Sikh college, working in the open, with arguments any trained reader could in principle check. This is precisely why it could be embraced so broadly — and also why some traditional ਟਕਸਾਲਾਂ, whose authority rested on lineage, would later regard parts of it with caution. The next lessons turn to the heart of the method itself.

lessons.title: Gurbani Viakaran: The Grammar Beneath the Darpan
lessons.summary: The 1939 grammar that supplies the rules every Darpan entry applies.
lessons.html:
ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ ਵਿਆਕਰਣ: The Grammar Beneath the Darpan

The ਦਰਪਣ cannot be understood apart from the work that made it possible: Sahib Singh's 1939 ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ ਵਿਆਕਰਣ. If the Darpan is the cathedral, the ਵਿਆਕਰਣ is the structural engineering. Every meaning the Darpan offers is, in principle, derivable from the rules set out in this earlier book. This lesson explains what those rules claim and why they were revolutionary.

The Central Insight

The foundational claim of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ ਵਿਆਕਰਣ is deceptively simple: the language of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ is not loose or merely poetic in its forms, but governed by a consistent grammar — and that grammar is visible in the script itself, particularly in the ਲਗਾਂ ਮਾਤਰਾਂ, the vowel signs. Where a casual reader might treat a final ਔਂਕੜ or ਸਿਹਾਰੀ as incidental, Sahib Singh argued that these marks systematically encode case, number, gender, and syntactic role.

Consider the implication. In ordinary modern Punjabi, the noun ਗੁਰੁ and ਗੁਰੁੂ might seem like spelling variants. Sahib Singh demonstrated that within Gurbani such differences are not arbitrary: the presence or absence of a vowel sign on a final consonant frequently marks whether a noun is singular or plural, nominative or oblique, a vocative address or a subject. The text, on this view, is grammatically self-disciplined to a degree earlier readers had not fully appreciated.

What the Grammar Covers

ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ ਵਿਆਕਰਣ is organized like a true descriptive grammar. It treats the noun (ਨਾਂਵ) and its declensions; the pronoun (ਪੜਨਾਂਵ); the verb (ਕਿਰਿਆ) and its tenses, moods, and persons; the adjective (ਵਿਸ਼ੇਸ਼ਣ); and the particles and postpositions that knit a sentence together. For each category Sahib Singh adduces numerous examples drawn directly from the scripture, showing the pattern and noting exceptions. The method is inductive: he reads the whole text, observes regularities, and formulates rules that account for them.

A Worked Principle

One of the most consequential rules concerns nouns ending in a consonant. Sahib Singh showed that a masculine singular noun in the nominative case very often carries a final ਔਂਕੜ, while the same noun without it may signal a different case or a plural. This single principle, applied consistently, resolves countless ambiguities. A line that earlier commentators read as addressing many gurus might, by the vowel signs, clearly be speaking of the one ਗੁਰੂ; a word read as a noun might reveal itself, by its ending, to be a verb.

ਲਗ ਮਾਤ੍ਰ ਦਾ ਫ਼ਰਕ ਅਰਥ ਦਾ ਫ਼ਰਕ ਹੈ।
"A difference in vowel-marking is a difference in meaning."

This sentence captures the engine of the entire Darpan. Because the marks are meaningful, attending to them is not pedantry but the very act of understanding.

Against Two Errors

The grammar guarded against two opposite errors. The first was the careless reader's error of ignoring the vowel signs altogether, flattening grammatically distinct forms into a vague devotional blur. The second was the over-eager interpreter's error of importing a preferred theological meaning and bending the words to fit. By anchoring interpretation in observable grammatical form, Sahib Singh aimed to discipline both. The reader is not free to mean whatever they wish; the text, through its grammar, constrains the field of legitimate readings.

The Status of the Rules

It is important to be precise about what the grammar claims. Sahib Singh did not assert that he had invented the grammar of Gurbani; he claimed to have discovered and described it, much as a linguist describes a living language. The rules are presented as features of the text put there, in his understanding, by the Gurus and ਭਗਤ themselves, who wrote in a disciplined idiom. This is why the grammar functions as evidence: if the patterns are really in the text, then anyone can verify them, and a reading that violates them bears the burden of proof. The next lesson examines the ਲਗਾਂ ਮਾਤਰਾਂ in closer detail, for they are the smallest units on which this whole edifice rests.

lessons.title: The Power of the Lagaan-Matraan
lessons.summary: Close study of the vowel signs and how their grammatical reading transforms interpretation.
lessons.html:
The Power of the ਲਗਾਂ ਮਾਤਰਾਂ

If there is a single idea on which the authority of the ਦਰਪਣ rests, it is the grammatical significance of the ਲਗਾਂ ਮਾਤਰਾਂ — the vowel signs and diacritics of the Gurmukhi script. This lesson takes a closer, more technical look at these small marks and at the interpretive revolution that follows from taking them seriously.

What the Marks Are

Gurmukhi consonants carry their vowels through attached signs. The ਔਂਕੜ marks a short 'u' below a letter; the ਦੁਲੈਂਕੜ marks a long 'oo'; the ਸਿਹਾਰੀ marks a short 'i' before a letter; the ਬਿਹਾਰੀ marks a long 'ee'; and so on, alongside the ਕੰਨਾ, ਲਾਂ, ਦੁਲਾਂਵਾਂ, ਹੋੜਾ, and ਕਨੌੜਾ. In everyday writing these simply spell words. Sahib Singh's claim is that in ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, especially at the ends of words, they additionally do grammatical work.

The Final Aunkar as Grammatical Signal

The clearest and most discussed case is the final ਔਂਕੜ. Sahib Singh showed that a masculine noun in the singular nominative case characteristically ends in ਔਂਕੜ, whereas the bare consonant ending often marks an oblique or plural form, and other endings mark vocatives or verbal forms. Take a familiar word such as ਸਚੁ versus ਸਚ. The reader trained by the Darpan does not treat these as interchangeable; the vowel sign tells them how the word functions in its sentence — whether 'Truth' is the subject being predicated, or 'true' is operating differently. Multiply this discrimination across the tens of thousands of words in the scripture, and the cumulative effect on interpretation is enormous.

ਜਿਹੜੀ ਲਗ ਗੁਰੂ ਨੇ ਲਾਈ, ਉਹ ਅਰਥ ਦੀ ਕੁੰਜੀ ਹੈ।
"The vowel-sign the Guru placed is the key to the meaning."

Why Earlier Readers Missed This

It is fair to ask how generations of devout, learned ਟੀਕਾਕਾਰ could have under-used such a systematic feature. Several factors contributed. Oral ਟਕਸਾਲ recitation traditions sometimes pronounced these final vowels lightly or not at all, so their grammatical force was not always salient to the ear. Manuscript practice and the influence of Sanskrit and Braj conventions led some to treat the marks as metrical or euphonic rather than grammatical. And the dominant interpretive frameworks, often Vedantic, were more interested in mystical sense than in morphology. Sahib Singh's achievement was to step back and read the marks as a system, asking not 'what does this verse mean spiritually?' first, but 'what does this word's form tell me about its role?' — and to let the spiritual meaning follow from the disciplined reading.

A Note of Caution

The grammatical reading of the ਲਗਾਂ ਮਾਤਰਾਂ is powerful, but Sahib Singh himself acknowledged limits. Gurbani is poetry, and poetry sometimes bends grammar for meter (ਛੰਦ) or effect. There are forms inherited intact from Sanskrit or Persian that follow their own rules. There are scribal questions about the earliest manuscripts. A mature use of the Darpan recognizes that the grammatical principle is a strong default, not a mechanical law that overrides all other evidence. Sahib Singh navigated these tensions case by case, and part of the Darpan's value is watching a master judgment at work where the rules and the poetry pull against each other.

The Pedagogical Payoff

For the student, the lesson of the ਲਗਾਂ ਮਾਤਰਾਂ is also a discipline of attention. To read Gurbani with the Darpan is to slow down, to notice the vowel sign one might have skated over, and to ask what it is doing. This is why teachers say that working through the Darpan trains the eye. Even a reader who eventually disagrees with a particular gloss has, by engaging the grammatical argument, learned to read more carefully. In the next lesson we assemble these small marks into the full structure of a Darpan entry, seeing how grammar becomes a finished explanation of a verse.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Darpan Entry: Pad-Arath and Arath
lessons.summary: The repeatable structure of every Darpan passage, from word-gloss to running translation.
lessons.html:
Anatomy of a Darpan Entry: ਪਦ-ਅਰਥ and ਅਰਥ

What does the ਦਰਪਣ actually look like on the page? Its enduring usefulness comes not only from its method but from its remarkably consistent format. Once a student learns the structure of a single entry, they can navigate all ten volumes. This lesson dissects that structure.

The Building Blocks

A typical Darpan treatment of a passage proceeds through recurring components. First, Sahib Singh reproduces the original ਤੁਕਾਂ of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ. Second, and most distinctively, he provides the ਪਦ-ਅਰਥ: a word-by-word gloss, in which each significant term is isolated and given its meaning, often with the grammatical form noted. Third, he gives the ਅਰਥ: a flowing Punjabi paraphrase that renders the sense of the whole passage in clear prose. Where needed, he adds a ਭਾਵ or explanatory note drawing out the theological or contextual import, and frequently a grammatical justification (ਨੋਟ) explaining why a word was read as it was.

Why Word-for-Word First?

The decision to lead with ਪਦ-ਅਰਥ is not stylistic; it is epistemological. By glossing each word before paraphrasing the whole, Sahib Singh shows his work. The reader can see exactly how the running translation was reached, term by term, and can check each step against the grammar. This transparency is the opposite of an oracular commentary that simply announces a meaning. The ਪਦ-ਅਰਥ invites the reader into the reasoning and, crucially, makes disagreement specifiable: if you doubt the ਅਰਥ, you can point to the precise word in the ਪਦ-ਅਰਥ where you part ways.

A Schematic Example

Imagine a short line of Gurbani. A Darpan entry would handle it roughly thus. The ਪਦ-ਅਰਥ would list, say, three or four key words, each followed by its meaning and, where relevant, a grammatical tag — noting that a word is a singular nominative noun, or a feminine adjective, or an imperative verb. Then the ਅਰਥ would weave these into a single coherent Punjabi sentence capturing the line's message. Finally, if the line is contested, a ਨੋਟ would explain: 'this word is read as a verb, not a noun, because of its ending,' and might compare a parallel usage elsewhere in ਬਾਣੀ.

ਪਹਿਲਾਂ ਹਰੇਕ ਲਫ਼ਜ਼ ਦਾ ਅਰਥ, ਫਿਰ ਸਾਰੀ ਤੁਕ ਦਾ ਭਾਵ।
"First the meaning of each word, then the sense of the whole line."

This sequence — part to whole — is the Darpan's pedagogical heartbeat.

Internal Cross-Reference

One of the Darpan's quiet strengths is its use of the scripture to explain the scripture. When a word is rare or ambiguous, Sahib Singh frequently cites its occurrence elsewhere in ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, where the context is clearer, and reasons from the parallel. This intratextual method — letting ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ interpret itself — is a hallmark of his approach and a major reason scholars trust the Darpan even when they question a particular reading. It keeps the interpretation anchored in the text's own usage rather than in external systems of thought.

Coverage and Organization

The Darpan follows the ਅੰਗ-by-ਅੰਗ order of the ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ, treating the bani in its canonical sequence. The ten volumes together cover the entire scripture, from ਜਪੁ ਜੀ ਸਾਹਿਬ through the closing compositions. This completeness is itself a monumental achievement: earlier ਟੀਕੇ were often partial, concentrating on the more popular ਬਾਣੀਆਂ. To gloss every line of the whole ਗ੍ਰੰਥ with a consistent method is a feat of stamina as much as scholarship.

Using the Structure as a Student

For the learner, the practical takeaway is a reading workflow. Find the passage; read the ਤੁਕਾਂ aloud; study the ਪਦ-ਅਰਥ to absorb each word's meaning and form; read the ਅਰਥ for the whole sense; and attend to any ਨੋਟ for the difficult points and grammatical reasoning. Practiced over time, this workflow does more than convey information about particular verses — it trains the very skills of close reading that Sahib Singh embodied. In the next lesson we step back to compare the Darpan with the ਟੀਕੇ that came before it, and to ask why it eclipsed them.

lessons.title: Earlier Teekas and Why the Darpan Surpassed Them
lessons.summary: Comparing the Darpan with the Faridkot and earlier commentarial traditions.
lessons.html:
Earlier ਟੀਕੇ and Why the Darpan Surpassed Them

The ਦਰਪਣ did not arrive into an interpretive void. The ਪੰਥ had long traditions of explaining ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ, both oral and written. To appreciate what Sahib Singh accomplished, we must place his work alongside its predecessors and ask what made the Darpan, in the judgment of so many, the new standard.

The Inherited Traditions

For centuries, the meaning of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ was carried chiefly by the ਟਕਸਾਲ lineages — schools of recitation and exposition transmitted from teacher to student — and by the learned ਨਿਰਮਲਾ and ਉਦਾਸੀ scholars who produced written ਟੀਕੇ. These traditions preserved invaluable knowledge: correct ਪਾਠ (recitation), the pronunciation of difficult words, and a wealth of contextual and devotional understanding. Their custodianship kept the meaning of the scripture alive across generations when few could read.

The Faridkot Teeka

The most ambitious written commentary before Sahib Singh was the so-called Faridkoti ਟੀਕਾ, a large multi-volume exposition prepared under the patronage of the Faridkot state and associated with ਨਿਰਮਲਾ scholars. It was a genuine landmark, covering much of the scripture. Yet from the perspective of the ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ reformers, it had a characteristic limitation: it tended to read ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ through the lens of Vedanta and Puranic lore, mapping the Gurus' words onto categories drawn from Hindu philosophical and mythological systems. Where the reformers heard the Gurus declaring the worship of one formless ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ and rejecting ritual and caste, the older ਟੀਕੇ sometimes assimilated these declarations into a more familiar pan-Indian devotionalism.

The Darpan's Distinct Contribution

Against this background, Sahib Singh's contribution can be stated precisely. First, method: he grounded interpretation in the internal grammar of the text rather than in an external philosophical system, giving his readings a public, checkable basis. Second, consistency: he applied one coherent grammatical apparatus across the entire scripture, so that the explanation of a word in one ਬਾਣੀ was answerable to its explanation everywhere else. Third, theology by evidence: where the reformers wanted to show that Gurbani teaches a distinctive message, Sahib Singh let that message emerge from disciplined reading rather than from polemic. The grammatical argument did the theological work.

ਅਰਥ ਪਰੰਪਰਾ ਤੋਂ ਨਹੀਂ, ਬਾਣੀ ਦੀ ਆਪਣੀ ਬਣਤਰ ਤੋਂ।
"Meaning comes not from tradition alone, but from Bani's own structure."

What the Darpan Did Not Discard

It would be a mistake to cast the Darpan as a wholesale rejection of earlier learning. Sahib Singh drew gratefully on the lexical work of predecessors, above all Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's ਮਹਾਨ ਕੋਸ਼, and on the accumulated knowledge of word meanings preserved by tradition. His innovation was not to throw away the inherited vocabulary but to organize it by a rigorous grammar and to correct, where the grammar demanded, readings he judged mistaken. He stood on the shoulders of the ਟੀਕਾਕਾਰ even as he revised them.

Why It Won the Field

Several factors explain the Darpan's ascendancy. Its method appealed to a modern, literate, reform-minded readership that wanted reasons, not just authority. Its completeness made it a one-stop reference for the whole ਗ੍ਰੰਥ. Its clear Punjabi prose made it usable by ਗ੍ਰੰਥੀ, ਰਾਗੀ, ਕਥਾਵਾਚਕ, and educated ਸੰਗਤ alike. And its publication in an age of cheap print put it within reach of the many. The combination of intellectual rigor, comprehensiveness, accessibility, and timing made the Darpan the default Punjabi ਟੀਕਾ within a generation. Yet, as we will see in a later lesson, this very triumph provoked debate, especially among ਟਕਸਾਲ traditions whose readings the Darpan sometimes corrected. First, in the next lesson, we examine the Darpan's handling of genuinely difficult Gurbani — the proving ground of any commentary.

lessons.title: How the Darpan Handles Difficult Gurbani
lessons.summary: Case studies in the Darpan's method for resolving obscure or contested verses.
lessons.html:
How the Darpan Handles Difficult ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ

Any commentary can explain easy verses. The test of a ਟੀਕਾ is what it does with the hard ones — the lines where the vocabulary is archaic, the syntax is compressed, the imagery is dense, or the tradition itself disagrees. This lesson examines, in principle and through representative types of cases, how the ਦਰਪਣ approaches difficulty.

Types of Difficulty

The difficulties in ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ fall into recognizable categories. There are lexical difficulties: rare words, or words borrowed from Persian, Arabic, Sanskrit, or regional dialects, whose meaning is not obvious. There are grammatical difficulties: compressed lines where it is unclear which word is subject, which is object, and what governs what. There are referential difficulties: pronouns or epithets whose referent must be inferred. And there are theological difficulties: lines that, read carelessly, might seem to support a reading at odds with the Gurus' broader teaching. Sahib Singh developed characteristic strategies for each.

Strategy One: Let Grammar Decide Syntax

Where the syntax is ambiguous, the Darpan turns first to the ਲਗਾਂ ਮਾਤਰਾਂ. If it is unclear whether a word is the subject or the object, the vowel sign on its ending frequently settles the matter: a nominative ending marks the subject, an oblique ending marks something else. By reading the marks, Sahib Singh often dissolves an apparent ambiguity that had generated competing traditional glosses. The grammar acts as a referee.

Strategy Two: Use Parallel Passages

For lexical and referential difficulties, the Darpan deploys its intratextual method. A rare word in one line is illuminated by its appearance in another line where the context is clearer. An obscure epithet is identified by comparing how the same epithet is used elsewhere for ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ or for the ਗੁਰੂ. This lets ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ define its own terms, which is both methodologically conservative and theologically apt.

ਬਾਣੀ ਦਾ ਅਰਥ ਬਾਣੀ ਤੋਂ ਹੀ ਖੁੱਲ੍ਹਦਾ ਹੈ।
"The meaning of Bani opens only through Bani itself."

Strategy Three: Respect the Rag and the Whole Shabad

Sahib Singh insisted that a ਤੁਕ be read within its ਸ਼ਬਦ, and the ਸ਼ਬਦ within the flow of its ਰਾਗ and theme. A line wrenched from its context can be made to say almost anything; embedded in its ਸ਼ਬਦ, its meaning is constrained by the argument the ਸ਼ਬਦ is making. The Darpan's habit of explaining the central theme (ਕੇਂਦਰੀ ਭਾਵ) of a ਸ਼ਬਦ before glossing its lines reflects this conviction that the part is governed by the whole.

Strategy Four: Distinguish Theology from Imagery

Gurbani frequently uses the imagery of other traditions — Puranic figures, yogic terminology, Islamic vocabulary — to make its own points, often by reframing or transcending them. A naive reading might take such imagery literally and conclude that Gurbani endorses the borrowed system. Sahib Singh's method, attentive to context and to the Gurus' consistent message of ਇੱਕ ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ, reads such passages as appropriating imagery in service of a distinct teaching. The discipline of grammar plus context guards against importing alien doctrine on the strength of a borrowed word.

Honesty About the Hard Cases

Crucially, the Darpan does not pretend that every difficulty is fully resolved. In genuinely contested places Sahib Singh sometimes presents his reading while acknowledging the grammatical reasoning that supports it, leaving the careful reader able to weigh it. This intellectual honesty — showing the reasoning rather than decreeing the result — is part of why scholars respect the work even where they dissent. A commentary that admits the difficulty and argues its case earns more trust than one that papers over the seams.

What Students Should Take Away

The deeper lesson is transferable. Faced with a hard verse, the trained reader asks: what do the vowel signs tell me about the grammar? Where else does this word appear? What is the ਸ਼ਬਦ as a whole arguing? Is a borrowed image being used or endorsed? These questions, modeled relentlessly across ten volumes, are the real gift of the Darpan. They turn the reader from a passive recipient of meanings into an active, disciplined interpreter. Having seen the method at its sharpest, we turn next to how the ਪੰਥ received it — including the criticisms it provoked.

lessons.title: Reception, Critics, and the Taksal Debate
lessons.summary: How the Darpan was received, and the substantive debates with traditional lineages.
lessons.html:
Reception, Critics, and the ਟਕਸਾਲ Debate

A work as influential as the ਦਰਪਣ inevitably draws both devotion and dispute. This lesson surveys its reception across the ਪੰਥ and engages honestly with the criticisms raised, especially by some ਟਕਸਾਲ traditions. Understanding the debate is essential to using the Darpan maturely rather than treating it as an unquestionable authority.

Broad Acceptance

The dominant story is one of remarkable acceptance. Within a generation of its publication, the Darpan became the working reference of countless ਗ੍ਰੰਥੀ, ਕਥਾਵਾਚਕ, ਰਾਗੀ, teachers, and ordinary ਸੰਗਤ. Its clarity made ਕਥਾ (discourse) easier to prepare; its completeness made it a reliable first stop for any line; its grammatical method gave it an authority that felt modern and checkable. Across much of the mainstream ਪੰਥ, to ask 'what does the Darpan say?' became a natural step in studying any verse.

The Grounds of Criticism

Yet the Darpan also met principled criticism, much of it from ਟਕਸਾਲ traditions such as those associated with Damdami and other lineages. Their concerns were several. First, on a few words the Darpan's grammatical reading produced a meaning at variance with the traditional oral ਅਰਥ transmitted through the ਟਕਸਾਲ; where Sahib Singh trusted the grammar, the ਟਕਸਾਲ trusted the inherited gloss. Second, some critics held that a living oral tradition reaching back toward the Gurus' own time carries an authority that a modern grammatical reconstruction cannot override. Third, there were specific theological points where critics felt Sahib Singh's reading flattened a deeper or more mystical sense in favor of a plainer grammatical one.

ਪਰੰਪਰਾ ਤੇ ਵਿਆਕਰਣ — ਦੋਵੇਂ ਅਰਥ ਦੀ ਖੋਜ ਵਿਚ ਸਹਾਈ ਹਨ।
"Tradition and grammar — both are aids in the search for meaning."

A Real and Productive Tension

It would be wrong to caricature this as enlightenment versus superstition. The ਟਕਸਾਲ critique raises a genuine question in the philosophy of interpretation: when a systematic modern method conflicts with a continuous living tradition, which should yield? Sahib Singh's wager was that the text's own grammar is the more reliable guide, because it is public and checkable, whereas oral transmission can drift. The ਟਕਸਾਲ wager was that the meaning was given alongside the text from the beginning and preserved by faithful transmission, so the tradition is itself evidence. A thoughtful student holds both considerations in view rather than dismissing either.

Academic Reception

In the scholarly world, the Darpan and especially ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ ਵਿਆਕਰਣ are treated with deep respect. Linguists and historians of Sikh scripture recognize Sahib Singh as the pioneer who first described the grammar of Gurbani systematically. At the same time, modern academic scholarship — represented by figures who study the textual history of the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ — sometimes raises questions Sahib Singh's grammar did not fully address, such as the role of scribal variation in the earliest manuscripts and the limits of treating every vowel sign as fully systematic. These are not refutations but extensions of the conversation he opened.

The Question of Over-Reliance

A further, more practical concern voiced by teachers is the risk of over-reliance: that students may consult the Darpan as a shortcut to a finished answer rather than as a model of how to reason. This worry is, ironically, the opposite of what Sahib Singh intended. His ਪਦ-ਅਰਥ structure was designed to show reasoning, not to replace it. Used well, the Darpan trains independent reading; used lazily, it can substitute for it. The remedy is to engage the grammatical arguments, not merely the conclusions.

Toward a Balanced Use

The mature position that has emerged in the ਪੰਥ is neither uncritical adoption nor dismissal. Most serious students treat the Darpan as the indispensable starting point — comprehensive, rigorous, and clear — while remaining attentive to ਟਕਸਾਲ readings, to academic textual scholarship, and to the poetry's own resistance to over-systematization. This is, fittingly, the very stance of disciplined humility that Sahib Singh modeled. In the final substantive lesson we consider how the Darpan lives on today, in print and in the digital age.

lessons.title: The Darpan Today: Digital Life and Enduring Authority
lessons.summary: The Darpan's continuing role in the digital era and its place in contemporary Sikh study.
lessons.html:
The ਦਰਪਣ Today: Digital Life and Enduring Authority

More than half a century after its publication, the ਦਰਪਣ is arguably more accessible and more widely consulted than ever. This lesson considers how the work has been transmitted into the digital era, how it functions in contemporary Sikh life and scholarship, and what its endurance tells us about the questions it answered.

From Ten Volumes to the Open Web

The original Darpan was a ten-volume printed set, a serious investment of shelf space and money. The digital era transformed its reach. Sahib Singh's commentary has been digitized and integrated into the major online ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ resources, where a user reading any line of ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ can call up the Darpan's ਪਦ-ਅਰਥ and ਅਰਥ alongside the original. Searchable databases and ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ apps frequently include the Darpan as a default commentary layer. The practical effect is that the method Sahib Singh devised — word-by-word grammatical explanation — now reaches a global ਸੰਗਤ at the tap of a screen, far beyond the Punjab classrooms where it began.

The Darpan in Contemporary Kathaa and Teaching

In ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰੇ and study circles around the world, the Darpan remains a staple of preparation for ਕਥਾ and ਵੀਚਾਰ. A ਕਥਾਵਾਚਕ preparing a discourse, a teacher leading a ਸੰਥਿਆ or Gurbani class, a student writing on a ਸ਼ਬਦ — all routinely consult it. Its clear structure makes it easy to extract a reliable meaning quickly, while its grammatical notes provide depth for those who want it. For the diaspora especially, where access to traditional ਟਕਸਾਲ training is limited, the Darpan functions as a portable teacher.

ਦਰਪਣ ਅੱਜ ਵੀ ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ ਦੇ ਪਾਠਕ ਦਾ ਪਹਿਲਾ ਸਾਥੀ ਹੈ।
"Even today the Darpan is the Gurbani reader's first companion."

Within Modern Sikh Studies

In the academy, the Darpan occupies a foundational place. Scholars working on the language, theology, and textual history of Sikh scripture engage Sahib Singh's grammar as the necessary point of departure, whether to build on it or to refine it. Studies of the formation of the ਆਦਿ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ, of Gurbani's vocabulary, and of Sikh exegetical traditions repeatedly reckon with his contribution. Even where contemporary scholarship complicates his picture — for instance by emphasizing manuscript variation or by situating Gurbani's language within wider North Indian devotional idioms — it does so in dialogue with the framework he established.

What Its Endurance Reveals

Why has the Darpan lasted? Partly because it answered a real and persistent need: a reliable, comprehensive, accessible Punjabi explanation of the whole scripture. Partly because its method is genuinely powerful, dissolving ambiguities that had long troubled readers. And partly because of its tone — reverent yet rigorous, confident yet showing its reasoning. The Darpan models a way of relating to ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ that combines devotion with disciplined study, refusing to choose between the two. That synthesis is its deepest legacy.

The Darpan as a Model, Not a Ceiling

The healthiest contemporary attitude treats the Darpan as Sahib Singh would have wished: as a magnificent tool and a model of method, not as the final word that ends all inquiry. New manuscript scholarship, ongoing ਟਕਸਾਲ wisdom, comparative linguistics, and the living engagement of the ਸੰਗਤ all continue the work of understanding Gurbani. The Darpan is the great trunk from which much contemporary study branches, but the tree is still growing.

Coda: The Convert Who Gave the Panth Its Standard

There is a fitting symmetry in the story this course has told. A man born outside ਸਿੱਖੀ, who had to learn the language of Gurbani from the ground up, ended by giving the ਪੰਥ the most trusted Punjabi key to its scripture. His outsider's rigor became the insider's standard. Whenever a student today opens a Gurbani app, sees the ਪਦ-ਅਰਥ unfold word by word, and grasps a difficult line at last, they are the heirs of Prof Sahib Singh's lifetime of patient labor — a mirror, as he named it, still reflecting the meaning of the Guru's word.

ਹਵਾਲੇ (Works Cited)

  • Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.
  • Mann, Gurinder Singh, and Kamalroop Singh. The Granth of Guru Gobind Singh: Essays, Lectures and Translations. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2015.
  • Nabha, Kahn Singh. Gurushabad Ratanakar Mahan Kosh. Patiala: Bhasha Vibhag Punjab, 1930.
  • Shackle, Christopher. A Guru Nanak Glossary. London: School of Oriental and African Studies, 1981.
  • Singh, Pashaura. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.
  • Singh, Sahib. Gurbani Viakaran. Amritsar: Singh Brothers, 1939.
  • Singh, Sahib. Meri Jeevan Kahani. Amritsar: Singh Brothers, 1968.
  • Singh, Sahib. Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. 10 vols. Jalandhar: Raj Publishers, 1962-1964.
  • Singh, Taran. Gurbani dian Viakhia Pranalian. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1980.
